en: Preface to the *Cuanzhu* (Compiled Annotations) of the *Mahābuddhahṛdaya-Śūraṅgama-sūtra*:

I once saw the old edition of the *Cuanzhu* compiled by Master Jieshi more than ten years ago. Last autumn, while meeting him at the official residence of the Southern Han, he presented me with this current edition, which has been revised and altered in fifteen or sixteen places.
It appears to have been produced by selecting the explanations of various schools and pruning away [redundancies].

This work is voluminous; its ultimate aim is to return to what is essential and concise. Yet, interspersed within it are my own interpretations. Not only does this make me a filial son to the Sacred Scriptures, but it also makes me a loyal minister to the various masters.
Is the merit of this endeavor not indeed great? Nevertheless, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* possesses both exoteric and esoteric aspects. As the opening of the sutra states:

Immediately, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in tranquil repose. For the sake of those in the assembly, he proclaimed the profound and abstruse Dharma. The pure multitude at this Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before.
The *kalaviṅka*-like celestial voice of the Tathāgata pervaded the worlds of the ten directions. The Tathāgata manifested his teaching, and the pure multitude attained realization.
The sounds are heard everywhere, yet there is not a single word; this is the Esoteric Śūraṅgama. Ānanda earnestly requested it, and the Tathāgata expounded it with wondrous eloquence;
this is the Exoteric Śūraṅgama. If the exoteric is used to explain the esoteric, then the ten fascicles of the sūtra text already serve as its commentary.
To add further commentaries beneath these commentaries is like entering the ocean to count its sands—what benefit would that ultimately bring? In response:
The blind describe heaven as being like a canopy or like an egg; this is necessarily so for them. Those with eyes, however, need only look up once.
Master Jie’s intent in citing the views of various schools was not merely to provide for the blind, but his expectations for those with eyes were even more profound.
I hope that those who are skilled at reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* will strive together toward this end.
On the tenth day of the third month of the year Wanyi (1615), the lay practitioner Feng Mengzhen, while traveling at Shuangjing, respectfully inscribed this at the Wenshu Tai hermitage.
In the year Wuyin (1598), while I was reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in the mountains, many renowned monks had gathered there. I questioned them regarding the contents of the scripture.
Regarding the principle that in this world sound arises from movement and form arises from sound, the respondent’s explanations were entirely prolix.
Only the Venerable Huanchu said to me: "Movement is the root of karma. All dharmas are fundamentally quiescent by nature;

yet when the mind moves for a single thought-moment, the six distractions arise in confusion. His statement that "sound arises from movement and form arises from sound" refers to the moment one enters [into delusion].
"If there were [such a thing], then every phenomenon would possess it. I was struck with a sense of clarity and wonder.

It turned out that the Master had been exploring this sutra morning and night without ceasing. By the year Jiawu—seventeen years later—the commentary he had compiled was finally completed after four revisions of the draft.
He showed it to me in Moling and said to me: "What was it that you asked of me in the past, and what was it that I told you?"
The purport of this single chapter truly encompasses the entire scripture. Now, sound arises from movement; it is because of this that sentient beings transmigrate in a cycle of delusion.
To enter the stream and lose all objective referents—this is how the Great Being Avalokiteśvara attained perfect penetration.

For the mind is fundamentally without mind, and appearances are fundamentally without appearance; yet sentient beings fail to realize this, and with a single thought of false movement, they give rise to cognition through sensory objects.

One falsely perceives within the mind; because of the sense faculties, appearances arise, and one falsely perceives within those appearances. From this, the seven realms of existence become turbid and chaotic, and one sinks into the long night of ignorance.

This is movement. If one realizes that both appearances and perceptions are devoid of intrinsic nature—like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other—then internally there is no mind capable of projecting, and externally there are no appearances manifested. From this, the two states of movement and stillness clearly do not arise. Emptiness.
When that which is empty is extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests; this is "perishing. When there is movement, one perceives emptiness and perceives form;
therefore it is said, "Due to delusive error there is space, and based on space the worlds are established. When there is perishing, both emptiness and form are truly real;

therefore it is said, "If one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away. Thus, that which is refuted by the seven inquiries is refuted.

This is movement. That which cannot be returned among the eight returns is the return to this state of non-existence (*māyā*). When there is movement, hearing does not transcend sound and seeing does not exceed form;
even one's own body is as distant as Hu and Yue. But when there is non-existence, the sense bases, elements, and spheres are all wondrously perfect.
Earth, water, fire, and wind do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another. This exhausts what the twenty-five sages have realized and reaches the ultimate limit of the fifty-five stages.
Wherever they go, they exhaust this movement; in the end, they perish. Therefore it is said: "Entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, one fulfills Bodhi and returns to non-attainment.
I asked: "If one returns to non-attainment, how can one see it? How can one cultivate it? How can one realize it? He replied:
"Movement gives rise to suffering. It is not by seeing non-attainment that one sees it; it is by cultivating non-attainment that one cultivates it."
Realizing that there is nothing to be attained, one has no means to extinguish suffering. Even those in the tenth stage still possess the afflictions of a learner;
how much more so for those bound by all fetters? Upon hearing this, I was like a traveler in the desert finding a cool breeze.

The Master then commanded me to read his book to its conclusion, as if he suspected there might be some points of disagreement between us. I closed the volume and said: "Since you have already shown it to me, I see the lion."
To wish to test its fierce strength while it is already crouching—is this not an excessive calculation?
Of the annotations, seven-tenths were derived from Changshui and Wenling; two-tenths were derived from Letan, Gushan, and other masters;
and one-tenth was derived from the unique insights of the Master (Shangren). The names of these various teachers are no longer recorded, as they have been harmonized into a single whole.

Thus, the essential points and structural threads of the sutra are interconnected, which will facilitate the reader’s understanding. Furthermore, the explanations provided by various masters are already familiar through worldly tradition;
the reader may verify them for themselves. As for what I have related here from the words of these superior persons, I have never once unrolled it until the very end of this volume.
Preface to the Compiled Annotations on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* by the student from Narayan Cave, Ju Rují, written on the final day of the tenth month in the Jiawu year of the Wanli era.
As for the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, it is inherently pure; it is not obtained through awakening, nor is it accomplished through cultivation. Nevertheless, the mirror of wisdom—

Long has one been shrouded in darkness; how can one attain great clarity by abandoning sublime awakening? The jewel of the mind has long been obscured; only through perfect cultivation can it finally be made clear and vast.

For this reason, Ānanda, prompted by his deluded attachments, inquired about the initial expedient means. The World-Honored One, relying on the conditions of his own delusion, interrogated him regarding the arousal of the Bodhicitta at the stage of practice.

To give rise to the mind based on the perception of marks is truly to be deluded regarding the Truth and to mistake the false for reality. To investigate the mind and discern the seeing is, in truth, [the path to liberation].
Shattering the false to reveal the true; though revealing the true while shattering the false, one still brings the false back to the true through successive layers of refutation.
The intent is to cause one to know the true and recognize the false, and to harmonize all phenomena so that one may realize that the false is itself the true.

Thus, when the audience hears this subtle and wondrous instruction, their inverted perceptions vanish and they suddenly awaken to the true mind. Pūrṇa, hearing this primary truth, [attains realization].
Yet, obscured by the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the winds of doubt arise.

Though fundamentally pure and luminous, the worlds and sentient beings emerge due to the arising of delusion and falsehood—like floating, empty, and illusory forms produced from a cataract within the clear stillness of space. To realize this is to see that they are fundamentally pure and luminous.

To be deluded is for mountains, rivers, and the great earth to turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust; by clinging to various marks, they lead to mutual conflict and mutual plunder.
To extinguish the dust and unite with awakening is to perfect the single nature, whereby all things attain mutual pervasion and mutual containment.

When one is deluded regarding the true, wondrous, and luminous awareness, mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly manifest from this point onward. When one attains the wondrous, empty, and luminous awareness, how could the outflows of conditioned habits ever arise again? Delusion...

Once one has attained awakening, one will no longer be deluded. If the illusory cataracts are removed, the phantom flowers will be extinguished forever. When gold is extracted from ore, how could it ever become ore again?
When wood is reduced to ash, how could branches ever grow back? Upon hearing this, the views concerning the sequence of reality and falsehood should be dissolved.

Having reached this realization, one awakens from delusion and the doubts regarding the beginning and end of existence are forever stilled. At this point, although it is known that phenomena arise from delusion, it remains unclear what causes that delusion.
Therefore, [the text] first cites the story of Śrīgupta running madly while looking into a mirror as a metaphor for the fact that the cause of deluded thought has no location.
Next, it exhorts Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra not to discriminate among phenomena, so that when the frantic mind ceases, it is itself Bodhi. Yet, the recipient of the teaching further...

One may doubt that the bodhicitta is attained through causes and conditions; therefore, the World-Honored One again cites the case of Upatiṣya to clarify that it is not accomplished by relying on external assistance.
Following this, he reveals the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), rebukes mere erudition, and exhorts the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

By means of this, one attains the dissolution of attachments and the awakening of the mind, securing the residence of the Heavenly King and seeking entry through its gate, thereby arriving at Great Nirvāṇa.
[The Buddha] said: "One must rely on the path of the original aspiration to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This requires the temporary subduing of the sense gates;
therefore, first examine the mind as it arises in the causal stage, causing it to revolve back from its state of birth-and-death to subdue it and return to original enlightenment.

Next, examine the root of afflictions, teaching one to rely upon the sense organs to go against the current of karmic flow and follow the path of perfect penetration. By striking the bell, the permanence [of hearing] is revealed, and one awakens to the nature of hearing."

By nature, one does not cling to permanence as being annihilation. By using a handkerchief to demonstrate knots, one realizes that the unravelling of the deluded mind immediately yields the wondrous realization of non-arising.
Although the meaning of "one" and "six" vanishing is known, the fundamental source of perfect penetration has not yet been fully understood;

therefore, he first commanded the various sages to explain the expedient means of cultivation, and subsequently charged Mañjuśrī to select the true and perfect penetration, proclaiming pure and clear instructions to guide those at the beginning stage.
By expounding secret verses, he causes past habitual tendencies to be dissolved; thus, the distant traveler recognizes the path home, and the wanderer finds the gate to the granted dwelling.
Through these fifty-five stages, one proceeds by way of this path; through these twelve single and double gates, one provisionally attains entry.
Thus, within the realm of True Suchness (tathatā), although the traces of awakening and cultivation have vanished, [this remains so] within the gate of birth and death.
Within this, how could the title "Entering through Understanding" be obstructed? Mañjuśrī requested the revelation of the scripture’s title so as to truly circulate the Great Dharma.
The World-Honored One meticulously investigated the realms and destinies, intending thereby to restrain deluded sentiments.

He further elaborated upon the demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) to completely eradicate the thorns of views, blocking the deviant paths at the ford of delusion and opening the straight steps to the Hall of Dharma. Thus, he brought Bodhi to perfection, returning to the state of non-abiding.
It is attained when both truth and falsehood are forgotten and the fruit and cause are unified in one. To reach the ultimate source, this sutra is supreme.

When I first examined the commentaries and exegeses, I found them to be largely in accord with the Buddha’s intent, leaving nothing omitted; yet, as I have long contemplated the scriptural text itself, I have gradually come to feel that the Sage’s mind has not been fully exhausted therein.

I have immersed my spirit in silent investigation and gradually grasped the initial outlines. Thereupon, I have searched through the commentaries of various schools and compiled the subtle refinements of numerous interpretations.
I have clarified the essential tenets while analyzing points of agreement and difference, and harmonized the questions and answers to elucidate what was obscure or omitted.

Yet, this is like attempting to increase the height of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff by scooping up soil, or adding to the depth of the Nine Abysses by cupping water; it is merely a vain endeavor. Nevertheless, disregarding my own ignorance and limitations, I have presumptuously attempted this synthesis.

I have collected various words and titled this work *Cuanzhu* (Annotated Compilation). My hope is that by relying on these texts to clarify the meaning, one may suddenly awaken to the eternally abiding true mind;
and by practicing according to the teachings, swiftly realize the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Written by the śramaṇa Zhenjie at Mount Jing. *Explanation of Doubts regarding the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Regarding the explanation for dispelling doubts: because students of the Dharma, upon reading this sutra, may rely on ancient commentaries or cling to their own views regarding the stages of śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna—taking mere reasoning for practice and confused views for cultivation—their essential intent remains unclear.
Upon reading the present compiled commentary, they cannot help but harbor doubts. Therefore, I shall first clarify the fundamental tenets and subsequently briefly cite several points.
I shall provide an explanation for each point. To examine the essence of *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*:

these constitute the fundamental basis of this entire scripture and the governing principle of its three divisions. *Śamatha* signifies the meaning of quiescence; *samādhi* signifies the meaning of luminous illumination;
and *dhyāna* signifies the meaning of the non-duality of illumination and quiescence. The intrinsic nature of the body is inherently awakened, which is termed "illumination. This awakened essence...
Fundamental quiescence is called "stillness. The non-duality of clarity and stillness is called the "essence" (*tattva*). This refers to the essence of clarity and stillness;
it is the ultimate, adamantine principle, which is also termed "abiding in concentration" (*samādhi*). This is because such is the essence of clarity and stillness.

Suddenly, it becomes obscured and dark. With the stirring of a thought, there is a fleeting arising; thus, what is fundamentally luminous becomes ignorance, and what is fundamentally quiescent becomes the stirring of thought.

Thereupon, one cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding) because of this movement, thereby stilling that movement; one cultivates *vipaśyanā* (insight) because of this dullness, thereby observing that dullness.

When the efficacy of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is manifest, dullness and movement vanish of their own accord, and luminosity and quiescence naturally restore themselves. This is according to [the method of] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This refers to the ultimate and steadfast practice; it is also called the "inducing of samādhi. As the Sūtra says:
"There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices.
Thus, it is clear that *śamatha* and the others pertain to both principle and practice. Therefore, Ānanda first asked how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain the realization of Bodhi.
Regarding "the initial expedient means for wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna":
the intent is to clarify the ultimate and steadfast principle as the foundation of practice; it does not concern the conduct of progressive cultivation.
Indeed, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the realization of Bodhi by clarifying this wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna as the initial expedient means.

This is the fruit of that [practice]. Therefore, Ānanda immediately pointed to the substance of the fruit to inquire about its initial cause; was this not intended to clarify the principle of ultimate solidity?
Thus, the initial expedient means should only point toward the genuineness of faith and understanding; it is improper to further discuss the "perfect penetration" of the ear-faculty.
Furthermore, since the three and a half fascicles of the sūtra all pertain to the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), how could this possibly be a question regarding cultivation?
Thus we know that the initial question constitutes a general inquiry regarding the stages of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, Ānanda’s request for instruction on the path of *śamatha* was intended to seek instruction on the path of the "Wondrous Adornment of Self-Nature Śūraṅgama," rather than seeking instruction on the practice of cessation (*śamatha*) alone.

However, since *śamatha* and the other practices already encompass both principle and application, taking them as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) not only does not contradict principle, but rather fulfills the original intent of the requester.

Therefore, after the World-Honored One emitted light, he first pointed to the two minds—true and false—to clarify the roots of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa; subsequently, he restated the purport of the question, saying:
If you now wish to know the path of *śamatha* with the aspiration to transcend birth and death,
you should understand that the deluded mind is the root of beginningless birth and death, while the true mind is the root for transcending birth and death and realizing *nirvāṇa*.
Since your desire to know the path of *śamatha* is rooted in the aspiration to transcend birth and death, is this not, in fact, a desire to know one’s own nature?
Thereupon, he raised his fist and questioned him, intending to test whether his mental application was true or false.
Because the other again recognized it as something capable of being inferred, [the Master] rebuked him, saying: "This is a false conceptualization of external objects. He concluded by pointing out:
"It is entirely because you grasp at these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality, that you fail to achieve the fruit of sainthood. However, what has been explained above...

[The Buddha] showed [him this]. He merely wished for Ānanda to recognize delusion and know the truth so as to transcend birth and death. Within the text, there was never any discussion of cultivation.
Thus, one knows that the request to show the path of *śamatha* was a request to show the self-nature (*svabhāva*), not a request to show cessation (*śamatha*).

Furthermore, when Ānanda heard that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," his confusion and distress redoubled; he immediately requested again, saying: "I only pray that Your Great Compassion will bestow upon me the eye of great wisdom."
"You have revealed to us that the awakened mind is luminous and pure; this is our desire for the delusions and confusions to be resolved so that we may attain clarity and purity of mind.
Now, the World-Honored One, wishing to expound the path of sublime cultivation for the various samādhis of the Great Dhāraṇī, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Although you possess strong powers of memory, it merely increases your learning; regarding the subtle and secret contemplation of śamatha, your mind remains—"
Not yet having understood this, you thus give rise to confusion regarding the essence and function of true seeing. For true seeing is the essence; tranquil illumination is its function.
Because the essence of true seeing inherently possesses the function of tranquil illumination, it is tranquil yet constantly illuminating;
therefore, it can illuminate and discern that the essence of seeing is false. It is illuminating yet constantly tranquil; therefore, seeing is not [true] seeing. Since Ānanda, regarding...

Those who truly perceive the essence and function [of the mind] do not fail to understand either of these two, yet they instead increase their confusion and distress. The World-Honored One then again pointed to both the identical and distinct views, reiterating the contemplation of *śamatha* as follows:
"The luminous mind of original enlightenment perceives conditions; it is not an eye disease. That which is perceived by the perceiver is the eye disease;
the perception itself is not within the eye disease. This is truly the seeing of seeing. Indeed, the luminous mind of original enlightenment is the Great *Dhāraṇī*.
"Awakening to conditions as not being eye-diseases" and so forth refers to the sublime path of cultivation for all *samādhis*.

Because the essence of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*) is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it is able to awaken to and understand that all conditions are illusory. Because it is illuminating yet constantly quiescent, it does not fall into the midst of the eye-disease.
This truly means that at the time of seeing the seeing, the seeing is not [itself] the seeing; this is a reiterated demonstration of the contemplative observation of *śamatha*.
This is to dispel the delusion of viewing views as non-views, thereby causing the awakened mind to become clear and pure. Some may object:

"Since you speak of the contemplation of *śamatha* and also refer to 'the excellent path of practice for all *samādhis*, does this not indicate the progressive cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
Why then restrict it to the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*)? Answer: Not so. This passage is intended to refute false views and false awakenings.

This reveals true vision and true awakening. Desiring Ānanda to know the essence of true vision and true awakening, [the Buddha shows that] its nature inherently possesses the function of tranquil illumination, which is capable of destroying delusion.
Thus the Sūtra says: "You should further know that when you see the seer, the seeing is not itself the seeing.
The meaning lies in knowing this first and then acting; by so acting, one destroys delusion. If Ānanda were to know true awakening...
Regarding essence and function: this refers to knowing the path of sublime practice for the various samādhis and great dhāraṇīs.
Now that Ānanda is confused and bewildered because he does not know the essence and function of true seeing, he is ignorant of both principle and practice.
Therefore, although it is called "the path of sublime practice for śamatha and contemplative observation," the text belongs to the section on destroying falsehood to reveal truth; such is its intent.

Because this involves both the knowledge of principle (*li*) and the practice of knowledge (*xing*), it belongs to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) rather than the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
However, since the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* penetrate both principle and practice, that which is "seen" on the Path of Vision is the seeing of this principle.

Thus, it is said: "One knows the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, which contains and nurtures the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions. This refers to the Path of Cultivation.
That which is practiced is the cultivation of this very path. Therefore, within the section on the cultivation of the Way, the two definitive meanings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are clarified.
That which is realized upon attaining the fruit is the realization of this principle. Thus it is said:

"This awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) within the Diamond Mind (*vajracitta*)," which is precisely the re-realization of the Buddha’s *samādhi*. Therefore, I call this the "Great [Awakening]."
Fundamentally, the three divisions constitute the core principle. As the ancients said: "Relying on the ultimate, firm principle, one cultivates the ultimate, firm practice;
by cultivating the ultimate, firm practice, one returns to realize the ultimate, firm principle.
Such is the great purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Annotated Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
Resolving Doubts Regarding the *Śrī-mahā-śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the Ultimate Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization,
and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty;
with the assistance of the Śramaṇa Migaśaka of the country of Udyāna of the Tang Dynasty for the oral interpretation;
and the Bodhisattva-śīla disciple, former Minister of Justice and concurrently Member of the Central Secretariat... [of the Tang Dynasty].
Recorded by Fang Rong, Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Coordinator of State Affairs, of Qinghe;
transcribed by the Śramaṇa Mingju of Li; compiled and annotated by Zhenjie. Regarding the resultant essence (*phala-bhāva*) of the Tathāgata:
its essence is inherently so; why rely on secret causes? Regarding the functional application (*prayoga*) of the Bodhisattva path: its function is... [unfolding].
What constitutes the myriad practices? There is no cause and no practice; there is no cultivation and no realization; there is neither understanding nor non-understanding.
All names and characteristics, whether great or small, are not established. This is the true Śūraṅgama, the ultimate and adamantine state.

It is simply because the Tathāgata is hidden within the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) of sentient beings that he is not revealed except through secret causes. Sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are submerged in...
Regarding the seven realms of existence, there is nothing among the myriad practices that is not cultivated.
Thus, the Buddha, the Sovereign of Awakening, revealed to them the Great Dharma so they would not become lost in minor paths, yet could silently attain the essence that is beyond all bounds.

He illustrated this through the metaphor of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa so they would not stagnate in the perception of forms, yet could reach the ultimate subtlety of the Unsurpassed. By pointing to the secret cause of the Tathāgata, he enabled them to clarify their original nature.

O Wondrous Mind! Know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time take this as their primary cause; clarify the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization, so that one may awaken to the ultimate Dharma.
Know that all sages rely upon this to realize the fruit, even unto the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices of a Bodhisattva.
Among all phenomena, there is nothing that does not ultimately reach the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), remaining firm and unshakable.
Because it destroys [all delusions], it is named *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-tathāgata-rahasya-hetu-bhāvanā-sākṣāt-kriyā-nītārtha-sarva-bodhisattva-sarva-caryā-śūraṅgama*.
Śūraṅgama is translated here as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.

This is the very foundation of the principles and practices of this sutra, and the essence of the bodies and environments of both the holy and the ordinary. Because this essence has not yet been clarified, all phenomena and dharmas...

They appear distinct and diverse, yet they are bound by phenomena. When this essence is realized, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness, the holy and the ordinary, defilement and purity—all phenomenal dharmas—are extinguished in their very place; this is precisely the eternally abiding nature of mind.
Therefore, it is said that "all matters are ultimately firm and solid. The *sūtra* refers to the written text that serves as the means of expression; "expression" (*quan*) is like a fishing trap.
If students can refrain from clinging to the trap as being the fish itself, then the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* may be attained.
As for the "Compiled Notes" (*Zhuànzhù*), this refers to the compilation of the words of various masters to provide commentary on this sūtra. Now, since the *Śūraṅgama* first arose...
From Fúxià downwards, there have been more than ten schools of interpretation.
Those compiled here draw primarily from the two masters of Chángshuǐ and Wēnliṅ; however, the names of these various teachers are all omitted.
This is likely because some passages synthesize the meanings of many texts, others slightly alter the phrasing of a single meaning, or some include additional material.
I have adopted both [the Chinese and the Indic], employing both the meaning and the phrasing, so that from the outset there is neither loss nor gain.

Nevertheless, if among my ignorance there is occasionally something gained, I shall also humbly append it therein. I seek only that the principles and phrasing be direct and penetrating, thereby elucidating the intent of the sutra.
If something does not accord with the sutra, then even if its discussion of principle is profound and mysterious, or its composition is beautiful and rich, I take no interest in it at all.
Indeed, in antiquity there were certainly those who stumbled over a thousand-li journey, and in the present day there are likewise those with the clarity of a single tube.
For this reason, even the masters of the past could not entirely avoid entering here and exiting there, or siding with their own while attacking others.
It is like those who drink from the ocean, each satisfied by a single flavor; or like those who gaze upon a mani jewel, each seeing but one color.
If one were to speak of ultimate exhaustion [of all phenomena], then it is only Buddha and Buddha.
A General Survey of the Scriptural Divisions:
Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, from the Tang through the Song dynasties, there have been successive sages who have produced commentaries and exegeses based on scriptural divisions (*kepan*).

However, their methods of dividing the scripture all maintain that the King Śuddhodana and King Virūḍhaka belonged to different eras, and thus they do not consider it to be a single assembly spoken all at once. As for their classification of the teachings (*pianjiao*), they all...

Regarding the matters of Guhagupta, Yaśas, and others, you have arbitrarily concluded that they occurred after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. I, being ignorant, privately harbor doubts about this and beg to first question you on it.
Now, the shifting of a riverbed at night occurs faster than the turning over of one's palms; the succession of kings in a hidden kingdom may take place in but a morning or evening.
Yet, the *Śūraṅgama* Dharma assembly lasted from summer until winter. One should not, therefore, insist on a different king or suspect a different assembly.
Furthermore, since the time of Dīpaṃkara, there has been no period when the various Buddhas have not preached [this] and no period when Bodhisattvas have not realized it.
Since the Earth-holding Bodhisattva (Dharaṇīdhara) stated that he had heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the wondrous Lotus Sūtra, how could this refer to Śākyamuni alone?
Moreover, in the fourth fascicle of the sūtra, it is recorded that Mādrī’s divine powers were neutralized by the power of a mantra, and she was reunited with Yaśodharā.

They awaken to their past causes; some attain liberation from the fetters, while others receive a prediction of future enlightenment. This is the Tathāgata’s prophetic revelation of what has not yet occurred.
Thus, in the sixth sutra below, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmitrā attains arhatship upon hearing the verses being recited.

At the Dharma assembly on Vulture Peak, Yaśodharā was granted a prediction of enlightenment. Since these predictions were bestowed after [the disciples] had emerged from the entanglements of worldly existence, they all follow the section on the preaching;
could this not be considered a prophetic indication of what was yet to come? This can be understood simply by examining the word "or" (或).

When the sutra speaks of the "final instructions," that refers to the concluding passage concerning the subduing of Māra at the end of the tenth fascicle; it is indeed the *Śūraṅgama* Dharma assembly.
Finally, this "last" does not refer to the final moment before death. Although many previous citations have been drawn upon, they cannot be detailed here;
none of them are sufficient to serve as a standard for structural analysis (*ko-p'an*). If the structural analysis lacks a standard, the underlying principles and meanings will naturally diverge.

Now, I shall follow the sequence of our Buddha’s establishment of the teachings, though I do not yet know if it is appropriate. Please allow me to set forth my humble view. Regarding the Dharma King’s preaching of the Dharma, there is...
The sequence is orderly and systematic. First, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) Sudden Teaching is expounded to establish the foundation; this is the *Avataṃsaka*.
Next, the Three Vehicles (Triyāna) Gradual Teaching is expounded to accommodate the capacities of beings; this refers to the *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.

Finally, the One Vehicle Perfect Teaching is expounded to reveal the ultimate reality; this is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* is situated within the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and its essence is truly vast.

This is the ultimate teaching of the Vehicle. Therefore, the secret cause of the Tathāgata, the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas, and the methods of cultivation and realization—all are ultimately complete herein.
From this point onward, there is no further progress or cultivation; one proceeds directly to the perfectly sublime path of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, there was no further discourse on the stages (bhūmi) of spiritual attainment;

it spoke exclusively of the Sublime Dharma, granting authorization according to individual capacities and bestowing predictions of Buddhahood. Indeed, regarding the manifestation of the Great Matter, the Lotus Sūtra is the ultimate and exhaustive culmination;
nothing more can be added. Following the Lotus Sūtra, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra was then taught, concluding with the upholding of the Vinaya and the discourse on the Eternal.
That which "supports the Vinaya" (fúlǜ) is for the purpose of entrusting future affairs; that which "discusses the Constant" (táncháng) is for the purpose of demonstrating true quiescence.
These are matters left behind solely at the moment of death; they do not add anything to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Yet, commentators who do not base themselves on the intent of supporting the Vinaya arbitrarily judge the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* to follow the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and likewise call it "supporting the Vinaya and discussing the Constant. If this were so, then...
Having completed one's cultivation, one further pursues cultivation; after upholding the Vinaya, one again upholds the Vinaya.

The former is superfluous to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while the latter is redundant to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. This is indeed an inversion of priorities and a proliferation of branches that brings disorder to the Dharma of the Dharma King.
Now, the matter of pursuing cultivation is like farming: it is like weeding and tilling; it is like a lotus flower: it is like the unfolding of its blossoms.
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is termed the "harvesting" and the *Nirvāṇa* the "gleaning," there should be no further weeding or cultivation within that harvesting and gleaning.

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is termed the "abandoning of the provisional to establish the real"—like petals falling and the lotus appearing—there should be no further blooming of petals after they have fallen.
To prove this by means of the sūtra: once the destitute child has received the treasure store...
Furthermore, what more remains to be sought? Once those who were led by the conjured city have reached the place of jewels, what further progress could they make?

After Dīpaṃkara had preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he entered parinirvāṇa in the middle of the night; after Śākyamuni Buddha had preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he announced his extinction before the fourfold assembly.
Why, then, do you continue with such prolixity regarding the *Śūraṅgama*? If the *Śūraṅgama* must necessarily come later, then Ānanda...
Having already exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they yet had not exhausted all outflows regarding the *Śūraṅgama*.
Having already been fit to receive the Buddha’s prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they yet did not possess the full power of the Path regarding the *Śūraṅgama*.

Having already attained realization of the wondrous Dharma, they yet did not know the destination of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Having already established themselves securely in the Buddha-way, they yet [were]...
That they subsequently fell into brothels is entirely a case of perversion; logically, it could not have been so. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is judged to follow after the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This is because, following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the study of wisdom (*prajñā*) flourished while the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) was not yet fully perfected.
Some people may become mired in extensive learning and lose the state of right concentration (*samādhi*).

Therefore, this [text] demonstrates the great samādhi of Śūraṅgama and provides the great wisdom of Prajñā, so that concentration and wisdom may be balanced and both study and practice may be perfected, ultimately leading toward the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle.
This is the purpose for which the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* was composed. Regarding the general purport of these three scriptures, they are all nothing other than...
For the sake of the one great cause and condition, one must first rely upon Prajñā to bring forth illumination; next, one proceeds through the *Śūraṅgama* to practice and realize;
finally, one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for confirmation. Only then can the capacities of all Buddhas be fully exhausted. Such is the nature of the introduction.
Nevertheless, for guiding one toward the vehicle of Chan and resolving correct views, nothing surpasses the *Śūraṅgama*. Its topical outline follows the standard major divisions.
It consists of three parts: first, the introductory section; second, the main body of the teaching; third, the section on dissemination. The introductory section is divided into two:

first, the presentation of the time, place, principal figures, and associates to establish faith; second, the presentation of Ānanda’s manifestation of traces to initiate the discourse. The main body of the teaching contains five sections.

The first is the Section on Seeing the Path, which initially employs seven investigations to reveal the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity (this constitutes the first fascicle).
Next, through the "eight returns," the wondrously pure essence of vision is distinguished to reveal the *tathāgatagarbha* (sections two and three).

Subsequently, the mountains, rivers, and myriad phenomena proclaim the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth (from section four, beginning to the middle). All of these serve to enable the practitioner to clarify the mind and perceive its nature, acting as the secret cause for cultivation and realization;
therefore, this is called the "Section on Seeing the Path. Second, the "Section on Cultivating the Path" first demonstrates the initial [stage].
The mind has two points of definitive meaning: first, to cause the causal mind to examine the resultant awakening;

second, to examine the root of afflictions so as to serve as the true foundation for practice (from the fourth section to the end). Next, the sequence for loosening the knots of the six sense faculties is shown, enabling the mind that unties the knots to attain wondrous, perfect penetration, which serves as the essential requirement for practice (from the fifth to the middle of the sixth section). This concludes one cycle of cultivation and progress for those of sharp faculties.

Thus Ānanda arrived here, having clearly understood the path to which Bodhi leads. Believing himself to have already awakened to the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas, he vowed to deliver those in the final age;
he further requested instructions on how to establish a site for practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the rules for concentrating the mind.

Thereupon, he heard the three trainings in the absence of outflows (*trīṇi śikṣāṇy anāsravāṇi*), the four types of restraint (*caturvidha-saṃvara*), and the great divine mantras (the seventh of the six sections). These constitute, in total, the method for cultivation.
First, the Section on the Factors of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-aṅga*). Second, the Section on the Factors of Realization (*abhisamaya-aṅga*).

From the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to Great Nirvāṇa, it sequentially demonstrates the advancement through fifty-seven stages until reaching the ultimate state of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the accomplishment of the Unsurpassed Way; therefore, it is named the Section on the Realization of the Fruit.

(End of 7, beginning of 8). Third, the Section on the Concluding Summary of the Sūtra. It enumerates five titles to summarize and clarify the great purport [of the teaching]. (Middle of 8). Fifth, the Section on Aids...
The Section on the Divisions of the Path. First, it clarifies that the seven destinies, including the hells, are created solely by the mind.

Next, it clarifies the subtle demonic activities within *śamatha*, for fear that practitioners might wash their minds with what is not correct, thereby falling into error and ruin; thus, it is called "Aid to the Path" (*aṣṭama-madhyama-daśama-anta*).

Now, one realizes the Path (*darśana-mārga*) before practicing the Path (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and one realizes the fruit (*phala*) after practicing the Path. This concerns the matter of cultivation and realization.
It is finished. Thus concludes the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Essential Dharma of the *Śūraṅgama*.

Yet, out of his great compassion, the World-Honored One further wished for sentient beings who uphold the precepts to remain pure and free from transgressions, and for true practitioners not to encounter divergent paths;
therefore, he taught the methods for assisting the Way as a final instruction. He then entered the stage of circulation, bringing this assembly to its conclusion. This is...
Once the threads are woven together, they form a continuous chain that cannot be severed; it is impossible to divide them into separate assemblies or categorize them as distinct doctrines.
This is but a general outline; a detailed explanation following the specific texts would exhaust all particulars.

Nevertheless, when viewed from the present perspective, there are somewhat more contradictions than before, and even those of established expertise in their respective schools cannot avoid internal inconsistencies. Only the person of comprehensive understanding should examine this.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling [at such-and-such a place] together with twelve hundred and fifty people.
Regarding this Dharma, I heard it from the Buddha. This assembly is established by the Buddha’s own words; it serves merely as a testimony that the Dharma has been transmitted.
It is not necessary for others to speak of it. The phrase "at one time" is also established by the Buddha and is used universally across all sūtras.
Therefore, it is not fixedly designated [by a single term]. *Buddha*—fully called *Buddha*—is here translated as "The Awakened One" (*Jue-zhe*).

*Śrāvastī*, or sometimes *Shewei*, is newly translated as "Abundant Virtue," because the kingdom abounds in four virtues: first, wealth; second, objects of desire; third, extensive learning; and fourth, liberation.
*Jetavana*—fully called *Jita*, correctly *Śreṣṭha*—is here translated as "Victorious in Battle. It was the Prince’s [park].
This is its name. When he was born, his father, the King, was victorious in battle against a foreign state and consequently established this auspicious title.
Thus, Sudatta purchased a grove for him and constructed a vihāra to offer to the Buddha; "Huan" (桓) refers to the forest. A bhikṣu possesses three meanings:
namely, a mendicant, one who destroys evil, and one who terrifies Māra. As for the one thousand two hundred and fifty people, they were those first ordained...
First, he converted the five men beginning with Cunda; next, he converted the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their one thousand disciples;
next, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with a hundred disciples; and finally, he converted the householder Yaśas and fifty others.
The scripture cites these as large numbers, which is why five individuals are subtracted from the total. "Together" (俱) refers to the meeting of teacher and disciples, gathering at one time.

Furthermore, these followers had previously served non-Buddhist paths, undergoing diligent hardships for many kalpas without attaining anything at all. As soon as they encountered the Buddha, they immediately attained the supreme fruits.
Thus, moved by their gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness, they constantly followed his transformation; hence, they are known as the "Constantly Following Assembly."
"All are untainted great arhats" (up to) "rescue the future and transcend all worldly entanglements.
This is a praise of their virtues. The first two phrases offer a general praise; from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it is a specific praise. As for what is called "maintaining and upholding":
Abiding in the Middle Way and maintaining it without loss is precisely the meaning of "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
To speak of being "outflow-free" means not falling into either of the two extremes. To "skillfully transcend all existences" (*bhava*) means not leaking into existence;

to be able to "descend into the realms" means not leaking into emptiness. What is called "skillful transcendence" is to transcend all existences while remaining within all existences. Regarding that which is...

This refers to one who is wondrously capable: able to transcend all realms of existence (*bhava*), yet also able to turn the wheel of the Dharma with the Buddha within the lands, remaining unattached to either emptiness or existence;

thus, such a person is worthy of being entrusted with the final charge. Furthermore, they adorn the *vinaya* to establish a broad model for the three realms and manifest response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to deliver sentient beings.
Their intent is not merely to benefit others for a single moment, but is directly aimed at rescuing and liberating those of the future.
He caused them all to transcend the defilements and burdens of the various realms of existence. Thus, they were able to benefit themselves and others;
for this reason, he was praised as a "Great Arhat free from outflows" (*anāsrava-mahārhan*). His name was Mahāmati Śāriputra (down to) Upānisaṭa, who served as the leader among them.
This is the list of names. Śāriputra: *Śāri* means "Sparrow" (*śārikā*); he was the son of a woman named Śārī.
Because his eyes were so distinct in black and white and moved with such fluidity like those of a sparrow, he was given a name derived from his mother’s.
Maudgalyāyana: this is his clan name (*gotra*), meaning "of the Mung-bean lineage" (*mudga*). His personal name was Kolita, which means "jointless tree. Mahā... [text ends]
Kauṣṭhila—this means "Great Thighs. Pūrṇa is the father's name; this means "Full.
Maitrāyaṇī is the mother's name; this means "Compassion. Now, by combining the names of his parents, he is addressed as "Son of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇī.

Subhūti is called "Born of Emptiness" because at the time of his birth, all the storehouses were empty. An astrologer declared that it was both auspicious and fortunate; therefore, he is also called "Good."
The present [disciples] are Śubhūti and Upānanda; the latter is here translated as "Dust-nature-emptiness.

Although their names appear differently in various sūtras—where they are ranked by seniority of ordination, Cunda is mentioned first, and where they are ranked by excellence of virtue, Śāriputra is mentioned first—this follows the precedent of ranking them by virtue.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *pratyekabuddhas* who had attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), with Mañjuśrī as their leader.

*Pratyeka* is fully called *pratyekabuddha*, which here means "individually enlightened" (*yuanjue*). They are so named because they awaken by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

These belong to the class of those who travel in groups (*vargacārin*), and are not the same as the "rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*). The "rhinoceros-like" refers to one who emerges alone, like a rhinoceros.

"In a world without a Buddha" refers to the Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers). "Those who travel in groups" means they proceed in a company; this occurs when a Buddha has appeared in the world, and thus refers to the Pratyekabuddhas.
Because both leaders and followers have assembled together, it is said that "they come to the Buddha's presence together with those at the initial stage.

*Shu* (屬) means "to encounter. *Zizì* (自恣), or the "Pravāraṇā ceremony," is permitted for three days by the Vinaya: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth days of the seventh month. It is for the purpose of confessing one's own transgressions.

[The term] *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) means to allow the Saṃgha to raise [criticisms] at will; hence it is called *pravāraṇā*. During the ninety-day period of restricted movement (*varṣā*), one has no means to behold the Buddha;

therefore, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, one consults [the teacher] to resolve doubts in one's mind. Both *pravāraṇā* and the resolution of doubts are means to examine the virtuous achievements of the ninety-day period.

Regarding the veneration of the Tathāgata as "Compassionate and Majestic" (*maitrī-vibhūṣita*): "compassion" refers to his benevolence, while "majesty" refers to his awe-inspiring power. This is the esoteric meaning.

The meaning of the secret cause is proclaimed as profound; this is why it serves as the prologue for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* takes the "Innumerable Meanings" as its prologue.
The *kalaviṅka* is a celestial bird whose song is harmonious and elegant; the Buddha’s voice is like it.
Mañjuśrī—meaning "Wondrous Virtue" in Chinese—symbolizes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). In the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama*, he acts as the one who selects [the true nature].
Dharmākṣa was therefore ranked as the foremost.
At that time, King Prasenajit, for the sake of his deceased father, also personally invited the great bodhisattvas.
Prasenajit—here translated as "Victorious Army"—was the King of Śrāvastī. "Memorial day" refers to the anniversary of his death.
"Palace quarters" refers to the king’s inner court; he invited the Buddha into this inner court, demonstrating the utmost reverence.
Within the city, there were also elders, lay devotees, and all sentient beings of immeasurable merit.
This passage describes the reason for his erroneous fall into the brothel. Regarding those who received separate invitations:

before Ānanda had accepted the general invitation from the assembly of donors to a meal, he had accepted a separate invitation and traveled far away, not yet having returned; thus, he was unable to attend according to the monastic order. "Monastic order" (僧次) refers to the sequence of seating based on seniority.

This refers to the sequential assignment of monastics to accept invitations. According to the Vinaya regulations, when the Sangha travels to a distant location, there must be at least three companions:
one *sthavira* (senior elder) and one *ācārya* (preceptor). This is done to solemnize their conduct and prevent errors or omissions. The *pātra* is called the "proper vessel" (*yogya-bhājana*).

Regarding the "last donor," this refers to those who have not yet provided a meal for the Sangha; through impartial compassion, they transform others by maintaining a mind of equality toward themselves.
They gave with a pure mind; regarding both the greedy and others, they were equal toward the Dharma as well.
Thus, the donor and the observer both obtained immeasurable merit, thereby accomplishing boundless virtue. As for the Mātaṅga, he was filthy and lowly;
since Ānanda made no such distinction, he fell into error. Kṣatriya refers to the royal lineage; Caṇḍāla...
"Luo" means "those who kill," namely the families of butchers, slaughterers, prostitutes, and liquor dealers.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, maintained strict and dignified deportment and observed the solemnity of the fasting laws.
This passage describes the intent behind practicing universal compassion. Subhūti abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to follow the poor;
one did so because it was easier for the wealthy to give, and the other did so to plant seeds of merit for the poor.
The Tathāgata rebuked them both, desiring that their minds be free from partiality and that they cease the slander arising from such inequality. Therefore, Ānanda held them in profound reverence.

This is based on the *Sugong jiefa* (The Ritual for Solemn Fasting). As for the "ritual for fasting" (*zhai fa*), it refers to maintaining a dignified and grave demeanor while proceeding in a prescribed order to beg for alms.

Some restrict this to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, claiming that it was not the Tathāgata who rebuked [the disciples]. How could one know that it was not the Tathāgata who rebuked them? Was it Vimalakīrti alone who offered the reprimand?
At that time, Ānanda, while on his alms-round, [encountered] a woman who, through her lewd advances and physical caresses, was about to cause him to violate his precepts.
This clearly illustrates how he mistakenly fell into a brothel. "Mātangī" is translated as "Original Nature"; she was a courtesan.
"Śābikara" means "Yellow-haired Heretic. The illusory spell transmitted by him was named "Primal Brahmā," which was in fact a demonic incantation.
This is merely a skillful means. To "lustfully caress" refers to drawing near with the body in order to destroy the essence of the precepts; it means intending to ruin the substance of pure morality.
The subsequent statement that "because the mind is pure, one has not yet fallen into ruin" implies that [the act] was merely an attempt to destroy them.
The Tathāgata knew that [the city] had been subjected to the arts of seduction (until) Mātanga returned to the Buddha’s presence.

This clarifies that he went to protect them by reciting mantras. It is the Tathāgata’s constant practice: after accepting an invitation for a meal, he always preaches the Dharma once the feast is concluded.
Now that he has returned so swiftly, there must surely be a purpose; therefore, the king, his ministers, and the great assembly have followed him here.

The crown of the head is the fruit of the unsurpassed; its light possesses the colors of a hundred jewels, which is called "Fearlessness" because it can intimidate demons and heretics, such that no object can surpass it.
That the World-Honored One does not himself recite the mantra, but rather causes a manifested Buddha to speak from the light upon his crown, demonstrates—
This mantra is the unconditioned Buddha of the mind; it is the unsurpassed Dharma of the mind.
Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself in worship, and wept with grief (until) he withdrew to sit silently and receive the holy instructions.
Self-reproach and petitioning are the primary expedient means for attaining Bodhi.

For the wisdom born of extensive learning must rely upon the realization of one's nature (*darśana-dhātu*) to fully manifest the power of the Path and prevent one from being ensnared by the heterodox. Now, Ānanda has been devoted solely to extensive learning.
Because he had not yet fully perfected the power of the Way, he inquired about the primary cause for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to attain the fruit [of Buddhahood].

This implies that the attainment of the fruit of Bodhi by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all relies upon the realization of the nature (seeing the nature) as the cause; therefore, he points to the essence of the fruit in order to inquire about the primary cause.
This is precisely analogous to the request made by Mañjuśrī in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* regarding the original ground of practice for all Tathāgatas.
*Śamatha* means tranquility; *samādhi* means luminous clarity; *dhyāna* means the non-duality of luminosity and tranquility.
Although there are three meanings, the essence of the mind is one. To raise one is to include all three; to speak of the three is to refer to the one.
Since both "one" and "three" are ultimately non-existent, it is designated as "wondrous"—this is the self-nature *śūraṅgama*. This refers to the initial expedient means.
This refers to requesting instruction on the self-nature of Śūraṅgama. The intention is to awaken to this in order to establish the secret cause (*guhyahetu*).

Therefore, in the explanation of the title, it says: "Pointing to the Tathāgata’s secret cause, so as to clarify the fundamentally wondrous mind; to know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time all rely upon this as their primary cause.
This is precisely that meaning. Now, although this question concerns the secret cause, it speaks of the "initial" [stage].
As for "expedient means" (*upāya*): within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, even cultivation and realization are transcended; how, then, could one rely on secret causes?

What is now called "attaining *bodhi*" is clearly just an expedient regarding the self-nature. Speaking in terms of the three stages of seeing, cultivation, and realization, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) constitutes the initial expedient;
thus, Changshui also points to correct faith and understanding as the initial expedient.
I have observed that because Ānanda inquired about the initial expedient means, the Tathāgata subsequently questioned him regarding his original aspiration for enlightenment;
this was intended to verify the authenticity of the causal ground. Thus, this "initial expedient means" [is the subject of inquiry].

Is this not precisely the inquiry into the initial mind that attains fruition? Since the attainment of fruition depends upon the causal ground, and yet Ānanda employed delusion to obscure the truth, [the teaching] first discriminates between the true and the false; next, it brings delusion back to the true;

and finally, it proclaims the nature of the ultimate truth within the supreme meaning, continuing until the conclusion of the section on the Path of Seeing—all of which serves to elucidate one's own [nature].
It is simply the nature of *śūraṅgama*. If one awakens to this nature, then faith and understanding become authentic, which is termed the "Path of Seeing" (*darśanamārga*).
Upon seeing the Path, one immediately attains the initial skillful means. Therefore, it should be known that this question constitutes the general heading for the section on the Path of Seeing.

Some say that because the power of the Path is not yet complete, there is much wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) but a lack of right concentration (*samādhi*); thus, they request instruction on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the "Perfect Penetration of the Auditory Faculty," the intention is to cultivate this in order to perfect the power of the Way.
I, the humble one, consider that if one possesses much learning but has not yet seen the Way, then the functional power remains incomplete, and one consequently falls under the influence of Manoharā.

Therefore, [Ānanda] requested instruction on the *Sūtra-lakṣaṇa-śūraṅgama* (the Self-Nature Śūraṅgama), intending to awaken to this in order to perfect the power of the Way and thereby establish the primary expedient means. Please examine this in detail.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and I share the same breath of life... for this reason you have yearned with thirsting devotion to follow the Buddha and shave your head.

Because you previously requested the initial expedient means of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, I now inquire after the stage of the ground upon which you first resolved your mind, in order to verify whether it is true or false. How is it that Ānanda’s perceptions are all subject to arising and ceasing?"

This means that the characteristics of phenomena are seen as truly existent, and their arising and ceasing are manifest. Taking this as the basis for generating the bodhicitta, one securely proceeds toward the eternal fruit.

Therefore, the sutra below states: "If, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither born nor extinguished—such a thing is impossible.
Ānanda: This is his name, meaning "Joyous Celebration"; he was the Buddha’s younger cousin. Thus...
"Of the same breath" means sharing the same origin. "Heavenly relations" refers to brothers.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Ānanda! You all should know [up to] that because this perception is not true, there is cyclic wandering."
This first praises his resolve and further causes him to know that all sentient beings, deluded regarding the truth and employing the false, transmigrate through birth and death.
Desiring that their minds become true and direct, he first causes them to understand the root of sentient beings' saṃsāra;
next, he restates the intent of the question and commands them to cultivate a direct mind. This is because all sentient beings...
It is because the causal mind was not true that you have transmigrated through birth and death. Now, as you wish to investigate the truth and manifest the nature, you must employ a direct mind;
thus, the causal mind must indeed be true and direct. Although previously your causal mind was not direct, [it is now time to rectify it].
Furthermore, this praise is offered because I take pity on their extreme delusion and desire to guide them with gentle patience.
"Now you wish to investigate unsurpassed bodhi... therefore I have resolved my mind to abandon birth and death."
I desire that he state directly what he is confused about; thus, I cite his previous request to compel him to answer with a straightforward mind.

Furthermore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions have transcended birth and death by means of a straightforward mind. Since you now wish to investigate the truth and manifest the nature, you too must employ a straightforward mind.
From "You, now" below, I cite his prior inquiry; from "You should immediately" below, I command him to provide a direct answer.
"Throughout the ten directions," etc., clarifies the root from which the Tathāgata attained the fruit. The question, "Who loves and delights [in this]? is a further inquiry into the root of delusion.

The answer, "Because of the mind and the eyes," precisely states the root of delusion. "Eyes" refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); "mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).

These faculties and consciousnesses are empty and false, like flowers in the sky. Because one clings to them as having substantial reality, one is able to see and to delight; thus, one does not know the Truth.
Using false conceptualization, how could one investigate the truth, manifest the nature, and abandon birth and death? Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"The six [sense organs] act as intermediaries for thieves, robbing one of the family treasure. Beginningless, empty habituation and the ignorance that dwells in the ground all arise through the sense faculties and consciousnesses;
the cycle of birth and death does not fail to proceed from these. Thus, the following inquiry and examination are intended to make one realize their falsity.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said [up to the point where you asked], 'Where now are the mind and the eyes located?
By answering regarding the mind and the eyes, I am thereby inquiring as to their location. The mind and the eyes are the very root of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one does not know the location of the mind and the eyes, one will be unable to subdue these afflictions. It is like a country invaded by bandits; one must dispatch troops to quell them."
It cannot be removed. If one does not know the location of the thief, the thief cannot be removed. Now, that which causes you to transmigrate is entirely due to the mind and the eyes;
where, then, do the mind and the eyes currently reside?
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...in this way, the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body.
This answer concerns the location of the mind and the eyes; it is precisely the reckoning that the mind is inside. That is to say, the mind is inside and the eyes are outside.

This applies to everyone from ordinary sentient beings up to the Tathāgata, Ānanda; the texts simply present these points in different places. There are twelve types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Excluding earth, wood, space, and scattered matter, these are not of the same category as the physical eye or the mental consciousness. The "floating root" refers to the four sense objects;

this is what is meant by the "eye. This is explained in detail in the fourth fascicle. Although this passage involves a dual reckoning of both the mind and the eye, the following section first refutes the mind.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you are now sitting here [until] 'therefore I am able to see from within the hall at a distance,' this first cites an event to establish the point.
It establishes the distinction between internal and external objects; it intends to clarify that if the mind were located within, one should perceive things in successive order.
It establishes the sequence of perception in order to refute the notion that the mind resides within."
First, the internal [objections] are presented; having thus identified them, they are subsequently cited and refuted.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the midst of the great assembly (until: Ānanda prostrated at his feet and humbly received his compassionate instructions.
Since the preceding section has already established the point by citing scriptural evidence, one should now directly refute the notion of a mind existing within.

Why, then, was it previously permitted to demonstrate the Śūraṅgama Samādhi? Answer: This was because, based on the preceding reliance upon the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the question regarding the initial expedient means was raised.

Therefore, he stroked [Śāriputra’s] head and granted him permission to reveal the *Svabhāva-śūraṃgama*, desiring that he clarify this so that he might know the path of wondrous adornment and thereby establish the primary expedient means. Some may ask: "What is it that the *Svabhāva-śūraṃgama* reveals?"
Answer: That which Ānanda clung to all involved a mind that has a location, attachment, and limited measure.

That which the World-Honored One refuted all revealed a mind that has no location, no attachment, and is expansive, filling the Dharma-realm. Is this not demonstrating the self-nature Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
If one can awaken to this, one will immediately know the path of wondrous adornment, thereby accomplishing the initial expedient means.
Because he did not awaken to this, he subsequently requested further instruction on the path of *śamatha*.
Both *śamatha* and this *samādhi* refer to the self-nature *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; "path" refers here to the Path of Wondrous Adornment (*Miao Zhuangyan Lu*).
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... [up to] 'it is impossible for it to reside within the body.
This refutes the attachment that the mind resides within. From the words 'As you... below, he restates the previous matter and questions it in reverse;
the intent is to clarify that if the mind were indeed within, one would necessarily first perceive what is inside the body, just as a person in a hall must first see what is within the hall."

"Come forward. You too must step down. [The Buddha] proceeded to refute the notion that the mind resides within the body by having him observe his own internal organs. "Is it possible? he asked. [The monk] replied, "It might still be possible.

[The Buddha] then led the assembly to question him: "The heart and stomach are internal organs; even if one cannot know them, the nails and veins are external and manifest. How can you not perceive them?
Since you do not know what is inside, it is clear that the mind is not within. How then can you claim to know what is outside?"
This means that the five viscera dwell together and are most intimate; the myriad phenomena are separated and distinct, and are truly remote.
If one does not understand what is within the body, how could one possibly know external objects? Therefore, the following section concludes by refuting [this view].
Now, while the preceding text presented both the location of the mind and the eyes, here we first refute the deluded mind. Although it is called "refuting the deluded mind," it merely says:

This mind has no location; yet, rather than explicitly stating that this mind is illusory, [the Buddha] intended to lead Ānanda through successive investigations until his emotional attachments were exhausted and his reasoning brought to its limit.

It was only after these seven locations had been examined for the mind that he finally told him, "This is not your mind," and so forth. Thus, the purpose of refuting [the mind] by pursuing it through these seven locations is as follows:
Furthermore, the deluded mind is refuted as having no location.
Ānanda bowed his head and said to the Buddha: [omitted] "How can one person cause many people to be satiated?
He again calculated that the mind exists outside, providing the following analogy to establish that the mind does not exist within, but rather exists outside.

Regarding the external object (*bāhyārtha*). The Buddha’s discourse below [begins with] "Because they further reckon the mind to be external," and thus he again cites an example to definitively establish this point:
namely, that food cannot satisfy this [body], meaning that an external mind cannot know the body. "Ssu" (宿) means "in advance. There are four kinds of food.
"Tuan" (摶) refers to "morsel" (*kavaḍīkāra*); it has a physical form and can be grasped as a segment, distinguishing it from mental food (*manah-saṃcetanāhāra*) and the others.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you were to perceive [the body] as residing outside the body...

there is no such possibility. This refutes the attachment that the mind resides outside. Below the section "The body and mind are external to one another," he distinguishes that they are not external.
From "I shall now demonstrate to you" onwards, he verifies that they are not external. *Tūla* (fully written as *Tūṣāra*), here translated as "frost"; the Buddha’s hand was as soft as this.
"Soft, like *tūla* cotton; therefore, it is called the 'tūla-cotton hand.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One... [up to] ...those who are unobstructed [do so] because their faculties are hidden within.'"
This theory posits that the mind is hidden within the sense organ (*indriya*). As follows, an analogy is established to prove this theory of the hidden organ:
lapis lazuli represents the organ; the eye represents the mind. The visual organ is pure in color and does not obstruct the mind, just as a lapis lazuli bowl does not obstruct the eye.
When one object is illuminated, the mind perceives it through the organ. Thus, [the text] concludes the theory of the hidden organ.
The meaning [of this]. The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... (up to) ...it would be like a crystal [vessel] being joined [to another], which is impossible.

This refutes the hidden root [of the opponent's position]. From "As you... onwards, he restates the [opponent's] calculation to pose a question. From "The Buddha told... onwards, he clarifies that the dharma and the analogy do not correspond.

The error of the Qi [position] is like the analogy of seeing lapis lazuli: in the actual teaching, one does not see the sense organ (*indriya*). Even if one were to grant that the sense organ is seen, the sense organ would then be the object (*viṣaya*).
If it were an object, one could not say that [consciousness] "follows" it; for the preceding text states: "That sense organ follows the seeing, and immediately thereafter it discriminates."
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One... [up to] ‘this is called seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?
This is because one further calculates that the mind is located within; therefore, taking the perception of darkness as the perception of the internal organs.
Thus, although it is said that perceiving light is called seeing the external, the essence of the mind one clings to still remains within. This is because when one opens the eyes and sees...”
This is because it is clarified that they are not like lamps situated outdoors. "Organs" (*fùzàng*) refers to the five viscera (*wǔzàng*) and six hollow organs (*liùfǔ*).
"Apertures" (*qiàoxué*) refers to the seven orifices. The *Báihùtōng* states: "The five viscera are the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys.
The six hollow organs are the palaces and offices of the five viscera. The stomach is the office of the spleen; the bladder is the office of the kidneys; [and] the triple burner (*sānjiāo*)."
The gallbladder is the palace of the liver; the large and small intestines are the palaces of the heart and the lungs.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You should close your eyes... (until) if there is no correspondence, how can seeing be established?"
This correctly refutes the view that darkness is what is called "seeing internally. You should now cite the opponent's position to question them.

Then, following that position, you must refute it with a challenge: namely, if darkness were to face the eye, then darkness would be in front of the eyes and could not be established as being internal.
If you claim that seeing darkness is itself seeing the internal organs and thus constitutes the "internal," then while dwelling in the dark without light,
the darkness within the room would all be your own internal organs. Furthermore, if you do not concede that one has never seen an object without it being present before the eyes—
since such a thing does not constitute "seeing"— how can it be established as "internal"?
If one were to separate external seeing from internal correspondence (upamiśra), [it would follow that] if the face is not seen, internal correspondence cannot be established.
This is a concessive refutation (*abhyupagama-prasaṅga*). The objects before the eyes are called "external seeing," while the objects within the body are called "internal correspondence.

Previously, it was argued that because [the face] faces the eye, it is external and cannot constitute the internal. Now, even granting that it is separated from external seeing and constitutes internal correspondence, [it still follows that it cannot be seen].
This eye is capable of looking back. Now, if it can look back at the body when the eyes are closed, then it should likewise be able to look back at one's own face when the eyes are open;
if this were not the case, the principle would not be established.
If one claims that upon meeting [the object], this "knowing mind" is established, it is impossible for such a person to be called one who sees internally.
This verse exhaustively refutes all conceptual attachments to demonstrate their destruction. Suppose you maintain that one can see the face;

then your mind and your eyes must reside in empty space, because seeing is established only through the mutual confrontation of the sense organ and its object. If they were to reside in empty space, [how could there be contact?]
If it is manifest as being outside, how can it be established as being inside? Furthermore, if it were in space, it would be the same as that of others; naturally, it would not be your own body.
If you insist that although you see my face, it must certainly be your own body, then since the Buddha also sees you, he should likewise be your body.
Moreover, if your mind is able to see the face, then the place where your original body resides should be devoid of it.

Regarding consciousness: because it resides in the space within the locus of the eye-organ, if one were to insist that both [the eyes] possess consciousness, then two distinct entities would be established;
consequently, there would have to be two Buddhas. Therefore, the following concludes the refutation.
