Ānanda said, "I have heard the Buddha teach the fourfold assembly (up to) that it is neither within, nor without, nor in between—these three locations.
This calculation follows wherever they meet. From "I have heard" onwards, he cites what the Buddha taught to give rise to his conceptual attachment:
"When the mind arises, dharmas arise; the objective realm originates from the mind. "When dharmas arise, the mind arises; the mind shifts following the objective realm. By means of the mind...

When mental phenomena arise, they follow along with the objects of perception through thought; this is the very substance of the mind. Where the mind and its phenomena unite, that is where the mind resides.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "As for what you have just said—that if [the mind] came from the outside, it would first meet the face..."
This restates the previous calculations in order to distinguish between the existence and non-existence of the substance (*tattva*).

If there were no substance, then it would be empty of its name; how could it then follow [the body] in conjunction? It would be like the nineteenth element or the seventh sense-object—merely empty names.
If, however, there were a substance, where would it be located? One should touch the body to verify this, thereby clarifying that the substance truly has no location. "Ting" (挃) means to touch.
Ānanda said, "It is the eye that sees; it is the mind that knows, not the eye" (up to the point where he asks), "If it were the seeing of objects, how could one be called dead?
The passage beginning with "Ānanda said" below explains the preceding objection. It means that while the mind can only know, it cannot be said to see; [it] has never...

Wu was able to see that [the Buddha-nature] exists within the mind; it is merely that his eyes could not see it. Below the words of the Buddha, because he resolved the difficulty, he used the metaphor of a gate to illustrate that the capacity for seeing exists within the mind, and cited death to clarify that it is merely the eyes that fail to see.
"Ānanda, as for this mind of yours that is conscious and capable of cognition... [omitted] ...it is impossible for the mind to follow along with existence or non-existence.
This section re-examines its essence in order to refute the notion that it follows wherever it conjoins. First, four propositions are established; below, each proposition is examined in detail.
"If one" and so forth examines that it is not a single entity and has no fixed location—that is, it has no determinate place. "If many" and so forth examines...
It is not a manifold entity. If it were pervasive throughout the lower part, then—distinguishing this from a non-pervasive entity—it would be identical to the previous case;

one should then perceive all four parts upon touching a single branch. If it were not pervasive throughout the lower part, then—distinguishing this from a non-pervasive [entity]—since both meanings are untenable, one cannot claim that the mind exists wherever it happens to contact an object.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...furthermore, if there is no seeing within, it must be in between.
This calculation considers the mind to be in between. "As for 'I' also being below," this refers to what was heard in the past.

"As for 'like me' below," this refers to the arising of a calculation through reflection, whereby one thinks it is inside; yet then one does not see the internal organs. If one thinks it is outside, then it does not accord with the body.
[The opponent] says: "I understand. Since the two meanings [of 'middle'] are untenable, it must exist between the sense organ and the object.

The Buddha said: "As for your statement that the 'middle' must necessarily be non-delusive, since the defining characteristics of the substance are thus conflated, the mind ought to be in a state of confusion."

This is based on the calculation of the intermediate [position]. Here, the "sense faculty" (*indriya*) refers to the body and the "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the location; thus, one infers the intermediate position by means of these two. The "body" is the sense faculty and the "location" is the object.
If it were located within the body, there would be two meanings: the center and the periphery. If it were at the periphery, it could not be considered the center.
Regarding "in the middle," it is the same as "within" mentioned previously; one should perceive the interior. As for "at a location," this also implies that the central position is not fixed.
"To manifest" means to mark an object in order to make it clearly evident. If there is confusion, there will be no basis for grasping the center.
Ānanda said: "Among what I have spoken, it is not these two kinds [of extremes]; it must be in between—this is impossible. This refutes the notion that the mind exists in the middle.
Above, he had separately examined the sense organs and their objects to investigate the position of the middle;

this is not like those two [extremes], as it clarifies the space between the sense organ and the object. The Buddha’s words below [begin with] "If... and so on, citing the opponent's calculation to question them. If one includes the following...

This is difficult to refute according to your calculation. "Object" refers to the sense-field (*viṣaya*); "substance" refers to the faculty (*indriya*). If these two are combined, then cognition and non-cognition would be conflated.
Even if they were not conflated, the object would not be the substance of cognition; since the faculty and the sense-field would stand as two separate entities, how could this be the "Middle"?
Furthermore, if the combination of the two is untenable, then not combining them cannot constitute the Middle. If one does not combine them with the faculty, then it is not [the Middle].

[The Buddha said: "If you know [the object] but do not simultaneously perceive the sensory field (*viṣaya*), it is not that you do not know. Since both of these meanings are untenable, what, then, constitutes the characteristic of the 'intermediate' [consciousness]?
Therefore, the following concludes the refutation. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... (up to)... would this not be called my 'attachment-free mind'?"
The Buddha’s intention is precisely to reveal that the mind fundamentally has no location; that which is able to be without dwelling or attachment is what is called "mind.
Now, although Ānanda speaks verbally of non-attachment, his heart actually harbors attachment. Therefore, the following passage draws out that underlying sentiment and refutes it.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Your statement that from the awareness of knowing [up to] there is one who does not cling cannot be called 'non-existence.
Because you calculate it as non-attachment, I have cited material objects and images to draw out your underlying sentiment. When I say 'both are non-existent,' 'both' refers to all things;
'non-existent' means non-attachment. As for the question 'is it existent or non-existent?'—this refers to your mind being without attachment."
Furthermore, as for those objective phenomena, do they exist or are they empty and non-existent? If they were empty and non-existent, they would be like the hair of a tortoise;
how could one be attached to them, such that you speak of "non-attachment"? If things exist, then they are entities; how then could there be non-attachment?
Therefore, it is said that they cannot be called non-existent. These [preceding points] all set forth the objections; what follows is the refutation.
If there were no marks, then "non-existence" would itself be a mark; (up to: it is impossible for one to claim that the awakened mind perceives nothing of the sort.
This refutes all forms of non-attachment. If things were truly without marks, they would be like the hair of a tortoise. Yet, things are certainly not non-existent.
This is precisely the existence of characteristics. To know that characteristics exist is for the mind to have a locus. How, then, can this be called non-attachment?
The preceding seven rounds of refutation have pursued and shattered [delusion] so that the mind which clings has no place to escape.
When deluded sentiments perish, the true mind awakens of itself. The primary expedient is attained herein. Thus, those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom are already in accord.
While [the Buddha] had attained latent awakening, Ānanda had not yet awakened; therefore, he requested further instruction in the subsequent passage.

The World-Honored One then again emitted light and manifested auspicious signs, demonstrating the two kinds of fundamental natures. Next, He raised His fist to test his vision and repeatedly interrogated him regarding his mind.
Because Ānanda again identified it as the faculty capable of discernment, the Buddha then rebuked him and instructed him, leading him to a subtle and refined realization.
The passage beginning with "Examining that which is detached from dust has no substance" and so forth, serves to refute the false mind’s lack of substantial reality.
At that time, Ānanda was among the great assembly (until) he leaned forward in thirsting anticipation, reverently awaiting the instruction.
This passage describes the cause for sinking into the houses of lust; it requests instruction on the path of *śamatha*.

This is because those who, having not yet eliminated the outflows (*āsrava*), are driven by perverse defilements and sink into the houses of lust, do so precisely because they do not know the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and have not yet reached that true limit.
As for the "path of *śamatha*," it refers to the initial demonstration of self-nature mentioned previously.
The Śūraṅgama is the path of wondrous adornment. One desires to awaken to this in order to know the path;
since one has not yet awakened, one again seeks instruction on the path of the self-nature Śūraṅgama wondrous adornment. Thus it is called the path of śamatha.
The intent lies in awakening to this to know the path, not in seeking instruction on the practice of cessation (śamatha). Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "Unable to comprehend..."

Regarding one's own mind: how does one know the right path? This indicates that only when the mind is clearly illuminated does one come to know the correct way; the meaning is precisely the same as this.
If the principle is clear and the path is correct, evil views will naturally perish. Therefore, it is said: "To cause all icchantikas to destroy their *mleccha* [barbarian] ways."
At that time, the World-Honored One, from his face (extending to... all remained in their respective lands with palms joined, listening attentively.
Because he was about to reveal the Fundamental Illumination (*mūla-vidyā*), he first manifested auspicious light.

When it is said that "various lights were emitted from the face," this means that the lights from the mouth, eyes, ears, nose, and the space between the eyebrows were all emitted simultaneously, demonstrating that this Fundamental Illumination is present in all the sense faculties (*indriya-dvāra*) without exception.

It manifests; because there is nothing it does not manifest, it shines forth equally and illuminates all at once, like hundreds of thousands of suns throughout the entire Buddha-world, which is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As for the "sixfold earthquake," it symbolizes the shattering of the ignorance of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) that gives rise to and binds one to delusory objects.
That the lands of subtle atoms are simultaneously revealed means that the fundamental luminosity clearly illuminates so that delusory dust does not create separation.
That the worlds of the ten directions merge into a single realm means that the sphere of wisdom manifests perfectly so that the measures of the emotional mind do not obstruct it.

That the Bodhisattvas and the assembly all abide in their original lands means that the measure of the mind is fundamentally the source, and the hearing of the mind is fundamentally lucid. To realize this light...
Śrī (the Auspicious One) immediately awakens to his own nature and thereby knows the path of wondrous adornment.

As for the "sixfold earthquake," it refers to shaking, surging, trembling, rising, roaring, and crashing. To sway unsteadily is called "shaking. To have undulating ridges and depressions is called "surging.
To have a deep, rumbling sound is called "trembling. To rise from below upward is called "rising. To emit a crashing resonance is called "roaring. To strike and pound is [called "crashing"].
"Holding an object is called 'striking.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "All sentient beings... [omitted] ...enter the various realms of existence in vain without realizing it.
This refers to the deluded multitude. It indicates two kinds of fundamental roots, so that they may recognize the false and know the true, thereby attaining the wondrous.
It is the path of adornment. "Karmic seeds" refers to inverted, deluded confusion. The *akṣa* fruit has three seeds on a single branch;

they must necessarily grow together. This is a metaphor for the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—which must necessarily arise together. "The essence of consciousness, fundamentally luminous" points to the true essence, original luminosity.
"Able to give rise to all conditions" means that based upon this fundamental luminosity, the sense organs, the physical body, and the material world arise.

The various conditions, such as the realms and so forth—namely, the primordial clarity that gives rise to the perceived object—once these conditions are established, the original clarity is immediately lost.
Therefore, that which remains after the conditions have ceased is the originally pure essence; it is what is meant by "the nature of illumination, once established, has vanished."
Sentient beings, having lost their fundamental luminosity, remain unaware throughout their daily lives and thus wrongly enter the various realms of existence.
This is because Ānanda did not know where the true limit leads; he requested instruction on the path of *śamatha*. Therefore, the World-Honored One pointed out two kinds of roots.
I desire that you recognize delusion in order to awaken to the *śūraṃgama* of your own nature, and thereby know the path of wondrous adornment.
Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of *śamatha*—up to the point where "that which is capable of investigation I shall take as the mind"—[you must understand this].
Having restated his previous request, [the Buddha] immediately raised his fist to test his perception, thereby rigorously interrogating his mind.

Now, one who wishes to know the path of *śamatha* and transcend birth and death must achieve awakening to the original mind; therefore, he again raised his fist to test his vision and strictly questioned his mind.
Yet Ānanda had not yet eliminated the marks of sensory objects and remained deluded, identifying the false as true; thus, he was still obscured regarding *śamatha*.
He departed by another path and entered the cycle of birth and death.
The Buddha said, "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind" (and so on, until), "This is not my mind; what should it be called?"
This directly refutes the mind that performs the act of deliberation. When the Buddha says "Ho! (*dhik*), he laments the gravity of their delusion; thus he rebukes them with these words.
This is not a lowly expression, but one intended to dispel their deluded attachments. *Jue* (矍) is an expression denoting astonishment and alarm.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is the external object" (up to) "...please bestow your great compassion and reveal [the truth] to those who have not yet awakened.
Because he refuted that the capacity for discernment is not the mind, Ānanda gave rise to fear regarding insentient things and sought instruction.

The phrase "This is" below points out that the aforementioned capacity for discernment is not real and should not be clung to as such. However, Ānanda still [perceives] awareness in relation to objects.
"I understand. It is different from earth or wood; you have taken this [consciousness] to be my mind, and thus I have expressed my alarm and doubt to seek your instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed Ānanda (up to the point where he explained that) the nature of all minds is itself without substance.

Because they are terrified by this, they claim there is no mind; therefore, [the text] cites what is commonly said to lead beings and prove that the original true mind fundamentally exists, so that they may know where to apply themselves.
"Desiring to cause the mind to enter the patience of non-arising dharmas" means desiring that they recognize arising and ceasing in order to awaken to the non-arising and non-ceasing.
Since the three realms are but mind and the myriad dharmas are but consciousness, it is said: "All dharmas are..."

Birth is merely what is manifested by the mind. "All causes and effects" refers to the primary retributions (*pratyātmabhāva*) of the ten realms; "the motes of dust in the world" refers to the secondary retributions (*bhājanaloka*) of the ten realms.
All of these take the mind as the substance of their existence. Within them, even down to blades of grass, leaves, threads, and knots, all possess their own substantial nature.
Even empty space has its name and appearance; how much more so the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence? How could it be said [that this essence does not exist]?
To be without mind is not the same as being like earth or wood. That which is inherently undefiled is called "pure";
that which is defiled yet remains undefiled is called "wondrously pure. As for the nature of all minds being itself without substance:
this refers to the eternally abiding true mind, which can serve as the fundamental nature of all myriad phenomena; how could it itself lack a substance?
If you persist in clinging to the discrimination of vitarka and vicāra (up to the point where it is said), it is still merely a reflected image of the discrimination of dharma-objects.
This is based on the six objects of sense to demonstrate the absence of self-nature. "Discrimination of vitarka and vicāra" refers to the mind that is capable of inference.
If you insist that this is the mind itself, then it ought to possess a nature independent of objects; as you will see below, I shall cite examples to demonstrate its lack of such nature.

This is their nature. For distinguishing auditory objects is movement, while internally maintaining a state of profound stillness is quiescence. Movement belongs to the external sensory objects (*viṣaya*), and quiescence belongs to the mental object (*dharmadhātu*).
If one is separated from these two objects—movement and stillness—there is ultimately no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) whatsoever;
therefore, both are merely matters of conceptualized reflections. To "internally maintain a state of profound stillness" is precisely to dwell with attachment to the realm of quiescence.
I do not command you to hold that which is not the mind as being the mind (up to the point where it asks), "Who then cultivates and realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
This clarifies that phenomena are devoid of substance in order to shatter the mind of arising and ceasing. I do not command you that what you grasp must necessarily be the true mind.
You should first attempt to scrutinize this mind with subtle discernment: does it possess a substantial body apart from sensory objects, or...
Furthermore, apart from objects, it has no substance. If this deluded mind had a substance apart from objects, it might be the true mind;

since it has no substance apart from objects, how could it be anything other than deluded? As for the statement that "the objects of the six realms are like forms and discrimination is like their shadows," it means that the six objects are like forms and discrimination is like shadows. Since a shadow exists because of a form, it has no independent substance; since the mind exists because of objects, how could it...

Does it have an essence? Since you recognize the capacity for inference as being real, yet that capacity has no essence apart from its objects, your Dharma-body would be identical to total annihilation.
How then could you cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly [realized that] although they had attained much learning (*bahuśruta*), they had not achieved the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*).
The preceding section refuted arising and ceasing, desiring them to awaken to the non-arising and non-ceasing. Upon awakening, one attains it spontaneously with a sense of vast clarity;
failing to awaken, one remains silent and lost. Because they did not awaken, they clung to the delusory as real and thus failed to achieve the fruit of sainthood.
I speak thus to inform you, so that you may recognize that the capacity for inference is not ultimate reality, thereby awakening to non-arising.
Indeed, to awaken to non-arising is to awaken to the self-nature of Śūraṅgama and to know the path of wondrous adornment.
Having heard this, Ānanda again shed tears of grief (until: "awaken my wondrous, luminous mind and open my eye of the Way").
Moved by what the Buddha had uttered, he lamented his former failings and requested that the wondrous mind be awakened and the eye of the Way be opened.
This question arises from the aforementioned attachment to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality. It concerns the two obstacles.
"Those" refers to the afflictions regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). "Objects of knowledge" refers to the discriminating mind that takes conditioned phenomena as its object;
it arises and ceases according to its environment, like a guest who comes and goes. "Afflictions" refer to the mind that flows within the nature;
its arising and ceasing never cease, like dust swirling in the air. In sum, these are all the deluded thoughts of birth and death. If one knows this...
If one realizes the nature of the mind as quiescent and eternal, one will not mistakenly take delusive thoughts to be real, and the entanglements of delusion will naturally unravel.
Now, because you do not know the nature of the mind, you are entangled by delusive thoughts; therefore, I request that you give rise to the wondrous mind so that the eye of the Way may be opened.
Thus, the World-Honored One cited the example of a blind man staring into darkness to provide instruction, so that you might know that the faculty of seeing is the mind itself. Understand this!

There is no deficiency, for it is through awakening to the nature of the mind as quiescent and eternal. Yet, although Ānanda and the great assembly heard this instruction, they ultimately did not awaken;
this was truly because their attachment to the deluded identification with body and mind had not yet perished.
Therefore, he first had the five bhikṣus speak of the "guest-dust," desiring that they recognize the mind capable of cognition as being like guest-dust.

Yet one does not recognize the delusive as real. Next, by counting the fingers and flicking the light, one seeks to awaken to the fact that the body and its objects of perception are likewise adventitious dust, so as not to be deluded by the real and instead recognize the delusive.
If one can truly do this, then the delusive attachment to both body and mind will naturally vanish, and the nature of the mind—quiescent and eternal—will naturally be realized.
At that moment, the Tathāgata caused [the light] to spiral from the *svastika* on his chest down to Ānanda and the great assembly.

As for the emission of precious light from the *svastika* on his chest to reveal the wondrous mind and the eye of the Way, it symbolizes that right knowledge and vision are produced from the jewel-bright wondrous mind.
That the Buddha’s chest bears a *svastika* symbolizes the gathering of all auspicious myriad virtues.
That light is brilliantly radiant and intensely magnificent, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors; it signifies that the illumination of the wondrous mind is fully endowed with myriad virtues.
That the light pervades the Buddha-realms demonstrates its pure and fundamental nature. That it universally drenches the crowns of the Buddhas’ heads...
The "manifestation" indicates what is common to the ultimate fruit; "reaching the great assembly" demonstrates that it is shared by all sentient beings.
This is the true light of the wondrous mind and the eye of the Way; it does not increase in sages nor decrease among ordinary people, but merely appears in accordance with their capacities.
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "I now do this for you... [up to] "...attain the pure and luminous mind and obtain the eye of purity.

Because he had previously requested instruction on the wondrous mind and the eye of the Way, he here grants permission to establish the Dharma-banner (*dharmadhvaja*). The banner symbolizes the subduing of the heterodox and the establishment of the orthodox.
Below, by means of the manifestation of seeing, he causes [the disciple] to realize that the nature of seeing is the mind, thereby subduing heterodox and divergent views and attaining the correct.

Knowledge and vision—this is called erecting the great Dharma banner. When heterodox deviations are crushed and knowledge and vision are rectified, the wondrous mind is attained and the pure eye is gained.
Thus, the previous question struck both the mind and the eye; here, both the mind and the eye are revealed.

That which is equally present in sentient beings and Buddhas, yet cannot be measured or known, is called the "wondrous, subtle, and secret. It cannot be defiled by impurities, nor can it be obscured by darkness.
It cannot be obscured; this is called the "pure and luminous nature. When vision is free from the affliction of cataracts, it is vast and clearly illumined; this is called the "pure and clear eye.
Ānanda, your previous answer that you see the light and the fist—up to the point where you said the matter and meaning are similar to the Tathāgata’s fist—is [in error].
The wondrous mind and the eye of the Way are fundamentally without deficiency; it is only because of delusion that one fails to realize this, and thus these metaphors are employed to bring it forth.
When the juice of the Jambu-tree enters the water, the sand and stones turn to gold. *Xi* means a brilliant crimson.
Ānanda compares the faculty of sight to a fist; while the phenomena and their meanings are not analogous, Ānanda, failing to awaken, replied that they were similar.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Your words are similar [to what I have said]... up to 'the objects before one are naturally dark; what loss is there to seeing'?
This precisely reveals that the nature of seeing is without deficiency. To see darkness is itself to see. Thus we know that blindness is not a lack of seeing;
it is simply the absence of eyes and ears."
Ānanda said: "The blind see only darkness before their eyes" (up to) "...thus this nature of seeing is the mind, not the eye.

This is because he did not realize that the nature [of seeing] is without deficiency; therefore, [the Buddha] again cites the contrast between those with clear vision and those in darkness to demonstrate it.
From "If the lamp were the seer" onwards, [the text] restates the preceding point to conclude that seeing does not depend on the eye. [This is] knowing-seeing...
By means of the eye, one directly awakens to the nature of the pure and luminous mind, which is fundamentally without deficiency, and thus attains the pure eye.
Although Ānanda had heard these words, he joined his palms, purified his mind, and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
The preceding section revealed that the nature of seeing is the mind, yet the great assembly had not yet awakened to this; they therefore hoped for further instruction.

However, the reason the audience present at the occasion did not awaken despite hearing the Buddha’s revelation was that their attachment to taking the delusory for the real had not been extinguished.
As long as this persists, how could they realize the quiescent and eternal nature of the mind? Therefore, he commanded the five bhikṣus to speak of the guest.
The "dust" is used for the purpose of opening up and revealing [the truth].
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand like cotton-wool... [omitted] ...asking why he had attained the fruit of sainthood through awakening.
He raised this question regarding the past to inquire about the cause of his awakening, intending thereby to have him explain the "guest-dust" (āgantuka-rajas) in order to reveal it. For this reason:
Regarding the demonstration of "guest-dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*): it is intended to cause one to realize that the moving mind and its conceptualizations are like guests and like dust.
By not being deluded by them, the nature of the mind—quiescent and eternal—can be known, and the holy fruit of *bodhi* can be attained.

If one correlates guest-dust with the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the "guest" refers to the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) and the "dust" refers to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*). The "host," which is emptiness, is the quiescent and eternal nature.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha [up to] “the meaning of ‘dust’ (rajas). The Buddha said, “It is so. This refers to adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*).
He wished for the assembly to hear what was shown: that the mind which conditions coming and going, arising and ceasing, through consciousness is the delusion of adventitious dust;
whereas awakening to the absence of coming and going, arising and ceasing, and realizing the quiescent permanence is the truth of the sovereign emptiness. As for "adventitious" (*āgantuka*):...
The analogy of dust: the "guest" represents the coarseness of the cognizable (*jñeya*), while the "dust" represents the subtlety of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The cognizable refers to the coarse, wandering thoughts that arise from the discrimination of objects; the afflictions refer to the subtle, incessant flow of the mind as it arises and ceases.

To say that the guest stays overnight and eats at an inn is a metaphor for the mind of conditions encountering an object—arising as soon as the causal conjunction occurs—and then consuming [the experience].
The completion of the evening tasks and proceeding onward is a metaphor for the mind of conditions ceasing and dispersing once it has detached from its objects.
The host having no destination of his own is a metaphor for the permanent mind not following the coming and going or the arising and ceasing of objective conditions.

Furthermore, the dust motes flickering and moving without rest are a metaphor for subtle thoughts arising and ceasing incessantly; the empty space, clear and still, is a metaphor for ultimate quiescence.

This metaphor illustrates that true nature is free from thought, profound, still, and immovable. If, through the various causes shown, one recognizes the false with the consciousness and realizes the true, then the sentiment of taking the false for the true will vanish, the entanglements of the two obstacles will be released, and the quiescent and eternal nature of the mind will be awakened.
How could there be any sacred fruition that is not attained?
At that moment, while the Tathāgata was among the great assembly... [who is it that causes this shaking? The Buddha said, "It is so.
Because the assembly did not realize the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal, they falsely identified with the appearances of body and environment.
Desiring to dispel their deluded attachments, the Tathāgata must respond to those present who are ready for the teaching, using dialogue and exhortation to illuminate this Way; therefore—
This bending of the fingers and the flying light are means by which teacher and disciple respond to one another to reveal the truth.
For the body undergoes birth and death, and objects come and go; they are like adventitious dust.

Because people do not understand this and instead grasp at them as real, the Tathāgata used his bent finger to point to objects and the flying light to point to the body, intending to show that these characteristics of movement, opening, and closing are inherently unstable.

This reveals the adventitious dust; it intends for one to contemplate the characteristics shown so that, by recognizing the body and its objects as adventitious and illusory, one may spontaneously dispel clinging attachments.
Quiescence and constancy are fundamentally without arising and ceasing, or coming and going, just like the host who occupies space.
Because they do not realize this, he further inquires about their vision regarding the head and hands, intending to elicit an answer showing that the nature of vision is immovable.

There is no opening or closing, for this reveals that the subject is empty space. This is intended so that, through the words of the response, one may awaken to the fact that the nature of seeing is the true emptiness of the subject.

Indeed, these manifested phenomena of movement, opening, and closing, as well as the words of the response stating there is "no movement and no opening or closing," are expedient expressions employed to reveal that adventitious dust is the guest and the subject is empty space; they are expedient expressions.

This refers to the "intention" (*yi*). Desiring that they recognize delusion and awaken to the truth, he immediately had them contemplate the image to grasp the intention, so that they might know their point of return upon hearing his words.
However, when the occasion arose and the Buddha twice questioned him regarding his vision, he answered according to his own understanding of what he had heard;

this perfectly accorded with the Buddha’s mind, and thus the Buddha confirmed it by saying, "So it is. The meaning of what was realized was first used to confirm that his words accorded with principle.
[The Master] followed [the sequence]. One person present among the assembly attained awakening to the mind upon hearing these words.

Because the rest of the assembly did not awaken, he subsequently rebuked them. Nevertheless, since those present were likewise unawakened at this point, they could not escape being included in the rebuke as well.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly at length (up to the point where it says): "Within this cycle of rebirth, they themselves undergo the process of wandering.
The master and disciple respond to one another to leave behind these words and images, desiring that they recognize delusion and awaken to the truth.

Yet, although the great assembly observes these images and hears these words, they remain confused about the truth and continue to identify with delusion; therefore, he raises awakening to point toward their confusion in order to reprove them. He said:
"Furthermore" (若復) means that it is provisionally explained through the dialogue with sentient beings so as to bring about clear awakening; hence it says "furthermore.

This is because Dignāga, by virtue of his awakening, realized that the conditioned mind is a delusion like adventitious dust and thereby achieved fruition. Thus, it is said: "If there were further sentient beings..."
One contemplates the image of the head moving of its own accord; that which moves is taken as "dust. One contemplates the image of the Buddha’s hand not remaining still;
that which does not remain is taken as a "guest. Thus, one knows that the body undergoes arising and ceasing, like dust motes in a crevice that move without ceasing.
That objects have coming and going is like travelers who pass through without staying. In this way, one awakens to the fact that both body and objects are likewise [impermanent].
Regarding the delusion of adventitious dust, one must not mistake the false for the real. This clarifies the principle of observing the sign (xiàng) to grasp the meaning (yì).
The passage beginning with "You observe" points out the error to reprimand those who, despite observing the sign and hearing the words, have failed to grasp the meaning.

Specifically, it reprimands those who, having observed that Ānanda’s head was moving of its own accord, should have realized that the body is but adventitious dust, and that hearing and seeing have no fixed locus.
When it moves, you should immediately realize that the mind is quiescent. Furthermore, as you observe my hand opening and closing, you should recognize that objects are adventitious.
Since hearing and seeing have no expanding or contracting, you should realize that the nature is eternal.

Why is it that you now do not awaken to this quiescence and eternity, which are without movement or expansion and contraction, yet still regard the body—subject to agitation and birth-and-death—as the self?
The realm of coming and going, which does not abide, is taken as the object; hence it is said, "taking movement as the body" and "taking movement as the object.
This is precisely to reproach the multitude for recognizing false movement while remaining deluded regarding non-movement.

Since the text only reproaches the recognition of the false while implicitly omitting the delusion regarding the True, it simply asks: "Why do you now take movement as your body, etc.? From this point downward...
This means that beginning from the initial delusion of ignorance, one pointed at the fingers and chased after the light; and even until now, one still mistakes the false for the true.
Therefore, it is said that from the beginning until the end, every thought-moment arises and perishes.

Thus, the body and environment that are recognized are the realm of arising and perishing, and the mind that recognizes them is the mind of arising and perishing. Not awakening to the quiescent and eternal is to lose the truth; this is delusion.
To identify with the body and its objects is a perversion. Having already identified with things and lost the truth, one acts perversely;

thus, within saṃsāra, one takes upon oneself the cycle of wandering. If one can directly and thoroughly illuminate that the body, its objects, and the mind all arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature—being like guests or like dust—then the deluded attachment to body and mind will naturally fade away.
Thus, the nature of the mind, quiescent and eternal, is awakened. To transcend birth and death by turning back from this very point—how could this not be a source of joy?

Ānanda and the great assembly— down to all those with outflows— were all desirous of hearing [this teaching].

This passage describes what has been realized and requests instruction on the nature of non-arising and non-extinction. It means that although he had realized that the conditioned mind is not real, he had not yet realized the fundamental mind;
therefore, upon hearing the previous reprimand and instruction—that movement constitutes the body and movement constitutes the environment—he was moved to speak.

Furthermore, as thoughts arise and perish moment by moment, they lose sight of their true nature; thus, they do not know how the body and mind are illusorily subject to arising and perishing, nor how the true nature is without arising or perishing.
Therefore, they all joined their palms, prostrated before the Buddha, and wished to hear [the teaching].
King Bimbisāra deeply understood what Ānanda and the great assembly were harboring in their hearts, and he himself also remained in doubt regarding the nature of non-arising and non-perishing.
Therefore, he cites the doctrines of external schools to clarify the inquiry, hoping that the Buddha would provide an exposition.

Yet, the Tathāgata immediately reveals the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing within the body of arising and ceasing; this serves both to refute the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists nearby—causing them to know that death is followed by rebirth—and to deeply lead Ānanda and others toward the realization of the Truth, which does not depart from illusory arising and ceasing. This, then, is [the teaching] within arising and ceasing.
This is to demonstrate that there is neither arising nor ceasing. Kātyāyana is his clan name; his personal name was Kālodāyin.
This non-Buddhist adhered to the view that all phenomena both exist and do not exist. Sañjayin is the name of Vairaṭīputra, so named after his mother.

This non-Buddhist gave rise to the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Although the external calculations are many, they do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. Both of these...

Because they belong to the class of those with nihilistic views, they all claim that there is total annihilation. This person’s heterodox calculation fails to understand how the seeds of karma produce one another;
he falsely asserts that death itself is nirvana.

The Buddha told the Great King: "From 'Your body exists now' up to 'you must know for certain that this body shall eventually perish,' [the Buddha] intends to manifest that which is unchanging and imperishable by analyzing it in terms of the physical body itself.
He asks about what changes and what does not change because he wishes to reveal the nature of non-arising and non-perishing within this body of birth and death."
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King. As for your present age, how can it be compared to the time of your full vigor?
Desiring that you further examine the phenomenon of transition and decay, I have therefore asked by comparing the young with the old.
Furthermore, the Buddha asked about two periods, yet the answer provided three: namely, infancy, maturity, and senility. 'Infant' (hai) refers to one who has merely formed a skeletal frame."

"Rú" (孺) refers to one who requires others for nourishment. "Fū" (膚) refers to the skin on the surface; "còu" (腠) refers to the texture of the grain and lines [of the flesh]. "Máo" (耄) means being clouded and forgetful.
Although eighty years of age is called "máo," King Bimbisāra was only sixty-two at the time; thus, it is used here as a general term for being clouded and forgetful.
The Buddha said, "Great King, regarding your physical appearance... [omitted] ...therefore you know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.
Previously, he pointed to the countenance and asked about the changes in appearance from youth to old age; now, because the form does not decay instantaneously, he asks about the changes over years.
This is intended to cause him to minutely examine the signs of transience and passing away. Indeed, the intent behind the Buddha's question was to lead him toward the realization of change.
Once the profound scrutiny of the Madhyamaka view of cessation has been extinguished, one may then demonstrate the nature of non-alteration and non-cessation; this will surely be easy to comprehend.
"Cao-lo" (殂落) is synonymous with "transmigration and decline. Although the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) takes "cao-lo" to mean death, that is not the meaning in this present scripture.

Furthermore, the limitation of ten years is a broad estimation for a coarse observation; from the perspective of a refined observation of the immediate moment, [the mind] is truly never-stopping from instant to instant.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Did you see the transformations? [The King replied: "No, World-Honored One.
This was intended to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is without birth or extinction; it first causes one to know that this seeing is free from childhood or old age.
For although the physical countenance undergoes change and transformation, this nature of seeing has never changed. How, then, could birth and extinction occur within it?
Jīva—here translated as the Deity of Longevity—brought his son to visit the Buddha, seeking longevity.
The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled... [and so forth], until the king leaped for joy with a delight such as he had never experienced before.
This is precisely to demonstrate non-extinction within the midst of transformation and extinction. Makkhali Gosāla was a follower of Kātyāyana;
since he maintained that there is neither birth nor death, this is your own true permanence. You should not be deluded by such heterodox theories of annihilationism.
Upon hearing this, the King attained realization that there is no extinction; thus, he leaped for joy to express his shallow awakening, speaking only of "casting off one life to move toward another.
Yet, if one examines its profound meaning in detail, one must know that extinction from the very beginning is non-extinction.
If this is so, it not only refutes King Ajātaśatru’s external views, but also fulfills Ānanda’s double request.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and said: "I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements.
Having heard what was said above, he had mistaken the false for the true; consequently, he harbored doubts regarding the previous reprimand and thus requested the Buddha to provide clarification.

This means that since the vision of the river’s flow is devoid of arising and ceasing, the vision of the Buddha’s hand opening and closing previously observed must likewise be without arising or ceasing.
How, then, can it be said that we have lost our true nature and act in delusion?

However, while the preceding section demonstrated this based on the nature (*dharmatā*), the present section addresses it in terms of the grasping at characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). That which is thus recognized possesses two types of inversion:
taking the unchanging and indestructible nature shown by the Tathāgata to be the perception that discriminates objects is to mistake the true for the false.
To take what is correct as inverted is like recognizing the perception that engages with objects as being neither born nor extinguished;

this is to mistake the false for the true. To take what is inverted as correct is precisely what constitutes a perversion of one's nature. The Tathāgata regards nature as true and appearances as false;
he takes what is correct as correct and what is inverted as inverted. Therefore, he is named the One of Right Universal Knowledge (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm [down to] your bodies, saying: "Your nature is inverted.
Because you take the false for the true, I extend this hand to reveal this inversion. Indeed, the Buddha-body is fundamentally free from either correctness or inversion;
it is because Ānanda and the others possess inverted views that one speaks of "inversion. It is like an arm hanging down naturally, yet [they perceive it] in reverse.
This constitutes an inversion. To turn what is upright into what is inverted is an inversion; to regard it as correct when it is not is like taking the head for the tail and the tail for the head.

Therefore, it is said that "head and tail have been exchanged. Since people of the world universally possess such doubled inversions of view, we know that by comparing and illustrating them through these two bodies, the body of the Tathāgata is taken as correct because it is indeed correct, and is thus named "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha). You—
Such a body is specifically termed "inverted by nature" due to perverted views (*viparyāsa*).
*Mudrā* means "seal," which is one of the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*). "Beholding" refers to seeing.
"Examine your own body and the Buddha’s body with careful attention" (until you no longer know where the inversion of body and mind resides).
This teaches one to carefully observe the locus of inversion. That is to say, when your body is contrasted with the Buddha’s body and called "inverted," from where does this name "inversion" derive?
The intent is to lead one to realize that what is falsely taken as real is but delusion.
This is to mistake awakening for delusion; it is the very locus of perversion. At that time, the assembly did not yet understand and remained in a state of confusion.
The Buddha, arising in compassion and pitying Ānanda, [said]: "The wondrous nature of precious clarity mistakes awakening for delusion."

Because they do not understand where the inversion lies, this passage cites what is commonly said to clarify it. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers collectively to the five sense faculties and the six sense objects.

"Mind" (*citta*) refers collectively to the six consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness. "Various conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to all phenomena that serve as the objects of the faculties and consciousnesses.
"Mental concomitants" (*caitta*) refers to the fifty-one mental factors. "Various objects of perception" refers to all phenomena that are taken as objects.
Extensively citing mountains, rivers, and the great earth; light and darkness, form and emptiness; the nature and characteristics of the real and the false;

and the causes and effects of the heterodox and the orthodox—all lack inherent substance and are manifested solely by the mind. Thus, your current illusory and false body and mind are all objects manifested by the wondrously luminous mind.
To awaken is to recognize the false and know the true; to be deluded is to forget the root and identify with the false. Now that you have identified [with the false]...
To take the false as true is to fail to recognize illusion and delusion while claiming to have awakened to the wondrous essence;
conversely, it is to abandon the fundamental wondrousness and cling to illusion and delusion. This is to mistake the confusion within awakening. This is precisely where the inversion lies.

While the wondrous mind is one, the multiplicity of its designations arises from the differences in how it is applied according to the teachings. This clarifies that objects manifested by the mind are like...

It is like a mirror; therefore, it is called the "wondrously luminous true essence. What is referred to as "originally wondrous" means that it is inherently and naturally wondrous, requiring no cultivation or effort.

"Mind" (*citta*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*) are mutually designated according to their essence and function. Mind arises from the wondrous and manifests luminosity, pervasively and perfectly illuminating and discerning, like the light of a mirror;
hence it is called the "perfectly wondrous and luminous mind. Nature, however, is the wondrousness inherent within that very luminosity.
It is still, profound, and tranquil, like the substance of a mirror; therefore it is called the "wondrous nature of precious clarity.
When obscured and darkened, it becomes empty space within the darkness of emptiness... (up to) ...the Tathāgata says that such persons are to be pitied.

This clarifies the meaning of perversion in order to conclude the eulogy. "Obscuration becomes emptiness" means that because one does not realize the oneness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, one is universally deluded regarding the *dharmadhātu*, thereby forming a state of stubborn emptiness; this is what the sutra below refers to when it says, "from delusive ignorance, there is empty space.
Regarding "within the obscurity of emptiness, darkness coagulates to form matter": this refers to the stubborn emptiness that has been transformed, which, together with the transforming agent...

The union of the two factors of ignorance transforms and gives rise to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which constitute the external forms of the mountain-rivers and the environment of retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).

This is what is meant by "thoughts clarifying and forming the land. Because the four great elements and their material forms mix with the mind of deluded thought, they transform and give rise to the internal forms of sentient beings as the primary retribution (*upapatti-vipāka*).

Therefore it is said: "Material forms mix with deluded thoughts; the characteristics of these thoughts constitute the body. Here, "thought" refers to the deluded mind, and "characteristics" refers to [the objects of] delusion.
Form. When form and the mind conjoin, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are complete; thus, one knows that sentience is precisely the sentient being.
Regarding the phrase "the gathering of conditions stirs within," it means that illusory conditioned energy accumulates therein. Internally, it fluctuates and roils according to thoughts;
externally, it rushes and scatters after objects. Taking this state of turbid agitation as the nature of the mind—this is all merely the true mind [in its deluded state].

The objects appearing therein are both unreal. Since you are deluded by these confused and agitated appearances and take them to be the mind, you are certain that the mind exists within the illusory substance;
thus, you do not know that the empty void and the world are the vast mind manifested from the true mind.
If this is so, how is it different from abandoning the boundless oceans of lands to recognize only one?
To take a floating bubble for the substance of the entire tide and the capacity of the vast ocean—is this not indeed a perversion?

You who are below [in the hierarchy of beings] are said to turn your back on the Truth and pursue delusion, like abandoning the ocean to recognize a bubble; you cling to the delusive as true, like taking a bubble to be the ocean.
Having already abandoned the ocean to recognize a bubble, you were already lost; to further take that bubble to be the ocean is yet another loss.
This is what is called "twice as deluded as others. Since their delusion is such, they are no different from those who mistake the correct for the inverted and the inverted for the correct.
Therefore, the matter of the hanging hand is cited to conclude this exclamation.

Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, up to the point where he said, “You have pulled out the root of my doubts and led me back to the Unsurpassed Way,” followed this wondrous sound and awakened to the fact that his wondrously luminous mind was originally perfect and complete, with nothing lacking.

Yet, regarding the perceiving faculty—the causal mind by which he had obtained this—he still harbored lingering doubt, taking it to be the true self. This has already been refuted previously. He took it to be...

"It is not real. As for the rest, nothing can be apprehended; thus, I still do not dare to recognize it as the fundamental source. Therefore, I pray that the Buddha will proclaim and reveal it to uproot the root of my doubt.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others [still regard]... because there is nothing to be understood, you are also like this."

Because the distinction between the real and the false has not yet been clarified, this passage demonstrates that the true nature is devoid of subject and object. For the true nature is without conditions and is free from the marks of subject and object;
yet, when one uses the mind that acts as a perceiving subject to perceive the Buddha’s Dharma-sound, there is already a duality of subject and object, and thus one does not attain the Dharma-nature.

The phrase "as with a person" and following first clarifies that the object of perception is not the ultimate reality. Here, the person is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata, and the finger serves as a metaphor...

The "voice-teaching" (śabdopadeśa) uses the moon as a metaphor for ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Showing people" is a metaphor for transforming sentient beings. The teaching elucidates the truth, and that truth is the very mind of sentient beings.
Upon hearing the teaching, one should naturally turn to contemplate the mind; only by letting go of the pointing finger can one recognize the moon.
If, however, one regards the pointing finger as the moon, then both the finger and the moon will vanish, and neither light nor darkness can be discerned. "You are also like this" means:
If you identify the dharmas as the mind, you are like those who mistake a pointing finger for the moon. Why?
Because if one identifies the dharmas as the mind, both teaching and principle are lost, and one remains ignorant of the distinction between the true and the false.

If you take this discriminative mind of mine—which speaks of the Dharma—to be the "Dark Principle" (tamas-tattva), such as that held by the Kauśikas and others, it clearly demonstrates that the subject which perceives is not real; it simultaneously demonstrates the unreality of the Dark Principle itself.

This means that the perceiving mind is like a traveler who stops for a while and then departs. If your own mind were truly real, it would have nowhere to go; how then could it be separated from sound and cease to exist?

"Distinct nature" (bīexìng) refers here to the following: it extensively clarifies Ānanda’s underlying intention. "The mind that discriminates sound" refers to the mind that takes sound as its object;
this is precisely the one who awakens to the Buddha’s Dharma-sound. "The mind that discriminates my appearance" refers to the mind that takes form (color) as its object.

This refers precisely to that which is to be venerated. It means that not only is the mind that discriminates sound devoid of intrinsic nature apart from sound, but the mind that discriminates form also lacks intrinsic nature apart from the characteristics of form. Thus, proceeding downward, it further reveals that the *pradhāna* (the Unmanifest) is not real.
This refers to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) of the non-Buddhists; excluding the *pradhāna*, these are neither form nor...
The mind is not empty; all else does not transcend matter, mind, and emptiness. Regarding the realization of truth:

my mind consists of the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the organ of the mind, and the divine self (ātman); all of these are mind. The five sense objects and the five great elements are all matter.

Among the five great elements, space is the greatest; this is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Now, when one analyzes them, they are entirely non-existent; this is precisely not the mind. It is neither form nor emptiness; it is not the realm of form.
Since it is neither form, emptiness, consciousness, nor mind, the nature of mere-consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*) is profoundly obscure.

Yet the heterodox do not understand this and establish it as the "Obscure Ultimate" (*tamas-tattva*). This is because, even if there were no external objects, discrimination would still not be true. Thus, it is not merely due to the presence of sense-objects that discrimination is unreal. Even in their absence...
Discrimination is neither form nor emptiness; this is called the obscure principle (*tattva*), yet it is not the ultimate truth.
Apart from the conditions of all dharmas, there is no nature of non-discrimination; thus, the various objects to which your mind-nature returns—how can they be the master?
This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature each has a place to which it returns" (up to) "...please deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

This question concerns the wondrous mind being "without return. To subsequently point specifically to the "seeing-essence" as that which does not return is to rely upon the non-returning of the seeing-essence in order to manifest the non-returning of the true nature.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Furthermore, you see me... now I shall show you the ground where there is no returning.
As for Ānanda’s question regarding how the wondrously bright, original mind has no place to return, the Buddha answers by means of the essence of seeing (*darśana-vijñāna*).
This is because the true mind is without trace; since it is difficult to awaken to it directly, he relies upon the essence of seeing as a skillful means to provide instruction. This...
Although it belongs to the realm of delusion, it is closely proximate to the truth; like a second moon, the analogy is not far-fetched.
One should know that this vision is also the very vision that previously took objects as its conditions.

However, while the vision that discriminates objects is refuted by stating "it has a place of return," the nature of the seeing-capacity that perceives objects is indicated by stating "it has no place of return. As the subsequent text says: "You now pervade..."
Observe the assembly of sages in this gathering; as your eyes survey them all around, it is merely like reflections in a mirror, without further analysis.
This is the essence of seeing (*darśana-vijñāna*), which is the aspect of the capacity to see that can be returned [to its source]. Furthermore, it is said:
"Your consciousness sequentially identifies and points out within this assembly, 'This is Mañjuśrī,' and so forth. This is the discrimination of objects (*viṣaya-vikalpa*).
"Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east... [until]... when the sky clears and the mists subside, one again perceives its purity.
This was intended to demonstrate the nature that cannot be returned; thus, I first pointed to the characteristics that can be returned. These eight instances merely cite the essentials.
However, regarding these eight conditions, seven of them refer to the objects of discrimination, while only the condition of discrimination itself [refers to the faculty]."

Thus, one gives rise to discrimination regarding the seven objects. This is what was previously called "the vision that discriminates based on sensory objects," which was refuted by the statement, "there is a returning.
Ānanda, you all gaze upon these various changing phenomena... (up to)... for this reason, the Tathāgata is called "one who is to be pitied."
This concludes the praise by demonstrating the nature that cannot be returned, based upon these characteristics that can be returned.

That is to say, the eight factors such as light and darkness each return to their respective eight causes; yet as for the luminous essence of the seeing-nature that perceives these eight kinds, to what place should it return?

The section beginning with "For what reason" interrogates and explains why there is nothing to return. If there were something to return, it would depart along with its objects and no longer possess the capacity [to perceive].
"It is seen. While the objects naturally have distinctions, the nature of seeing has no differentiation; thus, it does not follow the objects in their manifestation.

From "All that can be returned" onwards, this concludes by demonstrating that which cannot be returned is your true nature. From "Then you will know" onwards, this concludes with an exclamation of praise to awaken [the listener].
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has nothing from which it can return, how can I know that it is my true nature?

He asked this because he had mistaken the true nature—which the Tathāgata had shown to be without anything from which it returns—for the mere clarity and precision of the faculty of sight. Thus, he raised this question.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I now ask you... (up to) "...sentient beings see through with a clarity that does not exceed a few inches.

This passage describes how the functions of vision differ; its intent is to reveal that the nature of vision is without distinction. There are five types of visual function: first, śrāvakas; second, arhats;
third, bodhisattvas; fourth, Tathāgatas; and fifth, sentient beings. The intent is to clarify the four classes of noble ones and the six realms of ordinary beings.
Although the modes of perception differ, the nature of seeing is not distinct. *Āmalaka* means "difficult to distinguish";
its fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach, and resembles a crabapple but is not a crabapple. Regarding the statement that it does not exceed the measure of a *fen-cun*:
when separated by paper or film, one cannot see external objects; when separated by skin, one cannot see the internal organs.
"Ānanda, furthermore, when I and you observe the Four Heavenly Kings... [down to] grasses, weeds, humans, and animals—all things are not you.
This is intended to demonstrate that their nature is no different [from yours]. The preceding section pointed to the characteristics of differentiation to lead them toward discernment.

From 'Furthermore' onwards, I first indicate the objective phenomena, and subsequently require discernment to reach the ultimate source of your vision; that is, to exhaust the limits of what you perceive."
It extends upward to the sun and moon, downward to the Circular Mountains (Cakravāḍa), and reaches into the midst of all things; let each be examined and discerned in detail.
Ānanda, these various natures of existing things, near and far, right up to this subtle, wondrous, luminous, and sincere essence, are your own nature of seeing.
This correctly demonstrates that true nature is without distinction. The previous question asked, "How can one know this to be my true nature?
This [passage] shows that while the myriad objects of experience are differentiated, when seen, they are without differentiation. That which is without differentiation is precisely your true nature.

This true nature is "pure" (*jing*) because it encompasses coarse turbidity without being defiled by it; it is "sublime" (*miao*) because it traverses the myriad distinctions without ever changing. It is ultimate.
To look at things both far and near with the same gaze is clarity.
If you see these objects, then you too [should be able to see]—why do you not see the place where I do not see?
By taking these objects as the basis to clarify the nature of seeing, there is a danger that one will mistake the act of seeing for an object; therefore, this is raised in response to clarify it.
This is to clarify. If you recognize seeing as an object, then my seeing is likewise an object, and you should be able to see it.
That which is "identical to seeing" is a trace dependent upon an object; that which is "not seeing" is the essence detached from an object.
If you claim that you and I both see the same single object, this is merely seeing my seeing—it is simply a trace. I, however, am detached from objects and do not see.
At that time, where does its substance reside? Since it cannot be seen anywhere, it is certainly not a material thing. This distinguishes seeing as not being a material thing.
If seeing is non-seeing, it naturally is not that characteristic of non-seeing.
This distinguishes what is seen from what is not seen. If you claim that you can see my "not seeing," then that [seeing] would naturally not be the characteristic of "not seeing.
Furthermore, the characteristic of "not seeing" is fundamentally without characteristics; how could it be something you are able to see?
"If you do not see the ground of non-seeing, it is naturally not a thing; how could it not be you?
This passage clarifies that the nature of seeing is not a material object. The 'ground of non-seeing' is the essence of true nature (*tathatā*).
If one were able to see it, it might be permitted as a thing; since it cannot be seen, it is naturally not a thing. How could it not be you?"
This is the true nature. Therefore, it was said previously that this subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is indeed your seeing-nature.
Furthermore, when you now see objects—[extending] until "and all the worlds would fail to be established."
Furthermore, by examining the confusion between subject and object, it is established that seeing is not a material thing. If seeing were a material thing, then material things would possess seeing;
consequently, the natures of sentient and insentient beings would become intermingled and indistinguishable.

Thus, it is said that no stable order could be established, which clearly demonstrates that seeing is not a material thing. This applies to all worlds, namely, both sentient beings and their environment (*bhājana-loka*).
This refers to sentient and insentient beings.
"Ānanda, when you see, it is you and not I" (up to) "your nature is not true;
you seek reality from me"—this again points to pervasiveness in order to reveal the true nature. For while the former demonstrated that there is no distinction, this points to pervasiveness.

All of these merely reveal the true nature. As for the passage beginning "How could it be...": this means that since you have realized that the faculty of seeing has no source from which it returns, it is your own true nature.
Why then do you doubt that your nature is not true, and seek to verify it with me?
This concludes the answer to the question, "How can I know that this is my true nature?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [omitted] ...I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound this for me.
He followed up with a question regarding the expansion, contraction, and total cessation of the seeing-nature. By "expansion and contraction," he meant that the seeing itself expands and contracts.
"Constricted and severed" means that one perceives the fundamental field of vision as being obstructed and cut off by walls.
This question arises because Ānanda suspects that the essence of his vision expands and contracts according to the breadth or narrowness of what is being viewed.
Since he was observing the first heaven, he saw only a single set of four continents; the term "Sahā" is used here merely as a general designation and does not refer to a great trichiliocosm.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Regarding all worlds... (up to)... 'the nature of their meaning is thus; how could they have expansion or contraction?

This is raised as a metaphor to demonstrate that there is no expanding or contracting in what is seen. 'All worlds' refers to such things as the sense organs, the physical body, and the receptacle world.
'Large and small, internal and external' refers to such things as a single realm or a single room. 'All activities' refers to expansion."

"Contracting, pinching, and cutting"—these collectively indicate that all phenomena belong to the external objects (*viṣaya*). They have no connection whatsoever with my seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*).
Therefore, whether the external objects are large or small, the seeing remains neither expanded nor contracted. To illustrate:

the vessel below represents the external objects, while the empty space represents the essence of seeing. My subsequent statement—that squareness and roundness depend on the vessel and do not reside in the empty space—refers to size.
Since this is due to external objects, what has it to do with the nature of seeing? Therefore, he concludes by asking: "How can it be said to exist?
Ānanda, if you further wish to cause [the mind] to enter into that which is neither square nor round, you must further eliminate the characteristics of space and its location.
This is a further demonstration that emptiness has neither square nor round dimensions; it again reveals that vision has no expansion or contraction.

However, in the preceding section, emptiness was explained in relation to the vessel, which caused the void to appear as if it possessed the characteristics of squareness and roundness. Now, this passage intends to cause the void to enter into a state devoid of squareness and roundness;
by merely removing the vessel, the void itself is then without squareness or roundness, for emptiness is fundamentally without such dimensions.

Therefore, one should merely remove the vessel; one should not remove the space. This serves as an analogy for discerning the seeing by means of objects, which causes the nature of seeing to appear as if it has a form of large or small dimensions.
Furthermore, if one wishes to make the seeing devoid of large or small dimensions, one need only depart from the preceding objects, and the seeing will then be without large or small dimensions.
Since seeing is fundamentally without large or small dimensions, one should merely depart from the objects; one should not remove [the seeing].
I see it thus. Therefore, the ancient masters said that by observing the nature apart from sensory objects, one spontaneously attains one's own original truth.
As for your question regarding the time of entering the room—asking whether there could not be a continuous trace of movement—that interpretation is incorrect.
This is precisely how he addresses and refutes the question. Since it cannot be drawn out, it certainly cannot be contracted;
since it cannot be continued, it certainly cannot be severed. As this is not the case, there is no use for emotional calculations.
"All sentient beings, from beginningless time... [up to] being able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
This passage summarizes the assembly to demonstrate Ānanda’s false conceptualization. "Deluded regarding oneself as an object" means mistaking one's nature for external dust.
"Being turned by objects" refers to the resulting inverted delusion. Being turned by objects is like empty space.

It transforms according to the vessel. Therefore, within this state, one contemplates the great as small; yet ultimately, for the sake of sentient beings, one who can transform objects is like removing the vessel to contemplate the emptiness [within].
Thus, body and mind are perfectly luminous, universally containing all lands, and are identical to the Tathāgata.
What is called the "Tathāgata" is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. Because one can transform objects, all phenomena are identical to suchness.

As for the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*), it refers to the meaning of the arising of manifold phenomena (*dharmas*) which are turned by external objects; this is because one perceives them as being large or small.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, [please] deign to bestow great compassion and reveal that which we have not yet awakened to."
Because he had heard that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, he immediately suspected that this wondrous nature was present before him; thus, he cites it to pose his question.

His underlying thought is that the essence of seeing must be his own wondrous nature, and that this very essence of seeing is now manifest before him, distinct from his body and mind. Since that which is seen is the true nature, what then is the "I" that sees? If...
This means that the body has no nature of seeing, yet its current differentiation is not false.

If one says that what is present before one is seeing, then apart from that external object, there would be no separate mental consciousness to discern my own body. If that external object were truly my own mind, [how could it be otherwise?]
If what you can see now were to constitute external objects as being "me," then since those [objects] are truly "me," you yourself would not be "me.
How does this differ from the previous objection? Since you see objects, the objects must also see you.

However, the intent of this question is that because Ānanda’s realization of the nature [of mind] was not yet perfected, he distinguished between objects and self within that single nature. Thus, the Tathāgata directed him to point it out.

Commentary: Although these words refute his views, they do not concern what lies before him. Their intent is to reveal that the myriad dharmas are of one essence, devoid of the marks of right and wrong, so as to lead him to realize that the nature of perfect luminosity is fundamentally without the distinction between self and other, nor any difference between right and wrong.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Regarding what you have just said... [up to] the Buddha saying, 'So it is, so it is.

Because the nature of seeing was suspected to be located in front, he immediately raised up the myriad phenomena and had him point them out; yet among these objects, there is no such thing as seeing."
Therefore, even a Great Sage cannot, within the objects themselves, cause one to see that which is apart from objects, thereby manifesting the nature of seeing.
"Thus it is, thus it is" is the Tathāgata’s teaching according to reality, whereas Ānanda pointed to objects and claimed there was no such seeing.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda: "As you have said... (up to) the Buddha said: 'So it is, so it is.

Because he was unable to point it out specifically, the Buddha questioned him again using the term 'not seeing. He first replied that he did not know, because the meaning could not yet be definitively established.
[The Buddha then considered: If the tree is not seeing, how can one see the tree? If the tree is itself seeing, then the tree should be named..."
[Mañjuśrī] said, "I see. [The Buddha asked,] "What do you mean by 'seeing'? Therefore, he further reflected that there is nothing that is not seeing.
However, when the Tathāgata seals both the words "is" and "is not," it is because within the realized state, seeing and the conditions for seeing are like flowers in the sky;
therein, fundamentally, there is no meaning of "is" or "is not. Thus, in accordance with reality as it is, he seals both.
In this regard, the great assembly consists of those who are not yet learners (*aśaikṣa*) [up to] you; contemplate this carefully so as not to disgrace my compassionate concern.

Because the assembly does not realize that there is no principle other than what has been stated, I point to the fact that it is not false according to what was said, so that you may contemplate it with earnest devotion.

"To be bewildered" means to be dark and obscured, lacking clarity. This indicates that one has already lost the correct view of phenomena (*dharma*) and further deviates from the vision of principle (*li*).

From beginning to end, it is difficult to clarify; to what can one turn for refuge? Furthermore, one does not realize that both the subject that sees and the object perceived are equally laborious appearances.

Whether "is" or "non-is," whether "thing" or "self," all are but conditioned dusts. Since the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) has not yet opened, the delusions of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are difficult to dispel.

[The opponent] refutes [this], saying: "Because of this, those who are not yet *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training) are simultaneously struck with alarm; their spirits are unsettled and they tremble with fear.

This is what is meant by 'being alarmed and losing one's composure. Regarding 'true speech' (*bhūtavāda*) and so forth: these refer to the two points answered above, which are called 'true words' because they are not deceptive arguments.
The four types of evasive equivocation (*cātuḥ-prakāra-vikṣepa*) of the heterodox *mārga* are seen in the tenth fascicle. 'Tian' (忝) means disgrace."
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, [proceeded] until he reached this point; in the interval between them, there was neither "is" nor "is not.
Because [the assembly] was terrified and lost their composure, Mañjuśrī took pity on the multitude and requested the clarification.

This was because the Buddha’s intention was to reveal that seeing and the conditions for seeing are like flowers in the sky; within them, there is fundamentally no meaning of "is" or "is not. Therefore, by means of...
