Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
These passages concerning the six sense bases each point to a single easily understood delusive phenomenon in order to clarify that the three characteristics are empty and false.
The six objects, such as form, share the characteristic of being objective spheres; the six sense bases, such as the eye, share the characteristic of being the capacity for seeing;

and the toil of the six sense bases is metaphorically likened to the characteristic of karmic activity. Although all three characteristics are false, the primary intent lies in refuting the six sense bases.

"Ānanda, that very act of staring with the eyes until they become fatigued (up to) 'is likewise a sign of fatigue produced by staring at Bodhi' refers to the previous instance of staring into empty space.
Because the faculty of the eye was fatigued, one saw flowers in the void; this previous example referred to the objective realm of form."

This metaphor applies generally to all three phases [of consciousness]. Therefore, it is said that both the "gazing" and the "fatigue" are equally the phase of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.

This is because the phases of karma, transformation, and manifestation all arise from delusion regarding the fundamental nature, just like the fatigue from staring with one's eyes; thus, they give rise to the appearance of empty flowers.
Because of the two kinds of delusive objects—light and darkness—[the visual faculty arises], yet fundamentally it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

Because seeing is triggered by objects and because the sense organ draws in those objects, it is called the "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*). However, since it has no substance apart from its objects, one can know it is empty and false.
Even as far as it is said that [seeing] does not come from light or darkness, nor does it issue from the sense organ, and so forth—if there is nowhere from which it comes, then it is not [real].

The causes and conditions are spontaneous; they are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. According to the preceding scriptural text, this should be divided into three sections:

first, from "That very pupil of the eye" downward, it explains how delusion arises based on the truth; second, from "Because of brightness and darkness" downward, it distinguishes that delusion has no reality;
third, from "Therefore one should know" downward, it realizes that delusion is itself the truth. This is because delusion lacks self-nature, and its entire substance is [the truth].
It is true. The remaining five cases are analogous to this.
Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who uses two fingers... [up to] ...it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

In these passages concerning the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the phrase "staring until weariness arises" uses the metaphor of flowers in the sky not merely as a singular metaphor for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), but as a general metaphor for all six faculties;
therefore, it is applied by analogy to all of them as "staring until weariness arises."
Ānanda, it is like a person who suddenly pinches his nose [until he smells a scent]. "Pinching" (*xi*) refers to the contraction of the breath.
"Trigger" (*ji*) refers to the barb of a crossbow. Since the faculty (*gen*) possesses the sense of "triggering" the act of hearing, this analogy is employed.
Ānanda, it is like a person who uses the tongue to lick the lips. (Up to: "It is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
To take up an object with the tongue is called "licking. The "lips" (*khan*) refer to the corners of the mouth.

Ānanda, it is like a person who has one hand that is cold [and another that is hot]. (Omitting intermediate text) Fundamentally, this is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The hand does not touch itself; rather, because of their coming together, one perceives the touch. Therefore, it is called "the touch perceived through conjunction. Conjunction does not conjoin itself; rather, because of their separation, one knows the conjunction.
Therefore, it is said to be manifested through the knowledge of separation. As for the phrase "if the momentum were established," etc., this refers to the mutual interaction of cold and heat.

Śāriputra, these two characteristics mutually establish one another. Because of contact, they have long since formed a state of fatigue; it is from this that these false appearances arise. Therefore, it is said: "Due to the contact of fatigue.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep... (up to) "...these are all equally the appearance of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi."

When the mind does not engage with objects, there is fundamentally no distinction between waking and sleeping. When the mind dwells upon objects for a long time, the consciousness becomes weary and the body exhausted;

only then does sleep occur. After sleeping for a long time, the exhaustion is relieved, and one immediately awakens. Therefore it is said: "When weary from toil, one sleeps; when sleep has matured, one awakens."

When one perceives sensory objects (*viṣaya*), there is recollection; this is called the time of awakening. When one contemplates sensory objects, perception and recollection arise immediately. The loss of such recollection is "forgetting";

this is called the time of昏寐 (deep sleep or stupor), when there is no object of contemplation and what was lost is extinguished. Yet, within the midst of abiding and change, it exists through delusion and falsehood;

therefore, it is called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*). "Inhalation" (*xi*) means to take up; "habituation" (*xi*) means to contemplate objects. "Returning to the center" refers to the mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).

They do not exceed one another; these are the four phases. This refers to the absorption of the four phases of the objective dharmas (dharma-āyatana) by the faculty of cognition (manas-indriya), which accords with the will.
Just as the internal objects are inhaled and grasped below, their arising and ceasing are termed the nature of awakening-cognition. Delusion does not depart from the True;
therefore, the mental toil during both waking and sleeping is likewise the appearance of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.
Regarding the two kinds of delusive objects, arising and ceasing (up to the point where it is said they are neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous):
previously four characteristics were cited, but here only two are mentioned. This is because "abiding" is subsumed under "arising," and "change" is included within "ceasing.

With the faculty of cognition situated between them, that which grasps and extracts this arising and ceasing of mental objects (*dharmas*) is called the nature of awareness. The "internal object" refers to the *dharma*-object (*dharmāyatana*).

Regarding "seeing and hearing flow against the current," the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: When the eyes and other faculties grasp external objects, they flow instantaneously into the mental ground (*manas*).
To enter from the outside into the inside is called "flowing against the current. This refers to the mind having an object of perception;

that is, when awake, one perceives objects, and this recollection arises. As for "the flow not reaching the ground," this refers to the time of deep sleep, when the sense organs do not perceive [objects].
As for "dust" (rajas): there are no external dusts flowing into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), and the mind itself has no object of perception.

This is what is meant by "sleeping"—losing memory and forgetting—which constitutes cessation. Awakening and knowing consists in surveying these two types of dust, waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing, as its essence.
Therefore, apart from those two kinds of objects, there is ultimately no substance [to the consciousness]. Regarding the two phases of waking and sleeping as the opening and closing of the body:
the *Liezi* says, "When one awakens, the form opens; when one sleeps, the form joins. "Joins" means "closes.

This implies that when [the senses] open, they perceive objects and thus recollection arises; when they close, they do not engage with mental objects (*dharmas*), and it is called cessation. As for your nature of awareness and cognition:
Apart from these states of waking and sleeping, arising and ceasing, they ultimately have no substance; therefore, they are like flowers in the sky.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
In the first six bases (*āyatana*), although they are analyzed by means of the objects (*viṣaya*) in relation to the faculties (*indriya*), the primary intent lies in the faculties themselves.

Now, in the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), although the faculties and objects are mutually analyzed, the primary analysis concerns the objects. Finally, in the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), although the three—faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—are mutually examined and analyzed, the primary intent lies solely in the six consciousnesses.
Ānanda, you should observe this Jeta Grove... [up to] it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
If the eye could produce form, then the eye would be the nature of form; yet when one sees space, it is no longer the characteristic of form, and thus the nature of form should dissolve.
Since the nature of form that can produce [perception] has dissolved, this dissolution is manifested from the very root.

All marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are entirely non-existent. Furthermore, the two dharmas of form and emptiness manifest in mutual dependence. Since the marks of form are absent, by what means could emptiness be manifested?
Therefore it is said: "Who clarifies the substance of emptiness? Thus, to calculate that the eye arises from the locus of form is an error.
That emptiness is likewise so means that, by analogy with form, emptiness also has no fixed location. If, moreover, there were the dust of form...
"Below" means that if one holds that form can produce seeing, then at the time of contemplating emptiness, seeing has nothing from which it is produced; hence it is said to "dissolve and perish.
When it perishes, both the object of form and seeing are entirely non-existent. Who then would perceive emptiness and form? Thus, the calculation that form produces the locus of the eye is an error.

Therefore, the section "Below" concludes by clarifying that [these phenomena] are false and illusory, so that they may be reconciled and returned to the nature of the treasury (the *tathāgatagarbha*).
Ānanda, listen further to this: within this Jeta Grove (up to the point that it) is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.

Just as when I enter the city, the Jeta Grove is devoid of a self; likewise, when sound comes to the side of the ear, there is no sound in other places, yet a thousand people all hear it—thus, the locus of sound has no reality. "If again, your ear... and so forth, meaning it is like my returning.

In the forest city there is no self. This is analogous to the ear going to the location of sound; if the ear were to go to that place, it would not exist elsewhere, yet sounds from various different locations are all heard.
Thus, the locus of the ear is not real. If there is no coming or going—meaning that sound does not come to the ear and the ear does not go to the sound—the meaning of "hearing" cannot be established.
Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... [it is] fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The nose is not the sandalwood; it does not arise from the sandalwood itself. It exists by depending on heat; it does not arise from space.

If it were produced from the wood, it would have to arise from breaking the wood. This refutation is based on the coarse and manifest characteristics of the smoke, rather than its subtle fragrance. If...
This is indicated by means of smoke. In reality, it has not yet reached [the distant place]; thus it is said that "the smoke rises into the air but has not yet traveled far.
Furthermore, while the smoke is still nearby, the fragrance is already perceived at a great distance; therefore, one knows that the fragrance does not emanate from the wood.
Since it is neither in the nose, nor in space, nor in the wood, the locus of the fragrance has no reality.
Ānanda, you always hold the almsbowl among the assembly during the two times [of meal]. (Up to: It is neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Flavor arises beneath the tongue; it is produced by breaking the faculty. This means that flavor is said to arise because of the tongue.

Since the tongue and its base are of one substance, they should not distinguish many flavors. If they do not distinguish many flavors, then it cannot be called "knowing flavor. If they do distinguish many flavors, then...
Taste does not arise from the tongue. "Stone honey" (śarkarā) refers to granulated sugar; because it is as hard as sand or stone, it is called "stone honey.

If taste were produced within the food itself—meaning that the food does not know for itself, but rather knows the flavor by means of the tongue—even if the food could know it, then that knowledge would not reside in you.
It would be the same as someone else's food; you would have no involvement in it, for taste is not something known by you. Since this principle is not so...
If that were so, then taste would not arise from food. If it were to arise from below in space—given that empty space is devoid of taste—then taste would not arise from space either.
Ānanda, when you regularly rub your head with your hand at dawn [up to the point where it is said]: "This is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
Because contact arises from the mutual resonance between the agent and the object, whether it is located in the hand or the head, in neither case is there a true contact.

If each possessed its own separate contact, there would have to be two bodies. If they were produced by a single contact, they would constitute a single entity. Thus, contact cannot be established as a reality.
This means that contact requires two things; if there is only one, it cannot be established. It is neither the object nor the agent, and so forth.
That is to say, being in a single location, contact cannot be established. Therefore, it is said that empty space cannot enter into contact with you.
"Ānanda, regarding what you have always considered as objects of the mind—whether good or evil (up to: that which is not an object of the mind—how could these constitute a 'base' (*āyatana*)?

The principle of their arising and formation is precisely the *dharmaviṣaya* (mental objects). This means that the objects of the mind’s perception do not go beyond the mental objects produced by the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
Below this [passage], he poses two simultaneous inquiries. Below the words 'Ānanda,' he first explains that there are no mental objects apart from the mind itself."

If phenomena were identical to the mind, they would not belong to the sensory objects; since they would not be objects of cognition (*ālambana*), how could they constitute the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
If they exist apart from the mind as having a distinct location, they would—by their very nature—not be produced by causes and conditions, nor would they be of spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*).

This clarifies that there are no objective phenomena (dharmas) apart from the mind. That is to say, if objective phenomena existed separately from the mind, would the intrinsic nature of those phenomena be conscious or unconscious?
If it were conscious, it would belong to the mind; yet its substance would be distinct from yours, and furthermore, it would not be an object (dharma).
Thus, it would be equivalent to another's mental representation (*cittamātra*). The statement "it is you, it is the mind" is intended to prevent such a counter-argument. Why is this so?
The following is a refutation: Your mind is singular; how can there be two? Since both the sense organs and their objects are cognized, these must be two minds.
Even if it were not cognition, since this dharma-object is not form (*rūpa*) or the like, where would its locus be?
It cannot be manifested within form or emptiness (*śūnyatā*), nor should it exist outside of form and emptiness; moreover, emptiness itself is not a thing that exists.
It is external. Since the object-field of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*) does not exist, the mind has nothing upon which to depend; from what, then, could its locus be established?
Thus, the mind’s dependence on the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) ultimately lacks any reality.
Furthermore, Ānanda, why are the eighteen *dhātus* fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of *tathatā*?

The three—sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—each consist of six; when divided into internal, external, and intermediate, they constitute the *dhātus*. Moreover, "realm" (*dhātu*) means cause and lineage.
This is because the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—mutually serve as causes for one another, yet each category remains distinct.

"Ānanda, as you have understood it—that the eye and forms serve as conditions (up to) being born from form and having form as their realm—this 'as you have understood it' refers to what was explained in the first fascicle.
Furthermore, the dharmas produced by causes and conditions as interpreted by the Hīnayāna are all considered substantially existent;
they do not realize that these are empty. Now, I am questioning him based on that [Hīnayāna view] in order to break his attachment."
All other cases are to be understood in this same way.
Ānanda, if [consciousness] were produced solely because of the eye, then since there would be neither form nor emptiness (up to:

it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature), if there were only the eye and no forms or emptiness, then consciousness would have nothing upon which to depend, vision would have nothing to manifest, and the realms would not exist.
What is established here does not arise from the eye. If it arose because of form (*rūpa*), it should perish along with the form.

When the form perishes and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) appears, one would not know that emptiness. Since one does indeed cognize emptiness, it does not perish along with the form; this demonstrates that it does not arise from form.
If form undergoes change, you likewise cognize the shifting and transforming characteristics of that form. Your cognition does not shift; since the form has changed, then...
From what basis is this non-transmigrating consciousness established? If it were to arise from the transformation of form (*rūpa*), then consciousness would itself undergo transformation;

thus, the characteristics of the realms (*dhātu*) would inherently be non-existent. If it does not transform, it must be permanent. Furthermore, since it arises from form, when emptiness manifests and form perishes, consciousness should likewise perish and consequently fail to cognize emptiness.
This reasoning is also untenable; therefore, it does not arise from form. If [it were to arise] from the conjunction of both eye and form...
The co-arising consciousness-element would be half-conscious and half-unconscious; therefore, it is called "separated in the middle.

If it were separated in the middle, it would be half-conjoined with the sense faculty and half-conjoined with the object; therefore, it is called "conjoined in two places. If such dual conjunction were established, there would be the fault of confusion;
thus, the consciousness-element is not established.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have understood—that the ear and sound serve as conditions (up to the point where ear-consciousness arises)—from what, then, is the element of ear-consciousness established?

If it were produced because of the ear, this refutes [the claim] from the perspective of the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense-faculty). This means that when the sense-faculty is not in contact with its object, the faculty itself lacks cognition.
If, in reality, there is no cognition, the faculty itself cannot even be established; how much less could consciousness exist? If [you argue] that it is "taking the ear" as hearing, this...

This refutes [the existence of] the coarse sensory organ (*audārika-indriya*). Even if one were to assume that the coarse ear-organ has the capacity to hear, if there is neither movement nor stillness, hearing cannot be established.
The passage beginning with "How could... clarifies that an insentient organ cannot give rise to a sentient consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
Then, regarding the passage beginning with "As for the ear": since consciousness does not arise from the organ, from what else could it be established?

If auditory consciousness arises because of sound—and [this applies] up to the point that [the object] is fundamentally neither a causal condition nor a spontaneous nature—then since sound can produce consciousness, why depend on hearing? If there were no hearing, sound would not exist either.

Even if one claims that consciousness arises from sound, yet admits it exists by depending on the sense organ (the ear), then at the time of hearing sound, one would be hearing consciousness itself. If this were not so...
If one hears consciousness, then there would be no realm of consciousness. If one hears consciousness, then consciousness is identical to sound.
Since that which can discern consciousness makes it the object heard, who is the subject that knows?

If there is no knower who knows this hearing-consciousness, one would ultimately be like grass or wood, and there would likewise be no consciousness. It should not be said that [consciousness] depends on sound and hearing.
Since it is not the case that the sense-faculties and their objects are discussed individually, it is illogical for the two combined to constitute the element of consciousness as a middle position.
If the middle position does not exist, how can the boundary positions be established?
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the nose and fragrance acting as conditions: [this extends] until "the nose itself has no name; how then can a realm be established?
If one takes the physical form of the flesh to be the lower level, it destroys the notion of the *bu-chen-gen* (the superficial sensory organ). To call it "body" is not the nose;
to call it "touch" belongs to the object-field (*viṣaya*) corresponding to the body-organ. Therefore, it is said that "the nose itself has no name."
If you claim that it is known through smelling, then within your mind—[up to] "the two natures do not exist"—from what could the realms be established?
This refutes the ultimate sense-faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*). Since the physical form and the two claws constitute the cognition, it belongs to the body;

therefore, it is said that the primary contact is not of the nose. Since space constitutes the cognition, it belongs to space; therefore, it is said that the flesh should not be the faculty of awareness. Since fragrance constitutes the cognition, it belongs to [the fragrance].
Fragrance—what concern is it to your nose? Hence it is said: "What business is it of yours? If [the opponent claims] fragrance arises below [the nose], this is cited to refute their calculation.

The primary refutation is that fragrance and stench do not arise from the sense organ (*indriya*). From the phrase "not coming from two things," the sense organ is refuted by means of its object (*viṣaya*);
thus, one falls into the error of having two noses. If the object is refuted by means of the sense organ, then no object can be obtained. Why? Because of these two...
Since their nature does not exist, the natures of fragrance and stench cannot be apprehended. From what, then, could the realm of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) be established?
This means that although the words refute the idea that fragrance and stench arise from the sense organs, the underlying intent is to show that fragrance and stench mutually cancel one another out;
being both absent, they cannot produce consciousness. Thus, we know that if fragrance and stench do not exist, consciousness cannot arise.
If consciousness arises because of fragrance and exists because of fragrance (and so on), it would fundamentally neither be caused by conditions nor possess a spontaneous nature.
Since the seeing-nature exists because of the eye, yet cannot see the eye itself; and since nose-consciousness exists because of fragrance, it should not know the fragrance.
If it is said that it can know it, then it does not arise from the fragrance. If it is said that it does not know it, then it cannot be called "consciousness. In all cases, this is not so.
That may be so. Furthermore, if fragrance were not perceived through cognition, the fragrance-element would not be established.
If consciousness did not perceive fragrance, then the consciousness-element could not be posited on account of fragrance. This calculation that consciousness arises because of fragrance is an error.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the tongue and flavor serving as conditions—up to the point where flavor does not arise of itself—how can you establish the [taste] element?

Take sugarcane and so forth; these refer to the five tastes. If consciousness were produced because of the tongue, then when all worldly things are devoid of taste, one ought to taste the tongue itself.
Why? Because it is said that consciousness is manifested through the act of discernment; yet now, since worldly flavors...
No. One must necessarily taste with the tongue; therefore, I teach you to taste your own tongue to see whether it is sweet or bitter.
If the root of the tongue were inherently bitter, there would be no one able to taste it. Furthermore, since the tongue does not taste itself, who could perceive this bitter tongue?
If the base of the tongue were devoid of flavor, then taste would have no basis for arising. Without taste and its corresponding object, from what could the sensory realm be established?
This calculation that consciousness arises because of the tongue is erroneous.

If consciousness were to arise from flavor and itself constitute flavor—up to the point that it is neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature—and if consciousness itself constitutes flavor, meaning that consciousness is identical to flavor, then it would be the same as the tongue faculty. That is to say, flavor does not taste itself.
Since it does not taste itself, how can it know flavor? If it does not know flavor, then there is no consciousness. Furthermore, consciousness...
"Because consciousness arises from taste: if tastes were many, consciousness should also be many; if consciousness has but one taste, it should also be one.

This establishes that the substance of consciousness necessarily arises from taste. "If salty, bland, sweet, and pungent were all the same single taste," this concludes that since consciousness has but one taste, it should also be one.
Since diverse tastes have become identical, there is no differentiation. If there is no distinction, it is not [consciousness].

Consciousness. If there were no consciousness, there would be no realm. This calculation that consciousness arises from the flavor is false. [The phrase] "it should not be said" clarifies that it does not arise from space.
[The phrase] "the tongue and flavor combine" means that if consciousness were to arise from the combination of the faculty and the object, then it would fundamentally lack self-nature;
how then could consciousness arise? Saline, bland, sweet, and pungent—these four flavors are briefly cited for detailed explanation.

There are six [types]. Adding bitter and sour [to the four mentioned previously] completes them. "Harmonized" (saṃskṛta) means that various flavors are combined to form a single whole. "Innate" (sahaja) refers to that which is naturally so and whose fundamental nature is not altered.
"Transformed" (vikṛta) refers to that which has changed from its original state through processes such as burning or boiling.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that the body and touch serve as conditions (up to the point where you ask):

"Who is there who knows union and separation apart from the body?"—discernment and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*) are themselves bodily consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), which takes the two objects of union and separation as its conditions. If there were no conditions, then there would be no consciousness.
To reckon that [feeling] arises from the sense-faculties is false. If it arises because of contact, then if there were no body, one would not know union or separation.
Who, possessing no body, could know union and separation? Thus, where there is no body, there is no contact. To reckon that it arises from contact is likewise false.
Ānanda, objects do not know their own contact; it is the body that knows there is contact (up to: "it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature").
That "objects do not know their own contact, but the body knows there is contact" means that the object does not know its own contact of itself;

it is only through the body that one knows there is contact. That "knowing the body is itself knowing contact, and knowing contact is itself the body" means that the body does not know itself; it is itself contact.
Only then does one know that contact does not know itself; it is the body that knows. Thus, body and contact are mutually identical.

When they are mutually identical, they cancel each other out and both vanish. Therefore, there is no location. When contact joins with the body, it becomes the very self-nature of the body; therefore, there is no state of contact.
When contact separates from the body, it is identical to the characteristics of empty space and so forth; therefore, there is no function of contact. This, then, is the internal...
If it is not established externally, how can it be established internally? This calculation that the element of consciousness arises from the contact between the body and the object is false.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand as the mind taking dharmas as its condition—up to the point where, in the absence of conditions, there is no form—what use would consciousness have?

This is a refutation based on the fact that [the sense organs] have no substance apart from their objects. For the mental faculty (*manas*) arises from what is thought and is produced in relation to mental objects (*dharmas*).
If separated from mental objects, the faculty would have no form and consciousness would have no function; thus, to calculate that the faculty arises [independently] is an error.
Furthermore, as for your consciousness-mind and its various faculties of deliberation (up to the point where) these two natures are not established, how can a realm be posited?

This is a refutation based on the non-arising of identity and difference. "Consciousness-mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "Deliberation and discernment" refers to the mind-faculty (*manas*).

If they were identical, there would be nothing further to be produced; if they were different, there should be no object of cognition. If there is indeed no object of cognition, how [can a realm be established]?

This arises from the mind-faculty (*manas*). If there is anything at all that is cognized, how could cognition be different from the mind? Since the two are not different, there is no cognition either.
As stated below, both together fail to constitute the element of cognition (*vijñānadhātu*).
If the various phenomena of the world arise from the *dharmas*, then since their characteristics do not exist within the [six] elements (*dhātu*), how could they be produced?

By assigning each of the five sense objects to its corresponding five sense organs, none of them are subsumed under the mind (*manas*). [The phrase] "your consciousness" below instructs you to investigate the characteristics of the *dharma-āyatana* (the sphere of mental objects).
As for "phenomena and phenomena," this refers to the phenomena of the *dharma-āyatana*: form and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction. That is to say—
Form, sound, and fragrance are the three objects [of the senses]. Union and separation are the two objects of taste and touch. Arising and ceasing are the object of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
However, arising and ceasing are merely the common characteristics of the five objects; they have no essence apart from the five. Therefore, it is said: "When there is arising, all dharmas arise."
When [the object] ceases, all dharmas cease. That which serves as the cause is the dharma-object (dharmāyatana).
Since the dharma that serves as the cause has no inherent reality, what form could the consciousness produced by it possibly have? If there is no form, then the realm (dhātu) also perishes.
Therefore, you should know that mind and dharmas serve as conditions (up to: they are fundamentally neither causal conditions nor spontaneous natures).
Since they are neither causal conditions nor spontaneous, this is called the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Previously, based on the four categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), sense-fields (*dhātu*), and elements (*dhātu*), it was clarified that [all phenomena] are fundamentally neither causal conditions nor spontaneous; yet Ānanda had not yet realized this. Therefore, what follows again uses—
The inquiry was made regarding the causes and conditions of the combination of the four great elements.
The Tathāgata, in turn, addressed the seven factors—the earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, and seeing—to clarify that they are fundamentally neither combined nor non-combined.

He integrated all phenomena so that they return to the Tathāgata-garbha, causing both the view of birth and attachment to dharmas to vanish instantly, such that the true mark of non-birth is fully revealed.
This refers to the manifestation prior to [the arising of] phenomena. It is called "Great" because its nature is perfectly round, pervasive, and encompasses the ten directions.
As for why there are seven: the generation and completion of the myriad dharmas do not depart from the four great elements;

they are established upon space, arise through the faculty of sight, and possess cognition through consciousness. Thus, the first five are possessed by insentient things, while the latter two belong to sentient beings.
To combine these: if one now enumerates seven of them, then the myriad dharmas are encompassed. Yet that Great Nature was originally neither water nor fire, nor was it emptiness or consciousness;
it is entirely the substance of the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting in accordance with karma. As it is with these seven great elements, so it is with all dharmas:

all that we rely upon and our own bodies were originally neither the sense organs and physical body, nor the vessel-world (the environment); they are all, in their very suchness, [the Tathāgatagarbha].
The characteristics of karma follow its course; yet the nature is truly perfect and harmonious, fundamentally devoid of arising or ceasing.

Thus, when Ānanda received the Buddha’s instruction, his body and mind became vast and open, attaining freedom from all hindrances. He clearly understood that all things in the world are the wondrous mind itself, encompassing the ten directions.
Looking back upon his illusory body, he realized it has no source for its arising or ceasing, and he knew with perfect clarity that he had attained [this realization].
"The fundamental wondrous mind is eternally abiding and never extinguished.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [up to] the Middle Way of definitive meaning, free from frivolous discourse.
This passage cites the Tathāgata’s constant teaching on the harmony of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), thereby refuting both the doctrines of causality and spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
"Rejecting. Regarding the request for an exposition of the definitive meaning of the Middle Way:

the intention is that what was previously taught—that causes and conditions are existent—and what is now being rejected—emptiness—are both not the Middle Way, but rather merely dharmas of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, he again seeks an exposition of the dharma that is free from conceptual proliferation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda... (until) Ānanda silently accepted the Buddha’s holy command.

Because he had previously requested [the teaching on] the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, the Buddha granted his permission to reveal it, so as to enable him to penetrate the true nature (*dharmatā*).
"You were previously weary and detached... refers below to the passage in the first fascicle beginning with "I have been devoted solely to much hearing since beginningless time. Therefore, I...
"Below" refers to seeking the path of enlightenment; therefore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is revealed.
Having heard this Dharma, it is called "the true medicine appearing before one," whereby one penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*) and attains the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Ānanda, as you have said, from "the combination of the four great elements" up to "like a whirling firebrand, it never rests," you have raised a doubt regarding the combination of the four great elements.
This first examines whether the nature of the great elements is combined or not combined.
If that nature of the great elements were indeed not combined, then it would be like empty space, which does not combine with various forms; yet this is hardly the case. If, indeed...
If they were to combine, they would be identical to those myriad transformations, forming and succeeding one another in a continuous cycle of mutual delusion; yet this is not so.
A whirling firebrand has no substantial reality; it serves as a metaphor for the appearance of mutually formed and continuous delusive phenomena.
Ānanda, it is like water becoming ice, and ice returning to become water again.

This directly demonstrates the principle that the Great Nature is neither harmonious nor disharmonious, thereby initiating the subsequent text; for this reason, he calls out and addresses him once more.
It is like water forming ice; this is not due to a lack of harmony. When the ice returns to water, it is not due to a process of combination.
Observe the nature of earth: from its gross form as the great earth (down to its subtlest aspects), even matter can be analyzed away. How, then, could emptiness be combined with anything?
This causes one to observe that form (*rūpa*) is analyzable, whereas emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not composite; thereby it is revealed that the nature of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is not a composite.
The subtlest part of a particle is called a minute atom (*aṇu*); subtler than that is the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*); and subtler still is the *anu-śūkṣma*, or "near-void" (*paramāṇu*).
An atom (*paramāṇu*) still possesses subtle form; therefore, it is called the "limit of form" (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*).

When an atom is divided into seven parts, its subtle form is almost non-existent; therefore, it is called the "near-atom" (*anu*). If one further divides the near-atom, it becomes emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Since the analysis of form can result in emptiness, emptiness should likewise give rise to the characteristics of form. However, when form is now recombined, it cannot become empty again. Re-...

Furthermore, emptiness cannot produce form; from what, then, would form arise? Therefore, one knows that this form has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the beginning and is not a product of combination.
You fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha—[as it is said]—there is nothing but verbal expression and a total absence of real meaning.
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is such that the myriad dharmas are one and the same; yet, as they unfold in accordance with conditions, they appear to differ.

Consequently, there are the names of the "Seven Greats," which are merely designations for differences in their characteristics and natures. Because characteristics are identical to the absence of characteristics, it is said that "the nature of form is true emptiness.

Because the absence of characteristics is identical to characteristics, it is said that "the nature of emptiness is true form. This state where there are no characteristics and yet no non-characteristics is called "purity"; it is neither harmony nor disharmony.
It is said that it is "fundamentally so" (*bennian*). That it is nowhere absent is called "pervasive" (*zoubian*).

Since it is neither identical with nor distinct from phenomena, neither joined with nor separate from them, yet is able to give rise to the seven great elements and all dharmas, it is simply a matter of responding to the mind according to its capacity and manifesting in accordance with karma.
As stated later: "If you clarify through emptiness, then emptiness appears; earth, water, fire, and wind each manifest their own clarity."

Thus, each manifests individually; this is the matter of responding to the mind according to its measure. Turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses gives rise to worldly toil (*rajas*);
extinguishing the dust and uniting with awakening gives rise to True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is the matter of manifestation according to karma.

As for the characteristics of the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—and the subtle principles of their myriad forms, there is nothing that does not manifest in accordance with response and following conditions.

Furthermore, the characteristics of this contemplation are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described. The nature of this contemplation is fundamentally real, consisting solely of wondrous, enlightened clarity;
its principle transcends emotional conceptualization and does not admit of arbitrary conjecture. Therefore, while there are words to express it, they possess no substantial meaning.

Thus, regarding the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), any mental formulation immediately deviates from it, and any stirring of thought immediately contradicts it. Only by abiding at all times without giving rise to [such thoughts] can one remain within it.
Regarding deluded thoughts: do not employ the conscious mind to discriminate or calculate; only then will you be in accord. The same applies to all other phenomena.
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self and is merely dependent upon various conditions (up to: there are only words and explanations, but no real meaning).
Fire has no self-substance; it takes form by depending on other things, and is therefore said to be "without self.
When various names are combined, if one examines them, each has its own root; this is true combination. When the name "fire" is combined [with other names], if one examines them, each lacks a root;
thus, it is not a true combination. Upāli-vilva means "Pumpkin Grove"; Kāśyapa means "Turtle Clan"; Gautama means "Star."
As for the name: his clan was established based on the stars, and in later generations, it was changed to Śākya. Regarding the *yángsuì* (sun-crystal):
Cui Bao’s *Gǔjīnzhù* states that it is made of copper and shaped like a mirror; when reflecting an object, its image appears inverted, and when facing the sun, fire emerges.
*Yū* means "to bend" or "to curve."

Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy. (Up to: Within the void, it exists spontaneously, coming from the moon. When sought, it flows; otherwise, it ceases.
This is what is meant by "flowing and ceasing without constancy. Kāpiḷa and the others—these four are all non-Buddhists skilled in illusory arts.
"The essence of the Great Yin" refers to the water within the moon. Before the full moon, it is called "white. It remains still...
Midday is called "day. Fangzhu refers to the water-gathering pearl.
Ānanda, if [the moon] came from the moon, it would still be able to travel such a great distance; yet all there is is mere verbal expression, devoid of any real meaning.
Since the forest trees neither emit nor discharge it, we clearly know that this water does not descend from the moon;
the water does not come from the moon, nor does it emerge from the pearl, nor is it born from space. It is thus inherently pervasive and is not a product of combination.
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant (until: it is merely words and lacks any real meaning. When one waves one’s robe, there is movement;
when one lets the robe hang down, there is stillness. This is what is meant by "movement and stillness are not constant.
As for "waving in reverse": if one faces oneself while waving, wind arises on one's own face; this is called waving in reverse. Since it is not waving in reverse, it does not arise from [the face].
It faces you. You examine it closely below: you claim that the three natures do not intermingle and that two natures are mutually exclusive.

Yet, when seeking the source from which the wind arises, it is utterly unfathomable. Since it does not emerge from the garment, nor is it produced from space, nor does it arise from that face, it is entirely without origin.
"It is not a matter of conjunction. It is primordially pervasive, manifesting according to karma.
How can you fail to believe this? Ānanda, the nature of emptiness has no form; it is revealed through form (until: ... through digging, that which exists arises without a cause of its own)."

Dugging into the earth, one finds empty space; this is what is meant by "manifesting through form. In the Western Heaven (India), among both the noble and the common, society is divided into four castes (*varṇa*).
This corresponds here to the four classes: the Kṣatriya, the royal caste; the Brāhmaṇa, the pure-minded, also called those of pure conduct.
Those who maintain the Way and abide in rectitude purify their conduct. Vaiśyas are merchants; Śūdras are farmers;
these are called the four castes (*catur-varṇa*). Pāraśava is translated here as "swift" and also refers to those of keen faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*). Caṇḍāla.
The *kuài* (魁膾). This is called *yánzhì* (嚴幟) in this language. Their evil karma adorns them as they carry out their distinctive insignia; that is to say, they shake bells and hold bamboo poles.
Furthermore, they belong to a race of both the wise and the foolish.
Ānanda, if this space were to arise spontaneously without a cause (up to the point where it is said that space should not emerge from nowhere),
or if it were to arise because of the earth— meaning that if space arose because of the earth— then at the time one digs through the earth to produce a well, [space would already exist there].
One should see empty space entering the well; yet since no space enters, how could it emerge because of the earth?
If space has no entering or emerging, yet space originally emerges because of the earth, then space and earth must originally have no different causes. If they are not different, they are the same;
thus, when the earth emerges from the well, why is it that one does not see space emerging from the well as well? If [space] were to emerge because of digging downward...
To say that "manifestation" is the cause is untenable; to say it is separate from the cause is also untenable. You should further examine below how these are not natural causes and conditions.

To "carve out emptiness and reality" means to carve reality into emptiness and the void. All the skillful arguments above serve to eliminate the deluded calculations of the conscious mind and reveal the perfectly interfused true essence.
"If this nature of space is perfect, pervasive, and all-encompassing... [it is] entirely the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

This connects the preceding text by means of the meaning established above. Since it has been clarified that [the elements] do not arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, one knows that the nature of space is perfect and pervasive, and is not a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
If this is so for the "one great" element, it is likewise for all other great elements; therefore, they are all non-existent [in terms of inherent arising].

Arising and ceasing. However, this great clarity-emptiness simultaneously integrates the preceding four [elements], so that one may know that although form and emptiness differ, their nature is identical.
"Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize whether the four great elements (mahābhūta) emerge or enter, or whether they are neither emerging nor entering.
If you were to realize that the nature of empty space is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally has no emergence or entry, nor anything that is neither,
then you would realize that the nature of the four great elements is truly perfect and harmonious, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing."
"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha... there is only verbal expression and no actual reality.
This "Great Emptiness" (*ākāśa*) in this assembly differs from the four great elements mentioned previously. In the former case, it was stated first that "phenomena are identical to the signless";

here, it is stated first that "the signless is identical to phenomena. Furthermore, fearing that the "true emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) might be confused with "insentient emptiness" (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*), the translator changed [the term].
True emptiness is the ultimate reality.

Ānanda’s inquiry—“I see that the faculty of seeing has no cognition of its own, yet it exists because of form and space” (extending to) “whether it is the same or not the same, or different or not different”—consists of four propositions:
first, identity; second, difference; third, both identical and different; fourth, neither identical nor different. However...

The scriptural passage consists of two pairs of similarities and two pairs of differences, each forming a single phrase; hence it is said: "either the same yet not the same, or different yet not different.
Ānanda, if this seeing were again [dependent] on light or on darkness... (up to) ...it would not be the case that the essence of seeing emerges from nowhere of its own accord.
"Ānanda, descend" [from the head]—this distinguishes that it is not of one substance. "If this essence of vision... [descends from the eyes]—this distinguishes that it is not of different substances.
"Light and darkness are mutually opposed" [and so forth]—this distinguishes that it is neither identical nor non-identical, and neither different nor non-different. "You, furthermore...
[and so forth]—this causes him to examine minutely that its nature is truly perfect and harmonious, not entangled in any delusions.

If one perceives, hears, or knows that the nature [of these faculties] is perfectly round and all-pervasive—[extending] to being neither subject to arising and ceasing, nor identical or different—if there is such perceiving, hearing, or knowing:

previously, regarding the six faculties, the seeing of the eye was extensively refuted, while the other faculties were treated briefly. Now, by analogy, it is shown that their natures are all pervasive.
"Hearing" refers to the faculty of the ear; "perceiving" (*jue*) refers to the faculties of the nose, tongue, and body; and "knowing" (*zhi*) refers to...
The faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is not explicitly called "cognition" (*buddhi*) here; this is an abbreviation. Regarding the phrases "arising" and "ceasing," and so forth:
since seeing, hearing, cognizing, and knowing are fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, they are originally neither arising nor ceasing, neither identical nor different, and so on.
This is intended to cause one to contemplate with clarity, desiring that one penetrate the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) wherein no marks whatsoever exist.
"You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha (up to) there is only verbal expression and no actual reality.
'The seeing-nature is enlightened clarity' means that the very nature of seeing is entirely the true essence of enlightened clarity.
'Enlightened clarity is the clear seeing' means that seeing is the clear seeing of enlightened clarity; therefore, it is pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire Dharma-realm."
As with the first [root], the same applies to the remaining faculties. "Tasting touch" refers to the tongue faculty; because it perceives only when in contact with flavor, it is also called "touch.
"Perceiving touch" and "perceiving cognition" refer to the body and mind faculties.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises from the six [sense bases] (up to: it is without cause and emerges suddenly).
The sense organs merely reflect objects, like a mirror reflecting things; consciousness possesses discernment, and thus it is able to point them out.
Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were produced within seeing—[and so forth]—why would you not perceive the bright moon separately during the day?

This nature of the conscious cognition of brightness is neither produced from the appearance of the object nor from space. If it were produced from space, [it would be perceived even when the object is absent].
Thus, it is neither this characteristic nor this vision. Where there is no vision, there is no discernment; where there is no characteristic, there is no object-condition.

Since both vision and characteristic are absent, from what could consciousness arise? Furthermore, if the substance of consciousness were empty within this interval between non-characteristic and non-vision, it would be like the hair of a tortoise.
If the substance of consciousness were existent, it would not be the same as material phenomena, even if it were able to manifest within empty space.
Your consciousness, since it lacks both the characteristic and the seeing, is likewise without function. "If there were not" below refers to the absence of the moon at midday;
since there is no consciousness that perceives the moon, one should know that it does not arise without a cause.
You should further examine this minutely and scrutinize it thoroughly [until you realize] that consciousness does not arise from nowhere on its own.

This is intended to lead you to carefully observe the source from which the nature of consciousness emerges. You see that perception relies upon the sense organ and its characteristics rely upon the object;

when there are forms, existence is established, and when there are no signs, non-existence is established. Thus, as for the source from which this consciousness arises in dependence upon conditions—is it from the seeing, or from the perceived characteristics?
Does it emerge? Is there an emergence or not? When one seeks the nature of consciousness, it is found to have no source whatsoever. You speak of their "harmonious union":

that consciousness possesses discrimination is called "movement," while seeing is without discrimination and is called "clarity. Since consciousness is movement and seeing is clarity, they are neither harmonized nor joined.
The same applies to hearing and cognition; they are all neither produced by combination nor are they spontaneous. This is the true nature, perfectly interfused and transcending all delusions.
Thus, this conscious mind is fundamentally without origin (extending to its ultimate state), being neither identical nor different, and neither empty nor existent.

If this consciousness-mind refers to the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), its discernment of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing corresponds to the aforementioned element of sight (*darśana-dhātu*).

It eliminates my inverted conceptions accumulated over billions of kalpas, so that without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one attains the Dharma-body.

From beginningless time, one has been deluded regarding the truth and falsely identified with the conditioned shadows of objects, giving rise to views such as those concerning causes and conditions or spontaneity;

this is precisely the inverted conceptualization that persists for billions of kalpas. Once one receives instruction and awakening, these inverted thoughts dissolve, and one realizes the original mind—this is what is meant by attaining the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
According to the aforementioned scriptural passage, since this pertains to the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), it describes the moment of complete awakening.

Furthermore, according to what is said below regarding Pūrṇa, although those like Ānanda have attained awakening, their habitual outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been eliminated; thus, we know this refers to intellectual realization (*prativijñapti*).

To praise the Buddha’s mind and offer it as a supreme repayment is the aspiration for the holy fruit; this is the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). To return and deliver the vast multitude is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*).
The simultaneous integration of wisdom and compassion, vast and inexhaustible, is what is called the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). It is the vow to enter the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
"Not attaining nirvana" is the very effect of the profound mind. Relying upon this to repay [the Buddha's] kindness, he requests the Buddha to serve as witness:

Now, since this has already eliminated inverted perceptions and allowed for the sudden attainment of the Dharma-body, one might suspect that the fruit has already been realized;

yet, while seeking further through aspiration, one must still eliminate subtle delusions. There are seven aspects of the Buddha-fruit, namely: Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, Tathatā, Buddha-nature, and Amala-vijñāna.

The *ālaya-vijñāna*, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—what is called the attainment of the *dharmakāya*—is precisely the realization of *bodhi* and the direct perception of one’s own Buddha-nature.

After perceiving this nature, one must carefully eliminate subtle delusions so that both arising and ceasing, as well as the cessation of arising, are simultaneously stilled, thereby harmonizing with *nirvāṇa*. This is to harmonize with the true suchness (*tathatā*), which is pure, white, and perfectly concentrated.
When the *āmalaka-vijñāna* (amala-consciousness) is suddenly and perfectly illuminated, it accords with the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

Yet, those who study today have barely attained two of these and have suddenly lost the remaining five. They lightly discard the teachings and no longer practice cultivation or severance; if so, when will birth and death ever end?
Yet it remains silent. When will the defilements be purified? Amidst this bustling clamor and agitation, when will there be vast clarity?

Amidst this obscurity and ignorance, when will there be perfect illumination? Even if one has realized the nature of reality, the habitual outflows of conditioned existence cannot be avoided from arising again.
I know that their inverted perceptions remain as they were; it will likely double again over the course of billions of kalpas—this is truly lamentable.
Upon hearing this ultimate teaching of the Śūraṅgama, one should joyfully strive to advance, swiftly bringing all things to ultimate completion.

*Śūnyatā* (Śunyata) means "emptiness" (*ākāśa*). *Śakala* means "solid" or "firm. This signifies that while emptiness has no substance and can still be extinguished, my mind is firm and shall never waver.

This is based on the power of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, binding the previously vowed mind and vowing to reach the ultimate end without ever falling back. When the vow is such as this, only then can the holy fruit be expected.

Characteristics are fundamentally without characteristics. It is due to deluded attachment that they appear as characteristics. Because Pūrṇa does not realize that the essence of dharmas is fundamentally without arising, he does not understand that arising exists only because of delusion;

Thus, they do not understand that all characteristics are illusory; therefore, they ask why water and fire do not overwhelm or extinguish one another.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa (until), who reverently listened to the Buddha’s Dharma-voice in silent obedience.

This nature causes those of the Two Vehicles to hear this, thereby attuning with true nature and giving rise to authentic cultivation. Thus it is said:

*Āraṇya* means "free from clamor and confusion. Because one awakens to non-arising and realizes the absence of clamor and confusion, one practices in reliance upon this; this is what is meant.

This was intended to demonstrate that birth arises from delusion, while simultaneously employing the principle of mutual fusion that you had heard to interrogate the nature of illumination."
The term "luminous" (ming) is intended to lead those who, by recognizing luminosity as falling into delusion, take it to be the origin of birth-and-death phenomena.

For the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening is luminous precisely because it is wondrous; it is not that it is not luminous. The luminous wondrousness of original awakening is wondrous precisely because it is luminous.
Furthermore, it is not illumination. Although Pūrṇa heard these words, he did not grasp their underlying principle;
he immediately identified illumination as awakening. Therefore, [the Buddha] said: "If this is not illumination, then there is nothing to be illuminated.

To say that Pūrṇa identified awakening as non-illumination is one error. Because he established "that which is illuminated," the Buddha showed him: "To have something [to be illuminated] is not [awakening]."
Awakening is such that there is nothing that is not clarity; thus one knows that both clarity and non-clarity are neither true awakening nor wondrous clarity.
Yet Master Yuan took the presence of something clarified to be delusion and the absence of anything clarified to be truth.

Therefore, his interpretation—that "in the absence of anything [to be clarified], there is no delusive clarity"—is a twofold error. Because one recognizes clarity and establishes an objective referent (*vastu*), the empty space, the world, and so forth arise.
Thus it arises. Therefore, it is said that "within the absence of sameness and difference, there is a blazing manifestation of difference," and so forth.

This is the manifestation of characteristics (lakṣa� Master Yue points to "establishing objects based on causes" and so forth as the three subtle [evolutions], and points to "the absence of sameness and difference" and so forth as the six coarse [evolutions]. These are his three errors. Such is the agitation.
The section beginning with "confusion and so forth" cites the three preceding subtle states (*sūkṣma*) to introduce the six subsequent coarse states (*audārika*).

Thus it says, "In this way, through mutual disturbance, they give rise to weariness," and so on. Master Yue’s identification of this as citing both the three subtle and the six coarse states constitutes four errors.
However, the subsequent text explains everything according to the authentic intent of the Sūtra; I fear that those who wish to understand the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Meaning) may [misunderstand].
I shall now annotate the differences and similarities; therefore, this is clearly explained.
Pūrṇa said: "If this lack of clarity were itself called awakening, then there would be nothing to clarify.
Pūrṇa, because he did not understand that true awakening is fundamentally neither clarity nor non-clarity, a single thought of deluded movement arose, and he identified with it.

It clarifies the establishment of the "object" (*viṣaya*). Therefore it is said: "If this is not clarified, then there is nothing to be clarified. This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) arising as the cause of the three subtle states.

and the object is the mark of manifestation (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*). Once these three marks have appeared, inexhaustible deluded karma arises from them. Thus...

The text below says: "Awakening is not that which is illuminated; it is because of illumination that an object is established. Since the object is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises," and so forth. The Buddha said:

"If there were no object to be illuminated, then there would be no illuminating awareness" (up to) "the nature of awakening is inherently luminous; it is through delusion that it becomes 'illuminating awareness'."
This citation is used to clarify that enlightenment is neither existent nor non-existent.
"If there is nothing to be enlightened, then there is no enlightenment" — these two phrases summarize the opponent's calculation.

If you insist that there must be something to be enlightened in order for it to be called enlightenment, [the Buddha] shows: "If there is something, it is not enlightenment; if there is nothing, it is not clarity."
Thus, both clarity and ignorance are neither true awakening. The passage beginning with "Ignorance" explains that the aforementioned awakening is neither existent nor non-existent.
Since ignorance is not the nature of the profound clarity of awakening, if there were necessarily clarity, it would be a deluded "clarity-awakening.
Therefore, one knows that true awakening is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent.
"Awakening is not that which is illuminated; based on illumination, the object is established" (up to) "therefore, one further establishes neither sameness nor difference.

This explains how the delusion of the preceding moment gives rise to the three subtle states. Now, the essence of the nature of awakening is fundamentally devoid of subject and object, and likewise devoid of sameness and difference.
Due to ignorance (*avidyā*), there is a single moment of false movement. One recognizes illumination and establishes it as an object; thus, subject and object [arise].

This establishes [the thesis]. Identity and difference are manifested through form; the establishment of the "proven" (sādhya) depends upon the "means of proof" (hetu). The proven exists because of your capacity [to prove it];

yet while the capacity and the proven are simultaneous, one merely speaks of them as having a temporal sequence. Once there is that which is illuminated by the means of proof, then within identity and difference, they blaze forth and become distinct.

Being different from that which is differentiated, one relies on difference to establish identity; thus it is said that "identity is established based on difference. Thus do identity and difference arise.
It is clear that "sameness" and "difference" are equally non-existent and without distinction; therefore, it is said that based on this, one further establishes "neither sameness nor difference.

However, these three characteristics cannot be fully manifested all at once through words, and thus they are explained in succession. Although they are taught sequentially, their arising is simultaneous.
The external vessel-world, empty space, and the sense organs of sentient beings that are perceived therein manifest instantaneously in a single thought-moment, and are likewise not sequential.
One should know that these three—when in a state of dullness and before movement—are identical as stillness and share the same essence as empty space.

When they move, they become differentiated and constitute the essence of the world. When one recognizes clarity and establishes it as an object, distinct from dullness and movement, this is the essence of sentient beings.
"Thus, through mutual disturbance, weariness arises" (extending to) "thereby giving rise to worldly toil and afflictions.

this restates that because of prior ignorance, there was a momentary false movement; the true nature was thereby disturbed. This restates the aspect of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*). "Mutual dependence gives rise to [weariness]"...

"Exhaustion" (*láo*) refers to the preceding states of subject and object, which arise in mutual dependence, producing the characteristic of exhaustion. "The subject" is the *zhuǎnxiàng* (transforming characteristic); "the object and so forth" are the *xiànxiàng* (manifesting characteristic);

and "exhaustion" is the *zhìxiàng* (cognitive characteristic), which is the characteristic of continuity (*xiāngxùxiàng*). "Exhaustion long gives rise to dust" means that, by means of the two aforementioned characteristics, one initiates grasping and calculates names;
this is the characteristic of calculating names (*jìmíngzìxiàng*). "The self-characteristic becomes turbid" refers to the four [characteristics], beginning with cognition (*zhì*).
The "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) intermingle with the true nature; therefore, they are called "turbid" (*hun*). They sully the pure essence, causing its stainless clarity to be lost;

therefore, they are called "defiled" (*zhuo*). From the phrase "thereby" (*you shi*) downwards, the text restates how the three subtle states give rise to the four coarse states, hence the mention of "dust-like toil and afflictions" (*chen lao fan nao*).
These four are precisely the substance of the afflictions (*kleśa*). The subsequent "karma, retribution, and sentient beings" refer to the latter two coarse states.
"Arising constitutes the world; stillness completes emptiness" (up to) "therein there is neither identity nor difference, for truly conditioned dharmas [do not exist].
This clarifies that the preceding single thought-moment of deluded movement constitutes the three characteristics. "Arising" is precisely "movement"; movement then constitutes "difference."

Movement constitutes the substance of the world (*loka*), while difference constitutes the substance of the realm (*dhātu*). Thus, the world is formed by movement and difference; hence it is said that "arising constitutes the world.

"Empty. The two lines following "empty space" (ākāśa) cite and clarify the two characteristics. The phrase "That which is non-existent... refers back to the absence of identity or difference in the preceding discussion;

Regarding "awareness and clarity, emptiness and dullness," etc.: it means that due to the delusion of a single thought-moment, one is unaware and undergoes false movement; through this movement...
Vacuity and darkness, one clarity and one obscurity, one movement and one stillness, exist in mutual dependence without ceasing. Internally, this arising and perishing is termed "shaking";

"Maintaining the land. The second and third lines of "Firm Awakening" (*kṣaṇabodha*) point to the preceding two natures as the cause for the production of fire.

It is only because the deluded mind moves falsely that there is what is called "clarity. Therefore, it is said that "the clarity of awakening is the fault.
Once the false has been established, it causes the six sense faculties to become obstructions; thus, the principle of clarity cannot be transcended.

For this clarity that is false is itself the object of falsehood, and the objects of falsehood are themselves the six kinds of falsehood. Internally, because the deluded mind moves falsely, there arises what is called "clarity."

Because one falsely perceives external causes, one consequently establishes that which is falsely conceived. From "By this" (*yìshì*) onwards, it demonstrates the characteristic of not exceeding [the source].

From "Form and fragrance" (*sèxiāng*) onwards, it cites the meaning of not exceeding mentioned above to clarify the nature of karma. That is to say, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally one perfectly integrated and pure jewel-like awakening;
however, they are accomplished solely due to the six false objects, such as form, and thereby become divided into one.

The perfectly interfused precious awakening manifests as seeing, hearing, knowing, and cognizing. Once the faculties and their objects exist, they constitute the nature of karma; thus, deluded karma is initiated.
Thereupon, those of similar karma entangle one another, and through union and separation, transformation occurs. This is the beginning of the six paths and four modes of birth.
Those of similar karma are the womb-born and egg-born classes; because the three—parents and self—share the same karma, they [are joined].
Birth occurs through entanglement; union and separation constitute the moisture-born and transformation-born classes. These do not depend on parents, but arise solely from one's own karma.
Some take form by uniting with moisture, such as crawling insects and the like; others are born by separating and undergoing transformation, such as the inhabitants of the heavens and the hells.
"Seeing bright forms gives rise to vision; the formation of perception is completed [and continues] through these causes and conditions so that sentient beings are perpetuated.
This explains the reason for the perpetuation of sentient beings. "Seeing bright forms gives rise to vision" means that the deluded mind perceives deluded objects;
this refers specifically to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) perceiving the parents. "The formation of perception is completed by clear vision" means clearly seeing the father...
One perceives and visualizes the mother as the objective field; thus, emotion arises from that field. Regarding the passage "different views" (*viṣama-darśana*) below:
when a male enters the womb, the father is the object of aversion and the mother is the object of affection; for a female entering the womb, it is the reverse.
Since craving is the root of saṃsāra, one emits the seed through craving. Because visualization serves as the medium for transmitting life, one receives [the embryo].

Regarding the phrase "conception is the womb; through union, birth occurs," this means that the union of the parents serves as the condition (*pratyaya*), while the desire and craving of those with similar karma serve as the cause (*hetu*).
Due to these causes and conditions, one enters the womb and takes up a physical form. The *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies that there are five stages within the womb:
the first seven days are called *kalala*, which is translated here as "coagulated mucus"; the second seven days are called *arbuda*.
*Tan* means "blister" (arbuda); its shape is like that of a sore or blister. At the third week, it is called *piśāca*, which means "soft flesh.
At the fourth week, it is called *ghanas*, which means "solid flesh. At the fifth week, it is called *praśākhā*, which means "the stage of limbs.

Here, I have briefly cited the first two [stages] to include the remaining three by implication. Among the four types of birth, the egg-born corresponds to the stage of *saṃjñā* (perception), and the womb-born corresponds to...
Sentiment corresponds to union; transformation corresponds to separation. Thus it is said that they follow what is appropriate to each.
As for sentiment and thought mutually transforming one another through union and separation—such as sentiment changing into thought, or union changing into separation—there is no fixed karma.
An egg can easily become an embryo; moisture can easily become a transformation-born being. There is no fixed substance. Therefore, as for the retribution one receives, one may rise or sink;
there is no fixed destiny.

Pūrṇa, conceptual craving (*saṃjñā-tṛṣṇā*) binds one to the same as fetter-craving (*bandhana-tṛṣṇā*), such that one cannot be separated from it; [this extends] up to the point where these are rooted in the greed for theft.
This refers to craving-attachment (*tṛṣṇā*) to clarify the root of karmic fruit. For if conceptual craving does not form a bond, then attachment can be severed.
Since they have become mutually entangled and cannot part due to their attachment, their mutual production continues without end;
such things take desire and greed as their root. If greedy attachment were not nourished, greed could be ceased; but since they nourish one another, greed cannot be stopped.
Greed inevitably leads to killing; thus, they prey upon one another without ceasing. Such instances have greed for killing as their root.
By taking "human" as the lowest [category], the greed for stealing is clarified. Regarding these two forms of greed—killing and stealing—at first glance they appear to be without distinction.

However, if one examines them through the principle of whether a life-debt is incurred or not, a difference emerges. If one kills someone who owes one their life, that belongs to the category of greed for killing.

If one does not repay the debt, they kill them; this immediately falls under the category of the greed for theft. Thus, we know that theft necessarily involves killing, whereas killing does not necessarily involve theft.

Therefore, regarding the greed for killing, it is simply said that beings "devour one another," while regarding the greed for theft, it is said that "when a person dies, they become a sheep," and so forth.
The distinction between these two can clearly be seen. Furthermore, the greed for sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) pervades all four [meditative absorptions].

Regarding birth, this discussion now specifically concerns birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*). Furthermore, while womb-birth encompasses various types, it is here primarily distinguished in terms of human beings, as these are the easiest to observe.
"You owe me my life; I return your debt" (up to) "by these causes and conditions, karma and its fruit continue in succession.
This clarifies the reason for the continuity of karma and its fruit. "Owing a debt" refers to the cause of killing and stealing. "Affectionate pity" refers to the cause of sensual desire and greed.
Only the phrase "killing [the lower beings]" explicitly concludes [the section]. The two phrases "life" and "debt" have their textual meanings seen in mutual relation. As it says: "You owe..."
"My life! Return my life to me! I owe you a debt; I shall repay your debt. These two lines concerning "affection" and "pity" should likewise be seen as mutually interchangeable.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted states continue in succession (until) this delusion ends only to begin again.
This summarizes the preceding text to conclude the answer regarding the karmic fruits of world-systems and sentient beings:

they all arise from the non-awakening of a single thought-moment of deluded movement, whereby one recognizes luminosity and establishes an objective realm, causing it to manifest. Therefore, it is said: "All are the clarity of awakening; the nature of clear and knowing awareness gives rise to appearances because of its discernment.

Thus, the "clarity of awakening" is precisely the phase of karma of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*), while the "nature of clear and knowing awareness" is the recognition of that luminosity as [an object].
