Furthermore, the cognition of "absence" is itself dependent upon the nature of hearing; one cannot say that hearing ceases simply because there is no sound. Therefore, the following section reiterates the preceding point to clarify it.
It is indeed so. Previously, Ānanda had generally doubted that the six sense organs have no substance apart from their objects;

how then could he take this state of annihilation as a cause while desiring to obtain a permanent fruit? The reason the Tathāgata separately reveals the nature of hearing as permanent is truly because he wishes to awaken the potential for the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
You are still deluded by inversion, mistaking sound for hearing; how then could this nature be extinguished for you?
As for the example you cited regarding sleep, it serves as proof that while the false consciousness reaches a state of profound darkness, the true nature does not sleep. "Even if you...
and so forth means that it is not only not extinguished in the present, but even if your life were to end, it would still not be extinguished.
"Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial... [up to] "...why would they not achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?
This passage clarifies the truth by refuting the false. It serves to refute the prior view of annihilationism and the absence of causes.

For previously, it was instructed that one must discern the nature of permanence as the mind of the causal ground; yet Ānanda raised an objection, and thus this conclusion is provided to resolve it. Because of these...
Sentient beings follow sounds and pursue thoughts; they do not realize that their nature is eternal. Following all processes of arising and ceasing, they thus transmigrate through birth after birth.
If one abandons arising and ceasing and maintains the true eternity, the light of the eternal will manifest before them, whereupon defilements will vanish and the Dharma-eye will become pure.
How could one then fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment? Why did you previously ask, "By means of what cause shall one seek the Unconditioned?"
The supreme awakening: these seven kinds of eternally abiding fruits can be attained and realized; how could they possibly be subject to annihilation?

Ānanda had perceived his nature but had not yet engaged in cultivation; it was as if he had found a magnificent mansion but was unable to enter deeply within.

Therefore, he requested the essential gateways for practice in order to seek realization and entry. For this reason, the preceding text first clarifies the two definitive meanings of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

This briefly indicates the essential gateways for cultivation and severance. Below this, the untying of knots is explained in detail, culminating in the twenty-five sages each presenting their method of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).

By decreeing that the faculty of hearing be chosen as the expedient means for beginners, the essential gateways for the cultivation and severance of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are extensively demonstrated, enabling one to enter deeply through a single door. This does not deviate from the two definitive meanings. Therefore, it is said below:
To know that there is no seeing—that is itself nirvāṇa. Not grasping at phenomena is called samādhi. Furthermore, it is said:

"If you wish to eliminate the fetters, you should do so within the mind of the fetters. In the passage where Avalokiteśvara describes his perfect penetration, he says: "Entering the stream, the objects of perception vanish; thus, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Mañjuśrī’s instruction states: "Reverse the mechanism of hearing; turn back the hearing toward its own nature. When this nature is perfected, [the state of non-arising is attained]."

The preceding [sections] all rely on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and observation (*samatha*) to go against the current of karma and follow the path of perfect penetration, thereby perfectly accomplishing the ground of fruition.

Thus, one should know that the extensive explanations on "untying the knots," as well as what has been presented by the various sages and what was shown by Mañjuśrī, do not transcend these two definitive meanings;
they differ only in their detailed or concise exposition.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One" (up to) "...awaiting the unsurpassed revelation of the Tathāgata.
This follows upon the preceding text to request instruction on the origin of bondage and liberation. For it concerns the very source from which the six sense faculties are bound.
This refers precisely to the subtle, wandering thought. This thought is none other than the co-nascent ignorance that has no beginning.

Because the six sense organs wander and rush toward external objects, one revolves through birth and death by means of this thought; if they do not wander, one leaves behind thought and swiftly realizes wondrous permanence.
Thus, we know that both bondage and liberation arise from thought. As long as thought is not extinguished, the root of the affliction remains unextinguished.

It is exhausted; thus it is likened to a tertian malaria. From this, one knows that the previous instruction to "detach from clinging and dwell inwardly" was intended to suppress the wild impulses of the afflictions of thought.
This question concerns the source of the binding and its resolution, with the aim of exhausting even the most subtle ignorance (*avidyā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda—[passage from] "is also not something other than your own six faculties"—this demonstrates the source of both bondage and liberation.
First, he rubbed the crown of his head, signifying the unsurpassed revelation. The sixfold earth-shaking signifies the shattering of the delusory knots of the six faculties.
The light from the crowns of all Buddhas pouring over the crown of Śākyamuni signifies the shared awakening.

This clarifies the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Summit. As for "speaking with one voice from different mouths," it shows that all Buddhas' liberation from birth-and-death and their realization of Bodhi are entirely due to this essential method.
"Co-arising" refers to fundamental ignorance. Regarding "birth-and-death and wondrous-constancy sharing the same cause within the six sense organs":
when one establishes cognition upon cognition and seeing, one revolves through birth-and-death; when one has no seeing within cognition and seeing, one realizes wondrous constancy.

As explained below: although Ānanda had heard such sounds of the Dharma [up to the point where he realized] that the nature of consciousness is empty and false, like flowers in the sky, this was because he repeatedly questioned the source of the binding and its liberation;
therefore, [the Buddha] first informed him that there is fundamentally no essence of either birth-and-death or nirvāṇa.

Indeed, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) likewise shares that same source. The nature of consciousness is illusory, and the sense organs and their objects are also illusory—the text omits certain repetitions for brevity.
As for "bondage and liberation being non-dual," it means that when one is deluded, one is bound by the sense organs and their objects, and thus revolves through birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Awakening to this, one is liberated from the sense organs and their objects; thus, one realizes wondrous permanence (*saccidānanda*). Although bondage and liberation differ, their nature is without distinction; hence it is said they are "non-dual.
Thus, both birth-and-death and wondrous permanence both arise from the six sense organs. Since they are said to share a common source and be non-dual, [they are one].

Thus, fundamentally, there is no characteristic of bondage or liberation regarding the sense bases and their objects; how, then, could there be birth-and-death or wondrous permanence? Therefore, the following verse says:
"The true nature is empty of the conditioned; the unconditioned has neither arising nor ceasing."
"Ānanda, cognition arises from the objects, and their characteristics exist because of the sense organs... (up to) how could any other thing be further contained within this?
This demonstrates the essential point of bondage and liberation, thereby resolving his doubts. It means that the sense organs and objects exist by depending upon one another.
It is like the two stalks of a reed, which stand supported by one another and both lack intrinsic nature.

Yet, within this state, failing to realize that things are illusory, one pursues the six sense organs and discriminates among the six sense objects; this is the very root of ignorance, what is called "deluded obscuration," which is ignorance itself.
If one realizes that both the perceived object and the perceiving subject lack intrinsic nature, and does not follow the six sense organs to discriminate among the six sense objects, this is—
Nirvana is truly pure; what is called "bringing forth illumination" is precisely liberation.

As for the question, "How could there be room for any other thing within this?"—it was because the Buddhas above had told Ānanda that whether one revolves in birth and death or realizes wondrous permanence, it is solely your six sense faculties and nothing else.
Ānanda, having realized this, harbored doubts and raised the question again to the Buddha; therefore, the Buddha first clarified it.

Fundamentally, there is no essence of birth-and-death or nirvana. In this context, when it is stated that "establishing knowledge within knowledge and views" and so forth, the two characters "knowledge and views" (zhìjiàn) comprehensively encompass the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). To say they constitute ignorance or nirvana is nothing other than these six sense organs;
how could any other entity possibly be admitted? This is intended to resolve Ānanda’s doubts and to provide testimony for all Buddhas.
These are his words. Furthermore, Ānanda previously said: "If one does not know the root from which the knot was tied, I believe that person will never be able to untie it.
He further asked: "Regarding today’s body and mind, what constitutes the knot? From what would it be called 'untied'?"
Therefore, when the Tathāgata answers that "establishing cognition upon knowledge and vision" constitutes bondage, this refers to the very root of what is bound.
That "knowledge and vision are without seeing" is what is called liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, [said: "Falsehood reveals the various truths; falsehood and truth are both equally false.
This verse shows that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source, and that bondage and liberation are non-dual.

Since they share the same source and are non-dual, it clarifies that within true nature there are no characteristics of sense organs, objects, bondage, or liberation; therefore, this verse states that both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are empty and false.
Because the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are themselves the characteristics of bondage and liberation:

that which is called "conditioned" refers to being bound by the faculties and objects through delusion regarding the fundamental nature; therefore, it is called "conditioned. Since this characteristic does not originally exist within the nature, it is said to be "empty.

Thus, the true nature is the existent phenomenon (*dharma*), while the emptiness of the conditioned constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it arises dependently. The concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is like...

Regarding "illusion": that which is called "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) is so designated because, through awakening to the fundamental nature, one is liberated from the sense faculties and their objects;

hence it is called unconditioned. Yet, within this nature, even this characteristic does not exist, and thus it is said to be unreal. This means that while true nature is an existent phenomenon, the unconditioned is unreal;

therefore, this constitutes the thesis (pakṣa). The reason (hetu) is: "because it is without arising or ceasing. The concordant example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is: "like flowers in the sky. Within this second formal inference (pramāṇa):
To state the reason first and the thesis later is merely a linguistic convenience of the translator; it entails no loss of meaning.

Since both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are false, then the "reality" that stands in opposition to the false is itself also false. Thus it is said: "By speaking of the false, all forms of reality are revealed;

yet the false and the real are equally two kinds of falsity. This passage is from the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Pal-zhen-lun). Master Yue did not interpret this by taking both the conditioned and the unconditioned to be false; this [interpretation of his] is incorrect.
The Sūtras and Śāstras are concluded. Therefore, I shall here adopt Changshui’s explanation:

"That which is neither real nor unreal—how can there be a seer and a seen? In the interval between them, there is no substantial nature; therefore, they are like bundles of reeds leaning against one another."

This verse shows that the mutual dependence of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other.

The phrase "neither true nor untrue" serves as a transition from what precedes to what follows: it means that since neither "true" nor "untrue" can be apprehended, how could there be further delusory faculties and objects?
The subsequent line states that the faculties and objects exist only by depending upon one another; since they lack any real nature in between, they are thus compared [to the reeds].
It is like the *naḍa* reed.
"The binding and the unbinding share the same cause" (up to) "delusion and obscurity are themselves ignorance; illumination and clarity are themselves liberation.
This verse means that birth-and-death and wondrous permanence are identical within the six sense faculties and are not other things. "The cause" refers to the six [sense faculties].
The faculties (*indriya*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) are simply the state of an ordinary person; liberation is identical to that of a noble one (*ārya*). Thus, there are not two paths.

"Observe what follows below" reiterates the previous analogy to ensure careful contemplation. To say they are empty means that while they depend on one another and thus appear to exist, this appearance of existence does not mean they do not rely on their fundamental emptiness—just as the faculties and objects depend on one another and appear to exist, yet do not rely on an inherent non-existence. If one does not understand them to be illusory and false, one will follow [them].

The discrimination of sensory objects is precisely ignorance; thus it is said that "delusive obscuration is ignorance. If one realizes their lack of intrinsic nature and does not follow after discrimination, one immediately attains liberation;

thus it is said that "the manifestation of clarity brings liberation. This corresponds to the verses regarding "establishing knowledge upon knowledge-and-vision" and "knowledge-and-vision being without vision."

"The sequence for untying the knots is sixfold; when the first is untied, even the faculty itself perishes. By selecting the perfect penetration, one enters the stream and achieves true enlightenment.

This passage takes up the meaning of the preceding section on untying the knots and initiates the subsequent text on perfect penetration. "Sixfold untying" means that the faculties are uprooted. "The first perishing" means that the nature is empty.
As for the term "entering the stream," it refers to emerging from it decisively; whereas the stream flows outward in wild pursuit of objects, here one moves against it.
And enters [the state of stillness]. "The returning flow becomes entirely one" refers to selecting a faculty of perfect capacity and relying upon it to initiate contemplation;
by thus reversing that karmic flow, one achieves perfect enlightenment. From this point onward, all are verses that arise independently.
"The ālayavijñāna, subtle and consisting of a torrent of habitual tendencies, is both real and unreal; fearing confusion, I have never openly expounded it.
This verse explains the initial arising of the root-knots (*mūla-granthi*). *Ādāna* (ādānavijñāna) is translated here as "grasping and holding," meaning that which grasps and holds the seeds.

It initiates and manifests activity; that is, the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*. Containing seeds constitutes its "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*); giving rise to all phenomena constitutes its "torrential flow.
Stillness arises from this differentiation, and bondage arises from this. This consciousness relies upon *tathatā* (Suchness) while conjoining with birth-and-death (*saṃskṛta*);
it is intermingled between the real and the false. Therefore, it is said that "the real is not real. If one were to take it as truly real, one would fear...

Deluded by habitual tendencies, they deceive themselves, regarding [the ultimate] as not being real. Fearing that they might mistake their own nature for something else and seek it externally, the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle do not expound [this truth].
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "The ādāna-vijñāna is extremely subtle."
"All seeds form a torrential stream; I do not reveal this to the foolish and ignorant, for fear that they might conceptually grasp it as a self.
That which the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) grasp as a divine self (puruṣa) is precisely this consciousness."
"The mind takes up the mind" (up to) "where even that which is not illusion does not arise, how could illusory phenomena be established?
This verse explains the essential point of entering perfection by unraveling the knots. All dharmas are manifestations of the mind alone; they originally lack intrinsic nature.
Because one fails to understand this, one grasps and clings within them, falsely forming the knots of the sense-faculties. This is what is meant by "the mind taking up the mind."
The mind is not an illusion, yet it produces illusory phenomena; because of false grasping, there is both the illusory and the non-illusory.

If one can, through the wisdom of contemplation, realize that all phenomena are like illusions and thus cease false grasping, then even the "non-illusory" does not exist. If the non-illusory itself does not exist, how could illusory phenomena exist?
When illusory phenomena do not arise, then the sense organs and their objects are suddenly purified, and perfect penetration manifests before one.
This is called the "Wondrous Lotus" (up to: "the single path to nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions."

This verse summarizes the preceding text. Because one contemplates phenomena as being like illusions and does not falsely grasp or cling to them, both the real and the false are forgotten, and neither defilement nor purity obstructs.
This is called the "Wondrous Lotus. When the faculties, objects, and binding afflictions vanish in that very moment, it is called "Vajra-King Awakening.
Being tranquil while illuminating, with both subject and object forgotten, it is called "Illusory Samādhi. Relying upon this—
Through diligent cultivation, in the space of a single finger-snap, one may transcend the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and enter perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
The *Abhidharma* (Sanskrit for "Incomparable Dharma") states that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all transcend birth and death and swiftly realize quiescent permanence through this very path;
hence it is said: "The Bhagavans of the ten directions share a single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. The title "Bhagavat" possesses six [meanings].
Meaning refers to sovereignty, brilliance, physical excellence, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly [were led] by the bestowal of the sound of the Dharma to wash away their deep-seated defilements.

This praises and thanks the preceding Dharma and further requests the subsequent teaching. *Ge ya* (Geya) means "to be chanted" or "repeated verse"; it refers to verses that chant over the preceding prose (*gadya*).
*Gāthā* means "recitation" and is also abbreviated as "verse" (*ge*). It does not depend on prose, but rather chants and praises with beauty.
Since these two types of verses are both chanted and mutually beautiful, they are said to be "intermingled and refined. This refers to—
The "Able to Express" refers to the wondrous principle that is pure and penetrating; this is called the "Expressed. "Unobstructed Great Compassion" describes its universal salvation.
The "Naturally Pure, Wondrously Constant, and True Dharma-phrase" refers to discourse that accords with the nature, wherein both the real and the delusive are forgotten.
The mind remains unsettled; I request that you explain this later. This doubt arises because the preceding verse stated: "The method for untying the knots follows a sequence;
when the six are untied, the one also perishes. Therefore, he is perplexed by this. "Sinking defilements" refers to subtle, latent fetters and delusions.
Immediately, the Tathāgata [sat] upon the lion throne... (up to) responding to the Buddha in succession; this is called "tying.
This refers to the demonstration of tying knots with a cloth. *Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner garment), *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe), *saṃghāṭī* (great robe), and *kambala* (woolen blanket).

It is said that "time" refers to the Yāma Heaven. However, because Ānanda had not yet realized that the six [knots] dissolve into the one and that the sequence of loosening and tying is lost, the Tathāgata displayed a single cloth to form six knots, thereby causing him to realize that the six dissolve into the one.
He demonstrated the sequential order of tying the knots, thereby causing him to realize that there is a systematic order to the process of loosening and tying.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "From my first tying of the cloth (up to) 'ultimately identical yet ultimately different,' this clarifies that a single cloth forms six knots, which serves as a metaphor for how the one true mind forms the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The substance of the cloth originally has no six knots;
this metaphorizes that the nature of the mind is fundamentally without the six sense-faculties. The movement of tying produces the delusion of six knots; this metaphorizes..."

The six sense faculties thus give rise to madness and delusion. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Originally based on a single brilliant clarity, they are divided into six harmonious combinations.
This refers to the emergence of ultimate difference from within ultimate sameness.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you must find this [unpleasant]... (up to) 'the six dissolve and the one perishes'—it is also like this. This clarifies that the six dissolve and the one perishes.
From "If you must" downward, it poses a question regarding the method for dissolving the six and attaining the one.

"Not accomplished" means that they do not form a single entity. From "This concludes" downward, it provides the answer, setting forth the meaning of the six dissolving and the one perishing. That is to say:
If the six knots remain, right and wrong arise like sharp spikes; if they are all completely untied, then there is neither "this" nor "that"—how could there be one or six?

The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" uses the Dharma to provide an analogy for this clarity: if the six sense organs are liberated, the true nature is likewise empty, and distinctions between identity and difference completely vanish.
It is just as when the six knots are untied, both "one" and "six" perish. Therefore, it is said: "When the six are liberated, the one perishes. Furthermore—
It is likewise so.
Because from time immemorial your mind-nature has been deranged (until) all these are but the delusive toil of inverted flower-like appearances.
It is clear that through this deranged mind the six sense-faculties are bound; by folding and twisting a single cloth, six knots are formed, and thus the wearying of vision arises.
Dust is like the appearance of flowers in the sky caused by fatigued eyes. It is not only the objective realm of dust that is like these flowers;
both birth-and-death and nirvana are likewise empty flowers. Therefore it is said that they are all "the flower-like appearances of wild toil and inverted delusion.
Thus, since the six sense organs arise from the deluded mind, if one simply resolves this deluded mind, the six organs will naturally be liberated.
Ānanda said, "This weariness is the same as the knots; how can it be untied? [The Buddha replied: "If you wish to untie the knots, you must act at the center of the knot.

This demonstrates the essential method for untying the knots. The two lines beginning with "This weariness" first apply the metaphor to the Dharma and then inquire about the method for untying the knots.

Pulling from either the left or the right is a metaphor for relying on the two extremes of existence and non-existence. One does not know that to untie the knots, one must rely on the Perfect [Middle Way].
Contemplation: When one unties the knot at its center, it immediately disperses. This serves as a metaphor for practicing the Perfect Contemplation (*yuan-guan*) to untie the root of the knots.

Thus, the Perfect Contemplation itself constitutes the "knot-center. Now, if one can employ the Perfect Contemplation to observe that all phenomena are like illusions, then naturally no discrimination will arise regarding the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and no grasping or attachment will be produced toward objects. In this way, the root of the knots is untied.
Ānanda, I say that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse appearances of worldly combinations.
Herein, one specifically takes the cultivation of perfect contemplation to unravel the root of the knots as the cause and condition for the Buddha-dharma;
therefore, it is said that one does not grasp at the coarse appearances of the worldly combination of the four great elements.
"The Tathāgata elucidates the mundane and supramundane dharmas" (up to) "all delusions vanish; what need is there for the unreal?
This clarifies the reason for not grasping at the coarse characteristics of combination. The Buddha possesses two types of wisdom: provisional and ultimate.
Ultimate wisdom darkly accords with principle; provisional wisdom mirrors phenomena. He elucidates the mundane and supramundane dharmas, even knowing that their various origins...

As for these matters, they are all that which is reflected by expedient wisdom. Since one has already clearly and unobscuredly illumined all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, sentient or insentient—how could the explanation of the causes and conditions for untying knots now involve grasping at the coarse appearance of their conjunction?

Therefore, whichever of the six sense faculties you choose to rely upon to initiate contemplation, once the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of the sense objects will naturally cease.
When the dust and grime have vanished, what need is there to wait for the True?
"Ānanda, I now ask you about this *karpāsa* cloth... (up to) 'the liberation of the six faculties is also like this. This clarifies the sequence of unfolding the knots.
From 'I now' [onward], he first clarifies the sequence of unfolding the knots by means of the analogy.

From 'The Buddha said' [onward], he clarifies it by applying the Dharma to the analogy. This refers to when one was originally deluded; it began with a single faculty, and through that single faculty..."
Because of delusion, all six sense-faculties are deluded; this is like the sequence of knots in a cloth.

Since the knots are thus, when one now wishes to untie them, one must necessarily initiate contemplation from a single faculty. When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are liberated;
this is like the sequence of unfolding the knots. Therefore, it is said that the liberation of the six faculties is likewise so.
"This root first resolves and first attains the emptiness of persons" (up to) "attaining the patience of non-arising from samādhi.

This clarifies the gradual sequence of attaining patience through the resolution of the faculties. For when the six faculties are first resolved, one realizes that the aggregates are without self, and thus attains the emptiness of persons.
When prajñā is perfectly luminous, one awakens to the emptiness and stillness of dharmas, thereby achieving dharma-liberation. Once dharma-liberation is achieved—

Contemplative observation is also empty. Since both object and cognition are empty, subject and object are simultaneously quiescent; thus, one immediately attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, [withdrew] to conceal their secret insights, hoping for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
The "Revelation of the Perfect Penetration of Wisdom-Awakening" refers to the teaching that when the six are resolved into one, both the true and the false are forgotten.
Because there is no longer any doubt regarding the meaning of the dissolution of the one and the six, the body and mind become luminous and unimpeded.

Nevertheless, although the meaning of the dissolution of the one and the six has been realized, the fundamental source of perfect penetration has not yet been fully mastered; therefore, [the practitioner] hopes for...
This is the Buddha’s secret bestowal. "Esoteric words" refers to the phrases such as "revealing the wisdom of perfect penetration.
"Original awakening" refers to the awakening to the true mark (dharmatā) through the mind itself; because the true mark is signless, there are no marks of either reality or delusion.

"Secret adornment" refers to the essential secret of the fundamental root of perfect penetration. This implies that having fortunately been admitted into the ranks of the celestial, if one further explains this perfection...

If one penetrates the fundamental source, then through this convergence the Way is accomplished. If the fundamental source is not spoken of, the secret mantra obtained will be identical to the original awakening;
it would be no different from never having heard it. Therefore, he immediately requested:

"May you, out of great compassion, bestow upon me the secret adornment, so that I may accomplish the final instruction of the Tathāgata. The Buddha did not speak of it explicitly, but rather unfolded it through the assembly.
[Chen: This is called "mysterious transmission. To withdraw and conceal the secret mechanism is precisely to still the thoughts and concentrate the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly at large (up to): "By what skillful means does one enter samādhi?"
Because he had previously requested instruction on the fundamental root of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong ben-gen*), he first ordered the various sages to each present their methods;

subsequently, he commanded Mañjuśrī to select among them to reveal that fundamental root. This is because it was previously clarified that the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) and the seven elements (*sapta-mahābhūta*) are of one identical nature as the *tathāgatagarbha*;
now, these twenty-five sages have each entered perfect penetration through one or another of these eighteen realms and seven elements. As it is said:

There are a thousand paths and nine thoroughfares, yet the royal city is but one; the subsequent selection of texts is intended to accord with regional suitability, not to reveal any superiority or inferiority among the Dharma-gates.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself testified that "the practices of those [disciples] truly possess no superiority or inferiority.

Thus, Master Yue’s differentiation of the *yuan* (perfect) from the *xiao* (small), *da* (great), *pian* (partial), and *yuan* (perfect) regarding the "perfect penetration" (*yuantong*) does not capture the true intent of the Sūtra. Therefore...
The current commentary does not preserve this.
"Kauṇḍinya and the five bhikṣus immediately rose from their seats" (up to) "...as I have realized, sound is supreme.
Kauṇḍinya means "Fire-Weapon"; this is his clan name (*gotra*). From "observing and seeing" below, it clarifies that he attained awakening by relying on sound. This is subtle and wondrous.

"Sound-secrecy-perfection" means that sound accords with its true nature. Now, regarding these twenty-five gates, the fact that the sense-object of sound is first designated is because it was the primary medium for the teachings in this land.
The Kukkuṭārāma (Chicken Garden Monastery) was built by King Aśoka to welcome the Buddha.
Upāliṣada rose from his seat... [up to] "...as I have realized, form (*rūpa*) is the primary cause.
Upāliṣada: what is the nature of the object (*viṣaya*)? Because one awakens to the nature through the object, he received this name.

Because he formerly had much desire, the Buddha instructed him to practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to awaken to the nature of all forms. This section clarifies the meditation from its beginning.
Regarding the marks (*lakṣaṇa*): it means first contemplating this body from its impure white bones until both form and emptiness (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) are non-existent;
thus, the materiality of the dust is exhausted. When the wondrous form is subtle and perfect, one immediately awakens to the nature of all forms.
Because one attains Arhatship by relying on these characteristics of form, the realization is described as "the cause of form being supreme."
The youth Incense Purity (Gandhārī-putra) immediately rose from his seat... [as far as] "...as I have realized, the excellence of incense is supreme.

He was taught to contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), yet through the perfection of his realization via incense, he attained the stage of the Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*); thus he is named "Youth.

Regarding "taking leave of the Buddha to dwell in seclusion," this means sitting in quietude and concealing one's traces while practicing contemplation in a pure retreat. It does not mean contemplating the emptiness of nature beneath a tree.
Furthermore, both wood and smoke are non-existent; since coming and going do not exist, the mind has no object of perception.

Thereby, the mind is dissolved, and one realizes the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). Mundane vapors suddenly vanish, and wondrous fragrance becomes subtle and pervasive. Thus, he described his realization, declaring that "fragrance is supreme."
The two Dharma princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata... (up to: "As I have realized, the cause of taste is primary. Bitter, sour, and so forth—these are the six tastes.
When these various tastes combine, it is called 'harmonized taste' (*saṃyuktarasa*). When used in its natural state, it is called 'innate taste' (*sahaja-rasa*).
When refined through processing, roasting, or baking, it is called 'transformed taste' (*vikṛta-rasa*). By virtue of serving the Buddha, one will certainly hear the True Dharma."
Thus, one is able to fully understand the nature of taste. Because it shines radiantly within sensory objects, it is not empty; because its characteristics cannot be grasped, it is not existent.
Since it is not existent, it is not identical to the body and mind; since it is not empty, it is not separate from the body and mind.

Having realized that the nature of taste has no basis, one immediately awakens to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is how, by means of tasting, one realizes clarity; therefore, this is the answer regarding what has been realized.
"Cloud Flavor" (Megharasa) is superior as a cause.
Bhadrapāla, together with his companions—[up to]—"as I have realized, 'Touch' (sparśa) is superior as a cause.
Bhadrapāla—here called "Worthy Protector" (Xiànshǒu) or also "Worthy Guardian" (Xiànhù)—protects himself through virtuous qualities and also protects others.
"Protecting sentient beings," and so forth, describes the past causes in order to set forth the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).

"Suddenly awakening to the cause of water" and so on means that upon a single awakening regarding water, all dharmas are seen as empty; thus, the substance of the dust does not exist, and the appearance of water is also empty.
Since both internal and external are empty, from where could there be washing? In the midst of this, one attains a state of non-existence, which is precisely the mind of luminous touch.
Therefore it is said, "The subtle touch is proclaimed as manifest. Yet the answer states that the cause of touch is superior.
From Mahākāśyapa and the Bhikṣuṇī Jālinīprabhā [down to], "As I have realized, the cause of the Dharma is superior."
Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Drinker of Light"—is so named because his body is of a true golden color and his radiance eclipses the sun and moon.

When [the Buddha] says, "I observed below," it means that by observing the transformation of sensory objects (*dharmas*), he realized the emptiness and stillness of all phenomena. He subsequently cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) to extinguish the faculty of mind (*manas*).

Consequently, he attained a state where body and mind transcend hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the duration of a finger-snap. Once the objects of the senses and all phenomena have been exhausted, [he remains].
When the Sublime Dharma is clearly elucidated, all outflows (*āsrava*) are extinguished; thus, he describes his realization, stating that the cause of the Dharma (*dharmahetu*) is supreme.
*Dhūta*—newly translated as *duōduō* (抖擻)—is rendered as "shaking off," so named because it is able to shake off the dust of phenomena (*dharmacūrṇa*).
Aniruddha immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...this is the first instance of returning to the source through the revolving of vision.
Aniruddha; this is translated as "Free from Poverty. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

While the Buddha was at the Jetavana Grove preaching the Dharma to the assembly, Aniruddha fell asleep there with his eyes closed. The Buddha spoke a verse in rebuke, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? Like a snail..."
As for the species of clams and oysters, they sleep for a thousand years and do not hear the name of the Buddha.
At that time, Aniruddha remained awake until dawn, whereupon his faculty of sight was lost. The World-Honored One then described the signs he had shown:

"He who delights in seeing illumination" refers to one who directs their attention toward the nature of seeing—the seeing-nature that illuminates the myriad dharmas. By directing the mind toward this seeing, [all other perceptions cease].

Conditions cease together with their causes; because conditions cease, samādhi manifests before one. As fetters and delusions are purified and exhausted, it is called the "Samādhi of the Vajra that Illuminates Joyful Vision.
Because one has attained this samādhi, one's self-nature becomes transparently clear; thus, one perceives the ten directions as clearly as fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
"Reversing vision to follow the source" means turning back from delusion to follow the truth.
Cūḍapanthaka immediately rose from his seat... [until] "reversing the breath and following emptiness; this is the foremost. Panthaka means "Successor of the Path" in Chinese;
he was the bhikṣu who recited the *sammārjanī* (broom). Because his mind was greatly distracted, he was taught to regulate the breath.
For the arising and ceasing of the breath follows the arising and ceasing of the mind. Because the mind arises and ceases, the mind does not... [continue].

He was unimpeded. Because the Venerable One contemplated the breath until he reached its subtlest limit, exhausting the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—his mind suddenly opened up and attained great non-obstruction; he became an Arhat.

As for "turning back the breath to follow emptiness," it means that having exhausted the moments of all conditioned phenomena, one immediately turns back from arising and ceasing. His mind suddenly becomes unobstructed, and thus he follows [emptiness].
"Non-arising is emptiness.
Kauṇḍinya then rose from his seat (until) "returning the flavor and revolving the faculty of cognition; this is the foremost.
Kauṇḍinya means "ox-chewer" in this language. "I have," below, recounts the cause of being an ox-chewer. "The Tathāgata," below, clarifies [the teaching].
The method of contemplation shown here teaches one to contemplate the cognition that tastes flavors, thereby attaining transcendence of all outflows (*āsrava*) until the Dharma-eye becomes pure.
This is called the "Dharma-gate of Entering Samādhi with Purity. Below the section on "Contemplating Flavor," the text correctly clarifies the characteristics of performing this contemplation;
it means contemplating that the cognition which tastes flavor does not arise from the sense organ, nor does it exist because of the object. By...
These faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and mind will accordingly dissolve and fall away at that moment. Thus, by mindfulness, one transcends all worldly outflows (*āsrava*).

Internally, one is liberated from body and mind—this is liberation of the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*). Externally, one leaves behind the world—this is liberation of the environmental retribution (*niśraya-phala*).
Because one has transcended all worldly outflows, one attains freedom from defilement and the dissolution of dust; the Dharma-eye becomes pure, and one becomes an Arhat.
Because he does not cling to the flavors of sensory dust and does not follow deluded cognition, this is called "returning to flavor and revolving cognition.
Pindola Bharadvaja then rose from his seat... [until] "...pure awakening leaves the body behind; this is the foremost."
Piliṅgavatsa—this is translated as "residual habit. I have first, below, related the circumstances of my entry into the Way:
hearing things that are unpleasant—that is, all manner of suffering—and contemplating things that are unpleasant, thereby coming into contact with things that are unpleasant.

Thereupon, he observes correctly. Because there is knowing, he knows this profound pain. Although there is the awareness capable of perceiving that which is perceived—the pain—he instead perceives his own pure mind, in which there has never been any sensation of pain.
Yet, because the subject-object duality still persists, his awareness is not yet pure; thus, he reflects further and advances until even the contact of the body has vanished, and the mind...
The marks also cease, and all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted in emptiness; this is the pure awakening that remains as the residual body.
Subhūti then rose from his seat... (until) returning to the Dharma and merging with the non-existent—this is the foremost.

The Venerable One’s understanding of emptiness did not pertain to a single lifetime; hence it is said to span "vast kalpas. Because he realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), his mind did not dwell upon phenomena, and thus his mind attained non-obstruction.
From knowing emptiness while in the womb until his full realization of the emptiness of the ten directions, this was still merely "emptiness as such" (*buta-kong*).
Furthermore, by manifesting the true emptiness of the nature of awakening, the nature of emptiness became perfectly luminous, whereby he was able to suddenly enter the precious clarity.
The ocean of the wondrous nature of true emptiness transcends the views of the two vehicles and accords with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

All phenomena enter into non-existence, such that subject and object are both exhausted; this is because they are fused within the ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness. All existing dharmas revolve back to the ultimate non-being;
this is because they return to the ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat... [until] "...this is the foremost among those whose light of knowledge and vision is supreme. Regarding "the purity of mental vision":

it means that it does not arise because of the sense faculties, nor does it exist because of objects. It transcends both the faculties and their sensory domains, being entirely free from the habits of delusion.
Because there are no habits of delusion, it illuminates all transformations with unimpeded penetration. Upon hearing this teaching...

Through causes and conditions, one awakens to the mind’s boundlessness; this is the seeing of the enlightened awareness as perfectly complete. All outflows are extinguished, and one attains great fearlessness, becoming an Arhat.

As for "the mind-seeing emits light, and the light reaches the ultimate limit of knowledge and vision," it means that by means of the light of the mind, one knows and sees all phenomena without anything being obstructed or unpenetrated—this is what is called "inner luminosity emitting light. All superficial dust-like phenomena...
Illusory appearances should be contemplated as transforming into unsurpassed awakening.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva then rose from his seat... [omitted] ...this mastery of discernment is the foremost.
To practice throughout the entire Dharma-realm is called "Universal" (Puxian). To occupy a station adjacent to the ultimate sages is called "Worthy" (Xian).

Generally, all who possess great roots and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva are said to perform the conduct of Samantabhadra. "Mental hearing" refers to the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). As for "discerning the knowledge and views of sentient beings":
He selects the practices of Samantabhadra and brings them to fulfillment. "The mind-hearing becomes manifest" refers to internal realization;
"discrimination is sovereign" refers to external function.
Sudhana and Nanda immediately rose from their seats... [until] "...this perfect clarity that extinguishes outflows is the foremost."
Sundarī means "beautifully beloved"; it is the name of his wife. Nanda means "joy"; it is his own name.
Although these two names from the Cien Monastery are both translated as "Radiant Joy," the wife's name is specified here to distinguish him from Nanda the cowherd. When I first descended...
"Clearly manifesting the source of contemplation" (from "The World-Honored One" downward) clarifies the signs produced by contemplating according to the teachings.

Previously, one regulated the breath based on the sense faculties (*indriya*) in order to collect the mind; now, this contemplation of the white [light] is based on consciousness (*vijñāna*), so as to stabilize the mind.

The breath arises from the movement of the lungs and stirs up the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, its appearance is like smoke. Those who are deluded do not perceive it; only through careful observation...

Contemplation is that which enables seeing. When pure contemplation brings forth illumination, turbidity gradually dissipates; thus, the interior becomes luminous and the exterior becomes empty, like smoke vanishing to become white.
When the mind is pure and outflows are exhausted, there are no further afflictions. As the inner clarity radiates light, the inhalation and exhalation are transformed into radiance.
"One shall attain Bodhi" means that the wisdom of unborn emptiness has already manifested before one.
It is purely wisdom; therefore, one shall attain Bodhi. "Dissolving" means that as the smoke vanishes, it becomes white;

"subsiding for a long time and manifesting brilliance" means that the inhalation and exhalation are transformed into radiance. "Brilliance becoming perfect" means illuminating the worlds of the ten directions;
"extinguishing outflows" means the mind opens and the outflows are exhausted—all of which arise from the manifestation of the nose-consciousness.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (up to: was foremost in extinguishing all outflows (*āsrava*) and foremost in preaching the Dharma, possessing unimpeded eloquence.
That he thereby subdued Māra and extinguished the outflows was entirely due to the power of his tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*).

To "proclaim suffering and emptiness while profoundly penetrating the true reality" means to realize that suffering has no characteristic of suffering and that emptiness has no characteristic of emptiness;
this is called penetrating the true reality. Thus, one proclaims the true reality within suffering and emptiness; this constitutes a subtle revelation of the secret Dharma-gate.
Because one has reached the source of all phenomena, there is nothing to fear. The Buddha responds through the three wheels of body, speech, and mind.

Objects are without obstruction; sound is the wheel of the mouth. Because one ascends to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) through the roar of the Teacher, it is sealed as the supreme for preaching the Dharma.

As for the statement "subduing Māra and extinguishing outflows," this means that by proclaiming the sounds of the Dharma with the consciousness of the tongue, one externally subdues the enemies of Māra and internally eliminates all outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, the consciousness of the tongue constitutes the [fifth]...
First: Upāli immediately rose from his seat... [until] "...he is foremost in all matters of universal benefit. Upāli;
this is translated as "Foremost" (*Upadeśa*), because he maintains the Vinaya as the guiding principle for the assembly. Alternatively, it is translated as "Near" (*Upa*).

[The interlocutor] says: Because he was a minister who served as an attendant when the Buddha was a prince, I personally descended [to that level] to first recount the conditions for entering the Path.

From the section on "Receiving the Buddha’s Teaching and Precepts" onwards, I formally present what has been realized. Regarding the rules of conduct (*śīla*) for walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, there are two hundred and fifty precepts each;
these, when categorized according to the three clusters (*triskandha*), amount to three thousand. Furthermore, these three thousand are assigned to the body.
The seven branches of verbal action constitute twenty-one thousand [types of affliction]. When these are further multiplied by the four categories of afflictions, they become eighty-four thousand.
Regarding natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*): killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are natural offenses;

they are inherently sinful and do not depend on a formal prohibition. To commit them constitutes an immediate transgression. Other [offenses] were established as prohibitions based on specific faults; prior to such a prohibition, committing them did not constitute a sin. Since both types of karma...
All are pure; thus, body and mind are quiescent. Regarding the phrase "I, by means of grasping the body," etc.:
it means that first, through grasping the body, because the body is pure, the body attains mastery. Next, through grasping the mind, because the mind is pure, the mind attains penetration.
Thereby, both body and mind become entirely unimpeded and sharp, and one attains wondrous, perfect penetration.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat... [until] having long since achieved crystalline purity, he was foremost among them.

He proclaimed the profound meaning of causes and conditions, namely that it is not a coarse phenomenon produced by worldly conjunction; rather, he elucidated the principle of the emptiness of all dharmas.
Thus, he was able to manifest his own mind, attaining great penetration, perfect clarity and purity, and unimpeded mastery.
It is fear. However, the reason why people fail to attain perfect clarity, purity, sovereignty, and fearlessness is that their mental consciousness flows outward and rushes toward objects.
Now, having heard this profound meaning and realized that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, the consciousness no longer flows outward but returns to the wondrous stillness;
thus, one attains perfect clarity, sovereignty, and fearlessness. The section beginning with "The Buddha asked" concludes [the discourse].

Answer: Regarding that which is realized: it means that as the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) turns back, it becomes again wondrously profound and still. The light of the mind shines forth, like clear water appearing after a long period of stilling the flow.
Therefore, the mental consciousness is considered primary.
Ucchuṣma, before the Tathāgata... [until] he attained unsurpassed enlightenment; this was foremost.
Ucchuṣma means "Fire-Head," which is the Vajra Fire-Head. From "I always... below, he recounts his past causes to describe what he has realized:
that those with much lust are fundamentally impelled by the sensation of warmth, giving rise to the fire of desire at birth and [extinguishing it] at death.
It is the fire of karma; because the power of karma increases and blazes, it becomes a mass of fierce flames. "Observing the pervasive warmth" means causing one to contemplate the element of fire.

"The divine light descends" clarifies that when contemplation is perfected, one enters realization—namely, transforming the fire of desire into the fire of wisdom, and changing the lustful mind into a mind of meditative concentration. "Clearly observing the unimpeded flow of the warm touch" refers to this very state.
This is the contemplation of the fire element as entry into perfect penetration. The arising of great jewel-flames is the Fire-Light Samādhi.
Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat... [until] ...he attained the unsurpassed way; this is the foremost.
Leveling the uneven prevents damage; by saving oxen for others, one is free from the notions of "self" and "other.
This is truly leveling the mind-ground, wherein there is no high or low. When practice reaches this point, upon hearing what was shown, my mind immediately opened.

As for the statement that "if one levels the mind-ground, then all grounds are level," it means to realize that the myriad dharmas are but the mind, and not to give rise to divergent views or distinctions.
It is distinct. One immediately attains equanimity of mind. If the ground of the mind is level, one no longer perceives such signs as self and other, high and low;
thus, all things are equal. Viśvabhū means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. This, too, arises from a level mind, whereby one attains sovereignty over all.
"I" refers to the speaker himself, who is now correctly describing what has been realized: namely, the thorough understanding of the two objects, the body and the sensory realm.
This is the Tathāgata-garbha; therefore, there is no mutual friction or contact. By realizing the nature of atoms, one immediately awakens to non-arising; hence it is said:

"I have attained the patience of non-arising regarding the Dharma-nature. The ground of the wondrous lotus-flower Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground of all Buddhas.
When practice is truly and perfectly in accord, and both defilement and purity are simultaneously forgotten, it is named the "Wondrous Lotus," which stands far beyond the three [realms].
By riding upon this, one profoundly attains the single reality, which is called the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. That which is upheld by the Ground of Holding is exhausted right here;
thus, the realms of body and dust are dissolved, and supreme wisdom becomes perfect.
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat... [until] "the perfection of Bodhi is foremost. *Candra* means the moon; it is the water-crystal.

In the past, he took Varuṇa as his teacher and practiced the contemplation of water (*āp-dhyāna*). Because the nature of water was perfectly luminous and clear, he was named Candraprabha ("Moonlight").

Regarding the phrase "contemplating below," this refers to forming the image of contemplation. This is because, in the initial contemplation, one contemplates the water within one's own body, the nature of which is not...
They contend with one another until they reach the observation of the various fragrant seas beyond the worlds, which are neither two nor distinct;

thus, the water-element attains perfect clarity and brightness. At that time, my physical body returns to its original state. I shall now describe the conditions for practicing this contemplation. When first accomplishing this contemplation, one sees only the water;
the color resulting from the fruit of clear concentration transforms according to the mind, yet one has not yet attained bodilessness. Upon emerging [from meditation],...
The mind suffers pain during meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For example, when Śāriputra entered concentration on the banks of the Ganges, he was struck by a malevolent spirit;

upon emerging from concentration, his head ached. This is because he had not yet attained the "bodyless" state (*an-ātmabhāva*). As for those who have long been free from the conditions of illness, this refers to Arhats whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted;
yet, since they have not attained the bodyless state, the fetters of the fruit (*phala-saṃyojana*) still remain, and thus their minds suffer pain upon emerging [from concentration].

That one does not yet know with certainty is due to the fact that ignorance has not been exhausted. When one contemplates that the water of the body-element is without distinction, its nature is then merged with true emptiness.
Because the natures of water do not encroach upon or supplant one another, it is said to flow through as a single flavor.

By contemplating that the natures of water do not encroach upon one another, one attains the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and fulfills Bodhi; therefore, the element of water is ranked first.
The Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha rose from his seat... [omitted] ...transmitting this one wondrous mind is the foremost.
Having attained great enlightenment through the wind element, his body and mind emitted light, penetrating all things without obstruction; thus he was named Vaidūryaprabha.
Buddha Amitaghoṣa, relying on the wind element to provide instruction to the Bodhisattva, desired that he realize immovability, and therefore commanded him to contemplate it.
Regarding all movements: if one realizes that all movements have no basis, one immediately realizes the unmoving state of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Thus, Vimalakīrti (Lapis Lazuli Light) contemplated the realms, the world, the body, and the mind; he saw that all flux, movement, and stillness are entirely due to the power of wind.
Therefore, it is said that "all movements are non-dual. Furthermore, he realized that this nature comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. From this...
He realized that the myriad movements within the great trichiliocosm are all merely frantic toil, like a hundred mosquitoes buzzing within a square inch.
Because he understood that these winds have no source, not long after meeting the Buddha, he attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Thus, he awakened to the immovability amidst the multitude of movements; consequently, he beheld himself as a Dharma Prince in the Buddha-land of Akṣobhya.
The east is the source of all movement, yet the Buddha is named "Immovable"; he is thus one who is still within movement.
Because he can be still within movement, his body and mind are unimpeded, penetratingly clear, and radiating light.

To say that he has unified with the Buddhas of the ten directions to transmit this single wondrous mind means that when one contemplates how the power of the wind has no basis, the mind realized therein is precisely what has been transmitted by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This is because of the wondrous mind.
Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat... [up to] "...this supreme perfection of wondrous power is foremost.
Because he contemplates emptiness, he attains realization of the nature of emptiness; thus, everything that exists within that nature is entirely empty, as is the body."
He penetrates the oceans of lands without obstruction and is named Space-Treasury (*Gaganagañja*). Because he has realized the nature of emptiness, he attains a boundless body;
by virtue of attaining this boundless body, he is able to use four precious jewels to illuminate the lands of the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.
The mirror manifests within the mind; light illuminates all lands, which enter into the mirror. Bodies and lands interpenetrate one another without mutual obstruction;
vast and compliant, they perform the Buddha-work. Below this "Great Supernatural Power," the cause of "Wondrous Power" is clarified:
it means that by contemplating the four elements, body, mind, empty space, and Buddha-lands as being equally false and illusory, they are seen to be solely the Perfect [Dharmadhātu].

The "Constant" [nature] darkly manifests this activity; how could it be restricted by spatial location? The passage beginning with "The Buddha asked" concludes the answer regarding what has been realized.

That the subtle power is perfectly luminous is precisely the matter of the mirror manifesting within the lands through illumination. Because one contemplates emptiness, this subtle power is attained; therefore, emptiness is the foremost of the great elements.
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat... [omitted] ...to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

this is considered the foremost. "Maitreya" is correctly transliterated as *Meitailiyena*. This translates as "The Kindly One" (*Maitreya*). It means that while his kindness flourishes in the present world, his compassion reaches the future kalpas;
because he pities sentient beings who are deluded regarding consciousness, he manifests traces to illuminate the truth. His mind values worldly renown and he delights in wandering about.
"Lineage and clan" refers to the clarity that deluded consciousness pursues objects, outwardly yearning for and falsely seeking them.
To "have the mind suddenly cease through the teachings of Dīpaṃkara" means to realize that objects are but consciousness; thus, delusion and falsehood are naturally eliminated.

When the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appears and one attains wondrous perfection, it is because once delusion and falsehood are removed, the true mind immediately manifests, whereby the myriad objects become wondrously perfected. Having attained this...
In the Samādhi of the Wondrously Perfect Consciousness-Mind, one realizes that all empty lands of the Tathāgatas are transformations of my own mind;

that purity and defilement, existence and non-existence, are likewise transformations of my own mind. From this, immeasurable Buddha-nature is manifested; this is called the flowing forth of immeasurable Tathāgatas.

Even upon attaining the stage of the "Place of Rebirth" (the Bodhisattva stage immediately preceding Buddhahood), one does not depart from this. When the consciousness-mind is perfectly luminous, one enters the Perfect [Enlightenment].

The *Tattvasiddhi* and other treatises state that because the consciousness-mind is wondrously perfect, one realizes the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). No longer deluded by consciousness or pursuing external objects, one abandons various forms of conceptual attachment;

thus, one is able to distance oneself from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), thereby attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The *parikalpita-svabhāva* refers to the arbitrary grasping at sentient beings, a life-principle, a self, and what belongs to a self, extending even to [the realm of] feeling...
The insentient is different [from the sentient] because it possesses substantial reality; thus, it is universally conceptualized.

The dependent nature refers to the construction of names and signs based on the conjunction of causes and conditions in the world, and the grasping of these provisional signs as definitely arising from seeds.
Although there is no grasping at a self, the natural lineage (prakṛtisthagotra) still clings to phenomena such as the five aggregates, which are certainly produced from seeds.
The perfected nature (pariniṣpannasvabhāva) is precisely suchness (tathatā). The perfected nature is like the hemp; the dependent nature (paratantrasvabhāva) is like the rope;
and the imagined nature (parikalpitasvabhāva) is like the snake. Now, entering the perfected nature is to realize the principle of suchness.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, together with his peers, has attained samādhi; he is the foremost among them.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta is also named Amitābha. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "With the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all things."
He causes beings to leave the three miserable realms and attain unsurpassed power; thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Now, one who recollects the Buddha must not, for even the duration of a finger-snap, think of the five worldly desires. This is called "binding the mindfulness. If one can remain thus, without a single moment of interruption or admixture, [one will achieve this].
Then the immeasurable nature-light will spontaneously manifest. This refers to what is described below as "not relying on expedient means, yet attaining the opening of the mind by oneself.

The analogy that follows demonstrates that one must fix the mind [on the Buddha] before resonance occurs. If one does not single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, then even if one encounters him, it is as if one has not;
even if one sees him, it is as if one does not. If one is stained with incense, one is permeated by its fragrance; if one recites the Buddha’s name, one beholds him.
Therefore, because of the wondrous permeation of mindfulness of the Buddha, it is called the "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

As for attaining patience through mindfulness of the Buddha, it is because pure mindfulness dispels turbid thoughts and right mindfulness extinguishes perverse perceptions; once the perverse and turbid are removed, the mind and its objects become empty and tranquil.
That all things are non-arising is called the "patience with non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In this way, the Buddha-land of intrinsic nature is pure;

thus, it gathers practitioners and brings them to a common goal. From "I have no [inferiority]" onwards, he correctly sets forth what he has realized. Regarding "completely gathering the six sense faculties":
because the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) universally gathers the six faculties, one immediately perceives the Great One—this is the first point.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat... [up to] ...entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

As for "Avalokiteśvara," it means observing the words and sounds of the world; it is a title for one who possesses perfect enlightenment and perfect response. Regarding the use of "observing" (*guan*) in relation to sound: *Note: The ellipses indicate the omission of the intermediate text provided in the source.*
One illuminates this with contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), rather than hearing it with the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*).

What is called "entering the stream and losing the object" can thus be understood as being through contemplation rather than hearing. The Buddha whom you take as your teacher is also named Avalokiteśvara;

cause and effect correspond, for the Way is one throughout past and present. Hearing refers to what reaches the ears; thinking refers to what attaches to the mind. This is the cultivation of practice.
This is called cultivation. These three are perfect clarity; they are called the three kinds of wisdom.
First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object (continuing until): "Since production and cessation have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one."
This describes the fundamental cause for entering the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*). Regarding the phrase "entering the stream and losing the object":
it means that, from the very beginning within the act of hearing, one employs the wisdom of perfect cultivation to reflect back upon the nature of hearing itself.

By not following the sensory dust of sound into its outward flow, one is able to turn against that karmic current, lose the characteristic of what is heard, and enter a state of stillness. Once that which is entered is stilled, movement and stillness no longer arise.
As the wisdom of contemplation gradually increases, the capacity to hear also comes to an end. Once the hearing that is perceived has departed, the wisdom that perceives it also becomes quiescent.

When neither object nor wisdom is established, the realization of emptiness reaches its ultimate perfection. When the wisdom that contemplates emptiness has vanished, the realization of the emptiness of that very wisdom also ceases.
Thus, the characteristics of arising and ceasing are exhausted, and the nature of perfect penetration manifests in its entirety before one. This is what is called "existence."
The illumination and that which is illuminated are both termed obstacles; the illumination and the illuminator simultaneously enter quiescent extinction.
Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds... (up to) sharing the same sorrow and longing as all sentient beings.
Because the nature of perfect penetration manifests before one, worldly and world-transcending phenomena cannot obstruct or limit it;

the ten directions and the dharma-realm are perfectly bright and thoroughly penetrated, thereby attaining two kinds of excellence. This is precisely the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination (*pariṣphuṭa-samādhi*), so called because of its perfect penetration.
Therefore, it harmonizes with all Buddhas above and with all sentient beings below, without any interval between them.

Harmonizing with all Buddhas above, it is thus able to take pity on beings and bestow compassion, responding to their capacities by granting them joy; this refers precisely to the thirty-two manifestations. Harmonizing with all sentient beings below:
Thus one knows his compassionate longing; wherever he encounters suffering, he immediately delivers them from it. This refers precisely to the fourteen fearlessnesses.
By virtue of my offerings to Avalokiteśvara, the World-Honored One has attained the thirty-two manifestations to enter all lands.
This is the fundamental basis for the thirty-two manifestations. "Like an illusion" means that the actions performed by an illusory person are fundamentally non-action;

this serves as a metaphor for cultivation through permeation responding to capacities, which is itself the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), wherein emotional attachments are lost and conceptual understanding is severed.

"Cultivation through hearing and cultivation by hearing" means that all permeation and cultivation are inseparable from hearing. Because one relies on the nature of hearing for cultivation, the fetters and delusions are purified.
When [all delusions] are exhausted and samādhi manifests before one, then one shares the same power of compassion as the Tathāgata. Thus, one is able to respond to conditions through transformation;

all such manifestations are merely like illusions. Regarding the thirty-two responses: one manifests bodies within the ten dharma-realms to perfectly respond to the various capacities of sentient beings.
When expanded, there are thirty-two; when condensed, they comprise only the four noble classes and the six mundane realms, encompassing all categories of beings.

World-Honored One, if various bodhisattvas enter samādhi (up to) being taught the Dharma so that they may attain liberation, because the nature of perfect penetration manifests and they share the same power as the Buddha, they are able to manifest the Buddha-body. Cultivating correct concentration and attaining the correct fruit, they advance in their quest for the remainderless state;
this is called "advancing cultivation of the untainted. Ignorance is nearly exhausted, and the knowledge of all modes is about to be perfected.
It is said that through the perfection of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one may attain Buddhahood;
therefore, the Buddha manifests his body to preach the Dharma of the fruit, so as to bring those who seek liberation to the fulfillment of Bodhi and their return to the state of non-attainment.

Even a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, sitting upon the Flower King Throne (*padmavikrānta-rāja*) on the verge of attaining perfect enlightenment, still possesses residual afflictions of learning and must yet rely upon a distinct Buddha.
He preached the teaching; only by severing the final ignorance could one attain the Buddha-way—this is precisely what that refers to.
If there are those in training who dwell in tranquil, wondrous clarity, [the Buddha] then preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve liberation.

The Pratyekabuddha appears in an age when no Buddha is present; by observing the transformation of phenomena and awakening to the state of non-arising on his own, he is called a "Solitary Awakened One.

Delighting in solitary tranquility and seeking natural wisdom, he is thus termed "Tranquil, Sublime, and Luminous. The Pratyayabuddha receives the teachings of a Buddha and awakens to the Way by contemplating conditions;
therefore, he is called a "Conditionally Awakened One. He realizes that delusion regarding the supreme nature arises from the twelve links of dependent origination. At [the stage of]...

When these [afflictions] are severed down to ignorance, the conditions are cut off and the supreme nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) manifests. Because this nature manifests through the severance of conditions, it is called "the supreme nature upon the severance of conditions.

As for "the supreme and wondrous manifesting in perfection," this refers to the fact that, according to the respective principles and wisdom of each vehicle, [the nature] has already manifested and is already perfected;
however, it had not yet been realized. Now, by manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma, he causes them to realize and enter [it], thereby bringing about their liberation.
Furthermore, for those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and have attained the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma to bring them to liberation.

From the stage prior to the third fruit, both the stage of the worthy (*ārya*) and the stage of the noble (*ārya*) belong to those in training. Through the sixteen moments of mind of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), [the afflictions are] severed.

Regarding the afflictions underlying the Four Truths: because one realizes the principle of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is said that "one attains the emptiness of the Four Truths.

Following the attainment of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one proceeds to sever the eighty-one grades of innate (*sahaja*) afflictions across the three realms; for each grade severed, one realizes a portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta*).

Therefore, it is said that "through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one enters cessation. The meaning of the teaching on liberation may be understood by analogy with the above. The four types of noble beings (*ārya*) are not enumerated here.
"Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation.
If there are sentient beings who desire clear awakening (up to: he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve it), this corresponds to the various devas.
The Brahmā King is the Lord of the Form Realm, named Śikhin; this is translated as "Crest."
The *Sīng-luo* (Necklace) Sūtra clarifies that each of the four dhyānas has its own sovereign. What is here called "Brahmā" should refer to the summit of the first dhyāna;
because it possesses the dharmas of vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and speech, he is able to become the lord of a thousand worlds.

Regarding his preaching the Dharma, as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the Great Brahmā Heavenly King expounds the *Vairāgya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Departure from Desire). As for "liberation," it means causing one to leave behind the dust of desire. [Emperor] Di...
Commentary: "Śakra" refers to the second lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who preaches the Dharma; this refers to the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśaladharma*).
"Īśvara" is the highest heaven of the desire realm. "Maheśvara" is Maheśvara, the lord of the summit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

However, by first mentioning the Brahmā King and then leaping from the heavens of the desire realm directly to the summit of the form realm, it is clarified that there is no land where he does not manifest.

If there are sentient beings who desire to preside over spirits and deities, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success. The preceding passage cited the orthodox rulers; this passage cites their ministers and assistants.

The Heavenly General is the supreme commander of Śakra-devānām-indra and presides over spirits and deities. The Four Heavenly Kings are subjects of Śakra and preside over the world. The Princes of the Four Heavens are... (namely, Nanda... *Note:

The original text appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist scripture, likely from the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* or a related text concerning the "Assembly of the Great Collection" (*Mahāsannipāta*). The fragment describes the hierarchy of celestial beings and the Buddha's skillful means in teaching them.*
The *ḍāka*s and their like are able to expel ghosts and spirits.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma for them so that they may achieve success as kings over ministers, officials, and commoners.
From the Golden Wheel-turning King down to the "scattered grain" kings, all are human kings. "Scattered grain" refers to...
The kings of the various states are scattered throughout the world as numerous as grains of millet. One who possesses the ten virtues is called a "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*):
namely, noble lineage, high rank, great wealth, majestic power, profound wisdom, advanced age, pure conduct, complete etiquette, being praised by those above, and being revered by those below.

Therefore, he is the head of his clan; the world defers to him. He dwells in seclusion to pursue his aspirations and practices righteousness to realize the Way; thus he is called a *jushi* (lay practitioner).

He delights in discussing sublime names and phrases, which refers here to elegant and refined discourse. [He may hold the rank of] the Three Ducal Ministers (*santai*), a Chancellor (*fuxiang*), or a Provincial Governor (*zhoumu*).
