Snowy-mountain cow’s milk is entirely *mahāmṛta* (clarified butter); its dregs are most fragrant and pure.
Simply blending it with a single flavor of *candana* (sandalwood) is sufficient to smear the ground. If this is lacking..."
Then, take deep, pure yellow earth and mix it with the powder of the ten fragrances to form mud.
Use this to smear the ground, creating an eight-cornered altar sixteen feet square (until) the incense is burned until the smoke has vanished, making offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This demonstrates the method for binding the maṇḍala, arranging the ritual implements, and making offerings.

The purpose of establishing these arrangements within the maṇḍala is to focus the mind upon a sublime realm, thereby eliminating distracting conditions so that one may devote oneself single-mindedly to the path of practice. Regarding the offerings presented, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not consume this food;
rather, they manifest eating it in order to increase the merit of others, thereby causing the practitioner’s merit and wisdom to flourish.
It is complete. Just as the Buddha accepted Cunda’s final offering so as to enable him to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, this case is likewise. Therefore, one must make offerings.
Have banners and flowers hung everywhere on the four outer sides (until) their forms and shadows overlap one another in layers.

This demonstrates the method for suspending and arranging [the icons] both inside and outside. At the central position facing the sun are Vairocana and others, the true lords of the site of tranquility.
Maitreya is the true lord of the future. Akṣobhya resides in the east; Amitābha resides in the west. Wisdom...
The Compassionate Lord is the true master. The various great transformations of the forms of Avalokiteśvara—uniting above and harmonizing below—are the true masters.
Vajragarbha, who constantly leads those who recite the Vajra-protective mantras, is the true master who subdues demons and severs hindrances.
To the left and right of the gate stand the assemblies of Śakra, Brahmā, and others; they are the powerful external protectors. In practicing during the Dharma-ending age, all rely upon these.
If even one of these is lacking, [the rite] will certainly not be accomplished. Ucchuṣma, Kṛṣṇa-jambhaka, Nīla-mukha-vajra, and Cundā are alternative names for Vajrapāṇi.
Bhṛkuṭī is also a deity of great supernatural transformations, and so forth.
The *Vairocana-vikurvāṇa-sūtra* states that this refers to the three-eyed Piṅgala with a topknot on the left side.
Piṇāka is the pair of messengers with the heads of a pig and an elephant. The mirrors for the upper and lower directions face each other across the cardinal points.
The fact that their forms and shadows are layered and interpenetrating is intended to demonstrate the characteristic of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

It seeks to cause one to accord with this in order to cultivate the great practice of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If one can cultivate the great practice of the Dharma-realm, then a single flower or a single incense offering will universally reach all lands as numerous as atoms;
a single action or a single characteristic will expand infinitely. Thus, these arrangements above and below are established.
This is not merely a matter of formality.
During the first seven days, one should perform prostrations with utmost sincerity until the body and mind become as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.
Whatever one aspires toward, taking refuge in the Triple Gem must be regarded as the primary expedient means; therefore, on the first seven days—

I sincerely prostrate to the names of the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats. It is by relying on their inconceivable power that one initiates the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
However, without the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), there would be no means to sustain it;

therefore, during the second seven-day period, one should single-mindedly make vows in accordance with the Vinaya teachings. When conduct and vows are firm and strong, one attains great valor (*vīrya*); thus, the third...

If one recites and maintains this divine mantra continuously for twenty-one days without interruption, one will ultimately be able to move the deities through sincere devotion and achieve success through diligent effort.
When mirrors reflect each other’s light, the Buddha-wisdom arises as illumination; thus, the path of response and resonance intersects.
That the body and mind become clear and pure means that the obstacles of past habitual tendencies have been utterly eradicated; this is the achievement of success through resonance.
This is the matter.

Ānanda, if this bhikṣu’s original preceptor [is such], and you ask about the establishment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in this manner, one who attains *srotāpanna* is said to have entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*).
However, regarding the ritual procedures and characteristics of the altar (*maṇḍala*), in this land at the end of the age...
The practices of the world are indeed difficult to perform. However, regarding the dhāraṇī to be recited, the subsequent text also permits its use outside of the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*).
Thus, those with the karmic affinity may receive benefit according to their capacity.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, [saying]... until... the Tathāgata Prabhāsa proclaimed this divine dhāraṇī.
In the past, Ānanda secretly relied on the power of mantras to resolve his difficulty regarding lust; thus it was said that he had "darkly obtained what had not been heard.
Now he requests a public exposition once more, his intention being to compassionately save those present in this assembly as well as those of the future.
*Namastathāgatāya* (up to) *svāhā* (427). This refers to incantation (*dhāraṇī*), also called "incantatory prayer" (*dhāraṇī-praṇidhāna*).

With these words, the Buddha invokes blessings for sentient beings, so that they may give rise to goodness and extinguish evil, transforming from the mundane to the sacred—just as the *gonglo* wasp incants over the *mingling* caterpillar. It is also a secret exposition of the *Śūraṅgama*.
The meaning of "strict" (or "solemn") is no different from the previously mentioned power and function of explicit teaching; it merely differs in its application to sentient beings.
Some say that explicit teaching brings about understanding and thus generates wisdom, while secret teaching brings about recitation and thus generates merit. This is generally the case.
Ānanda, even if one were to spend eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges reciting this *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-raśmi-samuccaya Sūtra*, one could never reach its end.
This "mantra-heart" (*dhāraṇī-hṛdaya*) is the Great White Parasol, vast and untainted, which completely covers the Dharma-realm;
it is the secret dharma-gate of the Tathāgata-garbha mind. Because it is vast and all-encompassing as the Tathāgata-garbha, one should uphold it.

By means of this, one is able to give birth to all Buddhas and achieve unsurpassed enlightenment; to subdue demons through responsive transformations; and to rescue and deliver beings from manifold sufferings, as well as other meritorious qualities.
Even if one were to speak for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could not exhaustively describe them. [This applies to] those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and so forth.
This briefly enumerates four of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), such as enmity, hatred, and separation from loved ones; it briefly enumerates four of the eight sufferings (*aṣṭa-duḥkha*).

According to the *Guǎngdìng jīng* (Consecration Sūtra), there are nine great calamities and innumerable minor calamities. "Gathering those with karmic affinities" means gathering all those who possess the conditions for connection.

It is also said that this mantra is named "The Tathāgata’s Crown" (tathāgatoṣṇīṣa). [The phrase] "...it is impossible for various demonic activities to exist" reveals the realm of the Tathāgata above;
this clarifies that it also encompasses gradual cultivation; and the following reveals the benefits of upholding the mantra.

Ānanda, if in all worlds, according to their respective lands... [down to] ...they shall all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection—such that fire cannot burn them and so forth—this is precisely what is meant by "protecting the world and attaining great fearlessness.
Because one benefits others through the recitation of mantras, all the evil kings of ghosts acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection. Gold and silver enter...
Medicine. Or it may provoke poison.
Ānanda, you should know that this mantra always [leads to] thorough and pervasive knowledge, such that one attains freedom from doubt;
this is precisely what is called "accomplishing the supramundane wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings. "Refined mind, secretly swift," etc., refers to refinement.

The mental aggregate serves as a support. When the spiritual consciousness is swiftly developed and becomes penetratingly clear, one is then able to remember and fully comprehend the events of eighty-four thousand Ganges-sands of kalpas, attaining freedom from all doubt.
From the first kalpa until the final body—down to states that are impoverished, lowly, and unpleasant—the "first kalpa" refers to the initial time of generating the mind and practicing.
Up until the time of the Bodhisattva’s final body, one does not fall among the various intermediate classes during this interval;
even if born among humans, one is neither poor nor lowly, because of [the power of] upholding...
Because the Dharma is most honored and supreme, the body is also honored and supreme.
Thus, even though these sentient beings do not themselves observe the fast or the precepts, they naturally come to possess the fast and the precepts.
This clarifies the benefits of reciting, copying, and making offerings to the divine mantra mentioned previously.

It means that by not engaging in conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) karma, one spontaneously attains untainted (*anāsrava*) merit. The term "raising the *ṛṣi*" serves as a metaphor for sentient beings; the "merits of all Buddhas" refers to the qualities of the Buddhas.
These three factors must converge. Therefore, below, the attainment of the fruit by Mātaṅgī serves as proof that this is not false.
However, one must find the right person to uphold [this practice]. Thus, it was said previously that if even one factor is impure, success will generally not be achieved;

and it was said later that if one maintains the precepts according to the Dharma, one will surely attain mental penetration (*cittābhijñā*). Let the practitioner examine this carefully; do not harbor vain expectations.
Ānanda, when these good men uphold this dhāraṇī (up to the point where it says) "all are completely extinguished and removed, without even a hair's breadth remaining.
This clarifies that upholding the dhāraṇī can eliminate karmic offenses. "Before receiving it" means before upholding the dhāraṇī.

The "four abandonments" (*catur-pārājika*) of a bhikṣu refer to the four fundamental grave offenses: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. In the Sanskrit language, these are called *pārājika*. This...
"Parājika" (Defeat) means that one who commits this offense is forever cast outside the boundaries of the Buddha-dharma, like a corpse that the great ocean will not accept.

For bhikṣuṇīs, four additional parājikas are added, namely: touching, the eighth [offense], concealment, and following. That is to say: fifth, one must not, with a defiled mind, touch the body of a man;
sixth, one must not, with a defiled mind, allow a man to grasp one's hand or one's robe, nor enter a secluded place [with him].

The eight matters [of improper conduct] include: standing together in a secluded place, conversing together in a secluded place, walking together in a secluded place, physical contact, making mutual appointments, and so forth.

The seventh is that one must not conceal the grave offenses of others. The eighth is that one must not follow those who have been formally censured by the Great Saṃgha by providing them with food and clothing;

specifically, one must not associate with those who have been censured by the Saṃgha and for whom the rite of communal residence (*sāṃvāsika-dharma*) has not yet been performed. This applies to all the aforementioned cases.
It is called the "Eight Abandonments. That which is "proposed by the Saṃgha" carries the sense of being formally accused or exposed.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings... [up to] ...all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished.
"Miscellaneous forms" refers to categories such as ghosts and animals. "Caitya" (支提) means a place worthy of offerings; it is a general term for a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*).
"Dhvaja" (脫闍) means a banner or standard.
"Ānanda, in every land and in every place where sentient beings dwell, no evil calamities or portents can ever enter.

When the heavens act contrary to their seasons and things oppose the natural order, these are what constitute disasters; yet such contrariness and opposition are fundamentally caused by human beings, while the heavens and the material world merely respond to them.
What are called 'calamitous transformations' and 'malevolent stars' are simply responses to the misfortunes of humanity."
These are the evil ones. There are eighty-four thousand, corresponding to the afflictions and karmas of sentient beings. Twenty-eight represent the regulations of the four directions;
eight represent the principles of the five elements, as well as Rāhu, Ketu, and Bhauma. If one follows them correctly, blessings respond; if one acts contrary to them, calamities respond.

This is what is meant by "following the path of kindness brings good fortune; following the path of rebellion brings misfortune. Those capable of producing disasters and anomalies likewise correspond [to these principles].

It is merely a matter of reversal. Like comets, meteors, and flying stars, these are manifestations corresponding to the collective karma (*sabhāgatā*) of beings, not the actions of the constellations themselves.

Now, through the power of incantations, a hundredfold auspiciousness is harmonized; thus, all malevolent transformations are extinguished in the heavens, and neither calamity nor ill omen enters its borders.
"Auspicious" (*xiáng*) refers to the preliminary signs of good or evil fortune.
Therefore, if the Tathāgata were to proclaim this mantra [and it were ineffective], then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods.
Regarding "penetration of the mind," based on what was previously explained, it does not exceed three meanings. First is the realization of the fruit:

that is, by sitting upright for one hundred days, those of sharp faculties shall attain the stage of *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) without rising from their seats. Second is the development of understanding; namely—
Even though their physical and mental bodies have not yet attained the holy fruit, they know with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood will not be in error.

Third is the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*): this means that such a person, at the appropriate time, is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas, knowing them exhaustively and without any doubt.
Having spoken these words, immeasurable [beings] within the assembly attained the realization of Bodhi, such that they would forever be free from demonic interference.
As for the Wind Master who sets the wind in motion and the Wind King who presides over the winds: this refers to the raising of the Earth Deities following the Heaven of No Form.

Previously, Brahmā and Śakra were raised, reaching as far as the three heavens; subsequently, Earth and Water were raised, yet Wind and Fire remained unexhausted. Therefore, it concludes by raising Wind.
"By means of 'deities,' he encompasses the four great elements; by mentioning 'formless realms,' he encompasses the three realms.
At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas [of deities]... (until) they shall always cause this person’s actions to be fulfilled according to their wishes."
The aforementioned multitude of spirits have all attained their fundamental wondrous mind and abide in Śūraṅgama Samādhi;

they are able to establish great principles and manifest the forms of bodhisattvas, devas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth, to protect and sustain practitioners. As for the statement that [the demon] had his head crushed by a precious vajra-pestle:
when Great Sages instruct sentient beings, they may employ either methods of gathering and receiving or methods of subduing and suppressing. Regarding the various wicked ones...
As for their withdrawal from the world, some were moved by his kindness, while others were struck with awe by his majesty; through these two paths, he enabled all to attain deliverance.

Now, he practices subjugation to cause them to revere his majesty—just as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of killing the icchantikas, the *Lotus Sūtra* of destroying all afflictions and disturbances, the execution of Śrīprabha against those of pure conduct, and the punishment of sentient beings by Pūrṇa—all of which arise from abiding in non-attachment.
By relying on loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one attains the stage of being the only child (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*); only then can one act in this manner.

From the passage in the fourth fascicle where [the Bodhisattva] requests entry into the jeweled house until this point, it is collectively termed the "Section on the Cultivation of the Path" (*bhāvanā-mārga-vibhāga*).

The subsequent text begins separately and is named the "Section on the Realization of the Fruit" (*phala-sākṣātkriyā-vibhāga*). Indeed, the reason the Section on the Realization of the Fruit extensively demonstrates the stages of cultivation and realization is that these stages possess causes.
Regarding the fruits: delusions have degrees of coarseness and subtlety; wisdom has degrees of clarity and obscurity; severance has degrees of shallowness and depth;

realization has degrees of partiality and fulfillment; and function has degrees of superiority and inferiority. If one is ignorant of these principles, one’s practice is not genuine. Thus, one passes through fifty-seven stages, entering and deepening gradually;
this is unlike the non-Buddhists and celestial demons, who possess no such stages at all. If one does not discern this in advance, one’s progress will deviate from the source.
Since they are ignorant of both severance and realization, they mistakenly recognize a minor attainment and consider it sufficient, thereby falling into the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*).
This matter is not a trivial one; therefore, it must be clearly explained so as to avoid incurring great error.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and—[omitting intermediate text]—stood waiting for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up with a fixed and vacant stare.
He recounted past events and set forth his benefits, inquiring about the stages of cultivation and realization.

Regarding the phrase "attaining correct cultivation," it means to cultivate based on awakening, with the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings complementing one another and precepts and meditative concentration providing mutual support; thus, he attained a state of physical and mental bliss and obtained the Great [Dharma].
This refers to benefit. The ultimate fruit of the noble stages is called *nirvāṇa*. The initial cause is called "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

From dry wisdom, one enters the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and dedication, as well as the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), which constitute forty-four moments of mind. These include the practices of application and dedication.
"Practice" refers to the cultivation [of the path]. Advancing further through the ten stages (*bhūmi*) is called "entering the stages," which constitutes the initial realization.

Reaching the eleventh stage is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); this is still a partial realization. Upon reaching *nirvāṇa*, it is called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*), which is the ultimate realization.
To fix one's gaze is called "staring"; to darken the mind is called "blinding. However, Ānanda has merely inquired about the stages of practice and realization.
As for the Tathāgata’s subsequent text, which first clarifies the nature of awakening (*bodhi-dhātu*), next distinguishes delusion and falsehood, and finally demonstrates the gradual stages:

this refers to the fact that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, fundamentally transcending both ordinary beings and sages, and is likewise devoid of cultivation or realization. Because of delusion, falsehood arises;

because of inversion, [the world] is produced. Only after the extinction of falsehood is it called "true," and only then do the stages of cultivation and realization begin to exist. For this reason, he next distinguishes delusion.

[The text] says that arising and ceasing are termed "delusion. Later, it demonstrates the gradual stages; by demonstrating the cessation of delusion as "truth," there thus come to be the stages of cultivation and realization.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, [extending] up to the two designations of the Great Nirvāṇa and the Two-fold Transformation of the Basis (*dvividha-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
"Proclaimed for display" means that it is first shown to those who practice *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna, so that they may not misrecognize [the path] and fall into error.
"Unsurpassed" means that regarding the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) shown for cultivation and advancement, there is no dharma that can surpass them.
"The correct path of cultivation" refers to the fifty-five stages mentioned below; these constitute the true path for the practitioner. "To hollow out the mind" means to hollow out...
Set aside discursive thoughts and receive the teaching with an empty mind. Birth-and-death, truth-and-falsity, bodhi, and nirvana—all these are what are called various names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*).
Within the wondrous nature, they are fundamentally and perfectly transcended. It is due to the causes of deluded and false appearances that there is cultivation and realization;
thus, one turns away from non-awakening to rely upon bodhi, and turns away from birth-and-death to rely upon nirvana. This is called...
These are the two names for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
"Ānanda, you now wish to cultivate the true *samādhi*" (up to) "...this is the Tathāgata’s true *samādhi*.
This restates the previous question, while first causing [the practitioner] to recognize the false and know the true. Now, one who wishes to cultivate *samādhi* must...
Regarding the Great Nirvāṇa: one must first recognize that these inverted delusions are without cause.
When inverted delusions do not arise, this is precisely the Tathāgata’s true samādhi—namely, to know that illusion is itself departure, and to depart from illusion is itself awakening.

If one can truly realize that delusion is fundamentally empty and that reality is fundamentally pure, and then practice in reliance upon this, the causes of inversion can be eliminated and Nirvāṇa may be attained.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion" (*viparyāsa*) of sentient beings? [This section] establishes the worlds and all sentient beings.
To clarify the inversion of sentient beings, this first explains the origin of the two types of inversion.

The two lines beginning with "By nature" (*xing*) clarify that the True [Nature] is fundamentally without birth. The two lines beginning with "Because of ignorance" (*yin ming*) clarify that birth arises due to delusion. From here it concludes.
The final two lines clarify that delusion arises based on the True. The following four lines clarify that deluded phenomena have neither cause nor origin.

The subsequent three lines conclude by clarifying how the world and sentient beings arise. The phrase "Because the nature is luminous and the mind-nature is perfectly bright" restates the preceding point to show that, fundamentally, there were no worlds or sentient beings; it was due to delusion [that they appeared].
This "fundamental luminosity" refers to the false perception of worlds and sentient beings within the state of signlessness (*animitta*).
Thus, worlds and sentient beings arise from false perception; hence it is said that "due to luminosity, the nature is manifested, and this nature gives rise to false perception.

Since all phenomena are falsely produced by the deluded mind, they depend upon the signless reality to constitute these signs of delusion; therefore, it is said that "from ultimate non-existence, [existence] is established."
Ultimately they exist. However, these phenomena that can give rise to ignorance are all falsely existent;
since they originally lack a cause to serve as their cause, it is said that "they are not caused by a cause. Furthermore, these phenomena that abide within ignorance originally have no root;
therefore, it is said that "they are utterly without a fundamental basis. Thus, since all phenomena arise from...
That which is ultimately non-existent yet becomes existent is precisely the establishment of all dharmas from the root of non-abiding. Thus it is said:

"Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established. This refers to the arising of the three subtle states with ignorance as the cause, as described in the *Awakening of Faith*.
To be deluded regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity is the phase of the karma of ignorance; to give rise to the nature based on that luminosity is the transformation [of consciousness].
Two aspects appear. "Manifestation" (xian) refers to the aspect of transformation; the nature of the worlds and sentient beings that are thereby produced is the aspect of manifestation.
To be deluded regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity is to give rise to false constructions. ... (up to) for this reason there are the inverted states of sentient beings.
This clarifies how delusion regarding the truth and pursuit of the false result in the perversion of sentient beings.
The first two lines of the second section clarify that delusion arises based upon the truth. The first two lines of the third section clarify that the nature of delusion is unreal.

The three lines beginning with "Wishing to" clarify that one does not know the essential means for returning to the source. The final two lines illustrate how seeking outwardly is not the way to give rise to [enlightenment].
The following eight lines correctly clarify the characteristics of perversion (*viparyāsa*). By means of the final two lines, the perversion of sentient beings is established.

Regarding the phrase "being deluded by the fundamental perfect luminosity gives rise to false constructs" and so forth: this means that all delusive phenomena arise from being deluded by the fundamental luminosity.

From the beginning, there has been no self-substance; it does not have anything upon which to rely. If one realizes that there is neither reliance nor substance, then right here and now is the true mind.
This is what is called the non-arising of inversion; this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi. How could there be a duality between the real and the false?
Because one fails to realize this, if one attempts to turn back from the false to restore the real, then the real and the false become two. Therefore, it is said:

Since that which has already ceased is not the true *tathatā* (suchness), how much more so when one seeks to restore what is not true—this merely results in the manifestation of non-characteristics (*animitta*).

Because one cannot realize that the delusive is itself the true, one consequently gives rise to the mind based on the Dharma, and the mind abides within the Dharma; thus it is said they "arise successively.
Since both the arising and abiding of the mind and its objects are delusive, it is said they are "not [real]. To give rise to the mind based on the Dharma is precisely the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

Taking the realms as conditions, the characteristic of wisdom arises; this is the characteristic of continuity. Because the mind abides in dharmas, through these two aforementioned characteristics, there further arises grasping;
this is the characteristic of calculating names and words. The mutual arising of mind and dharmas is precisely the power of birth that brings forth illumination.

These four are all delusions (*moha*). Perfumed by them, karma is formed; this is the characteristic of the arising of karma. Because there is responsive karma, birth and cessation continue in succession;
this is the characteristic of suffering bound by karma. Because these three—delusion, karma, and suffering—exist, sentient beings fall into perversion;
this is the arising of the six coarse states (*ṣaḍ-audārikatā*) with the objective realm of the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* as their condition.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world" (up to: "transforming sentient beings into twelve classes")?

This refers to how, based on the inversion of the world, one becomes born into the twelve classes of beings. These include such things as "existence," "that which exists," and the false arising of segmented [existence].
Because there is the capacity for existence, there is ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, there is the segmentation of east, west, south, and north. This points to this very segmentation.
The designation of "sections" is termed *dhātu* (realms). Now, since the characteristics of these realms are established based on delusion, what cause could they possibly have?
Therefore, it is said that they are "neither causes nor the basis for causes. Their abiding is merely an illusory abiding; thus, it is said that there is "no abiding and nothing to abide in.

Since they are not the eternally abiding true nature, they undergo the flux of past, present, and future without remaining still; thus, the three periods of time are formed. By means of these periods, the spatial dimensions are traversed.
When the directions and the world interpenetrate, they harmoniously combine to form twelve. Thus, the primary retribution of sentient beings also becomes twelvefold.
In the previous fourth fascicle, the directions and the world interpenetrated and were further augmented by the three layers of flux and transformation;

there, in contrast to the secondary retribution, the merits of the six sense organs of primary retribution were revealed to be twelve hundred each. Herein, they interpenetrate [in a different manner].
Because one follows the correct by relying on it, the twelve classes of beings are explained in relation to the world.
Therefore, from movement in the world there arises sound (and so forth), until, exhausting the twelve transformations, they become a single revolving cycle.
This is presented to clarify the causes for the cyclic transmigration of the twelve classes of beings.

However, the movement of thought and the arising of perception are fundamentally without priority or sequence; it is simply because [the truth] cannot be manifested all at once that they are explained as following one another.

Regarding the phrase "due to movement there is sound and so forth," this means that when a single moment of deluded movement arises within the inner mind, one then perceives external sounds and forms; since the mind has already arisen...
Thus it is. All phenomena arise simultaneously; therefore, form, fragrance, as well as seeing, hearing, and so forth, all arise together.

Since the faculties and their objects interweave to form six types of deluded conceptualization, which constitute the nature of karma, the twelve classes of beings revolve incessantly through these deluded thoughts.
Therefore, the following section reiterates and concludes the preceding text regarding sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, thereby reiterating and concluding the six [sense objects].

Chaos and deluded conceptualization exhaust the twelve transformations as a single cycle of return (*xuánfù*). By enumerating the twelve divisions, their differentiation arises from this revolving cycle.

This refers to exhausting the transmigrations and changes of the twelve classes of beings; because these are the cycles of return of the sixfold chaos and deluded conceptualization, it is said that "the twelve divisions revolve from this.
*Xuánfù* (cycle of return) is synonymous with *lúnzhuǎn* (revolving cycle).
Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted perceptions, [they reach] the state that is neither with perception nor without perception.
This vehicle, based on the cause of perception and the fruit of karma, generally clarifies the twelve classes of living beings.

Since inversion is the cause of perception and the cycling [of existence] is the fruit of karma, this section thus clarifies the twelve classes of living beings by way of their general characteristics. Below—
Regarding their distinct characteristics: in saṃsāra there are distinctions such as the false and the defiled; in perversion there are divisions such as agitation and desire.
Ānanda, from "due to the world's false saṃsāra" (up to) "fish, birds, turtles, and snakes, filling every category."
The egg-born arises from thought; this delusion is precisely thought itself. Because of these false thoughts, one transmigrates through egg-birth.

The essence of thought is buoyant and light, which is termed "movement" and "inversion. The egg is formed by the blending of vital energies, termed "the formation through the harmony of energies. Thought fluctuates between ascent and descent.
This is called the "confused thoughts of flying and sinking. Thus, the species of egg-birth that fly and sink arise from eighty-four thousand confused thoughts of flying and sinking.
That each category of deluded thought consists of eighty-four thousand is because each is produced by the transformation induced by eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).
*Kalala* means "coagulated slime," the initial stage of entering the womb, before the embryo has formed.
This is their characteristic.
From "due to the world of defiled saṃsāra" (up to) "humans, beasts, dragons, and immortals, their species fill [the world].
As for "the womb is due to emotion," defilement is precisely emotion. Because of this defilement, one undergoes saṃsāric birth from a womb; it is birth through emotion.
Regarding craving, it is called the inversion of desire. Regarding the union of semen and blood, it is called the formation through harmonious blending.

Regarding the partiality or correctness of mental states, it is called the confused thoughts of horizontal or vertical [orientation]. Thus, one is reborn among the various classes of humans and animals, characterized by horizontal or vertical [birth].

*Ārbuda* refers to the "blister," which is the stage where the embryo or egg gradually begins to differentiate. Sentient beings are all subject to false delusions, defilements, attachments, and obstructions.

[Included]. However, they are merely categorized according to what predominates in their respective retributions. Regarding the four modes of birth (*yoni*): that which arises from an egg is called oviparous (*aṇḍaja*);

that which emerges from being contained within a womb is called viviparous (*jarāyuja*); that which arises through the moisture of humidity is called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*); and that which suddenly exists where there was none is called transformation-born (*upapāduka*).
These four modes of birth have the internal mental volitions and karma as their cause, while external factors such as shells, wombs, and moisture serve as conditions.

These serve as conditions. Depending on the number of conditions required, they are established in this sequence: those born from eggs possess all four; therefore, they are mentioned first. Those born from wombs possess three;
those born from moisture possess two; and those born by transformation possess only one. This is according to the interpretation of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Due to the world’s attachment to saṃsāra (up to) its being filled with crawling and wriggling insects, moisture serves as the cause for conjunction.
Attachment is itself conjunction. Because of this attachment, one undergoes moist-birth within saṃsāra. Conjunction arises from the stagnation of craving;

by contacting objects, one moves toward and clings to them—this is called "perversion of movement. Moisture gives rise to life through yang-energy; this is called "formation through the union of warmth."
Their destination is not fixed; this is called "reversing and disordered thought. Consequently, they are reborn as wriggling and reversing creatures.
*Bishu* (蔽尸) refers to soft flesh, which is the initial sign of moisture-born beings. Since they do not enter a womb, they lack the first two stages [of embryonic development].

All ten types of birth are rooted in sexual desire and arise from emotional conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Because deluded emotions become increasingly false, the principle of transformation becomes increasingly [obscured].

They diverge, leading some to become as empty and dispersed as the wind, while others become as dull as wood or stone. Although these deluded manifestations differ at their branches, the root of delusion is one and the same.
From this cause, through the cycle of the world’s transformation and transmigration, beings evolve and migrate until they fill every space, flying and crawling in all their various forms.
Transformation occurs through separation and response; change is itself separation. Because of this change, one undergoes rebirth within saṃsāra, departing from this and entrusting oneself to that;

this is termed "false inversion. As it touches various categories and transforms, it is termed "the formation of contact through conjunction"; thus, by turning away from the old, one moves toward the new.
This is called "confusion between the new and the old. Therefore, the resulting retribution is likewise so. *Tui* (蛻) means to cast off the old and proceed toward the new;
it is like a worm becoming a butterfly, whereby walking is transformed into flying. Or like a sparrow becoming a clam, whereby flying is cast off for submergence.

Generally, whenever different forms are transmitted to one another, it is all a process of transformation and casting off (*zhuan-tui*). *Kalala* (羯南) refers to hard flesh; once the casting off is complete, the body is formed, and there is no longer any softness.
This refers to the stage of *saṃsthāna* (form). From this point downward, all are designated as *kalala*; this is the general designation for all classes [of beings].
If the fifth stage, *peśī*, were called "formed" (*saṃsthāna*), then it would apply only according to its specific appearance and would not be a general designation.

Due to the causes of worldly obstructions and the cycle of rebirth, [sentient beings] reach the point where they possess the spiritual power of prognosticating good and ill fortune; their kind fills the world.

They serve the sun, moon, water, and fire, blending with their light while clinging to them with firm persistence and refusing to let go. Because they create barriers that prevent free passage, this is called "obstruction" (*liuai*);
it is also called "obstructed inversion. Because their spiritual power is clear and manifest, they take birth based upon this; hence it is called "form" (*rūpa*).
Regarding signs: the stars, planets, sun, and moon—those that are auspicious are termed "rests" (xiū), while those that are inauspicious are termed "calamities" (jiù).
Even things such as torches and the pearls of oysters belong to this same category. Furthermore, all brilliant and spiritual entities are manifestations of refined radiance (*jīngyào*).
Because their conceptualization has already coalesced into refined radiance, they possess only form. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the eighty deities are all due to the persistence of obstructions.

One perceives that the source of thought constitutes this refined radiance. Although this is extremely refined and spiritual, it has not yet transcended the state of being carried along by the cycle of birth and death and its inverted characteristics.
Due to the world dissolving from its causes, beings revolve [in saṃsāra] until they become dispersed into emptiness and sink away, filling the void with their kind.
To loathe existence and cling to emptiness, to extinguish the body and return to non-existence, is called the cycle of dissolution. To be deluded and ignorant is called the inversion of confusion.

To loathe existence and return to non-existence is to rely upon the dark and obscure void; therefore, it is called "the formation through the union with darkness," and is termed the "subtle, hidden, and chaotic ideation.
Although this involves ideation without form, it is not without the substance of karma; hence it is also called *karma*.
South. Here, delusion and karma are heavy and dark; form and color are worn away; the body merges with empty obscurity; and consciousness clings to the hidden aggregates.
This is the category of those who are scattered, dissolved, and submerged in emptiness.
From the world’s cause of the phantom-like cycle of rebirth (up to) gods, ghosts, and spirits, their kinds fill the void.

They are deluded and have lost the truth, falsely attached to shadows and images. Just as non-Buddhists and ordinary people pray to deities and rely upon physical forms, they are thus called "phantoms" (*wangxiang*);
yet it is said that these are inverted shadows. Such beings as those who follow tracks and cling to shadows—

All arise from recollective conceptualization; thus it is said that they are formed through the conjunction of recollection. Because chaotic thoughts are secretly bound together, appearances and forms are secretly formed within the realm of the indistinct.
When the spirit is not luminous, it becomes a ghost in its obscurity; when the essence is incomplete, it disperses as a numinous being.
Having no substantial color, there exists only the appearance of conceptualization; therefore it is said: "The kalala flows and transmigrates through the appearance of conceptualization."
This refers to the land.
From the cycle of delusion and dullness within the world (up to) earth, wood, stone, and metal, which fill it to overflowing. Externalists reckon that insentient things possess life;
they consider stone and metal to be solid and firm, or they practice meditative concentration until their ash-like bodies congeal, their thoughts becoming exclusively withered and parched.

It is withered; hence it is called "delusion. What is meant by "withered and chaotic thoughts" is that the mind changes according to its objects and takes form upon encountering things, such as the case of the spiritual essence produced from a flower-pillar or the yellow-headed man turned into stone. This is because one does not understand the principle of the Truths.
They stubbornly cling to ignorance; being the very height of dull stupidity, they are obstinate and mindless, their spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone.
From the cycle of mutual dependence within the world (*yīn shìjiè xiāngdài lúnhuí*)... down to taking shrimp for eyes, such beings fill the realm.
Worldly people rely upon one another as mutual supports, using them as leverage to sustain their bodies and nourish their lives;

hence it is said they "depend on one another," which refers to the deluded thoughts of causal dependence. As karmic fruits revolve in succession, they do not receive bodies from within their own kind;
therefore, they are said to lack the characteristics of form and so forth, being like the water-jelly (*siphonota*), which takes water foam for its body and uses shrimp for its eyes. Fundamentally...
It is not that form exists inherently; rather, form is established in dependence upon other things. It cannot function by itself, yet it functions only in dependence upon other things.
Thus, one loses the true nature of heaven and becomes entangled in floating falsehoods. As these differing substances combine through the conditions of defilement, it is called "relying on causes."
Due to the mutual attraction of the world's phenomena, beings revolve in saṃsāra (up to: through curses and malevolent incantations, their kind becomes pervasive.

Drawn together by such perverse karma, their natures become inverted; they mount these incantations and entrust their consciousnesses to them, not according to the laws of natural physiology, but following delusively at the call of others.
This refers to those born from worldly evil arts, curses, and malevolent spirits or haunting objects.
Furthermore, if one does not follow the principle of arising, then fundamentally there would be no form. Since it is stimulated and becomes substantial, it is not without form.
Due to the world, false attachments combine to produce the cycle of rebirth (until: "different substances mutually form one another, their kinds filling all space").

Second, when false appearances combine with the nature and characteristics, they become utterly obscured. Different substances mutually constitute one another, and the principles of their existence interact in a circular manner.

This is like the *pulu* (a caterpillar), which originally is a mulberry worm; it does not possess the perception of being a bee, yet it comes to possess the perception of being a bee. Because its substance is different [from that of a bee], it does not initially possess the characteristic of that perception;

yet, because the substances mutually constitute one another, it forms the perception of a bee at the stage of the *kalala*. To discuss the cause: it is like the worldly phenomenon of turning one's back on one's kin and turning toward what is righteous.
Forgetting their own origins and ancestral sacrifices, they recognize those [beings] as their own kin; this is the cause.
Due to this cause, throughout the world of enmity and harm in saṃsāra—[extending] until all encounter being devoured by them—their kind fills every space.

They retaliate against one another with enmity and harm; they wound and kill in mutual opposition. Their natural disposition is perverse and strange, and they abandon the righteousness of kinship. Consequently, they give rise to species such as the earth-owl (*tǔxiāo*).
These take form through clods of earth or poisonous fruits because their parents possess affection; thus, they are not called "non-percipient" (*asaṃjñin*) in terms of their appearance.
However, because these offspring harbor resentment and lack affection, they are termed "non-percipient. *Xiāo* is the name of a bird that eats its mother and breaks mirrors.
The Shi-fu (Eater of Fathers). Its form is like that of a wild boar, yet its eyes are like those of a tiger.
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings;

this is the summary. Because they all fail to understand the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, they become deluded and ensnared by emotional desires, and their accumulated falsehoods give rise to [these forms].

Beings are born and delusively follow the cycle of transmigration; without correct cultivation, none can escape it. Therefore, the following text demonstrates the method for eliminating delusion and attaining realization.

Previously, it was commanded that one recognize the falsity as being without cause; here, it further commands the removal of the very root of that falsity.

This means that because one must recognize that deluded consciousness is without cause before being capable of practicing its abandonment, these three gradual stages are established for the purpose of cultivation and abandonment regarding the fundamental cause of chaotic conceptualization.
As the sutra below states: "This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
This means that one immediately eliminates the six types of distracted deluded thoughts and enters samādhi.

Regarding the statement, "From this point, one gradually cultivates, and according to what is practiced, establishes the stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*)," the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is itself a sage-stage.

Yet Master Yue judges that attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) constitutes the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*), and further identifies the first abode and above as the sage-stages. All of these interpretations miss the fundamental intent of this sutra.

The meaning follows what is taught in other sutras. Indeed, some sutras indicate that one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), while others indicate it is attained at the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*); thus, according to what each sutra teaches, they differ from one another.
What is not yet understood is that this sutra states that upon attaining the patience of non-arising, one immediately enters *samādhi*, and by virtue of entering *samādhi*, [one...]
One ascends through the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*). Thus, we know that Dry Wisdom is itself the stage of the sages (*ārya*). Therefore, the passage on the *saṃjñā-skandha* states:

"From this ordinary body, one ascends through the sixty sage stages of the Bodhisattvas. Master Yue further explains the three "advancements" (*vṛddhi*) as the practice of universal clarity (*sāmānya-prakāśa*).
The fifty-five positions are specifically designated to distinguish between the ordinary and the sage; it is not by means of the third advancement that [the distinction] is established.
Regarding "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā): not only do the preceding and following sections of the sutra text fail to connect, but it would also imply that Dry Wisdom arises without cause.
Moreover, the subsequent sutra states: "Thus, by means of the three progressive advancements, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
How could it be that the third advancement does not establish the stage of Dry Wisdom? Furthermore...

The Sūtra states: "From the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This means that upon reaching the mind of Vajra-wisdom (*vajra-citta*), one first attains the initial stage of dry wisdom.
Thus, from the initial mind one progresses to Equal Enlightenment, and at Equal Enlightenment, one returns to the initial mind;
hence it is said that one "attains the initial dry wisdom. Master Yue further asserts that there are two types of dry wisdom in this Sūtra, namely: the dry wisdom prior to faith (*śraddhā*).
Regarding the "Vajra Dry Wisdom" (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*): it is because the sutra states that within the Vajra-mind there is first the "Dry Wisdom.
However, one must not fail to recognize that the concluding summary text says, "All these various stages are entered into gradually by means of vajra-contemplation," and so forth.

From this, one knows that the dry wisdom prior to the stage of faith is itself the Vajra Dry Wisdom; there are not two distinct types of dry wisdom. This is all the more evident when considering the subsequent sutra passages.
If one can enter the Bodhisattva’s Vajra-dry-wisdom through the mutual functioning of these stages, how could one believe that the preceding dry-wisdom is not the Vajra-dry-wisdom?
Master Yue further explains the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi, stating that if dry-wisdom is not true, then the causal mind is not true;
how then could one reach the ultimate, unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment? Furthermore...

The opening passage of the *Shixin wen* (Text on Initial Faith) states: "From true, wondrous, and perfect [wisdom], one again gives rise to true, wondrous, and perfect [wisdom]. How could it be that the stage of Dry Wisdom (*ganhui*) is not true?

Nevertheless, the annotations below all explain according to the primary intent of the sutra. This analysis is provided here because I fear you may wish to know the differences and similarities between the *Huigui jie* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Text) and the present commentary.
Ānanda, within each and every class of sentient beings, they are fully possessed of such false and deluded discursive thoughts (*vikalpa*).
This "knot" demonstrates the arising of inverted and deluded thoughts. "Each possesses" means they mutually possess them;

that is, the twelve inversions, from the inversion of movement to the inversion of killing. Since these seeds of delusion are fully present within the mind of each individual class, it is said: [they are fully possessed].
Each possesses these [distinctions], all of which arise from the inversion of the wondrously perfect [nature]. Thus, it is like pressing upon the eyes so that illusory flowers appear.

Now, this concluding demonstration of what arises from inverted and chaotic thoughts is intended to establish the three gradual stages of cultivation and severance (*śikṣā-krama*) by means of them, in order to restore the original state.
Therefore, the text immediately below establishes the three gradual stages based on the fundamental cause of chaotic thoughts.
Otherwise, the successive stages of the path would arise without cause.
As you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi—up to the third stage—you advance by counteracting your present karmic activities.
This passage reiterates the preceding question to demonstrate the method for cultivating and severing [delusions]. The first two phrases restate what was previously asked;

from "In this regard" (*yú shì*) onwards, it demonstrates the method for cultivation and severance. Now, one who wishes to cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi must establish three gradual stages (*tri-krama*) for the cultivation and severance of the two causes of inversion and the six disordered delusive thoughts; only then can the Buddha’s samādhi be realized.
The ground is like a clean vessel containing poison and honey; it must be washed clean with hot water, ash, and incense before it can hold nectar.

As for the phrase "How does one [proceed] below?", this interrogates and enumerates the three characteristics of cultivation and abandonment. "Gradual" means that one intends to hollow out the fundamental nature.
One must first eliminate auxiliary causes and seek to oppose present karma. To do so, one must first maintain the precepts to hollow out and rectify one's nature;
hence it is called "gradual progression.
What are the auxiliary causes? Ānanda, such a world (up to) constitutes the first stage of progressive cultivation.

This demonstrates the faults of consuming pungent roots (śīla-virama) in order to prohibit them. Regarding the four types of nutriment: the nutriment of humans is "edible food" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), meaning that what is consumed must consist of distinct portions.

The nutriment of ghosts and spirits is "contact-nutriment" (sparśa-āhāra); they are satisfied merely by inhaling contact. The nutriment of the dhyāna-heavens is "volition-nutriment" (manahsaṃcetanā-āhāra); when nutriment arrives, they are satisfied either by merely intending it.
The nutriment of the consciousness-heavens is "consciousness-nutriment" (vijñāna-āhāra); as they lack form and color, they subsist solely through the faculty of consciousness.
This simply clarifies that all sentient beings subsist by means of food; therefore, one should observe the precepts regarding food and abstain from the five pungent plants (*pañca-garaka*).

It is not necessary to cite other sources. As for the five pungent plants: internally they assist lust and anger, and externally they attract malevolent spirits and demons; thus they are called "auxiliary causes. The five pungent plants are: [ginger, garlic, leeks, onions, and asafoetida].
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Onions, garlic, leeks, scallions, and asafoetida. Master Ying said that "asafoetida" (*xingqu*) is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound;
its correct form is "xingyi" (*hingyī*). The Tripiṭaka Master Cimin stated that its root resembles a radish and emits a pungent odor once it emerges from the soil.
The Compassionate One traveled to that land and did not see its sprouts; since they do not exist here, it was not translated.
What is "right nature"? Ānanda, for such sentient beings... [up to] ...they do not give rise to attachment toward pure discipline.
This [rule] requires the observance of pure precepts to cultivate the correct nature. One must not drink alcohol, as this is the ultimate prevention of disorder.

One must not eat raw meat, as this is the ultimate prevention of killing. Within the Vinaya, all five types of fruit must be "purified by fire," demonstrating that one should not consume things possessing raw vitality.
Lust is like a venomous serpent or a hostile thief because it can destroy the Dharma-body and kill the life of wisdom. To "possess the body" is to commit the transgression of being without a body;
to "possess the mind" is to commit the transgression of being without thought.
When one achieves the perfection of the precepts, then regarding the world (up to) one shall not return to the world to repay debts.

Sexual misconduct and killing follow one another; theft and robbery involve mutual indebtedness. Because there is no restraint, these things occur; therefore, when the perfection of the precepts is achieved, these two types of karma will forever cease, and the cycle of retribution will also come to rest.
This refers to a person of pure conduct who cultivates *samādhi* through the second stage of progressive cultivation.

This indicates that for one who has previously achieved purity in the observance of precepts, by cultivating *samādhi*, they will attain unimpeded supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) in this very life. "This then" concludes the title.
"What is meant by 'present karma'? Ānanda, when one is thus pure [up to] not allowing much wandering or dissipation toward the six external sense-objects.
This clarifies the cause for violating present karma. For it is only when the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) do not couple that one violates present karma;
therefore, this "not allowing much wandering or dissipation" is pointed out as the cause for violating present karma, and it is also the cause for entering right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

Because the mind does not flow outwardly but returns to the source, it naturally reverts; (up to: this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because the mind does not flow outwardly, it reverses its flow and becomes entirely unified. This immediately opposes the karma of the present moment, and one attains the patience of non-arising.

When it flows, it divides the profound stillness and joins with the sense objects; thus, the faculties and objects interweave, forming the six confused delusions that give rise to the karma of the present.

When there is no outward flowing, then the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another. By reversing the flow and becoming entirely unified, one is able to oppose and transcend present karma.

Thus, "reversing the flow and becoming entirely unified" refers to the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) from ethical discipline (*śīla*). "The lands of the ten directions" and so forth refer to the manifestation of wisdom (*prajñā*) from meditative concentration.
Because the mind that has attained concentration and wisdom is joyful and tranquil, it is the pure and wondrous nature of the Tathāgata.
They manifest within it, and one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Furthermore, as previously stated: "Now you cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi;
regarding the original causes of your fundamental deluded thoughts, you must establish three gradual stages before they can be eliminated.

Since this involves reversing the flow [of consciousness] to become entirely unified and attaining the patience of non-arising, one immediately eliminates the six perceptions and enters samādhi. Below...

It says: "From this point, one gradually cultivates and establishes the stages of the sages (*āryabhūmi*). One practices in reliance upon *samādhi*, gradually severing the fundamental causes and advancing through the sage-stages.
Later it says: "This awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*prathamā śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) within the Vajra-mind."
He immediately returns to realize the Buddha-samādhi, exhausting the fundamental causes and reaching the ultimate limit of wondrous enlightenment.
Thus, one knows that what is entered here, what is cultivated below, and what is ultimately realized—all are the Buddha-samādhi;
therefore, it was previously stated that one "cultivates and realizes the Buddha-samādhi."
From this point, one gradually cultivates according to the practices undertaken, leading up to the third stage of progressive cultivation.
This clarifies that the realization of the noble stages is achieved by relying on the mind of non-arising forbearance (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

For when karma is purified and the nature is luminous, one can then initiate practice and ascend through the noble stages. These fifty-five positions correspond respectively to the various aspects of practice within the state of non-arising forbearance.
Names are established so that one may contemplate their meaning and know what to cultivate and progress toward.

Furthermore, these three gradual stages are precisely the three principles of definitive practice previously demonstrated. Why is this? Because by eliminating auxiliary causes and excising the nature of the mundane, [one attains the ultimate].

This means that one immediately gathers the mind to establish the precepts; until the point where present karmic activities are contravened and the flow [of consciousness] is reversed to attain patience (*kṣānti*), it is because concentration (*samādhi*) arises from the precepts, and wisdom (*prajñā*) is developed through concentration.

From this point onward, as one gradually cultivates according to the practices undertaken and establishes the stages of the sages (*āryabhūmi*), up to the various combinations of the twelve stages—whether single or repeated—it is likewise a matter of advancing in cultivation based on concentration and wisdom, until concentration and wisdom are perfected.

When perfect luminosity eliminates all outflows (*āsrava*) and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way, one will know that the three gradual stages, as well as the twelve [methods]—both simple and combined—do not transcend the three of precept, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, the conclusion below states:
"These various stages all involve entering deeply and gradually through *vajra*-like cessation and contemplation."

Ānanda, these good men whose craving for desire has dried up—[up to] "have not yet joined with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma"—this refers to the inclusion of what was previously attained, thereby constituting the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
"Craving for desire has dried up" refers to the aforementioned absence of greed and lust in the mind.

"Root and object do not meet" refers to the aforementioned state where, since the sense objects (*viṣaya*) are no longer conditioned, the sense faculties (*indriya*) have nothing with which to meet. This is the remnant remaining before one's eyes.
As for the physical body no longer continuing its rebirth: it is because desire-love moistens karma, and the faculties and objects create karma, such that birth and death continue in succession;
this is all there is to it. Thus, when desire withers and objects fade away, they oppose the manifest karma; therefore, the residual body does not continue.

As for the mind of grasping becoming empty and luminous, being purely wisdom: this refers to the aforementioned reversal of the flow to become entirely unified, wherein the six functions [of the senses] do not [proceed outward].
This is practice. Because it maintains oneness, the mind is held in empty clarity; because the six functions do not operate, wisdom is purely pure.

As for "the nature of wisdom is bright and perfect, illuminating the ten directions," this refers to the aforementioned non-operation of the six functions, whereby the lands of the ten directions are vividly pure.
Below the character *qián* (dry), it clarifies the meaning of *qiánhù* (dry-wisdom); because one gives rise to wisdom by drying up desire, it is so named.
Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*). Furthermore, because the mind has not yet interfaced with the wisdom of fruition, it is called "dry wisdom.

One takes this very mind as the skillful means of faith. As for faith: it is defined as being pure, true, and without delusion; furthermore, it is defined as being in accord [with reality]. By means of the mind of the Middle Way—

Being pure and free from delusion, the causal mind and the resultant awakening correspond; thus, although the stages of Equality and Wondrous Enlightenment are vastly separated, one may proceed directly to them.
It is by means of this very mind flowing into the center that one reaches the state of pure truth in the Middle Way, which is named the Abode of Faith.

It is by means of this very mind—that is, the mind of dry wisdom (śuṣka-prajñā). Regarding the phrase "flowing into the center of the middle," it means that as for the mind, it is balanced such that neither śamatha nor vipaśyanā is one-sided;
as for the object, it is free from attachment to either emptiness or existence. By advancing in this manner, the wondrous mind is brought forth;

therefore, it is said to "flow into the center of the middle" and "the perfect wondrousness unfolds. This refers to the true, wondrous, and perfect mind of dry wisdom, from which this same true wondrousness is once again brought forth.
This is the stage of faith. By means of true and wondrous faith, one does not give rise to a mind that follows after emptiness or existence;

thus, all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder. When delusive thoughts are exhausted without remainder, the Middle Way is pure and true, and wondrous faith abides eternally; this is called the Abiding in Faith.
Subsequent stages advance by means of this, with no other distinct dharma, but rather proceed according to the position based upon the true and wondrous nature, becoming purified.

To remedy the habitual tendencies of delusion so that not even a speck of dust remains, one immediately ascends to wondrous enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*). As for the phrase "flowing into," it describes the manner of advancing and proceeding.
When true faith is clear and all is perfectly penetrating—up to the point where one attains freedom from forgetfulness—it is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness (*smṛti-sthiti*).

"Truly believing that all is clearly and perfectly penetrating" means that when the true nature is luminous and perfect, then all floating dust-like illusory appearances are transformed into unsurpassed awareness.
Because the nature is luminous and perfect, the three categories of aggregates, sense bases, and elements cannot act as obstructions;
thus, the habitual tendencies accumulated over countless eons all manifest before one, being remembered without omission.
"Wondrous, perfect, pure, and true; from this true essence, transformation is issued" (up to) "advancing toward true purity is called the mind of diligence.

When the nature of wondrous, perfect penetration is both pure and true, then the true essence penetrates and issues forth, transforming beginningless habits and unifying them into a single, bright spirit.
Because one advances toward true purity through this sole, bright spirit, one's practice is free from admixture; therefore, it is called diligence.
When the essence of mind manifests before one, it is purely characterized by wisdom; this is called the "abiding of the mind in wisdom.
Since delusive habits have been transformed, the essence of mind manifests before one, and as it advances toward activity, it is purely wisdom without habituation.

To maintain the clarity of wisdom so that it is pervasive, tranquil, and profoundly still, such that the essence of silent subtlety remains eternally concentrated and unchanging, is called the "abiding of the concentrated mind.
Once wisdom is purely luminous, one uses concentration to maintain it, causing it to be pervasive, tranquil, and profoundly still;
when the body of silent subtlety is eternally concentrated and immutable, this is termed the "concentrated mind."
The light of concentration illuminates the luminous nature; entering deeply with only progress and no retreat is called the "Non-retrogressive Mind.
Because one maintains wisdom through concentration until reaching profound stillness, the light of concentration illuminates;
by this, one is further able to enter deeply into the luminous nature, and thus there is only progress and no retreat.

When the mind advances with serenity, maintaining [this state] without loss, and the vital energy (*qi-fen*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is received in conjunction, it is called the "mind that protects the Dharma" (*hu-fa xin*).

Being able to penetrate deeply into the luminous nature (*ming-xing*), advancing serenely, and furthermore being able to maintain it without loss, one then connects with the vital energy of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
this is what is meant by "protecting the Dharma. This refers precisely to the principle-Dharma (*li-fa*).
To maintain the clarity of awakening through wondrous power—extending up to "interpenetrating one another in layers"—is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
To maintain the clarity of awakening without loss is the mind of protecting the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā-citta*).

To be able to turn the compassionate light of the Buddha through wondrous power is to turn the fruit toward the cause. To turn toward the Buddha and abide therein is to turn the cause toward the fruit. Thus, cause and fruit intermingle.
"Three. Because the lights mutually encompass one another, it is likened to two mirrors reflecting each other; this is termed the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

When the light of the mind secretly circulates and attains the Buddha’s eternal stillness—reaching the point where nothing is lost—it is called the abiding of the mind in precept (*śīla-citta-vihāra*).
Once the dedication is accomplished, one attains the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, wondrous purity and dwells securely in the unconditioned; thus, there is no loss.

"Eternally concentrated" means remaining unmoved in the face of objects; "wondrously pure" means being unstained while engaging with the dust of the world. In this way, the mind of precept is perfected.
Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla-vaśitā*), one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, proceeding wherever one’s vows lead;
this is called the "abiding of the mind of aspiration. Being unmoved by sense objects and untainted by worldly dust is what is meant by abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline.

When there is neither movement nor defilement, there is nothing that cannot be attained; thus, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, proceeding wherever one’s vows lead. At the very beginning of practice, one must...
Exhausting and severing the craving for desire causes the nature of the mind to become empty and luminous; only then can one enter the wondrous, perfect true nature (*bhūtatathatā*).

When this true nature is luminous and perfect, subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) manifest. Through their manifestation, they are subsequently transformed, causing pure wisdom to be free of habituation.

Furthermore, by maintaining this with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one causes the profound stillness to emit light, entering deeply into the luminous nature and guarding it so as not to lose it. This enables one to respond to the Buddha’s compassion.

Guang: Having attained the pure precepts of the Buddha, one traverses the mundane world without being defiled; wherever one goes, it is in accordance with one's vows. This is the sequence of the Ten Faiths.
Proceeding from faith, one enters [the path] and is born into the family of the Tathāgata. Relying on non-abiding wisdom, one never again regresses; this is called "Abiding" (Zhu).
Ānanda, this good man, by means of true skillful means (up to the point of) perfectly accomplishing the one mind, is said to dwell in the stage of "Initiating the Mind.
This refers to the subsequent stage being established upon the preceding one. The first three phrases refer back to what preceded:

"by means of true skillful means to initiate these ten minds" means that he relies on the truly wondrous, perfect mind of the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) as the skillful means for his progress, thereby manifesting the ten minds of faith.

Mind. After the essence of mind has been perfected below, it is called the "Ten Minds Entering" which perfectly accomplishes the One Mind. When the essence of mind radiates its brilliance, it is named the "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind" (Cittotpāda-vihāra).
From the stage of the Sages—beginning with Dry Wisdom (Śuklavidarśana) and ending with Equal and Subtle Wisdom—all are established in succession.

This is intended to cause the practitioner to enter from the beginning, abide in the ground of Buddha-wisdom, and, relying on that wisdom, give rise to practice, using practice to rescue [sentient beings].

Vow. By means of this, one transcends the stages of practice (*caryā-pratipatti*) and advances toward them; entering the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) and ascending to the Equal and Sublime [Buddha-stages]. This is the sequence of cultivation and realization.

When illumination dawns within the mind like pure lapis lazuli—[this stage] is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman-vihāra*), as one treads upon it to achieve the name of "ground."
The mind illuminates within; it is internally and externally refined and brilliant—this explains the meaning of the mind’s essence shining forth.

Treading upon the previously mentioned wondrous mind to establish the ground of reality is called "cultivating the ground" (treati). It is like one who intends to build a house: one must first prepare the ground before construction can begin.
When the mind-ground and cognitive awareness both attain clarity, and one traverses the ten directions without obstruction, this is called the "Abode of Cultivation.

Because the internal and external have been refined and polished, the mind-ground is perfected; the mind-ground is itself the principle (*li*). Wondrous practice (*xing*) is able to traverse it, and wondrous wisdom (*zhi*) is able to know it.
Since the triad of principle, wisdom, and practice all attain clarity, one traverses the ten directions without obstruction.
Furthermore,

when one’s practice becomes identical to that of the Buddha and one receives the Buddha’s *dharmatā* (spiritual resonance), up to entering the lineage of the Tathāgata, this is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).
Since what is traversed and what is known are attained without obstruction, the practitioner’s conduct then darkly accords with the conduct of the Buddha, and one receives [the Buddha’s power].

The Buddha’s vital energy enters the lineage of the Tathāgata, just as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) seeks out its parents; because this subtle faith communicates with the hidden, it is called "Birth in Nobility.
Having entered the womb of the Way and personally received the legacy of enlightenment, until the human marks are complete, it is called the Stage of Abiding in the Perfection of Expedient Means.

It shares the same vital essence as wondrous conduct; it is the wandering within the womb of the Way and the honoring of the lineage of enlightenment. Its prior practice is identical to that of the Buddha.
Because this skillful means is complete, it is likened to the physical features of a person in the womb being fully formed without deficiency.
To say that "skillful means are complete" refers to the perfection of the provisional wisdom that responds to capacities and engages with sentient beings.
"His appearance is like that of a Buddha, and his mental state is likewise; this is called the Abode of the Right Mind.
"His appearance is like that of a Buddha" reiterates the preceding text. "And his mental state is likewise" clarifies the nature of this stage.

If the appearance were identical externally while the mental state differed internally, it would not be the Right Mind. This is because both the skillful means are the same as the Buddha's, and the inner mind is likewise the same.
This is called the Stage of Rectifying the Mind.
When body and mind are unified and daily growth increases, it is called the Stage of Non-retrogression.
Possessing virtues equal to those of a Buddha, advancing without retreating, it is called the Stage of Non-retrogression.
The simultaneous perfection of the ten bodies and their spiritual marks is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*).
Because the form is complete yet minute, it is designated by the term "youth" (*kumāra*). As for the ten bodies:

the Bodhi-body (*bodhi-kāya*), the Vow-body (*praṇidhāna-kāya*), the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), the Sustaining-power-body (*baladhara-kāya*), the Ornamentation-body (*vyūha-kāya*), the Majestic-power-body (*vibhūti-kāya*), the Mind-born-body (*manomaya-kāya*), the Merit-body (*puṇya-kāya*), the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), and the Wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*).
The stage where one is formed upon emerging from the womb and becomes a direct son of the Buddha is called the "Abiding as a Dharma Prince.

From the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the "Noble Birth" (*janmakula*), it is called "Entering the Noble Womb. From the fulfillment of skillful means (*upāya*) up to the "Stage of Youth" (*kumārabhūmi*), it is called "Nurturing the Noble Womb.
Since the cultivation of this nurturing has reached its completion, it is metaphorically likened to a prince who has emerged from the womb; this is by way of skillful means.

Because the characteristics of the mind are identical to those of the Buddha, one is capable of succeeding to the Buddha’s position; this is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputrabhūmi*).

This represents the completion of one's personhood, like that of a great king of a nation; from the point of arranging the preparations for the consecration until the actual consecration itself, it is called the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣekabhūmi*).

The Great King of the nation is a Son of Heaven (*devaputra*); his legitimate heir is called the Crown Prince (*kumāra*). A Kṣatriya king is a sovereign among kings; his legitimate heir is called the Heir Apparent (*yuvarāja*).
