When about to entrust the national throne, one takes water from the great ocean to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), signifying that he shall become a king and employ the wisdom of the multitude.
Now, this position is already secretly endowed with all virtues and is capable of manifesting transformation throughout the ten directions to carry out the work of a Buddha.

It is like a prince who has reached adulthood; when the affairs of state are entrusted to him and the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is performed, it is called the "Stage of Consecration" (*abhiṣekasthāna*).

To say that the affairs of state are entrusted to him does not mean that the actual position of the kingdom has been formally handed over. It is only by reaching this stage that one completes the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

if the practices of the ten stages are fulfilled, one is then fit for the formal entrustment. Therefore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages receive the rank of a Buddha.
This is like the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning King receiving his office. Now, the arousal of the mind must first purify the ground; having purified the ground, one then practices;

and through practice, one is subsequently born into the family of the Tathāgata, endowed with the marks of awakening, sharing the Buddha-mind, extending the substance of the Path, perfecting the ten bodies, becoming a son of the Buddha, and undertaking the Buddha’s work. This is the sequence from beginning to end of the Ten Abodes.
Having already relied upon universal wisdom and abiding in the dwelling place of the Buddhas, he is thus able to extensively perform sublime practices for his own benefit and the benefit of others.
Ānanda, once this son of good family has become a child of the Buddha, [his practice] up to that of benefiting all sentient beings is called the "Beneficial Practice."
Possessing the wondrous virtues of a Buddha, one is able to accord with beings throughout the ten directions such that there is nothing unsuitable;

thus, the benefit of self and others is complete, and both the capacity [of the teacher] and the response [of the student] are joyful. Therefore, it is named "Joyful" (Prāmodya). Skillfully inferring these wondrous virtues to further benefit others, it is therefore named "Beneficial" (Ratiprada).
To awaken oneself and awaken others while being free from opposition is called the practice of non-anger and non-hatred.
Anger and hatred arise from opposition; now, because one awakens oneself and others and does not reject external objects, one attains freedom from anger and hatred.
Therefore, it is called the practice of being free from anger and resentment.
Arising from its own kind, reaching to the end of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions, it is called the inexhaustible practice.

It arises in contact with all categories and responds according to the capacities of beings; there is no time when it is not pervasive, and no place where it does not reach. Thus is the practice of beneficial conduct.
Exhaustion is called the practice of inexhaustibility.
The fact that all various dharma-gates are unified and accordant, attaining freedom from error, is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.

Although the above teachings respond to capacities with a thousand differences, and though they are explained through distinct names and categories, they all ultimately converge upon a single principle.

Therefore, it is said that all things are identical. When there is no discrepancy regarding the Dharma, one is free from confusion; when there is no error regarding the Dharma, one is free from delusion.
Since there is neither discrepancy nor error, one is thus free from both delusion and confusion.
Thus, within the identical, a multitude of differences manifests; each distinct characteristic is seen as the same, which is called the "practice of excellent manifestation.

Within the one, the infinite manifests; therefore it is said that "differences manifest within the identical. Within the infinite, the one manifests; therefore it is said that "identical characteristics are seen within differences.
Because one knows that all phenomena share the same single dharma-nature, one is able to produce various different explanations. And...
Thus, one does not lose the essential principle of the single nature and single characteristic. Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"One who is able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena remains unmoved within the ultimate truth. This is because of being free from delusion and confusion;
thus, one can manifest various dharma-gates in mutual correspondence as appropriate, which is called "skillful manifestation of practice."
Thus, even unto the empty space of the ten directions, there is no mutual obstruction; this is called the Practice of Non-Attachment.
This arises from the thorough expansion and perfect integration of the practice of skillful manifestation. Manifesting lands within atoms is called "manifesting realms";

not destroying the characteristics of the atoms is called "manifesting atoms. As for the term "non-attachment," attachment refers to dwelling and clinging, which is precisely what constitutes obstruction. World-systems.

Because even minute particles do not obstruct one another, it is called "non-attachment. This arises because the Bodhisattva has attained non-attached wisdom and dwells in inconceivable liberation, whereby such wondrous function is manifested.
The various manifestations that appear before one are all the practice of honoring the first *pāramitā*.
Whether manifesting as objects, realms, bodies, or teachings, they do not obstruct one another; hence, they are said to "appear before one in various ways.
Since these all emerge from the discovery of *prajñā*, they are called "the first. This wondrous practice transcends all others.
It is called "veneration. Therefore, the Vajra is termed the foremost *pāramitā*, which is precisely *prajñā*.
Such perfect interfusion can accomplish the ten directions; because its nature is inherently thus, it is called "true practice."
"Such perfect interfusion" refers to the unimpeded, wondrous function manifested above.

Being able to achieve such perfect interfusion and non-obstruction, one can fulfill the rules for benefiting sentient beings established by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; therefore, these are called "wholesome dharmas. Each and every rule...
All are in accord with purity and the unconditioned; therefore, they are called "real. These ten practices continue through to the subsequent stages without departing from the preceding dharmas.

Yet, they are established separately in succession for one reason: to enable the practitioner to progress through the stages, expand their innate awakening, purify the obstacles of affliction, and bring the fruit of Buddhahood to maturity.

In the first ten stages (bhūmi) and the ten practices (caryā), the mind of transcendence is predominant while the practice of great compassion is deficient; these must be supplemented by compassionate vows.

Abiding in the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, one turns the ultimate toward the conventional and turns wisdom toward compassion, so that the ultimate and the conventional are perfectly integrated and wisdom and compassion are non-dual.
This is called the Ten Dedications (daśa-pariṇāmanā), and it is also called the Ten Vows (daśa-praṇidhāna).
Ānanda, these good sons fulfill their supernormal powers (up to) the dedication that is free from the marks of sentient beings.
"Fulfilling supernormal powers" refers to the prior establishment of the fact that the present dusts and present realms do not obstruct one another;
this means that once this practice is fulfilled, one should cultivate the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). As for the practice of dedication, it is characterized by compassionate vows.

This is the most profound [teaching]. Therefore, one's duty lies in delivering sentient beings. However, if one perceives that there are beings to be delivered, one immediately enters the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and turns away from the path to *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, one must eliminate the mark of "delivering" and turn the unconditioned mind (*asaṃskṛta-citta*) toward the path to *nirvāṇa*.
To destroy that which is destructible and to distance oneself from all forms of distancing is called the "Non-Destructible Dedication.
To destroy that which is destructible is to depart from the mark of sentient beings; to distance oneself from all forms of distancing is to depart from both marks and their departure.
When subject and object are both empty, primordial enlightenment is serene and still; therefore, it is named the Non-Destructible Dedication.
"Innate enlightenment is profoundly still; its awakening is equal to the awakening of a Buddha" (up to) "is called the dedication reaching all places.
It is neither destroyed nor indestructible, neither separated nor inseparable; thus it is profoundly still and equal to the Buddha, and is therefore said to be "equal to the Buddha.

Because innate enlightenment is equal to the Buddha, the subtle and true nature is brilliantly manifested, and the ground is like the ground of a Buddha—this is what is meant by "the ground reaching all places," as mentioned previously.
That awakening is equal to all things means that the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal to all Buddhas.
That this stage reaches all things means that the realm of True Suchness pervades all places; that is to say, it is able to pervade all places by means of a single place.
The mutual interpenetration of the worlds and Tathāgatas, attained without obstruction, is called the Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit.
"Ascending to all Buddhas" refers to the Tathāgata; "reaching all places" refers to the world.

This is because the Bodhisattva has realized the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) and manifested its function; thus, they are able to bring about the mutual interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants. And...
Being unimpeded and sovereign, one becomes fully endowed with inexhaustible merit; therefore, it is called the dedication of the treasury of inexhaustible merit.
Within the stage that is identical to the Buddha-stage, up to [the point where] it is named the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality.
It is the same as the Buddha-ground; that is, the preceding ground is like the Buddha-ground. In all places, one gives rise to pure causes individually;
by relying on these pure causes, one takes up the path to nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is called "conforming to the roots of goodness of equality."
Once the true roots are established, all sentient beings of the ten directions [up to] are called the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.
Because the nature of these roots of goodness is truly perfect and harmonious, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, they are called "true roots.
Once the true roots are established, then all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own original nature; because this nature is perfected and accomplished, one accords with it.
One observes all sentient beings equally without losing [this perspective].
This is the dedication of the mark of *tathatā* (suchness), which is free from all marks of all phenomena and is non-attached to both [subject and object].
Because one contemplates all sentient beings from the perspective of the ultimate, it is said that they are "identical to all phenomena.

Because one contemplates in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), free from the characteristics of subject and object, it is said that they are "free from all marks. Since identity does not obstruct freedom, although there is contemplation, there is nothing to be contemplated.
Since freedom does not obstruct identity, although there is no contemplation, there is nothing that is not contemplated. Thus, emptiness and existence are identical.
Detachment. The second is non-attachment, which is called the dedication of the mark of *tathatā* (suchness).
Truly attaining that which accords with suchness, being unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the immeasurable dedication of the *dharmadhātu*.

Because one attains True Suchness (tathatā) and does not stagnate in either emptiness or existence, one is able to act without obstruction throughout the ten directions; this is termed "unfettered liberation.

Herein, the wondrous nature of the three virtues is perfectly realized. One no longer perceives the distinctions of high and low among the ten realms, and the measure of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) ceases;
therefore, it is said that the dharma-realm is immeasurable. Furthermore, upon first realizing this nature, one is considered equal to a Buddha.

As with the Buddha, regarding [the realization] that "he has reached all places" and so forth, as long as one still possesses the perception of finite measures (*pramāṇa*), the nature of the *dharmadhātu* has not yet transcended the finite.
When the qualities of this nature are perfected, one then extinguishes the perception of finite measures and attains the infinite.
This generally counteracts the limited emotional views of the preceding stages. Once this nature is perfected, one may enter the ten stages (*bhūmi*). However, regarding these various stages...

All [stages] are within the single realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); according to the specific practices undertaken, distinct names are established. All are equally able to perfectly realize the nature of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*).
Though not distinct, they are distinct; thus the various stages are differentiated. Though different, they are not different; they are solely this one mind.
As it is with the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), so it may be known for the subsequent stages.
"Ānanda, these good men are all pure... [up to] "...next they accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

This marks the transition from the preceding section to the subsequent one. Regarding the "forty-one minds": there is the one mind of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), and ten each for the stages of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Direction.
While both the Small Vehicle and the Shared Teaching possess these four preparatory stages, they are neither wondrous nor perfect; therefore, this text specifically designates them as "wondrous."

The preparatory practice of the Perfect [Stage] consists of taking the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind (up to the point where) one desires to ignite that wood; this is called the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*).
"Buddha-awakening" refers to original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). The previous measure of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-pramāṇa*) has ceased; it is equal and non-dual. This non-dual awakening is...

This is the Buddha’s awakening. Now, as one is about to ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*), one still takes that Buddha-awakening as one's own causal mind, further applying effort and practice to seek direct realization.
Because one is on the verge of realization but has not yet realized it, it is said that "it has emerged but has not yet emerged. The metaphor of fire represents the fruition-awakening.

The "original" (the wood) is a metaphor for the mind; the "drilling" is a metaphor for applied practice (*prayoga*). Since one has not yet ascended to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), it is likened to the heat that is first obtained when drilling for fire.

Furthermore, because there is still a slight obstruction beneath the state where one’s own mind attains Buddhahood—the ground upon which the Buddhas tread—it is called the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdhan-bhūmi*).
Previously, one took the Buddha’s awakening as the causal mind for oneself; now, one takes one's own mind as that which desires to follow the path trodden by the Buddhas.
That which the Buddhas have trodden is precisely the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), because all Buddhas ascend to awakening by means of these ten stages.
Now, the practitioner’s aspiration and course are directed toward the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which is precisely that which one who seeks to attain Buddhahood must traverse.
Nevertheless, because the ignorance (*avidyā*) that obstructs the first stage has not yet been exhausted, the fruit of the first stage is either realized or not yet realized.

Thus, it is likened to ascending a high mountain where the body enters the void, yet there remains a slight obstruction below. However, having already reached the summit, one need only wait a moment before proceeding further.
Subtle obstructions are eliminated.

When the mind and the Buddha are identical, one well attains the Middle Way. As with enduring a person, it is neither harboring resentment nor seeking fame; this is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
The practitioner’s mind becomes identical to the Buddha’s mind—this is termed "the two are identical. Having become identical to the Buddha’s mind, one well attains the Middle Way.
Thus it is. Yet, although this is attained, that which can be attained is not seen. When that which can be attained is not seen, there is likewise nothing to be spoken.
It is like a person who endures an offense; seeing nothing to harbor resentment toward, they likewise do not utter a word.
When quantity is extinguished and both delusion and awakening are beyond designation within the Middle Way, it is called the "World-First Ground" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

The preceding stage is termed "the two being identical," wherein one has already fallen into quantity; this is called "skillfully attaining the Middle Way," which is precisely awakening to the Middle Way.
Where there is awakening, there must necessarily be delusion; yet upon reaching this point of quantity, neither delusion nor awakening can be apprehended. One is liberated.

That which is measured by worldly conditions is still called the "Supreme of the World. If one advances through the ten stages to the ultimate state of Wondrous Enlightenment, fulfilling Bodhi and returning to non-attainment, this is the "Supreme Beyond the World."
Regarding the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*): they are so called because one accumulates the preceding dharmas until they reach fulfillment, and all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon them;

thus, they are termed "grounds. From the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward, each position follows upon the previous and mutually supports it, proceeding directly toward wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Within this, there is nothing that is not abandoned or realized; all these are abandoned without being abandoned, and realized without being realized.
Ānanda, when these sons of good family reach the limit of the Buddha-realm within Great Bodhi, it is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
The text below states: "One returns to non-attainment upon the fulfillment of Bodhi; by means of non-attainment, one attains Great Bodhi.
Since one has now realized that within the Middle Way of awakening there is nothing to be designated as either [delusion or awakening], one thoroughly penetrates Great Bodhi.
*Jin* (盡) means "to reach. "The realm of the Buddha" refers precisely to Great Bodhi. This is because, through Great Bodhi...
By practicing goodness, one attains thorough penetration; thus it is said that "awakening penetrates the Tathāgata and exhausts the realm of the Buddha.
Because joy in the Dharma increases further by means of this, it is also named "Joy" (Prāmodya).
When distinct natures enter into the same nature and that very sameness also ceases, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
It penetrates Great Bodhi and exhausts the realm of the Buddhas; thus, all obstacles are ultimate awakening.
Sentient beings and their lands share the same *dharmatā*. This is "distinct natures entering into the same. However, to perceive difference or to perceive sameness is still [delusion].
When the stains of affliction, including those of a similar nature, are extinguished, it is called "Freedom from Stains" (vimalā).

When purity reaches its ultimate limit and radiance arises, it is called the "Radiant Ground" (prabhākārī). When radiance reaches its ultimate limit and awakening becomes full, it is called the "Blazing Wisdom Ground" (arciṣmatī).
When emotional views are purified to the ultimate degree, wondrous awakening and clarity arise; therefore, it is named "Emission of Light" (Prabhākari).

When clarity reaches its peak and awakening is fulfilled, it is like a great mass of fire that utterly incinerates all shadows of objective conditions, whether identical or different; therefore, it is named "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī).
The stage where all similarities and differences cannot reach is called the Difficult to Conquer (Durjayā).
Because it has been incinerated and severed by the preceding stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), all similarities and differences cannot reach it;
furthermore, because the lower stages cannot surpass it, it is termed "Difficult to Conquer."

The unconditioned nature of true thusness (*tathatā*), being pure and luminously manifest, is called the Ground of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*); exhausting the limit of true thusness is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*).

Since the former [ground] has already clarified that ultimate awakening is full and that identity and difference do not reach it, the pure nature of true thusness is then luminously manifest before one.
Once true thusness is manifest, one transcends and reaches the ultimate limit by exhausting the boundary of true thusness; therefore, it is named "Far-Going."
Practice. Since suchness is the limit of the limitless, and since its principle is already boundless, how could practice approach it?
This single mind of suchness is called the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi).
Having reached the ultimate limit, one then fully attains its essence. Being the single, true, concentrated, and eternal, it is therefore called "Immovable.
The manifestation of the function of True Suchness is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī).
Having attained the true essence, one thereby manifests its true function; whatever is illumined and responded to is entirely true and nothing other than as it is.

For this reason, it is called "Excellent Wisdom" (*Sādhumati*). In the *Avataṃsaka*, this Bodhisattva is said to possess the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and acts as a great Dharma-preacher, expounding immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings without end. Therefore, it is called "Manifesting True Suchness."
[Application].
Ānanda, from this point onward [up to] these bodhisattvas also designate this stage as the "Stage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).
This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. From the initial arousal of faith until the ascent to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), all constitute the matter of cultivation.
This "Good Wisdom" (Sādhumatī) has already transcended the eighth stage, the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga*).
Since both wisdom and compassion are perfected, the merit of cultivation is completed at this point; therefore, it is called "cultivation" to conclude the causes of the ten stages.
What follows is the fruit of the ten stages, wherein there is no further cultivation. Question: If there is no longer cultivation in the subsequent stage, is there still anything to be abandoned?
Question: What is the matter regarding these hindrances? Answer: This refers to the completion of the merit of wisdom and compassion, at which point it is said that there is no further cultivation.

However, if one discusses the severance of hindrances, even the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) still involves cultivation; it is only upon reaching the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Suyunghak) that one is termed "beyond learning" (aśaikṣa).
The "Cloud of Compassion" (*maitrī-chāyā*) and "Sublime Cloud" (*vimala-megha*) that cover the ocean of *nirvāṇa* is called the "Dharma-Cloud Ground" (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

This "Cloud of Compassion" and "Sublime Cloud" represent the virtue of the tenth ground (*daśamī-bhūmi*). When the fruit of the tenth ground is perfected and the merits of wisdom and compassion are complete, there is no longer any self-interest;
it consists purely of benefiting others. Therefore, by means of unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), one raises the great Dharma-cloud to universally cover all sentient beings.
The great ocean of *nirvāṇa* is called the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

When a Tathāgata flows against the current and a Bodhisattva thus proceeds in accordance with it until their boundaries of awakening meet and intersect, this is termed Equal Awakening (*samyaksambodhi*).
Previously, it was said that on the Stage of Dry Wisdom one had not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma;
reaching this point, where the forward and reverse flows intersect, one then connects with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma. This "stream of Dharma" refers to the noble wisdom of the fruition-dharma.

As for the Tathāgata “flowing against the current,” this means arising from the Truth (the Absolute) to manifest as response (the Phenomenal), returning to birth-and-death—that is, entering from the fruition back into the cause. Thus, below...
This refers to entering the fruit from the cause, and entering nirvana from birth-and-death. Because one enters by following the current, it is called "reaching through following the course.

It marks the beginning of arising in response [to conditions] and the culmination of practicing the causes; as the point where the favorable and the adverse intersect, it is called "entering the intersection.

At this very stage, one is established as an Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) Bodhisattva. Thus, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages blend with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, and are equal to the Tathāgata...

They come together, yet the direction they pursue—whether contrary or with the current—is different from that of the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata flows against the current, emerging as one with all things;
the Bodhisattva flows with the current, entering toward wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Although these two are equal in this regard, it does not yet reach the ultimate subtlety.
Only when one reaches the "Original Cause" described below, exhaustively attaining the initial "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), does one finally perfect wondrous enlightenment.

"Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), [and] within the Vajra-mind, at the initial stage of Dry Wisdom—this collectively summarizes the preceding text to clarify the ultimate exhaustion of wondrous enlightenment (*miàojué*). The first two phrases collectively summarize the preceding text.

From 'This is awakening' (*shì jué*) onwards, it clarifies that one only attains the initial mind upon reaching Equal Enlightenment; this is precisely the ultimate exhaustion of wondrous enlightenment. Below, it is as follows.
The repeated phrases and so forth merely serve to reiterate and conclude this passage.

Since [the stage of] "Exhausting Wondrous Enlightenment" has already been reached, why is it said that this enlightenment is "initially obtained" within the Vajra-mind as the first stage of Dry Wisdom (*prathamā śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi*)? The term "this enlightenment" refers precisely to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This is because the Vajra-dry wisdom attained at the stage of Equal Enlightenment is itself the initial dry wisdom; by attaining this initial dry wisdom, one has exhausted wondrous enlightenment.
Because of this awakening, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are ultimately not two.
Thus, through these successive layers—twelve in total, both simple and compound—one exhausts the wondrous enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way.

This passage summarizes and concludes the preceding text. Beginning from *kandhā-vidyā* (dry wisdom) and ending with *sūkṣma-bodhi* (wondrous enlightenment), there are twelve stages in total, comprising both single and combined categories.

There are seven single stages, namely: *kandhā-vidyā*, *uṣmagata* (warmth), *mūrdhan* (summit), *kṣānti* (patience), *laukikāgra-dharma* (the supreme mundane dharma), *samyak-sambodhi-samīpa-bodhi* (equal-enlightenment), and *sūkṣma-bodhi*.

There are five combined stages, namely: *śraddhā* (faith), *vihāra* (abiding), *caryā* (practice), *abhimukha* (orientation), and *bhūmi* (ground). This is because within each individual stage, [the preceding qualities] are inherently complete.

Tenth, it is therefore called "repeated" (*fu*). Thus, at the eleventh stage, one still dwells in Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); only upon reaching the twelfth does one exhaustively attain Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and accomplish the Unsurpassed Path.
"These various stages are all [attained] through the gradual penetration of purification by means of the vajra...

This refers back to the preceding stages and positions to demonstrate the samatha and vipaśyanā that can realize them. "Various stages" generally refers to the twelve stages, both single and combined;
there is no stage that is not so. Therefore, it says "all by means of. "Vajra-observation" is the wisdom of contemplative illumination.
The ten profound metaphors of illusion are precisely the illumination that all phenomena are like illusions and so forth.

When one realizes phenomena in this way, emotional attachments and intellectual interpretations are suddenly forgotten, and not even a speck of dust remains established. Because contemplation is employed within stillness, it is said:

"Within *śamatha*, employ the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas. This is because stillness and contemplation are simultaneous—contemplating while in stillness, and being in stillness while contemplating. Thus, they are stillness and contemplation.

It is not partial; therefore, it is called "pure cultivation and realization. From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to the Stage of Faith (*adhimukti*), and from faith entering the [first] dwelling, continuing until the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*tathāgata-vyūha-jñāna*), it is therefore called "gradually penetrating deeper. As for the ten metaphors:

an illusory person, a mirage, the moon in water, flowers in the sky, an echo in a valley, a city of the gandharvas, a dream, a shadow, a reflection, and a transformation. Regarding the statement "the Tathāgata’s *vipaśyanā*," this serves to distinguish [it from other forms].
This differs from the Hinayana.
Ānanda, it is because of these three progressive advancements that [the teaching reaches] "if one views it otherwise, it is called a false view.

This concludes by demonstrating the distinction between the false and the correct, desiring that people turn away from the false through the correct in order to practice and realize [the truth]. Question: Regarding the third [section] mentioned previously...
Regarding the passage on "Further Progress" (*vṛddhi*), it says: "This person immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

From this point, they practice gradually; according to their initial resolve, they establish themselves in the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*). As for the question, "What does it mean to say that these various stages all involve 'gradually penetrating deep within by means of diamond-like observation'?
The answer is: among the three types of further progress, what is called "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" refers precisely to *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
This refers to the two aspects of the single mind. "Vajra-observation" and so forth refer precisely to *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

For the single mind is not separate from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are themselves the single mind. Therefore, the conclusion states: "Thus, all are by means of the three progressive advancements."
One is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
If one practices the contemplation of progressing through these stages, it is called "right contemplation"; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called "erroneous contemplation.
As for the fifty-five stages, they consist of the stage of Dry Wisdom up to the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding the term "path to Bodhi," *bodhi* means awakening. [The fifty...]
The five stages are the path leading to awakening; the two types of awakening—the equal and the wondrous—are awakening itself, not the path.
At that time, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince [said]: "How shall I and all sentient beings uphold this?"
The preceding section concludes the clarification of the realization of the fruit. The following portion is titled "The Section on the Conclusion of the Sūtra.

Although the primary teaching (*śāsanamūla*) has not yet ended, the sūtra is concluded abruptly because it first revealed the secret cause, then opened the path of cultivation and realization, and finally culminated in the ultimate fruit.
By providing a model for future generations with both a beginning and an end, the formal structure of the sūtra is complete. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī requested the sūtra: [Text follows]
The titles and the "Dharma to be Upheld" constitute the concluding text of the sutra; they still belong to the primary teaching (shōjū).
However, as for the "Aids to the Path," these are merely aids and therefore are listed separately at the end. This is the distinction between the primary and the auxiliary.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: [up to] "the pure ocean-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

This is a name established based on the principle that is expressed. "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Supreme Jewel Seal of the White Parasol" means that its essence is ultimate and all-encompassing, transcending emotion and departing from views; it is the heart-seal of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Thus it is realized.

The essential core of the Buddha-mind must surely accord with this. That which is called "the pure sea-eye of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions" refers to that which illuminates the entirety of the ocean of lands, purifying it so that not even a speck of dust remains;
it is the *śakara* Dharma-eye. To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision must necessarily rely upon this;
it is truly a matter of great significance and is not the teaching of those with limited wisdom. Therefore, Mañjuśrī was employed to pose the inquiry.
It is also titled *The Rescue and Protection of One’s Own Causes*, and it is also titled *The Definitive Meaning of the Cultivation, Realization, and Verification of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause*.
Ānanda represents the "own" (the object of affection), while Māraṇa represents the "cause" (the condition). By citing these two, it clarifies that all who possess the karmic affinity shall be saved.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the bodhicitta and so forth," this refers to supreme perfect enlightenment; it is by means of this sutra that one attains the ocean of all-knowledge.
"By entering through this sutra": this name is established based on its function for those to be converted. "Also called the Tathāgata... and so forth:

this name is established based on the meaning of the cause and effect that it explicates. That is to say, cultivation and realization based on the secret cause of the Tathāgata constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
cultivation and realization of the provisional vehicles are all non-definitive (*neyārtha*).
It is also titled *The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī-Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*.

This title is established based on its essence (*tattva*), function (*vṛtti*), and efficacy (*prabhāva*). "Great Vaipulya" refers to the Dharma that is taught: it is called "Great" (*mahat*) because it is eternal and all-pervading;

"Vaipulya" (*dharma*) because it serves as a norm and sustainer; and "Broad" (*vaipulya*) because it is comprehensive and vast—referring thus to the three greatnesses of essence, characteristic, and function, as well as cause and fruit.
Together they manifest, unimpeded in both defilement and purity, possessing mastery over all dharmas; thus it is named the Sovereign of the Wondrous Lotus.

It gives birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions, encompasses all dharmas, and upholds immeasurable meanings; thus it is named the *Dhāraṇī-mantra*, the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
As for "mantra," it refers to the Buddha’s use of spoken teachings to invoke blessings for sentient beings, transforming them from the state of ordinary beings into the state of sainthood.
It is also called "The Mantra-Phrases of Empowerment" and "The Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Foremost of the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas"; you should uphold it.
This is a name established based on its teachings and practices. This sutra has flowed forth from the *Abhiṣeka* section of India;
it is named "The Mantra-Phrases of Empowerment" because it concerns secret mantras (*mantra*). For those who recite and uphold it, the water of the Tathāgata’s wisdom shall be poured upon them.
It is the crown of the mind, just as a Kṣatriya receives his office. Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas receive the rank of Buddhahood through this, it is also called the "Mantra of Empowerment.

Since the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva take Śūraṅgama as their foundation, those who cultivate this samādhi possess the myriad practices within a single moment of mind; therefore, it is named the "Śūraṅgama of Myriad Practices. This concludes the sutra.

The section on the divisions is concluded. The following is the Section on Aids to the Path (*bodhipakṣa*), which consists of two parts. The first is titled "Specifically Clarifying the Various Destinies" (*gati*) to provide for the prevention of errors;
it begins from the subsequent text and concludes within the ninth fascicle. The second is titled "Detailed Discernment of the Spheres of Māra."
The profound and erroneous [interpretation] begins in the ninth fascicle and concludes at the end of the tenth fascicle.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda immediately [attained] the six grades of subtle afflictions in the cultivation of the mind.

This section concludes by describing the benefits obtained by the assembly; what follows is the expression of praise and gratitude. Regarding the "revelation of the meaning of the *Guhyamudrā-paṭala*":
this refers to the Supreme Jewel Seal of the Great Buddha-Crown *Siddhārthapratāra*. Furthermore, regarding the "hearing of the names of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)":
this refers to the *Tathāgata-guhyahetu-bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā-nītārtha* and so forth. [The term] "sudden awakening Chan" [is used here].

"Those [practitioners]" refers to those who, by hearing and practicing the advancement toward the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*), as well as the names and categories of the definitive meaning of the secret seals (*mudrā*), attain sudden awakening to the wondrous principle of *dhyāna* cultivation.
Their mental deliberations become empty and concentrated, thereby severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.

Regarding the delusions to be severed through the path of cultivation, in the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), there are nine stages within the three realms, with nine grades in each stage; first, one severs those of the desire realm.
By abandoning the first six categories [of afflictions], one realizes the second fruit; by abandoning the final three categories, one realizes the third fruit;

and by abandoning the nine categories in each of the two higher realms, one realizes the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Now, because these superior [afflictions] are abandoned all at once, it is said that "the six categories of the three realms" are abandoned.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, praised and thanked him for the preceding teaching, and requested the subsequent discourse.
Because that which is innate and obscure is hidden, it is called "sunk delusion. The previous teaching stated that the true, pure, and wondrous mind is fundamentally pervasive and perfect;
thus, the Dharma-realm is a single truth, and the ten thousand movements are one essence—there should be no [delusion].
The differences among the various realms of existence are as they currently manifest; this is what ordinary people doubt.
Consequently, some cling to the various realms and become confused about the wondrously perfect essence, while others cling to the wondrously perfect essence and deny the karma of the various realms.
Thus, they fall into error and ruin. Therefore, I specifically inquire of you, hoping that the Buddha will explain this in detail so that people may know what to guard against and prepare for.
World-Honored One, as in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā (up to the point where she) received it with joy upon her head, maintaining it with purity and without transgression.

There are two intentions behind the questions: namely, distinct karma with common retribution (*pṛthag-karma-sādhāraṇa-vipāka*) and distinct karma with distinct retribution (*pṛthag-karma-pṛthag-vipāka*). The first question concerns the three [offenses] of sexual misconduct, killing, and lying.

This refers to individual karma (*pṛthag-karma*). Because there is a fixed location, it refers to collective retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*). Furthermore, regarding the passage "naturally below," this asks about individual karma and individual retribution;
however, according to the intent of the subsequent answer, these are all cases of individual karma resulting in collective retribution. The text says:

"Following the commission of evil karma, although one invites [retribution] for oneself, within the commonality of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), there is also the original ground," and so on, up to "not severing."

The three karmas each have their own private [causes]; because they each have their own private [causes], these various privacies share a commonality (*sabhāgatā*). It is not that there is no fixed location.

Furthermore, this [text] says, "causing those who uphold the precepts to be cautious, pure, and free from transgressions," while the passage below says, "not entering into false views"—this is precisely the meaning of being prepared through the precepts.
Vairāṭya was the crown prince of King Nimi; having deposed his father to establish himself, he harbored a long-standing grudge and slaughtered the Śākyas.
The Buddha prophesied that he would enter hell after seven days. The king sailed out to sea to avoid him, yet he was spontaneously consumed by fire upon the water.
The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was able to expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras and had attained the fruit of the four dhyānas; however, due to his intimacy with evil friends, [he fell away].

They falsely claim that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Nirvana; therefore, they fall into the Avīci Hell. These are all instances of erroneously clinging to the wondrous perfection [of their own views] and utterly denying the existence of karma and its destinies.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "How excellent is this question! [This continues] until: "Naturally falling [into rebirth]—this is called the internal division.
This praises the question asked and explains how deluded habits give rise to the various realms of existence. The final two lines begin with "All... [and so forth].

This restates the meaning of the preceding question. From the phrase "Because of that" (*yin pi*) onwards, it clarifies that the arising of passionate attachment based on delusion is precisely the root of birth and death for sentient beings;
this is termed the "internal division" (*neifen*), which refers to matters within the sphere of sentient beings.

It can produce the water of craving, which moistens karma and moistens rebirth, ensuring that the cycle of transmigration continues without interruption; all such functions stem from this. These various forms of craving are not uniform, yet they are all capable of—

Because the karma of water is bound, it is said that the binding of the flow is identical [to the binding of the mind]. The nature of water is to sink downward; thus, karma accumulated through emotional afflictions mostly results in falling and sinking.
Ānanda, "external divisions" refers to what lies beyond the realm of sentient beings (up to the point where one) naturally transcends this; hence it is called "external division."
The cycle of birth and death for sentient beings fundamentally arises from their emotions (*qing*). When emotions become attached to defiled objects, one consequently falls [into suffering].
Now, taking a superior realm as the object of desire depends solely on one's mental conception (*xiang*); it does not belong to the realm of emotion.

This is therefore a matter beyond the ordinary lot of sentient beings, which is why it is called "external" (*wai-fen*). "Vapor" (*qi*) refers to the complexion of the breath; thus, the following cites actual events to verify that the body becomes light.
Purity; boldness and courage; dreaming of flying aloft; the manifestation of sacred realms; and disregarding one’s own body and life—these five are all sublime states resulting from mental ideation.
"Boldness" (*yi*) refers to being resolute and daring. Although these various ideations differ, they are collectively termed "delighting in external, superior objects."
It does not arise from emotional defilement. Since the perception (*saṃjñā*) is already light and pure, it naturally moves and flies; thus, one’s retribution shall be transcendent.
However, while perception can produce excellence, those born from eggs through perception differ due to the distinction between defilement and purity.

Here, for the time being, we refer to the perceiving mind of humans and devas as the "external division" (*bāhya-bhāga*); it is not the supramundane wisdom of the Three Vehicles. Why? Because of the preceding *ābhāsvara*...

He poses difficult questions concerning the realms from the hells up to those of humans and devas. Consequently, the Buddha, based on the habitual tendencies of delusion, divides these into two parts.
He then distinguishes the various destinies (*gati*) by means of these two divisions. Following the discussion of the destinies, he provides a summary, stating:
"These sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of saṃsāra," and so forth. Therefore, one knows that external divisions do not transcend the three [realms].

This is the realm (*dhātu*). Although the text states that when the mind dwells upon the Buddha-land, the sacred realm manifests in profound stillness, this is merely a general description of the signs of superior spiritual power.
Ānanda, from "all the worlds of birth and death continue in succession" up to "the two habits of death being contrary and birth being compliant intersect," [it describes the continuity of existence].
"Birth follows from habitual tendencies, while death proceeds from transformational flux" means that all sentient beings love life and loathe death.
Therefore, birth accords with their habits, whereas death opposes them. Thus it is further said that "death is contrary and birth is compliant;
these two habits intersect. This is merely a matter of mutual abbreviation in the phrasing; it simply means that birth follows from abiding and persistence.

Therefore, it is called "conforming habituation. Death follows the flow of transformation; therefore, it is called "contrary habituation. That which has not yet abandoned the sensation of warmth refers to the final moment of the present aggregates.

The intersection of the contrary and the conforming refers to the interval between the very moment of death and the very moment of birth. This concerns all karmic actions, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
At that very moment, according to the lightness or gravity of their thoughts and conceptions, they experience a corresponding lightness.
If their thoughts are purely positive, they will immediately ascend and be born in the heavens (up to) being reborn in any pure land according to their vows.
Because the substance of thought is light and buoyant, one ascends by flight when it is purely so. However, because this is specifically pure goodness, one merely attains birth in the heavens.
As for those who must be born in the heavens, based on the principle that inferior [mental] states are few while thoughts are many, they reside below the Four Heavenly Kings.
Examining where one is born through purely conceptual thought, it should be above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. If one practices wholesome dhyāna alone, then by nature one is born in the higher realms.
Regarding the realms: if one combines both merit and wisdom with pure vows, then at the time when the two practices intersect, the resulting transformation is doubly superior.
This is discussed as a digression on merit and wisdom within the context of the "flying mind" (feixin); therefore, in all cases, it is said that they are "combined."
With little emotion but much conceptualization, their light flight does not reach far. (Up to: These beings dwell intimately beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.

Because their superior conceptions are not pure and they are slightly hindered by deviant emotions, they experience this class of existence. Indeed, although they are hindered by deviant emotions, they possess virtuous aspirations;
thus, they experience these favorable conditions to dwell beneath the Buddha’s seat—namely, the classes of the eight divisions of devas, nāgas, and so forth. However, as for their emotions...
"Few thoughts and many [sensory] perceptions. This is a general statement. In principle, it is appropriate to divide this into four categories according to their relative proportions:

1. Those with nine perceptions and one emotion become flying immortals (*fei-xian*). 2. Those with eight perceptions and two emotions become powerful ghost kings (*da-li gui-wang*). 3. Those with seven perceptions and three emotions become flying *yakṣas* (*fei-hang ye-chao*). 4.
Those with six perceptions and four emotions become earth-walking *rākṣasas* (*di-xing luo-che*).
When emotion (*citta*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans; if thought is clear, one is intelligent, and if emotion is obscure, one is dull-witted.
Thus, present intelligence or dullness is felt as a result of past emotion and thought. Therefore, we know that what is called "equality" refers to karma as a collective retribution.

What is called "the obscure and the luminous" refers to the karma of individual retribution. Depending on the strength or weakness of the habitual emotions and perceptions one has cultivated, there arise differences such as being intelligent or dull-witted.
When emotion is predominant and thought is scarce, one flows into the transverse births (as animals), or else into the two kinds of hells: the [various] hells or the Avīci Hell.

When emotion is abundant and thought is scarce, there are likewise four divisions: six emotions and four thoughts lead to rebirth among the animals; seven emotions and three thoughts cause one to fall as a hungry ghost;
eight emotions and two thoughts result in birth in the *Sāntara* (Intervening) Hells; nine emotions and one thought lead to birth in the *Avīci* (Uninterrupted) Hell.
What is called the "water wheel at the limit of fire" refers to the eighth cold hell. To "receive the fierce fire of the breath" means to undergo [the torments of that hell].
Taking the element of fire as their body, they are constantly burned by flames; even when they obtain water to drink, it transforms into fire.
Thus it is said that water can harm them. As their afflictions and karma become increasingly stagnant, their retributions in hell sink ever deeper, falling down through the revolving wheels of fire.
This refers to the eight hot hells. When the body enters the ground where wind and fire intersect, it means one has transcended the cold hells and entered the hot hells.

Regarding the eighth hot hell, known as the Five Uninterrupted (Pañcānantarya), this discussion concerns only the seven hot hells, which are divided into those with intervals and those without based on their relative severity;
it does not refer to the [other] five uninterrupted offenses. Below, the eighth hot hell is explained.
These are the five immediate retributions (*ānantarya*).
Those of purely emotional nature sink directly into the Avīci Hell (up to) the *nikāya-sabhāga* (the class of beings sharing common characteristics), which also includes their original ground.

"Avīci" is translated here as "Without Interval. This refers to five things: the suffering of the retribution, the instruments of torture, the physical dimensions of the body, the duration of the eon, and the lifespan.
All of these lack any interval [of time], and are thus called the "five immediate" (*pañcānantarya*) offenses. Only those whose mental karma is most grave fall into them;

they remain there until the kalpa is destroyed before they emerge. However, if one commits these along with other sins such as slandering the Mahāyāna, then even when this kalpa is destroyed, one enters the Avīci hell in the ten directions once more, with no prospect of release.
This is because by slandering the Dharma and violating the precepts, one causes countless people to fall into false views.
Previously, you asked about the hells: whether they have fixed locations or arise spontaneously. Therefore, I replied that they are created by pure emotion;

although one invites them for oneself, they are nonetheless experienced through the influence of shared karma and thus do not lack fixed locations. As for "original grounds," each follows its original cause as the basis for the ground.
"Ānanda, all these are those sentient beings who... [have] created the ten causes of habitual practice and received the sixfold retributive responses.

This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. Previously, two divisions were opened to clarify how emotional and conceptual thoughts trigger transformations, providing a brief explanation of the seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*).
From here below, the detailed construction of the faculties and their objects will be examined, precisely investigating the seven realms of existence. The ten habitual practices are rooted in...
The ten delusions form evil karma through habitual practice. The six [delusions] intersect with the six sense organs, giving rise to intersecting evil retributions.
For example, when the eye creates the cause of karma, the other five serve as its assistants; thus, at the time of receiving retribution, they are all fully involved.
What are the ten causes? Ānanda, the first is the habit of lust (*kāma-vāsanā*). [This continues] until: "The Bodhisattva views desire as if avoiding a pit of fire.
Evil karma arises from emotional delusion, and among such delusions, lust is the most extreme; therefore, it is clarified at the beginning and end of both [the causes and effects].
Regarding the karma of the ten habits, each first describes the environment experienced as a result, followed by the specific retribution received. As for lust:

This is the retribution for karmic actions involving fire. It arises because the deluded mind is intensely inflamed, and through mutual friction, it is ignited. Consequently, the realm experienced as retribution appears as a great, raging fire.
King Shu said: "If the habit of lust is ground away without ceasing, one naturally consumes their own essence, causing the fire element to blaze up.
If, even while alive, one suffers from ailments such as emaciation, thirst, and internal heat, then at the moment of death, one will see [the same]."
A great, fierce fire is indeed appropriate; when the subject and object blaze together, it is called the mutual kindling of the two habitual tendencies (*dvaya-vāsanā*).

Thus, there is the retribution of the iron bed and the copper pillar, which corresponds precisely to those habitual karmas. The Tathāgata acts as the Guide, and therefore designates these [retributions] by name to warn them.
The Bodhisattva acts as the practitioner, and therefore feels profound dread to avoid them. "Designating by name" (*se-mu*) is like marking the eyes with an inscription.
Second, the habituation of greed arises from mutual calculation and mutual attraction. (Up to: When a Bodhisattva views greed, they avoid it as one would a sea of miasma.
The habituation of greed evokes water; it arises from the mind of craving calculatingly clinging to and absorbing [objects]. The accumulation of this suction through wind results in cold.

Wind congeals water into ice; thus there occur conditions of accumulated cold and freezing rigors. The *Ṭaṭa* and other such names refer to the retribution of cold ice, which is the Cold Hells (*śītanaraka*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The *Ṭaṭabha* and others are the sounds of enduring the cold; [the hells are named after] the blue, red, and white lotuses."
The color of the Cold Ice [Hell] is also [white]. The water of greed can moisten karma and nourish evil; the sea of miasma can poison the body with its venom.
The three—*Tāpana*, *Saṃghāta*, and *Raurava*—plus the three—blue, red, and white—further include the two signs of blistering and bursting; these constitute the eight cold hells.
Third, the habit of pride manifests as mutual aggression arising from mutual reliance. (Up to: When Bodhisattvas see pride, they avoid it as if avoiding a great abyss.

The habit of pride leads to arrogance and dissipation; it arises from looking down upon others and relying on oneself. Because one gallops and flows away in arrogance and dissipation, one is moved to encounter realms of surging and rushing turbulence.
Through the accumulation of this, malicious poison is brought forth, resulting in the retribution of being drenched and swallowed by rivers of blood. Pride is able to...
It nourishes delusion; thus, it is like drinking the water of delusion, which can bring about profound harm, and is therefore likened to a great drowning.
"The water of delusion" is the name of a body of water in the Western Regions, similar to the "Spring of Greed" in this land.
Fourth, the habit-energy of anger manifests as mutual conflict and opposition. (Up to: When a Bodhisattva perceives anger, they avoid it as if fleeing from execution.
The mind belongs to the element of fire, while the breath belongs to the element of metal. Anger arises from the mind producing the breath, yet it conversely agitates the mind.

When this is further compounded by impact and resistance, the fire of the mind becomes increasingly fierce and the metal of the breath becomes increasingly rigid. Therefore, it is said: "The heat of the mind gives rise to fire."
To forge one’s spirit is to become like metal. To sever the limbs in punishment is called *gong*; to mutilate the flesh is called "cutting.
These five [punishments] involve deceptive practices that entice and provoke one another. (Up to: When a Bodhisattva encounters deception, he views it as fearing a jackal or a wolf.
The habit of deception arises from crafty intelligence and produces evil that gradually spreads like weeds. Thus, it is like water soaking a field where grasses and trees grow;

because they are led and drawn along by irrigation, one experiences the consequences of being bound and dragged by ropes and wooden stocks. "Chán" (讒) refers to slanderers and thieves who subvert what is correct.
"Xiáo" (校) refers to the neck-shackle. The *I Ching* says: "The foot-strap shackle reaches the feet; the neck-shackle reaches the ears."
Sixth is the habit-energy of deception, which arises from mutual delusion. (Up to: When a Bodhisattva encounters deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous snake or viper.
As for the deceiver: for the sake of profit and fame, they harbor many ulterior motives;

they feign the possession of virtue to deceive others, causing others to remain in darkness and ignorance regarding their schemes. Their intent is fraudulent and their mind is flighty, like dust driven by the wind.
To cause others to see nothing, he thus experiences the realms of dust, soil, filth, and evil, as well as the retributions of drowning and being cast about.
Seventh, when the habit of resentment causes mutual hatred to arise from harbored grievances—[up to] "the Bodhisattva views an enemy as if drinking poisoned wine."

When the habitual tendencies of resentment harbor hatred, they inflict injury through hidden means; thus, like a secretly venomous creature harboring malice, one experiences the retribution of flying stones and being crushed by sacks.
The acts of hurling, throwing, and tossing are the retributions for such deeds. Flying stones and hurling refer to vehicles, boxes, and sturdy enclosures—all of which are matters of hidden intent.
As for "crushed by a sack," it refers to being stored within a sack and then beaten to death.

Eighth, the habit-energies of views interact with clarity, like the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)—up to the point of pervasive attachment to what is false, like standing on the brink of a precipice filled with poison. There are five types of habit-energies of views: first, *satkāya-dṛṣṭi*, here translated as the "view of a body," which refers to the attachment to various notions of a self within the body. Second, the "extreme views" (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), which consist of clinging to either annihilation or permanence regarding all phenomena. Third, "false views" (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), which involve erroneous understanding. Fourth... [text fragment]. Fifth... [text fragment]. Regarding the first, *satkāya-dṛṣṭi*: this is called the "view of a body," meaning the grasping that there is a self in the body and various forms of conceptual attachment. Second, the "extreme views": regarding all phenomena, one clings to either nihilism or eternalism. Third, "false views": erroneous awakening. Fourth... [text fragment]. Fifth... [text fragment]. [1] The view of nihilism (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which denies cause and effect; [2] the view of dogmatic attachment (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*), which regards what is not a fruit as a fruit, such as taking the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) to be *nirvāṇa*;

[3] the view of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*), which regards what is not a cause as a cause, such as observing the precepts of cattle or dogs as a cause for rebirth in heaven.
These five are collectively termed "evil views" (*pāpadṛṣṭi*). These various views clarify one another, yet they are mutually contradictory and oppose one another.
Because of this refusal and rejection, it is said that they arise from defiance and give birth to opposition.

Due to these transgressions, one encounters the realm of royal officials and judicial enforcement, receiving the retribution of being subjected to deceptive interrogation and investigation; even when meeting a stranger on the road, one must pass by them once and return again.
This metaphor illustrates how what is seen contradicts [reality]. These five evil views can cause one to fall into the Dharma-body;
therefore, they are called "pits of views. They can lead to the suffering of karma; therefore, they are called "poisonous ravines. Practitioners should swiftly extinguish them.
Ninth, the habit of injustice (*vaṅka*) intermingles and manifests as false accusation. (Up to: When a Bodhisattva encounters injustice, it is like being struck by a thunderbolt.

It is improper to bend what is not crooked; this is called "injustice" (*vaṅka*). For injustice is not true feeling; it arises from false accusation and oppresses others. Therefore, the retribution experienced corresponds to this.

To "push aside," "squeeze out," and "crush"—these are its meanings. To "press down" and "squeezing"—these also convey the same sense. To "filter" and "drip"—[these refer to the gradual exhaustion of the karmic flow].
"Horizontal" (*heng*) means "transverse. It refers to being squeezed and compressed in body, with one's blood drained away, as one is forced through narrow and agonizing instruments, transverse-wise.
This includes what are called "passing downward through," "hanging from nets," and "suspended head-downward"—all of which belong to the category of horizontal passage.
Because slander can injure people, it is called the "Slanderous Tiger"; because it is terrifying, it is called "Thunderclap."

Tenth: The habit of litigation arises from the concealment of faults within one's storehouse [of consciousness], leading to a state like "carrying a high mountain upon one's head while treading upon a vast ocean.

Litigation here does not refer to legal disputes before an official court; rather, it refers to publicly exposing what has been concealed. This is precisely the habit of concealment (*paryavasthāna*); by concealing this, one provokes that litigation.
It is said: "Mutual clamor. Thus, one encounters the realm of reflection and illumination; this is the retribution for being tested by evil companions.

When hidden malice is concealed, its eruption brings self-destruction. To conceal one's offenses is precisely what serves to crush and cast oneself down, like carrying a mountain upon one's head while treading through the sea.
The ten habitual tendencies arise from the ten delusions, encompassing both the root afflictions and their secondary concomitants. These secondary afflictions are of two kinds.

Tenth: The first ten are anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*). Here, "feigning practice" is precisely guile (*śāṭhya*).
"Enmity" (*yuān*) means resentment; "injustice" (*wǎng*) means harm; "litigation" (*sòng*) means concealment.
Ānanda, how do these six retributions arise? All sentient beings—down to the evil retributions they attract—all emerge from the six sense faculties.
The preceding section clarified the causes that are created; the following clarifies the retributions that are experienced.

Now, regarding the creation of karma and the summoning of its retribution, the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) must necessarily coexist. That consciousness is now treated as the karma while the retribution follows from the faculties is a mutual clarification of the textual meaning.
How do the retributions for evil emerge from the six sense organs? (Up to: "Like sparks scattering and spreading, fanning the void.
First, the brief indication. At the end of life, the explanation of the signs: first seeing fierce fires and so forth is what is called retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*).

"The consciousness of the deceased," and so forth, refers to retribution in the present life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*). Under "To reveal," he clarifies the two aspects based on the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

Under "In this way," he clarifies the mutual retribution (*miśra-vedanīya*) in relation to all the faculties; others should be understood by analogy. Regarding those whose karma of seeing induces fire:

because the faculty of seeing belongs to the element of fire, they experience fierce flames. They fear seeing objects and dread their concealment within the mind; in all six faculties, the mutual retribution is direct.

Regarding "entering the Avīci Hell," this is merely a way of speaking based on its gravity. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states that those who commit the most extreme good or the most extreme evil have no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and therefore enter directly.
Hearing belongs to water; thus, when hearing is scorched, it becomes boiling cauldrons and molten copper. The nose governs the breath;
thus, when the breath is scorched, it becomes black smoke and purple flames. The tongue governs taste; "balls of gruel" refers to the category of flavors.

The body is the locus of tactile sensation; it belongs to the category of ash and charcoal. The mind properly belongs to fire; when burned, it becomes even more intense. Thus, sparks fly and flames surge.
These two [body and mind] receive retribution and attract evil fruits (up to) becoming lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul.

Hearing belongs to water; therefore, by performing karma based upon it, one can evoke waves and surges. When hearing is activated, sound is emitted; thus, it serves as the basis for the retribution of offenses and the interrogation of circumstances.
When seeing is activated, there is the roar of thunder; this is because water transforms according to what is seen. When breathing is activated, there is rain and mist;
this is because water transforms according to the breath. When taste is activated, there is pus and blood; this is because water transforms according to taste. When... [the text continues].
Touch becomes a beast or a ghost; this is water transforming according to form. Mental attention becomes lightning or hail; this is water transforming according to the mind.
Indeed, among the retributions experienced herein, there are many that do not correspond to their respective sense organs.
Nevertheless, both karma and its retribution are inconceivable.
Third, the retribution for smelling [odors] invites and draws forth evil fruits: [it extends] until one’s body is shattered by flying sand and gravel.
Because of craving foul odors, one performs various karmic actions; as a result, one is affected by poisonous vapors, giving rise to various retributions.

As for the statement that [the consciousness] "surges up from the earth," it means that poisonous vapors fill the space both near and far, leaving no further way out; therefore, the *śūnyatā-vijñāna* (consciousness) emerges from the earth.
And they gush forth. "Substance" (*chih*) means obstruction; "treading" (*li*) means penetration. The basis upon which the karma of smelling depends does not depart from penetration and obstruction;

therefore, the surging breath can function as both substance and treading. That the surging of sight becomes a torch, and the surging of hearing becomes drowning or boiling water, is because the sense organs follow the transformations of the vital energy (*qi*).
That fish spoil is called "rottenness" (*nai*) and soup spoils is called "off-flavor" (*shuang*); hunger, rottenness, discord, and off-flavors all arise from this.

The flavors change according to the qi; this refers to the bursting, splitting, and rotting [of the body], which occurs because the physical substance changes according to the qi. The surging thoughts become ash and sand;
this refers to the mind changing according to the qi.
Fourth, the retribution of taste invites and draws forth evil fruits (extending to): flying hot iron raining down from the sky.
Following the examples of the eyes, ears, and nose, one should say "seeing, hearing, and smelling"; here it should be called the "retribution of tasting.

Regarding the term "retribution of taste," it is named after that which is tasted. This is because, out of greed for flavor, people set nets and burn the wilds to capture birds and beasts; thus, they see the iron.

It manifests the appearance of a fierce net of flames. As the basis for the faculty of the tongue, it never ceases its inhalation and exhalation; inhaling produces cold, while exhaling produces heat—this is the natural law.
When the tongue devours living beings, it causes them to endure suffering; likewise, by repeatedly tasting [objects], it gives rise to suffering so that it may cause itself to endure it.
Relying on the perception of craving for flavors, it is able to burn gold and stone; relying on hearing, it gives rise to evil. Therefore...
It can become a sharp weapon; relying on the sense of smell and indulging in greed, it captures various flavors like a cage, and thus becomes a great iron cage.

Because the taste of contact harms beings, one experiences arrows and bows that wound oneself. Because one contemplates objects due to the craving for flavor, one experiences flying iron that inflicts harm.
Fifth, the retribution of touch invites evil fruits—whether falling, flying, being fried, or being roasted;

whether amidst mountains or amidst swords and blades—all arise from attachment to the bodies of men and women. The iron city, the fire-dogs, and so forth, are all manifestations of the mixed retribution of unpleasant touch.
These are the bases of karmic touch, which do not transcend union and separation, or being slaughtered and torn asunder.

This is the departure from [ordinary] characteristics. The Path leads toward the road to hell. The "Observation" refers to observing the two watchtowers at the gate of the King of Hell, the hall, and the desk—these are the places where punishments are administered.
All are bases for bodily contact: the burning heat is visual contact; the clashing [of instruments] is auditory contact;

the "enveloping sack" is olfactory contact; the plowing and tongs are gustatory contact; and the flying and falling are mental contact. The "enveloping sack" is used to restrain the vital breath (*prāṇa*); as the karma of thought (*cetanā*) drifts about, one is bound.

Therefore, it gives rise to matters such as flying and falling. "Zi" (剚) means to thrust or insert a blade into the flesh. The acts of stabbing, shooting, torturing, and binding are merely secondary manifestations arising from that [primary cause];
they are not the primary characteristics of the root itself.
Sixth, contemplating the retribution that invites evil fruits [extending] from ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths, whether prostrate or supine;
because the thinking mind is drifting and turbulent, one first perceives signs such as an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land, for these are the supports for the karma of thought.
It does not depart from delusion and awakening. "Wandering wildly" refers to deluded thought. "Knowing suffering" refers to awakened thought. Thought must have an object;
therefore, when thought is bound, it becomes the locus where one undergoes punishment. When vision is bound, it becomes the matter of witnessing and proving one's offense.
When hearing is bound, it can become great boulders, carts, boats, and cages—thus the vital breath rests upon the turbulence of the mind.
That which is transformed by volition (cetanā) is always the tongue-faculty itself, from which sound is emitted. As for those of small stature and below, it is said that their bodies [perceive it];
this is because the karma of touch rides upon the transformations of distracted volition.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six fruits of hell (extending to) "undergoing immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.
This summarizes the ten causes and six fruits. Regarding those who create evil karma together:

when creating evil karma, one faculty acts as the primary agent while the remaining five assist it; thus, the six faculties create together, and the ten karmas are fully present. Therefore, they enter [hell].
The Nose Hell. One undergoes immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas; this is precisely the aforementioned sixfold mutual retribution, which is also the Five Uninterrupted Hells.
Therefore, it is said that one undergoes immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.
If the six sense organs each commit their own acts, and those acts are combined with their respective objects and organs, such a person enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells.
"The six sense organs each commit" means this is different from the previous case where the six organs collectively committed the ten causes.

"And those acts they perform," etc., refers to the former case where the six organs collectively created the ten causes, whereas here it is three organs that commit the three karmas; this corresponds to a single organ.
Furthermore, since they simultaneously possess three or four faculties, they must also lack two or three of the ten karmas;
thus, they enter the eight *ānantarya* hells, rather than the five *ānantarya* hells.
If one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three actions of body, speech, and mind, that person enters the eighteen hells.

Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct committed through body, speech, and mind are grave offenses; however, because they do not pervade all six [senses] and are not complete in ten [aspects], they are lighter than the former [offenses].
While there are only eight great hells—four cold and four hot—there are eighteen subsidiary hells (*kalpa*).
Furthermore, the eighty-four thousand subsidiary hells and their like are all branches of the great hells.
Depending on whether one’s three karmas are combined, intermediate, or otherwise, upon entering, one enters thirty-six hells.

The three karmas are not practiced simultaneously; that is to say, one possesses two while lacking one. Regarding the thirty-six hells, along with the one hundred and eight hells below, their specific names and numbers are not detailed.
If one perceives each sense-base individually and commits a single karma, such a person enters the one hundred and eight hells.

The former possesses both [the causes] while lacking one; this [latter case] incurs one [cause] while lacking two; therefore, it is also light. "Jian" (見) is pronounced "xian" (現). It means that they are clearly not concurrent.
Consequently, sentient beings act and create separately; from false conceptualization arises what was not originally existent.
This concludes the answer to the preceding question. In the five preceding sections, the various evil karmas were distinct;

that is, they were performed and created separately, and the resulting retributions in hell each followed their own kind, thereby entering into corresponding realms (*sabhāgatā*). This is as when one has separately committed an extremely grave offense.
"Entering Avīci together" refers to those who have committed grave offenses; "separately committing minor offenses" refers to those who have committed the one hundred and eight [offenses].
Passages such as "the arising of false conceptions" all respond to the questions previously raised by Ānanda.
Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings (until) later, when their retribution for sins is complete, receive the forms of various ghosts.
They have violated the *vinaya* discipline and lack a correct model; they have transgressed the Bodhisattva precepts and lack a correct cause;
they have defiled the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and lack a correct fruit. These three are incorrect; all else is deviant. Therefore, once the punishment for falling into hell is finished, immediately—
They enter the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*).
