If, due to their original cause, they committed an offense by coveting objects, once this person's retribution is exhausted and they encounter an object, they take form upon it and are called a "strange ghost" (*bhūta-preta*).

This is precisely because the habituation of greed serves as the cause; they give rise to greed for objects and seize them through improper means, and thus their remaining retribution remains among the ghosts.
They further rely upon material objects—such as gold, silver, plants, trees, and spirits—which are of many different kinds; therefore, they are called "strange ghosts" (guǐguǐ).
Those who committed the sin of lust and have completed their retribution encounter the wind and take on form; these are called "drought-demons" (póguǐ).
This is precisely because the prior habituation to lust serves as the cause. Form (*rūpa*) can agitate and disorder the body and mind, just as the wind blows upon objects.

This retribution brings about a ghostly form that, in turn, relies upon the wind; yet the substance of wind is fundamentally void. That this is brought about by habitual practice—cause and effect confronting one another—is surely not in vain.
Those whose transgressions were caused by greed and delusion, once their retribution is exhausted, encounter the form of an animal and are called *māyāvin* ghosts (魅鬼).

This is because their previous habitual practice of deceit serves as the cause; having thus established a foundation in fraudulence and deluded reliance on the void, they take refuge in the form of an animal.
They thus become ghostly forms; these include foxes, wild boars, dogs, and others possessing extraordinary spirits, of which there are many varieties.
Hence it is said that they "assume form upon encountering animals. A *mei* (魅) is one who manifests a beautiful appearance to delude people.
Those who commit the sin of greed and resentment, once their transgressions are exhausted, encounter insects that take form as *gudu* ghosts (poisonous spirits).
This is caused by the habitual tendencies of former enmity; with anger as the precursor, they harbor malice without relinquishing it, binding resentment within the mind.
With burning affliction dwelling in their hearts, when they undergo their remaining retribution, they likewise rely upon poisonous species— namely, snakes, vipers,
and venomous insects that possess extraordinary spiritual powers— to become *gudu* (contagious) poison-demons.
To harbor covetous recollections is a transgression; when such a person’s retribution for this sin is exhausted, they encounter a period of decline and take form as a *pūtana* ghost.

This is precisely because their prior habituation to anger serves as the cause. Not relinquishing hatred is what is meant by "covetous recollection. Thus, one eventually receives the retribution of a ghost.
When they encounter places of calamity and decline, they immediately possess the bodies of people; these are called *lìguǐ* (plague ghosts).
Such things as toxic plagues, *shānghán* (epidemic fevers), *chuánshī* (contagious wasting diseases), and *gùzhēng* (consumption) are all the workings of these ghosts.

To covet and imitate others is a transgression; when this person’s retribution for that sin is exhausted, they encounter the vital breath (*qi*) and take form, becoming what is called a hungry ghost (*preta*).
This is caused by their prior habituation to arrogance. Arrogance consists of looking down upon others and treating things with disdain, holding oneself aloft and being self-important.

When the karmic retribution reaches the class of ghosts, one encounters the vital breath as one’s substance. Lacking any real virtue within, one remains hollow-bellied yet haughty at heart, tormented by hunger. Therefore...
They are called hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Because their transgressions were rooted in greed and deception, when these people’s karmic retribution is exhausted, they encounter the realm of obscurity and take form as "demon-ghosts" (*yamadeva*).
This is due to the causal habit of prior delusion. Having sought profit and reputation, they harbored many heterodox schemes and feigned the possession of virtue.

They deceive and mislead others, causing people to become bewildered and ignorant of their schemes. Upon assuming the form of a ghost, they rely on the hidden and dwell in the dark, using their powers to bewitch those who sleep;
therefore, they are called *yāma* ghosts (sleep-bewitching ghosts).
Those who crave clarity commit a transgression; when their transgressions are exhausted, they encounter essence to form a body, which is called a *wangliang* ghost.

This is precisely the prior habituation of views acting as the cause. Clinging to views, they are born as distinct beings, each claiming clear awakening, and thus they summon rebirth in the realm of ghosts.

They take their form from whatever possesses a brilliant essence; thus, they rely on the sun and moon, the spirits of mountains and marshes, or anything possessing a radiant luster as the substance for their manifestation.
As for what is called a *wangliang*, it refers to a transformation or anomaly of wood or stone.
Greed becomes a transgression; when a person’s transgressions are exhausted, they encounter illumination, yet they remain bound by the names and forms that enslave them as ghosts.

This is precisely because their previous wrongful habits serve as the cause. They are unjustly suppressed and stripped of dignity, relying on empty fabrications and exhausting their minds and thoughts.
They afflict the innocent so as to make them guilty; they encounter manifest conditions and rely upon them to form their bodies, rather than belonging to the class of obscure, dark beings.
They are those who serve as runners in battle or laborers who carry sand and shoulder stones; hence they are called "servants" (yìshǐ).
To form factions out of greed is a transgression; when such a person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter human beings as a physical form known as a "transmitter of ghosts.
This refers to the habit of litigation practiced in previous lives. Because they loved others and favored themselves, they concealed their own faults while litigating against the errors of others;
thus, their retribution lies among the class of ghosts. Taking on a substance within the human realm—much like there are teachers of children in the world—they manifest in this manner.
As for those such as shamans and invocators, they all act as messengers for the divine way to transmit words concerning good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing;
these are called "messengers of ghosts. These aforementioned classes of ghosts are indeed numerous, yet when examining their fruits and verifying their causes, they do not exceed these ten types.
Ānanda, all these people fall because of their pure emotional attachments (down to: "then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous [nature] originally has nothing at all").

The water of accumulated emotional karma sinks downward until it is dried up by fire; thus, when the karma of emotion is exhausted, they again ascend by means of the karma of conceptualization—all of which is the work of delusive falsehood.
In the perfectly luminous mind of awakening, such things do not exist from the beginning.
Furthermore, Ānanda, once the karma of the hungry ghost is exhausted, one takes birth as an animal to repay former debts.

This is because the retribution of hell corresponds to the karma of emotion, while the retribution of the hungry ghost corresponds to the karma of perception; thus, when the karma of the hungry ghost is exhausted, both forms of retribution become void. One must then further repay the karma of indebtedness.
The ghosts of strange objects have their retributions exhausted; being born into the world, they mostly become owls. Through the habit of greed, one becomes a strange ghost;
when the retribution is exhausted, one is reborn among the species of owls. An owl is a "soil-owl" (*tǔxiāo*). It gathers clods of earth to serve as its offspring;
this is caused by its greed for material things. All strange and anomalous beings are subsumed under this category.
The ghosts of the *fēngbó* (wind-drought demons) are born into this world when their karmic retributions are exhausted; they mostly manifest as omens of calamity among all various classes of beings.

Sexual indulgence serves as the cause, and the retribution invites the *fēngbó*. These beings wander as animals, undergoing these signs of misfortune. "Jiù" (咎) means transgression or evil; "zhēng" (徵) means a portentous sign or verification.
These are summoned by wicked conduct and precede the arrival of disasters and anomalies, appearing first as such portents. As in the case of swarms [of locusts].

Flocks of sparrows and swarms of rats are omens of famine and scarcity. The *zhì* bird and the *yáng* bird portend floods; the dancing of cranes indicates frequent droughts. Such categories are not limited to these alone.
Those who were ghosts possessing animals, once their karmic retribution for animal existence is exhausted, are born into the human world, mostly as foxes.

This is the retribution for their deceitful causes; having been ghosts, they became malevolent spirits (*mèi*). Now that their basis [as spirits] is exhausted, they receive the bodies of foxes as animals.
The ghosts of *chong-gu* (insect-pests) and *gui-gu* (demon-pests), once their retribution for the *gu* has been exhausted, are born into the world mostly as classes of venomous creatures.
This is the retribution for the habituation of enmity: the ghosts create *gu*-poisons, while animals become venomous species, such as snakes and scorpions.
The ghosts of decay and pestilence, whose karmic retribution has been exhausted, are born into this world mostly as types of worms.
Due to the cause of habitual anger, these ghosts become agents of decay and pestilence; they rely upon calamities and attach themselves to misfortunes, entering into the body.
They subsequently take on animal forms, returning to lodge within the body as *kāṭaka* and *krimi* worms.
The ghosts of those who received vital breath have their breath exhausted and their retribution ended, so they are born into the world mostly as types of food.
Hungry ghosts attach themselves to the vital breath; arrogance and habituation are the causes. Ghosts suffer from hunger and emptiness, while animals satisfy the fullness of others;
thus they become types of food—namely, the animals in the world that may be eaten.
The ghosts of those who died in the depths of the cotton fields, their karmic retributions exhausted, are reborn in the world for the most part as types of clothing.

Due to the habitual tendencies of their past delusions, these ghosts manifest as "malignant darkness" (yakṣa-dhūma). Once this dark humor has dissolved, they become types of clothing for animals—namely, camels, donkeys, oxen, horses, silkworm cocoons, and the like—which are then used by humans for clothing and utility.
When the spirits of harmonious refinement have their retributions exhausted through harmonious dissolution, they are mostly reborn in the world as "responsive types" (*yinglei*).
Because of their habitual perceptions, these spirits manifest as *wangliang* (phantoms) or luminous entities;

once this is exhausted, they become animals and thus constitute responsive types—such as the swallow of the community and the wild goose of winter, which can respond to the seasonal cycles of the four times. To say "harmonious" (*he*) implies "mixed" (*za*); it refers to being mixed [with various conditions].
Those who were clever and sharp-sighted become ghosts.
These intelligent and numinous ghosts, when their brilliance fades and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the world as many auspicious omens among all classes of beings.

This is due to their previous habitual tendencies; these ghosts rely on their residual brilliance for birth and become a class of servile spirits. When the karma of the ghost realm is exhausted, their animal retribution comes to rest.

"Zheng" (to summon) signifies auspicious beauty. When auspicious omens are about to arrive, there are premonitory signs of them; these include such things as the magnificent phoenix and the auspicious qilin.
Ghosts that depend upon humans, when their retribution for past lives is exhausted and they are reborn in the world, mostly become creatures of this kind.
The cause for the habituation of litigation is that ghosts summon and transmit [the deceased]; when a person dies, they become an animal. The retribution lies in their cleverness and wit;
thus it is said they "follow their kind. This refers to those species that humans keep and raise as domestic animals.
Ānanda, all these beings have been withered by the fires of karma (up to the point where they are exhausted). Thus, these delusive conditions originally do not exist at all.

Having been in the two realms of hell-dwellers and hungry ghosts, their karma was withered by the fires; now they are born as animals to repay the remainder of their karma, which is why it is said they are "sideways.
They exist because of deluded thoughts, but in the awakened nature they are fundamentally non-existent. It is just like a circular shadow seen because of an eye disease.
As you have said, those such as Baolianxiang (Jewel Lotus Fragrance) and others [up to] all constitute the solidification of floating, empty, and delusory thoughts.
Regarding the three conditions you asked about: these were each created by those individuals through their own delusory karma and arose from them; they did not come from elsewhere.
Therefore it is said that "originally they did not descend from heaven," and so forth. They create delusion and receive delusion; within the nature of awakening, all are like this.
Like flowers in the sky.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from these animals [until] they return to being animals to repay the remaining balance, they pay for the livestock at the full price.
If they pay more than their share, then as humans they will be called upon to repay it in turn. Thus, whatever one takes by way of food, [it must be repaid].

One should not exceed the proper measure. If one possesses such power—namely, the power cultivated through meditative concentration and wisdom—and yet does not relinquish the human body, one will become a slave to those powers, or may even suffer their robbery or murder.
Ānanda, you should know that if one uses money and goods [to settle debts], even until the appearance of a Buddha in the world, one cannot cease [the cycle].
Only when the debt is fully repaid does it stop; thus there will be no further enmity. If the debt is not fully repaid and one does not stop, then the enmity will not cease.

Unless one correctly practices with the power of right effort, there is no way to block or cut it off. This refers to destroying delusions through the cultivation of meditative concentration; only upon seeing the Buddha and attaining the Way can one do so.
This exempts them from mutual harm. Although the effects of past karma do not perish and must be repaid when the fruit ripens, they are as unreal as a magical illusion.

You should now know that those of the owl species, once their retribution is fulfilled, will return to their original form and be reborn among humans, though they will be integrated into the ranks of the dull-witted.
Because of their greed for material things, ghosts manifest in monstrous forms; as animals, they exist as earth-owls that nourish themselves by clutching clods of soil.

Now, having returned to the human realm, their nature remains dull and ignorant, mingled with the stubborn and the foolish, and their minds forget virtue and righteousness; it is precisely because of these causes that they are thus.

As for what is called "intermingled" (*saṃmiśra*): when human beings receive retribution, it is summoned by wholesome causes. Although the general retribution (*vipāka-phala*) is the same, the completing karma (*pūrakakarma*) differs;

therefore, ten types are distinguished. Now, those who come here from the animal realm have received this as a secondary consequence of residual karma, rather than being summoned by primary wholesome karma.
Nevertheless, it is still induced by subsequent karma; because it is not [wholesome], it is called "intermingled."
Those who manifest as portents of calamity, having received their retribution in full, return to birth within the human realm, where they intermingle with various classes of beings.
This all begins with greed and desire; thus, ghosts take on the forms of drought-demons (*pabhāsa*), and those above become animals—these being the responses to the misfortunes of their past deeds.

When their karma is exhausted, they return to their original state and intermingle with various classes of beings. Because these portents of calamity originate from demonic anomalies, their residual habits again manifest as demonic anomalies.
Furthermore, those of the fox lineage, having exhausted their retribution and returned to human form, are born among the common masses;

yet because they follow the habits of deceit, they become ghosts that bewitch animals and enter the class of the "lateral births" (*tiryagyoni*), being possessed by foxes and wildcats. Therefore, they are now...
Humans are common and base, lacking discernment.
Those of the poisonous class, having received their retribution and returned to birth within the human realm, are integrated among those of a violent nature;

karmic habituation is the cause. Ghosts manifest as *gudu* (poisonous charms), while those on the periphery are born as animal species; snakes and scorpions are their forms, yet they may return to be born as humans.
The Way is muddled by the category of the obstinate. To be poisonous and unruly constitutes obstinacy; this, too, is the residue of habituation.
Those belonging to the category of worms, having received sufficient retribution and returned to form, are born into the human realm as minute beings mixed among the populace.

With the habituation of anger as their cause, they dwell among the hungry ghosts as pestilence; they are born as parasites such as *yū* and *hī*; and even when they receive the form of a human, they are those not even recorded in the registers of men.
Those who consume their peers, once their retribution is exhausted, return to form and are reborn among humans as members of the gentle classes.
Arrogance is the cause; it summons hungry ghosts who manifest from knotted qi and possess no substantial nature. Animals receive the category of food;
humans are weak and yielding. This is because arrogance and conceit conversely invite the retribution of gentleness and timidity.
Those who served as attendants are recompensed with sufficient sustenance and restored to human form, yet they participate among the class of laborers.
With habitual deception as their cause, they become ghosts when following the darkness of the underworld, or animals when serving as articles of use;
as humans, they undergo toil and hardship, belonging to the category of craftsmen and manual laborers.
Those who correspond to the human category receive full retribution and are reborn in the human realm among the class of literary beings.

Through this, they follow from their habitual perceptions; as ghosts, they descend into refined spirits; when their retribution as *wangliang* demons ends, they become animals according to the timing of their karma.
Entering the human realm, they possess a slight degree of literary refinement, yet this is not the result of a primary causal habit; it is also called "participatory integration."
Those who receive auspicious signs are sufficiently rewarded to return to human form within the realm of men, joining the ranks of the enlightened.
Those whose habitual practices were perverse receive the status of spirits; they are driven and employed with rapid speed, never pausing for a moment.
Those who have summoned auspicious responses among animals will possess a mixture of intelligence and clarity. Examining the fruits to verify the causes, there is necessarily no discrepancy.
Those who, through their various karmic conditions, have repaid their debts and returned to birth in the human realm, participate among the class of the enlightened (*dalu*).
Because of their habitual practice in litigation, spirits take them as their medium; they transmit divine utterances to reveal fortune and calamity.

They attract domestic animals that become tame and clever, and they reach a mastery of human affairs, penetrating both adversity and prosperity. Unmoved by honor or disgrace, they remain at peace and self-possessed; therefore, they are called the class of the enlightened.
Ānanda, all these beings have fully repaid their past debts [until] these types are called the "pityable ones.
Within the realms of hell-demons and animals, they repay their prior karma; once the retribution of the three miserable paths is exhausted, they return to being human.

According to the subsequent good karma they have summoned, their destinies differ. These are further divided into ten categories, all of which constitute inverted cycles of transmigration. One who desires to bring them to rest...
They are inverted. There is only morality, concentration, and wisdom; without these three, one does not cease from saṃsāra.
If a Buddha did not appear in the world, who would teach this Dharma to enable them to practice and study so as to escape saṃsāra? Therefore, such people are called those worthy of compassion.
Ānanda, furthermore, there are ten kinds of immortals (*ṛṣi*) who follow those who do not rely on perfect enlightenment—those who have not yet reached the destination of the enlightened ones.
These are those who practice *samādhi* without relying on the mind that is neither born nor extinguished as their foundation; that is to say, they do not take this as the basis for their cultivation.
They cultivate deluded thoughts separately, meaning they practice based separately upon deluded thoughts. They preserve their mental conceptions to solidify their physical forms.
This refers to those who set their minds on longevity, desiring that this physical frame remain firm and indestructible in order to seek eternal life.
"Xian" (Immortal) means "to transcend"; it signifies that a person's form and spirit can transcend [the mortal realm] and not die. Nevertheless, they ultimately return to decay and ruin;
compared to the heavens they are inferior, but compared to ordinary humans they are superior. Therefore, they are categorized separately. *Baopuzi* says: "Those who seek immortality..."

One must take loyalty, filial piety, harmony, obedience, benevolence, and sincerity as one's foundation. If virtue is not cultivated and one merely devotes oneself to esoteric arts, one will ultimately fail to attain longevity.

Ānanda, those sentient beings who firmly adhere to medicinal regimens (until they attain awakening and achieve the name of "Transcendent Practitioners") rely on drugs and tonics to prolong their life for one kalpa;
yet, because they cannot yet ascend lightly, they are "earth-walking transcendents" (*bhūmicara-siddha*). [The character] *xing* (行) is pronounced *qù* (去);
it refers to their spiritual practice. By consuming yellow radish, pine, cypress, and the like, their bodies eventually become light, and they are able to fly.

There are those who are *xian* (transcendents). Those who refine gold and stone into elixirs (*huandan*) and the like, transforming their bones and changing their forms, and who gather soil or touch stones to roam among humanity, are *youxing-xian* (wandering transcendents).

Those who stir the celestial pond (*tianchi*), swallow their own vital fluids (*jinli*), remain as pure and graceful as ice and snow, do not consort with worldly desires, and are no different from the heavens, are *tianxing-xian* (heavenly-transcending transcendents). They ride upon the movement and stillness of yin and yang to harmonize...
Those who consolidate their vital energy (*qi*) and refine their essence, casting off their physical forms to traverse the void, are *kōng-hsing* (Empty-Practice) Immortals.

Those who swallow the essence of colors, clothe themselves in rainbows, drink mists, and whose refined vital energy penetrates in hidden ways, are *tōng-hsing* (Penetrating-Practice) Immortals. Those who firmly maintain incantations and rituals until, over time, their path of arts is perfected, are *dào-hsing* (Path-Practice) Immortals.
Those who clarify and concentrate their refined contemplation until, over time, they are able to illuminate and respond, are *chào-hsing* (Illuminating-Practice) Immortals.
Some visualize the spirit exiting through the aperture at the crown of the head; others fix the mind on the navel wheel (*nābhi-cakra*) to refine the elixir (*candana*).
Both involve the contemplative recollection of perfecting the circle. Internally, they pair the male of the *kan* trigram with the female of the *li* trigram as husband and wife;

externally, they gather yin to assist yang and preserve the vital essence (*jing*). These are practitioners of the Way of the Spirit (*xingxian*). They visualize the entire world as being transformed and, thereby, realize transcendence.
The transformation then causes one to forget mental conceptions; the form is like withered wood and the mind is like extinguished ashes. This is called the perfect accomplishment of awakening.
When one's conduct transcends the world, it is called the "Transcendent Immortal of Transcendent Conduct."
Ānanda, all these [beings] refine their minds among humans... until their retribution is exhausted, they return once more and disperse into the various realms of existence.

The preceding passage states that when emotion is slight and thought is predominant, one is light and buoyant yet not far-reaching, thus becoming a Flying Immortal (*fei-xian*). The subsequent passage says: "One minutely investigates the seven realms;
all are the signs of the conditioned states of deluded sinking. One undergoes birth through deluded conceptualization and follows karma through deluded conceptualization. This refers to the mind.
This is to know what must be guarded against and prepared for. That which is called "refining the mind among humans" does not consist merely of taking medicinal elixirs to nourish life;

it must be accompanied by precepts and goodness before it can truly be called refining the mind. As for those who separately attain the principle of life, this arises from karma performed among humans that subsequently evokes the retribution of the realm of immortals.
As the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas) says: "Mount Kunlun, the Broad Capital..."
In the wilds of Mount Kunlun, at the Mound of Xuanyuan, lies the Land of the Immortals, where there is neither cold nor heat, and people all live for several thousand years.
This, too, is merely a common lot shared by many; it is not that such a place does not exist.

Yet, if one merely seeks to solidify the physical form without refining the mind, while hoping to reach a thousand-year lifespan, this is like seeing an egg and demanding a rooster at night—is it not far too hasty a calculation?
Ānanda, those people in the world who do not seek the permanent abode [up to] this class of beings are called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).

Although they have not yet been able to leave desire behind, they are able to obstruct it, preventing the waters of craving from flowing. Thus, their nature becomes limpid and translucent, and they are therefore able to take birth in this first heaven.
These six heavens are attained by practicing the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions; for now, we shall discuss them only in brief.
Regarding those who wish to slightly increase their excellence: first, Ānanda served as the catalyst for the teaching. Furthermore, sensual desire is the root of saṃsāra;
as previously clarified, it is from this that one’s downfall begins, and it is also from this that transcendence begins.
The intent is that for those whose initial resolve has not yet achieved meditative concentration and wisdom, they should swiftly sever the root; thus, saṃsāra—
They may emerge.
Regarding their own wives, their sensual desire is slight; such a class is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three).
Because this desire is thinner than that of those before, they receive retribution by dwelling above them; subsequent heavens follow this same pattern. "Pure Abode" (Śuddhāvāsa) refers to purity.
When one dwells within [the realm of form], the flavor of complete purity is not yet fully realized because of the presence of subtle attachment.
The sun and moon dwell at the waist of Mount Sumeru, while the Trāyastriṃśa heaven dwells upon its summit; because they are able to clarify and enhance luminosity, they are able to transcend it.
When encountering a desire, they engage in it briefly and then depart without further thought; such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven.

Because the mind of desire does not arise, movement is slight and stillness is predominant. Of the six heavens of the desire realm, the lower two are called the Earth-Dwelling Heavens (*bhūmi-vāsin*), and the upper four are called the Space-Dwelling Heavens (*antarīkṣa-vāsin*).
They do not require the sun or moon and are always luminous; day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of lotus flowers.
Because it is quiet at night, it is called "a period of time" (*samaya*).
Although all times are quiet, there is still the arrival of contact that must be encountered; such a class [of beings] is named the Tuṣita Heaven.
Although their minds are increasingly tranquil, they have not yet escaped encountering contact. This [state] is capable of having few desires, but has not yet reached the state of being without mind.

The Tuṣita Heaven consists of an inner court and an outer court. Although the three calamities reach up to the third dhyāna heaven, the present statement does not refer to them because it concerns the inner court.
Its subtle and refined nature is beyond contact; all such matters pertain exclusively to the inner court.
"I have no desire; you should perform the task for me" (up to this point)—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*).
Here, objects appear spontaneously without [the gods] having to form a mind [of desire]; thus it is said they "lie across" [the offerings] and "chew the wax," meaning the flavor is extremely thin.

All devas possess realms that are the result of their retribution (*vipākaviṣaya*), yet this heaven surpasses the lower heavens because its pleasures are enjoyed through spontaneous transformation. Therefore...
This is called "Transcending Transformations.

It refers to those who, while lacking a worldly mind, perform actions identical to those of the world (up to this point). This class is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
"Clearly transcending" means that [the lower realms] are entirely devoid of flavor. "Transformations" refers to the fifth heaven; "no transformations" refers to the heavens below.
Furthermore, as for the various objects of sensual pleasure, they do not manifest through one's own effort but are instead enjoyed with mastery through the transformations of others;

thus they are called "Mastery over Others' Transformations" (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). Ānanda, although the forms of these six heavens involve movement [and so forth], from this point downward they are collectively termed the Desire Realm (Kāmadhātu).
Although their forms involve physical movement, this designation of "physical union" (*rūpa-saṃyoga*) applies specifically to the two destinies of humans and *devas*.
It is said that their mental traces still intersect; that is, the traces of desire in their minds still manifest as the signs of physical union. Thus, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The six [classes of] desire-realm beings engage in sexual intercourse through embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing. This indicates that among the two classes of heaven-dwellers residing on the earth, there is physical union, whereas in Yāma...
In the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, they embrace; in Tuṣita, they hold hands; in Nirmāṇarati, they smile at one another; and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin, they gaze at each other.

One must know that those texts each describe the reception of desire according to the six heavens. The present sutra, however, distinguishes the gravity of sexual desire specifically among human beings in order to reveal how the retributions experienced in the six heavens differ.
Annotated Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Eight.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
Collated Notes, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty;
translated into Chinese by the Śramaṇa Mīghaśikṣā of the country of Udyāna during the Tang Dynasty.
Transcribed by Fang Rong, Dharma-hearer of the Bodhisattva Precepts under the Tang Dynasty, former Minister of Justice,
concurrently Participant in the Administration of Affairs with the Seal of Office,
and Duke of Qinghe; annotated by the Śramaṇa Zhenjie of Zhuili.
Ānanda, all those people in the world who cultivate their minds in such a manner—this class is called the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmapārisadya).

The preceding section explained the six heavens; although they have emerged from the disturbances of the mundane world, they have not yet severed desire, and thus they are collectively termed the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu).

From here downward, eighteen heavens are explained; although they are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form, and thus they are collectively termed the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu).

As for the realms (*dhātu*), they are also collectively called the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*) because they have already abandoned the defilement of desire. They are collectively designated as the four *dhyānas* because they have already abandoned distraction and agitation.

While the heavens of the desire realm are produced through the retribution of the ten wholesome deeds alone, these heavens are produced through the combined retribution of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and [wholesome deeds].
Nevertheless, they consist specifically of the six practices of impure (*sāsrava*) dhyāna-contemplation. As for the six practices: one views the desire realm as suffering, as coarse, and as...
This is the obstruction. To take delight in the realm of form as being pure, sublime, and free from defilement constitutes the worldly path of suppressing afflictions followed by ordinary beings.
As for the phrase "without relying on *dhyāna*," etc., it means this is not the authentic cultivation of true *samādhi*.

Lacking correct wisdom, one merely cultivates the six practices to suppress desire, ensuring that craving and attachment do not arise; thus, one does not remain in the desire realm. [This addresses] coarse afflictions.

Being unstained, the pure retribution manifests before them; thus, they are born into the Brahma-world. First, they are called the Brahmakāyika (Assembly of Brahmās), which refers merely to the common multitude.

Next, they are called the Brahmapurohita (Ministers of Brahmā), who are the great ministers and counselors of Mahābrahmā, culminating finally in the state of Mahābrahmā itself. Their advancement follows a sequential order.
Once the habitual tendencies of desire have been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests—up to this point—one such class is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).

While the first heaven [the Heaven of Brahmā’s Retinue] is merely able to maintain physical restraint and subdue desire, these gods further attain the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*), thereby conforming to the code of discipline (*vinaya*).

Because they practice the virtue of Brahma, they transcend [the lower realms]. Being conjoined with both precepts and meditative concentration, this is called "precepts concomitant with concentration" (*samādhi-sahagata-śīla*).
With body and mind wondrously perfected and their dignified deportment unimpaired—up to this point—one such class is named the Great Brahma Heaven (*Mahābrahmā-deva*).
Because his body and mind were already free from the defilement of desire, he attained a wondrous perfection of body and mind;
because he delighted in and accorded with all forms of discipline, his majestic deportment and moral conduct were pure and without flaw.
Upon reaching this stage, he further added the brilliance of clear awakening and transcendent penetration, thus reaching the pinnacle of sublime virtue and becoming a Brahma King.
Ānanda, these three superior streams—wherein all suffering and affliction (up to) the various outflows are unmoving—are called the First Dhyāna.
These devas have already emerged from the stream of desire; having turned their backs on the defilement of desire and moved toward supreme purity, all four dhyānas are thus termed "superior streams.

Having already abandoned the eight sufferings of the desire realm, it is said that they are not oppressed by suffering and affliction. Having already abandoned the scattered and agitated mind of desire.

Therefore it is said that "all outflows (āsrava) are unmoving. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*," meaning that one has abandoned the defiled and evil [states] of the desire realm and attained the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) through birth. However, from this heaven down to the lower heavens, they are all said not to be the "correct cultivation of true samādhi" (*bhūtasaṃmādhi*).
This distinguishes them as being with outflows (*sāsrava*), rather than without outflows (*anāsrava*)."
Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmās... [up to] this class is called the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*).
These have ascended by following the practice of Mahābrahmā; being fully endowed with precepts, concentration, and wisdom, they are said to be "perfected.
Because their Brahma-conduct is perfected, they are able to clarify and concentrate their minds, remaining unmoved by external objects, such that stillness and depth give rise to light. This light—

It is still inferior; therefore, it is named "Limited Light" (Parīttābha). From the second dhyāna upward, there is no verbal speech; light is emitted solely through the power of meditative concentration.
Because this light varies in degree of excellence, the levels are distinguished as higher or lower.
Light illuminates light, shining forth without end; such a class [of beings] is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*).

As their power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly luminous, wondrous lights flash forth in succession. From the previously mentioned Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), many lights flash forth in turn;

these lights illuminate one another, and thus they shine without end. As the objective realm becomes pure in accordance with the light, it reflects throughout the ten directions, universally becoming as clear as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
Because its illumination is inexhaustible, it is named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
It absorbs and sustains the perfect radiance to accomplish the essence of the teaching. (Up to: This class of beings is named the Heaven of Radiant Sound (*Ābhāsvara*).

The substance of the teaching differs across various worlds; thus, in this Sahā world, it is conveyed through written characters, whereas in the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavatī) world, there are no written characters.

There, the teaching is expounded solely by means of various fragrances. These devas inhale and sustain these fragrances, which form a perfect radiance (*maṇḍala-prabhā*) as the substance of the teaching.

This causes people to contemplate the light and know how to cultivate pure virtues (*brahma-guṇa*). Since there is no spoken language, transformation occurs through purity, and beings receive benefit according to their individual capacities.
Each is distinct; therefore, it is said that their application is inexhaustible. Because light serves as sound, it is called "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara).
Ānanda, these three superior streams—having subdued all anxieties and coarse outflows—are termed the Second Dhyāna.

The three heavens of the second dhyāna further surpass those below them; therefore, they are called "the superior stream" (*viśeṣa-āhāra*). Because one attains supreme joy (*prīti*), it is said that one cannot be oppressed by any anxiety or distress.
While in the first dhyāna one has just attained a mind free from outflows (*anāsrava*) and immovability, one has not yet been able to subdue [the afflictions].
This deva has already subdued the coarse outflows (*āsrava*); thus, karma gradually diminishes while conduct gradually excels. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"This is called the stage of joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That is to say, the water of concentration moistens the mind, the light of wisdom brings tranquility, and the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*) is harmoniously adjusted, so that sorrow does not arise.
[The character] "xuán" (懸) is likely an error for the character "chóu" (愁).

Ānanda, thus the celestial beings of the *Candraprabha-svara* (Moon-Light Sound) realm—up to this class known as the *Parīttābha* (Limited Purity) Heaven—because the sublime principle is revealed through the instruction of the circular radiance above, they are able to give rise to and perfect refined practice.

They depart from all agitations of joy and give birth to pure bliss. This bliss is not an external object; it emerges from the nature of purity, being tranquil, serene, and still. This is called [the state of]...
Although they experience the bliss of tranquility, their purity is still inferior; thus, they are merely able to access it but have not yet perfected it.
Because their purity is still inferior, they are called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttābha).
When pure emptiness manifests before one, it triggers an infinite [state]; such a class [of beings] is called the Immeasurable Purity Heaven (*apramāṇa-śubha-deva*).
As for "pure emptiness," it is the meditative mark that is free from all movement of joy and does not take objective objects as its condition. From this, it expands and pervades.
It causes the pure marks to be boundless and to accord with the wondrous nature; thus, body and mind become light and serene, and the joy of the nature is perfected.
Because they are boundless, it is called "Immeasurable Purity. Furthermore, because it has not yet pervaded the higher [stages] while being more extensive than the lower, it is called "Immeasurable."
The world, body, and mind are all perfectly pure (up to) this class known as the Śubhakṛtsna (Universal Purity) devas.
Their bodies and minds above are light and tranquil; this refers for now to their internal state. Now, regarding "the world" and so forth, these terms collectively encompass the external environment.
Because the pure space is boundless, they attain perfect purity in the world, body, and mind, and the merit of purity manifests before them.
Then body and mind return to the bliss of cessation. Because everything is perfectly pure, it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna).
Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity [to the path] up until the full completion of joy; this is called the Third Dhyāna.

These three superior streams are free from the agitation of joy and accord with the bliss of the fundamental nature; therefore, it is said that they possess great accordance and attain the bliss of tranquility.
"Perfectly endowed with joy" refers to the stage of wondrous bliss apart from joy; this means that although the mind is free from joy, the bliss of joy is spontaneously present.
Ānanda, furthermore, as for the gods and humans whose bodies and minds are not oppressed [down to] "this class is called the Puṇyaprasava Heaven.
Furthermore, the phrase "below" concludes the virtues of the third dhyāna. "Pleasure is not below" reveals the faults of the third dhyāna. "Suffering and pleasure are below."

This correctly demonstrates the arising of merit. For previously, the movement of joy was the cause of oppressive suffering; now, although joy has departed and the oppression of suffering has ceased, one attains immeasurable bliss.
Yet this bliss does not end in bliss, for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) will inevitably follow. This deity realizes this, and thus suddenly abandons both suffering and pleasure.
Because of this abandonment of suffering and pleasure, it is called the extinction of the signs of grossness (*dausthulya*). [This is] the abandonment of mindfulness...
Because it is pure, it arises from the nature of pure merit. From this point downward, the four *dhyānas* are explained as comprising nine heavens in total.

However, regarding the realms of retribution for the four *dhyānas*, there are only three heavens. The fourth, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), is a separate opening within the third, the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*) heaven;
both are realms of retribution for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Above these four are the five heavens of the Non-Returners (*anāgāmin*), which belong exclusively to noble ones (*ārya*).
They cultivate meditative concentration differently from ordinary beings;
with a mind of equanimity that is perfectly integrated and a pure resolve, they reach such a state as this, which is called the Heaven of Merit-Love (Puṇyaprasava).
Although previously one had abandoned both suffering and pleasure, the arising of the nature of pure merit was not yet perfectly integrated and purified.

Now, as the nature of merit becomes unobstructed, the mind of equanimity reaches perfect integration, resolute understanding becomes pure, and merit is without limitation, whereby one attains conformity.

To reach the furthest limits of the future is called "loving merit" (*puṇyaprema*). Because one delights in and accords with the nature of merit that is without obstruction, it is named "loving merit.
Question: This is a mundane dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava-dhyāna*); its lifespan is limited. How can it reach the furthest limits of the future? Answer:

This refers to those who have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and whose karmic retribution (*vipāka*) results in a lifespan so vast that it spans many kalpas, extending to the very limits of the future;
it does not refer to what is discussed regarding the period after such retribution has ended.
Ānanda, from this heavenly realm there are two diverging paths... [up to] ...this class of beings is called the Bṛhatphala Heaven (the Heaven of Vast Results).
From the stage of Merit-Love (*puṇyaprasava*), there diverge two paths: one is the direct path leading to the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*);

the other is the circuitous path leading to the Unconscious (*asaṃjñin*). If, in the preceding state of mind, one does not harbor divergent attachments and practices meditative concentration directly, causing the immeasurable pure radiance of one's own heaven to reach its full perfection of merit, then once the cultivation of merit is complete, one realizes the Vast Fruit. And...
They dwell in this heaven; because the merit resulting from the meditative concentration of this heaven is so vast, it is called "Vast Fruit" (Bṛhatphala).
If, with a prior state of mind, they simultaneously become weary of both suffering and pleasure—up to this point—a certain class of beings is called the Heaven of Non-conception (Asaṃjñisattva).
Although the preceding mind was able to subdue delusions and cultivate dhyāna, it still involved delusion and retained a sense of duality.

It took the presence of mind to be birth-and-death and the absence of thought to be nirvāṇa. Thereupon, simultaneously wearying of both suffering and pleasure, one single-mindedly investigates the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).

First, one abandons the coarse mind to enter the subtle mind; then, abandoning the subtle mind, one enters the extremely subtle mind. From this extremely subtle mind, there is a continuous succession.

Without interval, as objects and the body reach their limit, the mind reaches the limit of mental perception; when all are relinquished, it is called the "Path of Perfect and Ultimate Relinquishment," wherein both body and mind are extinguished.

When mental deliberations are as still as ash, this is the "Non-conceptual Samādhi. By virtue of this, one receives retribution and is born in the Heaven of No-Thought, with a lifespan of five hundred kalpas.
This is because such a person does not understand that the nature of delusion is essentially empty, and thus clings [to it].
They regard arising and ceasing as wearisome toil and, weary of this arising and ceasing, they seek that which is without arising or ceasing; yet this is not true non-arising.
They merely observe that the six consciousnesses do not function—like a fish trapped between ice—and, unaware of subtle arising and ceasing, falsely claim it to be *nirvāṇa*.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that when one is first born into this heaven, the state of non-conceptualization is not yet complete; it only becomes so after half an eon (*kalpa*), at which point their retribution [ends].
When that is exhausted, they again experience perception for half a kalpa, after which their retribution ends.
Ānanda, these four superior streams, whose efforts have reached full maturity throughout all worlds, are called the four dhyānas.

Regarding "unshakable by suffering and pleasure": because one has abandoned both suffering and pleasure through the fourth dhyāna, and because equanimity and mindfulness are purified, one cannot be shaken.
However, that vessel is not truly eternal; it arises and perishes along with the sentient being.
Although it is not the unconditioned true realm, the conditioned efficacy has here reached full maturity.
Ānanda, herein there are further five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who establish their dwellings within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).

Those who have attained the third fruit, having exhausted all nine grades of the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through cultivation, are born in this heaven and will no longer take birth in the desire realm;

therefore, they are called "non-returners. As for "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*), these are the afflictions in the form of seeds; both these and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are extinguished here. This...

This refers to the absence of karma that leads to rebirth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The phrase "forgetting both suffering and pleasure" further indicates the absence of such rebirth-karma from the fourth dhyāna downward.
Therefore, it is said that there is no "dwelling below. These five heavens are established separately from the fourth dhyāna;

they are collectively named the Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*). Hence, it is said that they establish their abodes through the commonality of the mind of equanimity.
Ānanda, when both suffering and pleasure are extinguished and the conflicting mind no longer engages [with its objects]—up to this point—one such class is called the Heaven of No-Heat (Atapa).
Previously, when there was equanimity toward or aversion for suffering and pleasure, the mind and its objects were in conflict, and one could not be free from vexation.

Only when both mind and object are released are afflictions severed. "Vexation" refers to intense heat; "heat" refers to subtle vexation. Above this, there is only the cessation of the conflicting mind.

There is no further engagement. Even if there were still grounds for engagement, one would merely extinguish coarse characteristics and attain freedom from vexation. This state further increases in excellence;
the mental mechanism has no counterpart, and as one investigates engagement until no ground remains, one can extinguish the shadows of conditions. Therefore, there is no feverish distress.
The wondrous vision throughout the worlds of the ten directions is perfectly clear and serene... this class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna (Good Appearance) Heaven.

"Ten directions" refers to that which is illuminated; "wondrous vision" refers to the capacity to illuminate. Although it illuminates the myriad phenomena, it does not give rise to thoughts or deliberations following after those phenomenal objects.
Therefore, there is no defilement from dust-like phenomena. Because the wondrous vision is perfectly clear and serene, it is free from all such dust and impurities. Thus [it is so named].

It is named "Excellent Vision" (Sudarśana). As for "Pure Vision": because it is free from the intermixture of dust and defilements, pure vision manifests before one; thus, one proceeds with purposeful action.
Since it consists purely of wisdom without habitual tendencies, it is said to be "unimpeded in its refinement. Therefore, it is called "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa).
"Exhausting the ultimate limit of the multitude of atoms and reaching the nature of the nature of form" (up to) "a single category called the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
"Atoms" (*jī*) refers to the subtlest particles of form. "Exhausting the ultimate limit of the multitude of atoms" means to exhaustively investigate all these subtle particles.

"Nature" refers to the fundamental basis of the subtle. "Reaching the nature of the nature of form" means to exhaustively reach the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*). Since the ultimate atoms and the multitude of subtle particles have already been...

When one has thoroughly exhausted [all forms], one enters into emptiness; therefore, it is said that one "enters the boundless. Because all form is completely exhausted, it is named the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha).
Ānanda, this heaven of the Non-returners is such that those in the four dhyānas—and indeed ordinary people of the world—cannot perceive it.

The deities of the lower heavens cultivate impure, mundane meditative concentrations (*sāsrava-vaipākika-dhyāna*), whereas these deities cultivate pure, noble karma (*anāsrava-ārya-karma*). Because there is a difference between the coarse and the subtle, they are unable to see [them].
Ānanda, from the "Eighteen Heavens Walking Alone Without Intercourse" downward is what is called the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).

This summarizes the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). They act alone without association because they are both devoid of sensual desire. Yet, they have not exhausted the burden of physical form, as they still possess material substance.
Furthermore, Ānanda, from this Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down [to the lower realms], they are called Great Arhats who have turned their minds back [from the world].

The Akaniṣṭha Heaven resides at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and is adjacent to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it is called the "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*) and the "limit of form.
There are two diverging paths: one leads out of the three realms, which refers to this passage; the other enters the formless realm, which refers to the subsequent passage.

All four dhyānas are cultivated by relying on equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti*). Here, the mention of the "mind of equanimity" points to the causal mind of the summit of existence. This is the causal mind.

To be able to give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), exhaust all defilements and delusions, and reach the state of perfect clarity (*paripūrṇa-avabhāsa*) such that one transcends the triple world (*tridhātu*) and does not abide in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle,
but enters the Bodhisattva vehicle— this is called "turning the mind."
If one achieves equanimity through a mind of relinquishment (up to this point), such a class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
From here downward, the four heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are clarified. Regarding "formless" (*ārūpya*): there is no form that is the fruit of karma;

there is, however, form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which applies equally to both the environment and its inhabitants. Thus, having extinguished the body and returned to non-existence, it is the dwelling place of those Śrāvakas of fixed nature, or—
They abandon the realm where gods and humans dwell together; their types are manifold, yet all lack the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The four heavens all advance by relying on partial emptiness (*ākāśa*): first, they loathe form and rely on emptiness; second, they loathe emptiness and rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*);

third, form, emptiness, and consciousness are all extinguished, and they rely on the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*); fourth, they rely on the nature of consciousness, exhausting their investigation through extinction, yet fail to attain true cessation.

All of these are the superior wholesome fruits of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); they have not yet transcended saṃsāra and do not constitute the Path of the Sages. If one is in the lower [heavens], one follows the previous method:

perceiving the body as descending, one clarifies the characteristics of this heaven. Although in this first heaven one possesses purity through the abandonment of mindfulness, one still perceives the obstruction of one’s own form.
By resolutely cultivating the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*), one extinguishes the body and returns to non-existence; thus, one grows weary of form and relies upon emptiness.
When the mind corresponds with empty space, it is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; thus one is reborn in the sphere of infinite space.
When all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation—reaching this state, such a class of beings is called the sphere of infinite consciousness.
When all obstructions have dissolved and ceased to exist, one no longer relies on form (*rūpa*). When even the non-obstruction of emptiness ceases, one no longer relies on space (*ākāśa*).

What remains is only the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manas*; this is the state of those who weary of emptiness and rely upon consciousness. It is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

Therefore, one is reborn in the sphere of infinite consciousness. The *ālaya* is the eighth consciousness; the *manas* is the seventh consciousness. [The remainder concerns] the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*).
Once these have been dissolved, the six consciousnesses no longer exist; thus, only two remain. Among these, the objects of the manas are the three—form, emptiness, and consciousness.
Since form and emptiness are absent in this stage, the coarse objects of form and emptiness are already gone; therefore, only the subtle aspects of the "half" and "all" portions remain.
When both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind has entirely ceased—up to this point—one such class is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Although the sphere of emptiness and form had already vanished in the preceding stage, the conscious mind had not yet been extinguished; now, this conscious mind has entirely ceased.
Therefore, the ten directions are tranquil and utterly devoid of any destination. Because it is tranquil and without destination, it is named "Nothingness. However, although this...
The mind of consciousness has perished, yet the nature of consciousness has not perished. Practitioners today do not penetrate deeply into this nature; they mostly stagnate at this point.

Though they may thoroughly comprehend the emptiness of form and extinguish their mental deliberations until reaching the state of non-existence, they ultimately remain bound by the nature of consciousness.
Profound and continuous, one cannot liberate oneself from it. The cave of birth and death truly exists herein.
When the nature of consciousness is unmoving and has been extinguished through exhaustive investigation, it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
The nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the profound and fundamental source of the conscious mind. "Immovable" means it is quiescent and has no destination.

Because one takes this immovability of the nature of consciousness to be the truth, one exhaustively investigates it through cessation; thus, within the inexhaustible, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion.
Therefore, it appears to exist yet does not exist; it appears to be exhausted yet is not exhausted. Because it appears to exist yet does not exist, it is not "perception" (saṃjñā).
Because it appears to be exhausted yet is not exhausted, it is also not "non-perception" (asaṃjñā).
"These who exhaust emptiness yet do not fully realize the principle of emptiness" (up to) "being deluded and leaking, they lack hearing [the Dharma] and thus enter the cycle of rebirth.

Regarding the phrase "these who exhaust emptiness yet do not fully realize the principle of emptiness," this refers to those in the aforementioned four heavens who all advance in their cultivation based on partial emptiness (*prādeśika-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, they are unable to exhaustively realize the wondrous principle of true emptiness. From the stage of Non-returner (Anāgāmin) downward, it is said that there are noble ones born in these realms;
these are merely those of dull faculties who have attained the state of a Non-returner (*na-han*). As for the term "Arhat," this is a designation applied based on their subsequent attainment.

If one proceeds from the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva) downward, referring to the various ordinary beings among the gods, even if they reach the limit of the Four Formless Heavens (*catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*), they do not return to the untainted state (*anāsrava*). Thus...
Deluded by the outflows (*āsrava*), they lack any sight or hearing; thus, they enter the cycle of transmigration.
Master Yue’s claim that those in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*) do not return is incorrect.
Ānanda, these various devas among the heavens—each being a celestial being—are [the ones who] dedicate themselves to the path of practice traversed by the assembly of the noble ones.
This clarifies that the hosts of devas receive retribution according to their karma; the King (the practitioner) thus entrusts himself to these stations to advance upward.

Their "wandering in *samādhi*," etc., refers to the "play" (*vikrīḍita*) of Bodhisattvas: entering and emerging from various *dhyānas* and *samādhis*, they progress through the noble stages, taking the heavens as their [basis].

Regarding the path of practice: this means that when a noble one (*ārya*) desires to hasten toward Bodhi, they must necessarily rely upon the various heavens as a temporary abode for their cultivation and advancement.
It is like a person who wishes to reach a royal city; they must necessarily borrow the roads to proceed there.
Ānanda, from the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) down to the extinction of body and mind of the *pudgala*, each follows its own kind.
"The extinction of body and mind" refers to the non-existence of the form-aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) and coarse consciousness.

All these, below, generally indicate that the three realms arise through delusion, and that the seven destinies (*saptagati*) sink into them through delusion. *Pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly takes up [existence]."
Gatis (destinies). This refers to how sentient beings, having given rise to afflictions and performed karma, are born into their respective destinies according to those actions.
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms... [up to] ...due to moisture, they are subsumed under the destiny of animals.
Asura is translated here as "Non-God. Their power of merit is equal to that of the gods, yet they lack divine conduct because they are prone to excessive anger.
Depending on the gravity of their karma, there are four different modes of birth. "Water-hole" refers to the Tailgate (the oceanic drain).

Ānanda, thus [the realms of] hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—[extending] to "how could one further follow the acts of killing, stealing, and lust"—are collectively shown to be the seven destinies arising from delusion (*mṛṣā*), thereby revealing that the true mind is fundamentally devoid of all delusions. For the seven destinies arise through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and are born according to karma;
therefore, they are called the "darkening and sinking" characteristics of all conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the wondrously perfect [nature], these are understood as such.

It has no root or continuity; thus, it is like a flower in the sky. To the previous question regarding how the wondrous mind can be all-pervasive and perfect while there are realms such as those of hell-dwellers, ghosts, humans, and devas, this is the concluding demonstration:
the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct serve as the root. When these karmic actions exist, one is termed a member of the ghostly class; this means one will inevitably fall.
When these karmic actions do not exist, one is termed a member of the celestial realm; this means one will inevitably ascend. Thus, birth occurs.

The absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitutes the celestial realm (*deva-gati*). By citing two [of the ten unwholesome paths] from among the seven realms of existence, both the wholesome and the unwholesome are comprehensively subsumed.
Because one falls due to the presence [of afflictions] and ascends due to their absence, it is said that the nature of saṃsāra arises through the mutual overturning of existence and non-existence.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of true samādhi, then the wondrous nature is eternally quiescent, and there will be no further saṃsāra; for both existence and non-existence are non-existent.
"There is neither good nor evil. 'Neither two nor even cessation' means that since good and evil do not exist, then even the absence of good and the absence of evil cannot be apprehended.
In this way, within the wondrous nature there is not even good; how then could there be what is not good?"
Ānanda, the three karmas are not cut off, yet each has its own private [cause] (up to: ...arising from delusion is without cause and cannot be investigated).
Because he previously asked whether hell has a fixed location or arises spontaneously, and that each person, having initiated their own karma, receives its retribution privately;
and furthermore, because he asked whether it exists inherently from the beginning, or whether it arises from the deluded habits of sentient beings—therefore [the Buddha speaks as follows].
This concludes the answer regarding the three karmas, namely killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
You must exert yourself in practice if you wish to attain Bodhi; as for what others say, that is the speech of Māra.

This exhortation to eliminate the three defiled states of mind serves to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox. Above, the various realms of existence were clarified, and one was cautioned against errors;
yet it concludes with an exhortation to eliminate the three types of defiled minds, such as killing, which constitutes the essential core of such caution.

The following section is the second division within the "Aids to the Path," titled "Detailed Examination of Mara’s Realms," which provides profound protection against heterodox errors and demonic influences.
This is Māra. It is translated here as "the Killer" or "the Robber," for he can kill the life of wisdom and rob one of wholesome dharmas. There are five types of Māra, namely:
the Māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*), and the ghostly Māra (*bhūta-māra*).

When combined, they are reduced to only the Māra of the aggregates and the celestial Māra. The Māra of the aggregates refers to the afflictions of birth and death that arise in dependence upon the five aggregates.

Furthermore, the celestial Māras, having cultivated perverted concentrations, delight in harming the true Path. They constantly accord with and follow those who have not yet resolved their minds, so as to remain without enemies;
however, they oppose and do not comply with those who practice correctly, specifically seeking to cause them distress and harm.
Therefore, one must discern them.

At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his Dharma seat—[until] they joyfully prostrated and waited in reverence for his compassionate instruction—the previous teaching having ended and no one among those present having asked a question, he was about to leave the Dharma seat when he again took up the precious desk and turned his golden countenance.
This "unasked self-exposition" is a subtle demonic affair within true *śamatha-vipaśyanā*; it is not the work of one possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajña*).
None can discern it; it can destroy the precious awakening and shatter the royal house of the Dharma. Therefore, it must be specifically warned against;

this is the ultimate expression of profound compassion. The true method of practice consists of the two previously mentioned principles of determination, the contemplative gate of Avalokiteśvara, internal precepts, and external mantras, combined with the aforementioned correct understanding—all of which are methods for practicing and entering awakening. To cultivate the sublime contemplation.

Wisdom cleanses internal defilements and obstacles; thus it is called "washing the mind. Because it is incited by demons and gives rise to conceptual discrimination and attachment, it is termed "not correct.

Regarding those who have not heard [the teachings] while in the fourth dhyāna: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that a bhikṣu who lacks the wisdom of extensive learning but diligently practices minor deeds may attain the fruit of the fourth dhyāna and then claim to have realized arhatship. When his celestial retribution is about to end, he beholds...
There are those who, having taken birth, subsequently slander the Buddha by falsely claiming that Arhats do not undergo further existence after death; because of this, they fall into ruin.
This is the fault of their own perverse delusions.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly, [saying] that all lands shall not be shattered or torn asunder.

This clarifies the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the realm of emptiness, thereby narrating the origins from which demons arise. The essence of the awakened mind is what is called the True Origin (*tathyamūla*).
Through delusion regarding principle and turning one's back on the truth, one becomes universally deluded throughout the *dharmadhātu*, thereby constituting the nature of emptiness.

As this delusive transformation does not cease, it forms the realm of outflows (*sāsrava-dhātu*), which serves as the basis for demons. "Delusive transformation" refers to changing in accordance with delusion. Only the True [is real].
The essence of the fundamental source is inherently vast and empty. Yet the void and the lands of the world are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false imaginings;
therefore, they are likened to a fragment of cloud. If even one among you were to give rise to true awakening and no longer be deluded, then these established forms would cease to exist.
Therefore, he shattered himself.
When you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and adorn samādhi—up until the time you enter samādhi—they all come to harass you.
Māra relies upon obscurity and darkness; now that you cultivate dhyāna and adorn concentration, your wondrous mind is brilliant and refined, and thus he is able to be torn asunder.
The realm of Māra is thereby brought to affliction and harm. "Adorning" (shì) means to embellish or adorn.

This refers to adorning the inherently existing true samādhi through the cultivation of the merit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because of this cultivation and adornment, one becomes identical with and merges into the nature of mind realized by Bodhisattvas and Arhats.
Consequently, the palaces of Māra and his followers naturally crumble and split apart; this is precisely the return to the source.
This was the preceding sign. Question: The great earth is insentient, and the various species of water and land are distinct;
why do they all tremble with fear together as if possessed by a demon? Answer: The majestic spiritual power of samādhi is inconceivable.

It is like the Great Tree Kinnara King, whose single movement of stringed song causes its sound to vibrate throughout the great trichiliocosm, causing even Sumeru, the king of mountains, to surge and submerge; how much more so for the head of a Bodhisattva!
By the power of the *Śūraṅgama*, how could one raise an objection based on the distinction between the sentient and the insentient?
The statement, "Ordinary beings are dark and dull-witted, unaware of the shifting and deceptive," is an explanation intended to resolve a latent doubt. It anticipates the doubt that one might ask:
"Since Māras and the various devas can perceive their manifestations, why do ordinary beings not perceive them at all? Therefore, this explanation is provided.

Yet, although those Māras may be filled with great wrath (up to the point where they) roll about and fall apart, unable to be pitied or saved, the wondrously enlightened true body is unmoving and indestructible.
Blasted by the power of the Right, the evil vapors naturally dissipate. The "master" of the five aggregates is the True Mind;
when the aggregates dissolve and enter into clarity, one points to that which gives rise to the True. Dhanagarga was but a lowly woman who merely violated the precepts.
As for the substance [of this]: the various māras are fierce and evil, capable of destroying precious awakening; one must certainly exercise deep vigilance.

The confiscation of a minister’s property serves as a metaphor for falling into the evil realms while at the stage of awakening. "Confiscation" (jimen) refers to the removal of one’s registration from the official registers.
Ānanda, you should know that from your sitting at the site of enlightenment (until this point) is what is called the realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
This teaches one to rely on the non-dual mind of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to enter right concentration.

To dissolve all discursive thoughts is to cause the delusory to vanish and the arising of birth-and-death to cease through the revolving of profound stillness. The clarity and brilliance resulting from the departure of thought is precisely the non-dual mind of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, the cessation of thought is *śamatha* (calm abiding); clarity and brilliance are *vipaśyanā* (insight). Because of this clarity and brilliance, one is not displaced by the objects of movement or stillness;
because of the cessation of thought, the notions of recollection and forgetfulness are as one. When thought ceases and defilements vanish, the essential nature is wondrously pure.
By relying on this to advance, one may enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Therefore, one should rely on this state to enter into the correct [path].
Although the power of concentration and contemplation is thus, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has not yet been shattered; it is like being in darkness despite having clear vision.

Though its essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. This is the characteristic of the aggregate of form. "Aggregate" (skandha) takes the sense of covering and obscuring.
Because it is the reality of distinct domains, it is called the "universe" (*qūyǔ*).
If one's vision is clear and bright, the ten directions open wide... [up to] ...taking solidified false imagination as its foundation.

This clarifies the destruction of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) in order to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). The characteristic of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form does not mean the extinction of the body into non-existence;
rather, it means that through the power of contemplation, one penetrates and illuminates reality so as not to be deluded or obstructed by the dharmas of form belonging to the realm of the body.

Therefore, it is likened to the eyes becoming clear and bright, with the ten directions opening wide. An "eon" (*kalpa*) refers to time; within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is no arising, and fundamentally, temporal divisions do not exist.
How could there be any characteristic of turbidity? Due to the mutual entanglement of the three perceptions, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is falsely established.

Because of this aggregate of form, the turbidity of the kalpa (kalpa-kaṣāya) arises; therefore, when form is exhausted, one transcends it. The initial cause of the aggregate of form is the false entanglement of the three—the father, mother, and self.
Thus it is said that solidified deluded thought is its root. The five kinds of deluded roots are explained by the Sūtra itself at its conclusion.
"Ānanda, you should investigate this wondrous clarity with precision (until) if you take it as a holy realization, you will immediately succumb to various delusions.
Herein, "this" refers to the non-duality of cessation and contemplation. The wondrous essence is fundamentally harmonious; it becomes obstructed only through the formation of deluded substance.
Therefore, when one exhaustively penetrates the subtle brilliance, the four elements no longer interweave, and the body is able to pass through obstructions.

However, this occurs specifically because it is compelled by a concentrated power that causes the subtle essence to overflow; it is temporary rather than permanent, and thus is not a realization of the sages.
Ānanda, you again take this mind and minutely investigate its wondrous clarity... (up to) "if you take this as a realization of holiness, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.

This mind is precisely the mind of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Previously, when the true essence of wondrous clarity overflowed into the external realm, there was nothing outside that could obstruct it;
now, as it overflows within the physical form, there is nothing inside that can hinder it. Thus, one is able to pick up and extract intestinal worms from within the body.

"O-whei. This too is merely temporary. This is precisely using the functions of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) to exhaustively investigate the wondrously luminous essence of the mind.
