Furthermore, if one uses this mind to scrutinize the internal and external with precision—up until the point where one forms a sacred interpretation—one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

The previous intensive cultivation was first able to achieve external emptiness, and subsequently able to achieve internal penetration. This [present stage], however, involves both internal and external intensive cultivation such that both are empty and penetrating;
thus, with the exception of the physical body, the six internal constituents—the *hun* (soul), *po* (ghost), intention, will, spirit, and consciousness—interpenetrate one another.
The five viscera are their presiding organs: the liver presides over the *hun*, the lungs over the *po*, and the spleen... [presides over intention].
The mind (*yi*) presides over the kidneys; the will (*zhi*) presides over the heart. As for their alternating roles as host and guest:

when the other five faculties enter the *hun*, then the *hun* is the host and the five are the guests; this continues until they enter the *shen*, at which point the *shen* is the host and the others are the guests.
They thus separate and unite with one another; that is, the essence (*jing*) leaves its primary position and unites with the *po*, or the *po* leaves its primary position.
Thus, it harmonizes with the essence (*sāra*) and other constituents. Since the *po* and *hun* spirits and so forth have all departed, they are constant;

because they interpenetrate one another, what was previously heard and perfumed can spontaneously manifest, and one suddenly hears something. Now, when one focuses the will and concentrates the spirit...
At the height of discussion, even those wondrous texts and elegant compositions that one has never intentionally studied often emerge brilliantly within dreams;
thus, it can be understood that when refined study triggers an inspiration, the spirit manifests spontaneously.
Furthermore, when this mind is clear, manifest, and brilliantly penetrating—up to the point where it might be misconstrued as a realization of sainthood—one immediately succumbs to various delusions.

The realms of purity and defilement constantly respond to the movements of the mind. When the mind is thus clear and penetrating and radiates light, the spirit is suffused with spiritual awakening, and the realm of the Buddha manifests within that luminous mind.
Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates the subtle brilliance (up to: "if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately be possessed by various demons").
One investigates the subtle brilliance and suppresses miscellaneous thoughts; when one's power and effort exceed the limit, the subtle brilliance becomes extreme and radiates forth.
Thus, the various appearances of objects manifest.

Furthermore, when one investigates with this mind until it becomes clear and transparent, if one takes this as a realization of sainthood (*ārya*), one will immediately succumb to a multitude of delusions.

There are indeed those among people who possess an innate clarity that naturally arises, such that darkness cannot obscure them; this refers only to the subtle, concentrated mind, which must be made limpid.
Only when there is no distraction can one see; yet as long as dark objects are not removed, one claims they are all real objects that do not change according to meditative concentration.

Furthermore, by means of this mind, one enters perfectly into the void and harmonious state (up to: if you take this to be the realization of sainthood, you will immediately be possessed by a host of demons).

When the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is empty and harmonious, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are simultaneously extinguished and the four elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are cast aside.
Pure awareness remains while the body is forgotten; thus, there is no injury from contact. Sustained by the power of meditative concentration, fire cannot burn it.

Even those in the world who sit upright to relinquish the self can cause their bodies to become like withered wood and their minds like extinguished ashes; how much more so, then, the power of true concentration!
Furthermore, by means of this mind, one achieves purity (up to the point where) if one forms a holy understanding, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.

One comes to loathe the coarse, turbid, and obstructive substance while delighting in the pure, wondrous, empty, and harmonious. As concentrated contemplation becomes increasingly profound, one thereby achieves purity.
Once the power of purification reaches its limit, the objective realm transforms according to the mind; thus, one is able to universally observe all objects and attain [realization].
There is no obstruction.
Furthermore, when one investigates with this mind to the point of profundity—if one forms a sacred understanding (*ārya-adhimukti*), one will immediately succumb to various delusions.
To "investigate to the point of profundity" means that the wondrous mind is deep without bottom and distant without limit; now, the practitioner...
If one seeks to exhaust its profound depth through the study of contemplating the mind, one will know that the application of the mind is likewise profound and far-reaching.
Therefore, by exerting the spirit and transcending the body, one’s perception and hearing reach far and wide.

Furthermore, when one investigates this mind with such extreme refinement—reaching the point where it might be misconstrued as a realization of sainthood—one immediately falls prey to various delusions.
"Investigating with extreme refinement" means that because the wondrous mind is pure and untainted, the practitioner now exhausts it through contemplation;
this is what is meant by "exhausting its essence. Moreover, it is so lofty as to be unattainable and so profound as to be unfathomable. Now, the practitioner...

Investigate this by examining the mind; that is to say, investigate it to its ultimate limit. This is because both the object investigated is refined to the extreme, and the subject capable of investigating it is likewise refined to the extreme.
Consequently, the evil seeds within one's own mind are stirred up, leading to the interference and confusion of external demons.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* (from "maintaining and protecting" up to "accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way") summarize the preceding meanings and constitute a formal injunction for their wide dissemination.

Regarding the phrase "the mind and its objects interact": it means that the mind engaged in *dhyāna* interacts with the solidified false conceptualization of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and thus these phenomena appear;
this should be understood by analogy for the other aggregates up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Why is this? It is because the five deluded thoughts, each within the domain of its respective fundamental aggregate (*skandha*), become the objects of contemplation for dhyāna.

As they are about to be destroyed but have not yet been destroyed, they are like a lamp about to go out, whose light flares up once more. Thus, they engage in a struggle against the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, whether one succeeds or fails depends upon this; it is here that the paths of the Mara and the Buddha are distinguished. Question: This is not [the case].
Regarding the sequential contemplation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): how can the five aggregates be exhausted in sequence? Answer:

Although the contemplation takes the general characteristics of the five aggregates as its object, the aggregates possess both coarse and subtle aspects; that which is coarse is exhausted first. It is like washing clothes: the coarse stains are removed first.
Since the five aggregates are accumulated through delusion (*moha*), when delusion is exhausted, the aggregates naturally cease. This proceeds from the coarse to the subtle according to principle.
This is necessarily so.
Ānanda, when that son of good family cultivates *samādhi* (up to this point), it is called "the realm of the aggregate of sensation" (*vedanā-skandha*).

This passage generally describes the cessation of form (*rūpa*) and the manifestation of sensation. As for "seeing the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a mirror," it refers to the minds of all Buddhas.

This is precisely my wondrously enlightened and luminous mind. By breaking through the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the internal and external become void and harmoniously integrated, allowing one to perceive the fundamentally wondrous mind.
It is like a mirror, empty and luminous, clearly perceiving forms and images; hence it is said, "like a mirror manifesting images.

Although it possesses this wondrous essence, it is as yet unable to exercise its function because it is shrouded by sensation (*vedanā*). Thus, it is like a person in a state of sleep or paralysis, whose limbs and body remain [unresponsive].
The six sense organs are clear and distinct, yet one cannot move them; this is the characteristic of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
If the affliction of nightmares ceases and the mind departs from the body—up to the point where it perceives a void clarity—it takes deluded thought as its basis.

This clarifies that the destruction of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) serves to transcend the turbidity of views (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya). As for the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha):

although one may attain the vision of the minds of all Buddhas, because one is still oppressed by sensation, one is unable to employ it. Therefore, when the aggregate of sensation subsides, one is immediately able to detach from the body and practice reflexive observation, remaining unimpeded whether moving or staying still.
The statement "transcending the turbidity of views" means that the turbidity of views derives its name from its dependence upon the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-āyatana).

The meaning of "feeling" (*vedanā*) is the reception resulting from the union of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Now that the aggregate of feeling is exhausted, there is no longer any reception of these faculties and objects;
therefore, one transcends it. Based on the illusory conditions of the agreeable and the disagreeable, false feelings of loss and gain arise.
Thus, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has no substance; it is a void that merely manifests clarity. Therefore, this void-clarity is a deluded thought.
Ānanda, when that virtuous man is within this state—[up to the point where] he loses his right concentration—he shall fall into ruin.
Within this, it is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) that is being focused upon. Since the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been shattered, there is no longer any darkness;
thus, one attains great radiance. As the mind becomes luminous and one recognizes the aggregate of sensation as a fault, one internally suppresses and breaks it down.
However, if this suppression is excessive, one loses their compassionate gentleness and becomes overly sorrowful, thereby allowing the demon of compassion (*karuṇā-māra*) to take possession.
Ānanda, furthermore, those sons of good family within that samādhi (up to) shall fall away from their correct attainment (*samyaksamāpatti*).

Regarding "the clarity of the aggregate of sensation" (*vedanā-skandha*): this refers to the state within the concentration on the aggregate of sensation where the nature of radiance is manifested, and the mind-ground becomes clear and bright.
As for "arousing and stirring": this refers to the signs of movement caused by joy. When form is exhausted and sensation is luminous, it constitutes the superior mark of concentration.
When superior signs manifest before one, if one does not give rise to agitation through joy, then no fault is incurred.

Because success is achieved through joy, if one becomes excessively moved by it, within that state of being moved, an infinite courage arises, leading one to think that the fruit of Buddhahood can be equaled and that meritorious practice is easily attained.
This results in the fault of rashness; "rashness" here refers to a bold and impetuous mind.
Furthermore, it is said that those sons of good family within meditative concentration (up to the point where they) lose right reception (*samyaksamādhi*) shall fall into ruin.

In all cultivation of contemplative practice, one must maintain the equilibrium of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to be free from error. Now, because concentration is strong while wisdom is weak, one falls into the error of dullness and forgetfulness.
Since the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted, there is no new realization to advance toward;

since the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already dissolved, one has lost the former dwelling place. Between advancing and retreating, there is a profound lack of support; this is called the "ground of mid-collapse. If...

There is the illumination of wisdom; thus, deep recollection does not arise. Because wisdom is subtle, within that state one may fall into desolation, withered longing, and deep recollection, and the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*) attaches itself there.
The mind of recollection is falsely bound, as if being suspended by a handful.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that concentration (until they) lose their correct reception (*samādhi*) shall fall into decline.

Previously, concentration was strong while wisdom was slight; now, the power of wisdom exceeds concentration. In both cases, there is mutual deficiency; therefore, one desires meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*).
The exhaustion of form and the clarity of sensation constitute the superior nature of concentration. If one can truly forget the self, one should not settle for little.
They are satisfied with this. Because they harbor the notion of "supreme nature" within their hearts, they suspect themselves to be Buddhas;

thus, they take little as sufficient and become complacent, allowing the demon of inferiority and easy contentment to possess them. Because the power of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is weak, they lose constant discernment;
because the power of their wisdom (*prajñā*) is excessive, they sink into speculative views.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right absorption shall fall into ruin.
Surveying both limits, if there were skillful means, they would not encounter hardship and peril, nor would they incur perverse anxiety.
Because they lose these skillful means, their minds give rise to hardship and peril, resulting in perverse anxiety and bringing about harm upon themselves.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that concentration (up to) shall fall away from right attainment (*samādhi*).

Pure pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is the meditative sign of the clarity of the perception of form. If concentration were accompanied by wisdom (*prajñā*), then joy would not arise, and the Noble Path could be traversed.
Now, since they lack the self-sustaining power of wisdom, joy arises in the mind; thus, as for concentration—
It will instead turn into distraction. Mara will find his opportunity and take delight in attaching himself to them.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that state of concentration (up to the point where they) lose their right absorption shall fall into ruin.

Having given rise to the notion of sufficiency within this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one lacks the wisdom to save oneself; thus, various forms of pride (*māna*) arise. There are seven names for pride:

relying on oneself to despise others is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"); imitating those of equal virtue is simply called *māna* (pride); contending for superiority among equals is called *atimāna* (excessive pride);
contending for superiority over those who are superior is called *mānātimāna* (the pride beyond pride); and claiming to have attained what one has not attained is called *abhimāna* (conceit).

Excessive pride (*adhimāna*) consists of boasting of one's own inferiority; this is called base pride (*ūnamāna*). To fail to pay homage to stupas and temples and so forth is precisely perverse pride (*mithyāmāna*).
The deluded people of today who neither pay homage nor recite [the scriptures] are all under the sway of the demon of pride (*māra*).
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) will lose their right concentration and fall away.
When form dissolves and sensation becomes luminous, one contemplates the clarity and brilliance of the mind. Within this clarity and brilliance, one perfectly awakens to the essential principle.
One attains great accord. If one does not give rise to thoughts or mental activity, one will not fall into error.

Because of this, the mind gives rise to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), leading one to claim for oneself that one has attained the freedom of a sage and no longer advance further; thus, one becomes like those who have heard nothing of the Dharma, inviting demonic possession and misleading sentient beings through doubt and error.
Furthermore, those sons of good family within that meditative concentration (until) they lose their right absorption and fall into ruin.
"Clear awakening" refers to the aforementioned perfect awakening of the refined essence.

Because they attain a nature of empty clarity within this clear awakening, they erroneously cling to nihilistic emptiness and repudiate cause and effect, thereby incurring various false faults. All who act in this way are victims of the demon of emptiness.

Furthermore, regarding the empty māra entering one’s heart and viscera: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that a māra can enter the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to take refuge in the faction of māras as if with lacquer or glue; they would not consider it difficult even to have their hands severed or their arms cut off.
Furthermore, those good sons within that samādhi (up to) will lose their right reception and fall away.
As form dissolves, they perceive light and attain a nature of empty clarity. If they do not greedily relish this state, craving will not arise;
however, because they deeply crave this empty clarity and give rise to boundless attachment, it becomes desire. This is precisely the meditative object that accords with the mind.
Lacking wisdom, they maintain themselves [in meditation] and mistakenly enter into various desires, thereby inviting demonic possession and misleading sentient beings with doubt.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states in *dhyāna* (extending to) maintaining and protecting [the mind] lead to the realization of the Unsurpassed Way.

The phrasing regarding the various aggregates (*skandha*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) all speaks of "maintaining," "sustaining," and "protecting. This refers to the intent of deeply guarding against error and assisting the path.
Ānanda, when that good man cultivates *samādhi* (up to this point), this is called the realm of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

This is a general account of the cessation of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). As for "perception," it refers to the floating characteristics of mental deliberation and the delusive habitual tendencies of consciousness that can obscure the wondrous luminosity and obstruct the Path of the Sages.

Although the aggregate of feeling has been exhausted, and the mind has become detached from the body such that one moves and dwells with freedom, thereby achieving the causes for ascending through the successive stages of the sages, and further attaining the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body) that proceeds everywhere without hindrance—nevertheless...
They are still shrouded by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); therefore, they are likened to those who speak in their sleep while fast asleep.
To say that although these people have no separate cognition, their speech nonetheless forms a coherent sequence, is a metaphor for those abiding in the state of perception:
though they do not know the realm beyond thought, they clearly perceive the beginning and end of birth and death. Those who are not asleep and all awaken to their words is a metaphor for...
"Exhausting conceptualization" means knowing that all sentient beings undergo birth and death through false grasping within the midst of deluded thoughts.
Regarding the "sixty stages of the sages," from the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) to Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-samyak-saṃbodhi*), there are actually only fifty-seven stages.
The reason they are called "sixty" is that the sutra cites a general number, thereby adding three positions.
"If every movement of thought ceases and all floating perceptions are eliminated" (up to) "the fusion of deluded perceptions serves as its root.
This clarifies the destruction of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) in order to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

To say that when perception is exhausted, one "perfectly illuminates the beginning and end of birth and death" means that the beginning and end of birth and death exist because of mental perception; therefore, when perception is exhausted, there is no beginning or end to birth.

Upon death, only the luminous clarity of perfect illumination remains, like a person waking from sleep; the words spoken in a dream cannot be found, for how could they possess phonetic tones or sequential order?

There is only the one who has awakened. As for the statement that it "transcends the turbidity of affliction," this is because conceptualization arises from the interaction of the sense faculties and their objects.

Afflictions arise from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); therefore, when conceptualization is exhausted, one transcends them. Conceptualization has the power to transform and integrate, causing the mind to follow objects and objects to follow the mind.
It is like imagining a sour plum, which can penetrate through material obstructions; thus, it is called "pervasive delusory conceptualization."
Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, yet he is deluded and fails to recognize this, he falls into the Avīci Hell.

Because the aggregate of sensation has been exhausted, his mind attains emptiness and subtlety; thus it is called the "emptiness and subtlety of the aggregate of sensation. Having reached this state, the ten mental states such as compassion are no longer present.

It is said that one does not encounter perverse thoughts because one is not obscured by them. Since the essence of the mind is clarified through cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is called "the clarification of perfect concentration.
Within *samādhi*, this occurs during the stabilization of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). "Perfect clarity" (*yuanming*) refers to the perfectly wondrous and luminous mind.
Those who cherish this perfect clarity and seek skillful means contemplate the essence of perfect clarity in order to give rise to *upāya* (expedient means).

Therefore, they sharpen their refined thoughts to greedily seek skillful means (*upāya*). When celestial Māras manifest transformations to teach and convert others, they demonstrate the skillful means of *upāya*.
"To attach to a person" means to attach to another person. As for "that person," it refers to the individual upon whom they attach.
Thus, when a flying spirit attaches to a person, it must necessarily attach to one who is suitable to be attached to—namely, one who has cultivated meditative concentration and practiced wisdom.
[End of section. Disciples and masters alike seek those who are skilled in their craft; this applies to all teachers of the Dharma, and the following cases are analogous.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if a son of good family [neglects his practice] while the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, he will become deluded and fail to realize the truth, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle emptiness of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and unaware and falls into the Avīci Hell—the phrase "the love for the lingering thread" refers to the desire for a secret union with the wondrous principle. Because he hopes for such a realization, the Māra grants him awakening.

From the section on "self-awakening" downward, all concerns the matter of secret union. Now, when the contrivances of the mind are forgotten and there is tranquil illumination, the principle naturally meets in mystery. If...
One seeks to achieve conformity; yet, the slightest movement of the mind brings error, whereupon the celestial Māras find their opportunity.
Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, one may become deluded and fail to realize this, falling into the Avīci Hell.
Love exhausts the root of the myriad transformations; thus, one clarifies the mind to analyze them.

Those who equate the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* with the fleshly body take this physical form as the fruit of virtue, regard illusory birth as eternal, and deny the existence of the retribution-body in the Pure Land.
All of them, because they rely on their own attachments to analyze the source of transformation, falsely propound theories of "blending and fusion. They take defilement to be true purity;
this is also intended to lead toward licentious desire. Now, the ocean of nature is perfectly clear and still, and the myriad phenomena manifest of themselves.
If one seeks worldly principles with partiality, it only serves to increase the tainted mind. This violates fundamental *dhyāna*, and thus malevolent spirits will enter.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle and wondrous state of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and unaware and falls into the Avīci Hell—the response from the sages will be suspended, yet the spiritual resonance will manifest within himself; this is the seeking of signs of cessation before the principle has been realized.

Furthermore, when the son of good family experiences the subtle voidness of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)—up to the point where he is deluded and unaware and falls into the Avīci Hell—their craving penetrates deeply into profound stillness, which is the power of maintaining clarity. Through this, those of false concentration can possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

"Past karma" refers to past deeds; "animal" refers to the subsequent retribution. These two constitute the supernormal power of knowing past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Knowing the beginning [of things] is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*).
"Exposing" refers to the supernormal powers of the eyes and ears. To reveal another's private affairs is called "exposing.
Furthermore, good sons, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, they may become deluded and fail to realize this, thereby falling into the Avīci Hell.

They delight in knowing hidden and extraordinary matters and greedily seek knowledge of past lives. Items such as bamboo slips, wooden tablets, and official documents are all the most marvelous and essential objects of the state;
they record great and small affairs and serve to unify the trust between ruler and subject, which is why they are employed.

By bestowing these extraordinary objects, they cause the mind to believe and submit, and only thereafter do they manifest [the truth]. In their mouths, they skillfully speak of things below, all of which they exploit for their own ends.
One is deluded by seeing them. Knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) is one of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

In the Hīnayāna, it is accomplished through cultivation; in the Mahāyāna, it is attained through its initial arousal. Now, you do not await its arousal nor follow its cultivation, yet you seek it by forming a deliberate thought; therefore, you invite demonic obstacles.
Furthermore, when the son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, he may become deluded and fail to realize that he is falling into the Avīci Hell.
The source of transformation is the root of all transformations. Desiring to attain this root and ride upon it to manifest spiritual transformations, he clings to such transformations;
thus, he manifests feats such as grasping fire and walking on water. If they were true spiritual transformations, he would not fear weapons or blades.
Furthermore, when a good man’s *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, he may become deluded and fail to realize that he is falling into the Avīci Hell.

He desires to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in order to attain emptiness and stillness. Regarding [the phenomena of] appearing and disappearing from emptiness and so forth, because he is fond of emptiness, he is deceived by it.
The following passages, which state that he "constantly speaks" and so on, all arise based upon his view of emptiness. In recent times...

This heterodox school falsely claims that "one must practice true practice" and "one must attain true insight. Consequently, they repudiate everything that is not personally witnessed, including cause and effect, future lives, and the realms of heaven and hell.
Thus, those who adopt their doctrine all claim that good and evil are vague and indistinct, and that this fleeting life will not be lived again.
Thereupon, they forget the restraints of the precepts and indulge in lust and pleasure, becoming mired in the darkness of drinking and gluttony.
They bring about their own ruin, yet hope for a prominent position; they plunder and oppress with such cruelty that it truly seems as though there is neither heaven nor hell.

I have always lamented this deeply, and thus, upon reaching this point in my commentary and sub-commentary, I was moved to take up my brush with vigor, hoping that those who follow demonic teachings might awaken and not sink into self-destruction.
When the sun and moon undergo eclipses, their vital energies flow and infuse, capable of producing things such as gold and jade. Even so...

Regarding "eclipses": when a vapor approaches and presses against [a celestial body], it is called a "partial obscuration" (bó); when it causes a deficiency or destruction, it is called an "eclipse" (shí).
Furthermore, good sons, from the state where the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, up to the point of being deluded and unaware, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Only when the delusions of the three realms are exhausted can one leave behind the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence and attain the *pariṇāma* (transformative) existence.

Now, while your merit is not yet perfected, you wish to suddenly transform this coarse body into a subtle essence and change a short lifespan into a long one; such a vain hope is merely to be deluded by the delusions themselves.

"Investigating the subtle" (*yanji*) means to investigate and exhaustively examine the most minute details in order to seek deeply. To traverse ten thousand *li* in an instant is the affair of those who have attained transformative existence.
In the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, there is the deity Cchamantra and the Viśa-children—namely, the Viśeṣas, who are ghosts (*piśāca*) under the command of the Four Heavenly Kings.
If they have already resolved their minds [toward awakening], they protect people; if they have not yet resolved their minds, they harm people.

Because they take as their benefit the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and its empty luminosity, they consume the vital essence and energy of others. Alternatively, those who do not rely on a teacher [are possessed] by demons (*māra*).
As for these teachers, they personally witness the manifestation of Māra; their speech is characterized by soliloquy, and from time to time they utter strange words.
Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of Māras [will] lose right universal knowledge and fall into the Avīci Hell.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the final age, those belonging to the faction of Māra will manifest in the forms of bhikṣus, arhats, and the like, corrupting and destroying the True Dharma and slandering the precepts. Their intent is the same as this.
"You need not first seek nirvana now; rather, you must maintain and protect [this teaching] until you have accomplished the Unsurpassed Way.
This sutra begins its instruction with Ānanda and concludes by entrusting him to propagate it.

From this, one can fully understand that the source and flow of the Great Teaching—its deep emergence and far-reaching influence—are entirely due to the power of Ānanda. Thus, it is shown that he encountered demonic events, was questioned regarding his mind, and underwent discernment.
Seeing this, he gave rise to great compassion for those in the Dharma-ending age, so that they would not be attached to demons and could attain right knowledge and vision.

One should know that although the four schools previously manifested their passing into extinction, the Dharma-transformation of today remains ever-present, like a shadow or an echo wherever it may be.
There is no body that is not one whose vows remain unfulfilled.
*The Compendium of Notes on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle Nine.
*The Compiled Notes on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas:
Definitive Meaning*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Indian Bhikṣu Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Meghaśikṣa of the Kingdom of Ujjayanī during the Tang Dynasty;
the words were interpreted by the Tang Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, Former Minister of Justice,
concurrently Chief Counselor of the Secretariat and Chancellery, Fang Rong of Qinghe, who recorded the text.
[Recorded by] the Śramaṇa Zhijie of Zili. Compiled Notes:
"Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi... this is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations)."

This is a general description of the cessation of *saṃjñā* (perception) and the manifestation of *saṃskāra* (volitional formations). Floating and shifting are deluded habits: when the day is bright, there is perception;
when the evening is dim, there is dreaming. These turbid disturbances cloud the true nature, preventing it from being unified; they agitate awakened clarity, preventing it from being still.
Therefore, for one whose *saṃjñā-skandha* is exhausted, dreams and fantasies vanish; waking and sleeping are always one, and awakened clarity is empty and still, like a clear sky.
The five aggregates are coarse at the beginning and subtle at the end; therefore, when ideation is exhausted, there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadowy phenomena.
Although one contemplates the myriad phenomena, there is no conceptualization. Thus, it is like a bright mirror: without attachment and without traces, it receives reflections in emptiness.

There is a complete absence of habitual tendencies; there is only the single, pure, and true reality. When clarity reaches such an extreme, the hidden *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is thereby revealed.

Furthermore, conduct is the root source of the arising and ceasing of the myriad transformations; thus, when its characteristics are revealed, there is nothing of the origins of the twelve classes of beings that is not fully seen.
Their respective destinies are their "life-threads" (*vijñāna*); they share a common foundation of birth, which is "conduct" (*saṃskāra*).

This means that although one may not yet have thoroughly understood the origins and causes by which those twelve types of beings receive their life-destinies, one is already able to perceive those classes of beings.
All arise through activity; thus this aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is called the "basis for co-arising. It is like a mirage—a shimmering heat haze or floating dust.

Because it agitates what is subtle and hidden, it is likened to a mirage. Because it arises and perishes momentarily, it is called "flashing" (yìyì). Because there are no longer coarse shadows, it is called "clearly agitated.
Although there is no longer the appearance of coarse currents or drifting forms, since the aggregate of formations has not yet been exhausted, then with respect to the faculties (indriya)...
Even within the sensory dust (*rajas*), there remains a subtle leakage; therefore, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is called the pivot and the cavity of the faculties and objects.
If this clear agitation—this shimmering primordial nature (extending to) its dark and hidden delusive thoughts—is taken as its basis.

This clarifies the destruction of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) in order to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. The habitual disturbances of the aggregate of formations constitute one's nature;

hence they are called "original nature" and "original habits. If one can extinguish these disturbing habits, one returns to the source, the clarity of the fundamental, and the marks of flux and transition are exhausted.

Thus, it is like the subsiding of waves, which transform into clear water. Birth and cessation ceaselessly alternate; karma and destiny are constantly shifting—this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Therefore, when practice is exhausted, one transcends it. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) shifts subtly and secretly, yet there is never any awakening to it; hence it is called "hidden and obscure false conceptualization."
Ānanda, you should know that this is the attainment of right awareness (*samyak-saṃprajanya*) within *śamatha*. (Up to: This person falls into two theories of causelessness.
When dreams and fantasies vanish, waking and sleeping are always one; therefore it is called "right awareness within *śamatha*," and it is also called "the concentrated clarity of the upright mind.

These are all signs of the exhaustion of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). External demons are all summoned by the mind; therefore, when conceptualization is exhausted and there is concentrated clarity, [they cease].
Then the celestial Māras will not approach. Because one is shielded by the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), one is finally able to investigate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

The fundamental basis of the class of beings is identical to the foundation of co-arising. When the generative source within that fundamental class is revealed, one perceives the generative source of one's own formations within that foundation of co-arising.
Because the generative source is thus disclosed, one gives rise to contemplation to observe it; for within the perfect source, one has been deluded.
Thus, giving rise to false conceptions, they fall into the two theories of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*). This is a general indication of their speculative views.
First, these people perceive that there is no fundamental cause [for existence], and thus they fall into the ways of external paths (*tīrthika*), deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.

Regarding "the vital mechanism is completely broken": because it was previously shrouded by the *asaṃjñi-skandha* (the aggregate of non-perception), the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is now revealed.

"Riding upon the lower" means that through the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) arising within meditative concentration, the faculty of the eye manifests this functional power.

The "meandering flow of karma" refers to the circulation of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. The conditions of good and evil karma are transformations produced solely by consciousness; such is the eighth [consciousness] of this person.
Even beyond ten thousand kalpas, one does not yet perceive the activity [of the cause], let alone consciousness. Therefore, from this point onward, they give rise to the view that there is no cause.

Since this has not yet been fully exhausted, one merely attains compliance within meditative concentration. Because of this compliance with the perfect interchangeability, one then falsely calculates within the midst of these perfect transformations.

All [of these] are capable of producing superior fruits. That is to say, fire can manifest light, and so on, up to dust particles which can bring about the formation of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

therefore, this is called "clinging to the non-arising as arising. This refers to the various outsiders, such as the three Kāśyapas.

Because their contemplation of principle is not authentic, they mistakenly fall into a void. Thus, within the nature of consciousness—which is perfectly luminous—they reckon everything to be empty and non-existent.

They cling to the notion that *śūnyatā* (舜若多) means "emptiness" (*śūnya*). To speak of "non-conceptual *śūnyatā*" is to cling to the nihilistic emptiness of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Because they cling to nihilistic emptiness, they take a pervasive voidness as their causal mind and thereby achieve the fruit of nihilistic annihilation.
This eternal extinction of the basis is the nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhist outsiders.

Furthermore, good son, from the thorough investigation of the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) [up to] turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa, the production of delusive seeds of extension occurs.

The "perfect permanence" and the "subtle perfection" are both the source of consciousness. Because this subtle perfection is long-lasting and does not perish, one consequently desires to firmly preserve the body so that it may coexist with it.
Yet, the body is fundamentally impermanent and truly not something to be craved; nevertheless, one delusively craves its solidity.
For a long time, one does not realize this is wrong; this is called "clinging to greed as non-greed.
Asita—here translated as "Non-existent"—is the Long-lived Seer (*Āyuṣmat Ṛṣi*). Although his life was prolonged, it ultimately ended in destruction.

"Lao" should be written as "Lao" (牢); it is an error of pronunciation.

They take the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to be the life-source of the twelve classes of beings, such that self and others are mutually interconnected.

They believe that if the aggregate of consciousness were to end, the lives of all beings would end, and their own lives would likewise end. Consequently, they wonder who could realize the true and eternal, and who could serve as a subject for transformation.

Thus, while in meditative concentration, they manifest various objects of desire to maintain their defilements and prevent them from being extinguished. Relying on such perverse thoughts, they proceed.
Desiring to realize the true and eternal, yet not knowing that it is not so, this is called the "attachment to the non-existent as real.

Ṭakkirāja can transform sensual objects to amuse himself; he belongs to the class of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods. Because of his perverse thoughts, he is reborn as a celestial demon (devaputra-māra).

This takes the "surging awareness" (*yuǎng jué*) as the causal mind, resulting in a stagnation within limpid clarity.

This very state described as the mind contemplating height (up to what is called) the second delusion, "empty clarity," involves the empty contemplation of height while a genuine sensation of acidity and astringency arises.

"Because your thoughts and reflections cause your physical body [to function], it is called the third delusive thought, 'interfusion.

It is through perception (*saṃjñā*) that they are fused. The mind gives rise to empty conceptions, while the form grasps at substantial objects;

When one interrogates the growth of nails and hair and so forth, if you insist that this change of essence is truly you, why do you not perceive this succession of phases?
Regarding these characteristics: because of non-awakening, the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is termed "profoundly hidden.
Furthermore, from your state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness where nothing stirs, up to the fifth stage, it is a subtle and refined inverted conception.
"Exquisite and unwavering" refers to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" refer to the function of consciousness.

Such appearances of delusion are manifold. Because profound stillness is not yet true stillness, it remains hidden in obscurity and goes unnoticed;
thus it is likened to a rapid current flowing beneath the surface, its course impossible to discern. This is the very source of recollective thought and the substance of delusive appearances.
One must directly dissolve the six sense-gates so that delusive habits have no place to lodge; only then can they be extinguished. This is the constant practice.

It is "habituation" (*xi*). It is "incipient" (*ji*). It is "subtle" (*wei*). This refers to the subtle marks of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) occurring in every thought-moment within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

that which seems existent is called "phantom" (*xiang*). Its essence is refined and subtle; therefore, it is named the "Inverted Refined Perception of Unseen Phantom Non-existence."

"Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by five kinds of false imagination... (up to) 'the profound entry merges with the profound, returning to the limit of consciousness.

These five aggregates originally arise in successive layers (up to the point where it is asked): "What is not yet clear? Let us inquire further.
The true analogy is the substance of the *kalpa*-cloth; consciousness is like the first knot, and form is like the final knot.

That "arising occurs because of consciousness" is like the subsequent knot arising in dependence upon the initial knot. That "cessation follows from the removal of form" is like the untying proceeding from the last knot.
Furthermore, the arising of the five aggregates proceeds from the subtle to the coarse; through delusion regarding true reality, consciousness arises and eventually form appears.
Their cessation proceeds from the coarse to the subtle: one must first destroy form before sensation manifests, continuing until one destroys formations before consciousness manifests.

As for the principle that "sudden enlightenment is attained, and by means of this enlightenment, [the afflictions] are simultaneously eliminated," it means realizing that the aggregates have no inherent substance, whereby the five aggregates are all [simultaneously dissolved].

"Extinction. Regarding the statement that "affairs are not eliminated instantaneously but are exhausted through successive stages": this means that while the principle is realized all at once, affairs must be eliminated gradually.
It is like a cloth which, though inherently unchanged, requires its knots to be untied step by step. If one does not eliminate them gradually, there will be liberation without practice;
one will cling to the principle while remaining deluded regarding affairs, and thus will ultimately fail to cultivate the true Samādhi of the Way.
"You should take this root of deluded thought (until) knowing that there is nirvana and not craving the three realms.

For it is through the teaching of this Dharma to others that one can eliminate severe retribution and transform suffering into bliss;
such is its excellence. It enables people to rely upon it to clarify the mind and see the nature, thereby shedding attachments and returning to the source.

With profound understanding, one transcends the six realms and abandons the one; by shattering the five aggregates and stripping away demons, one attains the fruit of the Treasure King without passing through the kalpas of the śrāvakas.
Since that is so, then this [attainment] which eliminates severe retribution is merely a shallow and proximate description. Truly, it shall be the same as that [ultimate realization].
"Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra... (up to) they will directly attain Bodhi and no longer have demonic activities.

To begin with, the Dharma attained by the Buddha is profoundly deep and difficult to understand; even Śāriputra, with his great wisdom, could not fathom it despite exhausting all his thought.
If this commentary were to exhaustively cover it, what would be the use of compiling [this work]? One might ask:

Among these, to gather all that is beautiful and achieve a great perfection—how could this be considered a minor contribution? This is the reason for the composition of this annotated compilation.

However, among the various commentaries, each excels in its own particular strength; if one cannot penetrate and illuminate the words of all these commentators through the notes, then they will remain entangled and difficult to discern.

As for Master Huan (Zhiyi), he devoted more than twenty years to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, revising his drafts four or five times.

The detailed explanations in the *Cuanzhu* (Compendium of Annotations) have already been seen in the introduction at the beginning of this scripture;
however, the verse text is appended here at the end of the volume for the convenience of reading. May those who observe it seek its meaning by following the map.
It seems that while one may not find [the truth] in the commentaries, one may still find it in the verses;
thus, the intention of this master of illusions to benefit others is truly profound and earnest. Someone said to me: "In recent times, lecture halls are already burdened with redundant commentaries;
yet you have now laboriously compiled and further versified these. Can you escape the ridicule of 'adding feet'? I replied: "These are the words of the Buddha."
The profound and subtle is such that it should be avoided in explicit exposition. It is sufficient that those who wish to study it seek and attain it for themselves.

Once it has been manifested in words, how does this differ from a commentary? Furthermore, verbal explanations can only provide aid for a single moment, and moreover, they do not continue unless passed on by others.

Even if there were never a lack of people to carry them on through the generations, what is transmitted over a long duration becomes distorted. One must therefore obtain the text itself as proof; thus:

It is known that the commentary does not delude people; rather, it is people who become deluded by the commentary. If one were to sincerely seek the truth for oneself and attain it, how could this be an impediment to the commentary?

Furthermore, to prevent those who cling to the commentary as if it were the scripture itself from abandoning the commentary to grasp only the words, it is also one purpose [of this work] to record both [the text and its meaning] together so that the listener may understand them through their own insight.

Lacking full mastery of the Way despite much learning, I was at a loss; Only by relying on his secret voice could I quell the impulse of lust. He took me up and guided me back to join you.

This verse demonstrates that delusion has no cause. **Chapter One: Showing That Delusion Has No Cause** The Buddha addressed the assembly: “Good sons, you should know that from beginningless time, sentient beings have been bound by ignorance and afflictions. Because they do not understand their own minds, they give rise to false thoughts. From these false thoughts, they produce karma; from karma, they produce suffering. Because they do not understand that suffering is empty, they undergo birth and death. Good sons, you should know that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams; they have no place of origin and no place of cessation. Why? Because the nature of the mind is originally pure and free from outflows. It is only because of deluded thought that one perceives the world as real. If one can suddenly awaken to the fact that there is no such thing as a real world, then the mind will naturally be at rest. Good sons, you should know that this deluded thought has no root cause. It is merely a false appearance arising from the interaction of conditions. Just as a person might mistake a rope for a snake in the dark, so too do sentient beings mistake the unreal for the real. If one examines the rope closely, one finds no snake; likewise, if one examines the mind deeply, one finds no world. Therefore, I say that delusion has no cause. At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, joined his palms, and said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if delusion has no cause, then how does it arise? And if it has no cause, how can it be extinguished? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that although delusion has no cause, it arises from the false perception of conditions. It is like a person who, seeing a mirage in the desert, thinks it is water. The mirage has no water, yet the person runs toward it. If someone were to tell them, ‘That is not water; it is a mirage,’ the person would then realize their error. So too, sentient beings perceive a world where there is none. If they can suddenly awaken to the fact that the world is empty and still, then the deluded thought will vanish of itself. Good son, you should know that this deluded thought is like an echo in a valley—it has no master, yet it responds to sound. If one understands that the echo has no substance, one will no longer pursue it. Therefore, I say that delusion has no cause. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if delusion has no cause, then why do sentient beings suffer in birth and death? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that suffering arises from attachment to the unreal. It is like a person who dreams of being in a prison. While dreaming, they feel fear and distress, but upon waking, they find there is no prison at all. Sentient beings are like this: they dream of the world, and while dreaming, they experience suffering. If they can awaken to the fact that the dream was empty, then the suffering will vanish. Therefore, I say that although delusion has no cause, its effects appear due to the power of habitual conditioning. If one can sever these habits through right mindfulness, then the cycle of birth and death will come to an end. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure, then why do we speak of cultivation and practice? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that although the mind is originally pure, it is covered by adventitious defilements. Cultivation and practice are like washing away the dirt from a mirror. Once the mirror is clean, its brightness is revealed. Likewise, once the defilements are removed, the original purity of the mind is manifest. Therefore, although the mind is originally pure, cultivation is necessary to remove the obstacles. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure, then what is the meaning of ‘delusion’? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that ‘delusion’ is simply the failure to recognize the true nature of the mind. It is like a person who, looking at the moon in the water, mistakes the reflection for the real moon. The reflection is not the moon, yet the person chases after it. This is called delusion. If one looks directly at the sky, one sees the true moon. So too, if one looks directly at the mind, one sees its original purity. Therefore, I say that delusion is merely a lack of recognition, not a substantial entity. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if delusion has no cause, then how can it be said that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that although delusion has no cause, the phenomena it produces do arise from conditions. It is like a magician who uses various props to create illusory forms. The forms have no reality, yet they appear before the eyes. So too, the phenomena produced by delusion are empty and unreal, yet they appear to exist. Therefore, I say that while the source of delusion is uncaused, its manifestations are conditioned. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure, then why do some people attain liberation while others remain in bondage? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that liberation and bondage depend on whether one recognizes or fails to recognize the mind. It is like a person who opens their eyes and sees the light, or closes their eyes and falls into darkness. The light and darkness are not external objects; they depend on the state of the eyes. So too, liberation and bondage depend on the state of the mind. If one recognizes the mind, one is liberated; if one fails to recognize it, one is bound. Therefore, I say that the difference between liberation and bondage lies in the mind’s recognition or non-recognition. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure, then why do we speak of the Three Poisons and the Eight Afflictions? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that the Three Poisons and Eight Afflictions are like clouds covering the sun. The sun is always bright, but when clouds gather, its light is obscured. So too, the mind is originally pure, but when afflicted thoughts arise, its purity is hidden. If the clouds disperse, the sun shines forth. If the afflictions cease, the mind is revealed. Therefore, I say that although the afflictions have no root, they arise from the conditions of false thinking. If one can cut off false thinking, the afflictions will naturally vanish. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure, then what is the meaning of ‘emptiness’? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that emptiness means that there is nothing to be grasped. It is like space: it contains all things, yet it has no form and cannot be grasped. So too, the mind is empty of self and phenomena; it is vast and boundless. To realize this is called the gate of emptiness. Therefore, I say that the mind is originally empty and still. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure and empty, then why do we speak of the Six Sense Bases and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that the Six Sense Bases and Twelve Links are like a dreamer’s journey. While dreaming, the traveler experiences many things, but upon waking, they find there was nowhere to go. So too, the sense bases and links of dependent origination are empty and unreal. They arise from the mind’s false projections. If one realizes that the mind is empty, then the sense bases and links will naturally cease. Therefore, I say that although the sense bases and links appear, they have no inherent existence. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure, then what is the meaning of ‘awakening’? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Good son, you should know that awakening means returning to the source. It is like a traveler who, having wandered far from home, suddenly remembers the way back. So too, when one realizes that the mind is originally pure and empty, one returns to the source of all phenomena. This is called awakening. Therefore, I say that awakening is simply the realization of the mind’s original nature. Pūrṇa said: “World-Honored One, if the mind is originally pure,

However, when the demons of the mind are utterly extinguished and the activities of arising and ceasing are exhausted, the subtle and secret aspects of phenomena manifest.

Thereupon, one recognizes the spirit and gives rise to false calculations; clinging to various views, one recklessly gives vent to deluded sentiments. One may dwell in the paths of demons or stagnate in the Lesser Vehicle, causing previously cherished habitual practices to fall into dormancy.
Thus, the demons of views are melted away, whereby the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is exhausted and the faculties mutually interact.
By practicing thus, one transcends from the stage of Dry Wisdom up to the final mind. Once the five aggregates are exhausted, the five perceptions no longer arise.

When perceptions do not arise, all demons naturally perish. In this way, both darkness and agitation are stilled; the essence of the mind becomes perfectly luminous, the demonic hordes are simultaneously subdued, and the city of Dharma is forever secure.
